title: Dull strings and dead spots
summary: A guitar that suddenly sounds flat and short-lived usually needs new strings. A single note that dies early, whatever string you play it on, is a dead spot - a resonance in the neck - and is handled differently.
symptoms: Tone sounds dull, flat and short on sustain
Strings look dark, flaky or discoloured, feel gritty
Strings won't stay in tune or won't intonate
One particular note (often around the 5th–7th frets on the G or D) dies much faster than its neighbours
A buzz or ring at one pitch that seems to come from the neck

causes.cause: Old, corroded strings
causes.check: Discoloration, flakes, dull or dead tone, poor tuning stability. A wound string with a broken winding gives a dead, buzzy note.
causes.fix: Replace the set. Wipe strings after playing to slow corrosion.

causes.cause: Pickup too close to the strings
causes.check: Lower the pickup a turn or two and listen for longer sustain.
causes.fix: Set pickups to spec [dx-pickup-height]; strong magnets close to the strings reduce sustain.

causes.cause: Dead spot: the neck or headstock resonates at that pitch and absorbs the string's energy
causes.check: Play the same pitch on two different strings. If it dies at the same pitch in both places, it is a dead spot. Clamp something on the headstock (a capo or clip-on tuner): if the dead note moves or improves, it is a neck resonance.
causes.fix: Small changes to headstock mass move the resonance: heavier tuners, a brass plate or a clip-on tuner left on. A different string gauge changes how the note couples. Tight neck screws and hardware also help.

causes.cause: Truss rod or loose part ringing at one note
causes.check: Rap the back of the neck; a rattling rod or loose truss-rod nut/washer can ring at certain notes.
causes.fix: Snug the truss rod nut lightly, tighten tuner nuts and bushings [dx-rattle-sitar].

causes.cause: Acoustic too humid
causes.check: Taylor lists dull, lifeless tone with high action as a sign of a wet guitar.
causes.fix: Bring humidity to 45–55% RH [dx-seasonal-changes].

tools: Clip-on tuner or capo (for the headstock mass test)

steps.title: Start with strings
steps.detail: Fit a fresh set; most 'dead' guitars come back to life here.

steps.title: Check pickup height
steps.detail: On electrics, back the pickups off slightly and compare sustain.

steps.title: Hunt for a dead spot
steps.detail: Play up each string one fret at a time, letting each note ring. Note any that die early, then play that pitch on another string.

steps.title: Try headstock mass
steps.detail: Clip a tuner or capo to the headstock and replay the dead note. If it improves, consider heavier tuners or leaving the clip-on in place.

steps.title: Tighten everything
steps.detail: Neck bolts, tuner bushings, bridge posts and the truss rod nut (just snug, do not change relief).

models.note: Dead spots are very common on long-scale basses; headstock mass changes are the usual remedy.
Check the neck screws are tight; a loose neck joint reduces sustain everywhere.

pro: A dead spot cannot be removed completely; a luthier can only move or reduce it.

title: String ball-end or wrap sitting on the saddle
summary: If the thick wrapped section near a string's ball end (or the wrong part of a taper-wound string) ends up on the saddle, the string cannot form a clean witness point: it buzzes, sounds dull, will not intonate, or breaks early.
symptoms: Sitar-like buzz or dull tone on one string, usually the lowest
Saddle has to go unusually far back or forward for intonation
The string sits visibly higher or crooked on the saddle
String breaks at the saddle or at the ball end

causes.cause: Strings too short for a through-body or deep bridge
causes.check: Look closely at the saddle: is the extra wrapping or colour silk near the ball end on top of the saddle?
causes.fix: Buy a longer set (through-body or extra-long). La Bella says ball-to-nut distance is not the same as scale, and to choose by wound length.

causes.cause: Taper-wound string installed wrongly
causes.check: On a taperwound string the exposed core should be what sits on the saddle (the outer wraps stop before it).
causes.fix: Reseat so the taper sits on the saddle; if the taper lands before or after the saddle, the set does not suit the bridge.

causes.cause: Ball end not fully seated or string twisted
causes.check: Pull the string toward the bridge with it slack and see if it moves further in.
causes.fix: Seat the ball fully and untwist the string before tuning (La Bella).

causes.cause: Short-scale bass with long-scale strings
causes.check: Wound section reaching onto the nut or tuner post too.
causes.fix: Use the correct scale set. See [bs-short-scale-setup].

steps.title: Inspect
steps.detail: Slacken the string slightly and look at exactly what rests on the saddle. Photograph it close up.

steps.title: Measure wound length
steps.detail: Measure from the ball seat to just past the nut and compare with La Bella's wound lengths: short 32-1/4 in, medium 34-1/4 in, long 36-3/4 or 37 in, extra long 38 in.

steps.title: Reinstall or replace
steps.detail: Reseat and untwist. If the wrong section still lands on the saddle, get a set designed for your bridge type.

steps.title: Re-intonate
steps.detail: After any string fit change, re-check intonation.

title: Action too high
summary: Strings that sit too far above the frets make the guitar tiring to play and push fretted notes sharp. Find out whether the neck, the bridge, the nut or the weather is responsible before you lower anything.
symptoms: Hard to press the strings down; barre chords tire your hand
Notes go sharp when fretted, especially near the nut
12th-fret string height well above the factory figure
Action rose noticeably during a humid summer (acoustic)
Saddles are already screwed right down and the action is still high

causes.cause: Too much neck relief
causes.check: Measure relief [dx-measure-relief]. Example limits: Fender electric 0.008–0.012 in depending on radius, Gibson around 0.010–0.012 in.
causes.fix: Tighten the truss rod (clockwise, seen from the adjusting end) a quarter turn at a time, retune and re-measure [fn-truss-rod-basics].

causes.cause: Bridge or saddles set high
causes.check: With relief correct, measure at the 12th fret (17th on Fender) [dx-measure-action].
causes.fix: Electric: lower the saddles or bridge posts. Acoustic: remove the saddle and sand its BOTTOM flat. Remove about twice the amount you want the 12th-fret action to drop (to lower from 7/64 to 6/64 in, take 1/32 in off the saddle).

causes.cause: Nut slots too high (action feels high only in the first few positions)
causes.check: Fret each string at the 3rd fret: a large gap above the 1st fret, and open chords that sound sharp, point to high nut slots [dx-measure-action].
causes.fix: Lower the slots with gauged nut files, a little at a time [fn-nut-problems].

causes.cause: Swollen wood from high humidity (acoustic)
causes.check: Taylor lists high action, dull tone and the neck plane sighting below the bridge as signs of a 'wet' guitar. Check the room with a hygrometer.
causes.fix: Bring humidity back to 45–55% RH and wait before cutting the saddle; the action often comes back down on its own.

causes.cause: Neck angle has changed (acoustic) or is too shallow (bolt-on electric)
causes.check: Acoustic: if the saddle is already low and there is not enough left above the bridge to reach spec, the neck angle is the problem (Taylor). Electric: saddles bottomed out and still high.
causes.fix: Acoustic: neck reset by a luthier. Bolt-on electric: a thin, full-pocket neck shim to tilt the neck back (careful DIY or pro).

causes.cause: A heavier string gauge pulled the neck forward
causes.check: Did the action rise after going up a gauge?
causes.fix: Re-set relief, then action, then nut and intonation [dx-string-gauge-change].

tools: 6 in steel rule (1/64 in or 0.5 mm marks)
Flat surface and 120–150 grit sandpaper (acoustic saddle)

specs.label: Fender electric action (17th fret)
specs.value: 7.25 in radius: 5/64 in bass, 4/64 in treble; 9.5–12 in: 4/64 in both; 15–17 in: 4/64 in bass, 3/64 in treble

specs.label: Gibson Les Paul (Jim DeCola, 12th fret)
specs.value: 5/64 in low E, 3/64 in high E

specs.label: Taylor acoustic (12th fret)
specs.value: 6/64 in low E, 4/64 in high E (12-strings 5/64 and 3/64)

specs.label: Acoustic saddle rule
specs.value: Removing x from the saddle bottom lowers 12th-fret action by about x/2

steps.title: Tune and measure relief first
steps.detail: Tune to pitch in playing position. Measure relief: capo at the 1st fret, hold the string at the body joint/last fret, feeler gauge at the 8th fret. If it is above spec, correct it before touching the bridge.

steps.title: Measure the action
steps.detail: With the capo off, measure from the top of the 12th fret (17th for Fender specs) to the bottom of the low E and high E with a steel rule, eye level with the string.

steps.title: Lower an electric bridge
steps.detail: Strat/Tele style: turn each saddle's two height screws equally, outer E strings first, then set the middle four to follow the fretboard radius. Tune-o-matic: slacken strings slightly, turn the thumbwheels down. Floyd/Edge: turn the pivot studs (release Edge stud locks first). Retune after every change.

steps.title: Lower an acoustic saddle
steps.detail: Slacken the strings, lift the saddle out (pliers on the ends if tight; pad the jaws). Mark a pencil line along its bottom showing how much to remove: twice the drop you want at the 12th fret. Tape sandpaper to a flat surface and sand the bottom, keeping it flat and square to the sides. Go in small steps; you cannot put material back.
steps.warn: Through-saddles and some under-saddle pickups need the saddle bottom perfectly flat or the pickup will be uneven; check all strings are balanced afterwards.

steps.title: Check the nut
steps.detail: If the first-position notes still feel stiff or sound sharp, check nut height [dx-measure-action] and lower the slots or have them lowered [fn-nut-problems].

steps.title: Play-test and re-intonate
steps.detail: Play the whole neck for buzz. Lowering the action changes intonation, so finish with [dx-intonation].

models.note: Tune-o-matic thumbwheels set height for the bass and treble side only; individual string heights come from the saddle notches. Stopbar height does not change action.
Saddle height on Gen II/III trem, Silver Sky and hardtail: 0.050 in hex key; SE models: 1.5 mm hex.
Overall height is set at the two bridge posts; individual saddle screws fine-tune each string. Low action reduces string-to-saddle downforce, which can make strings jump saddles.
Action is set by swapping neck elevation plates; each 0.006 in plate step changes 12th-fret action by about 0.015 in (a thicker plate lowers it).
Only the saddle and nut change action. If the saddle would have to go below the bridge top to reach spec, the guitar needs a neck reset.

warnings: Do not sand the top of an acoustic saddle to lower it; that changes the radius and the intonation points.
Never loosen the truss rod or remove the saddle on an acoustic with strings at full tension in one go; slacken first.
pro: Neck resets, neck-angle shims you are unsure of, and nut slot lowering beyond a light touch are worth taking to a luthier.

title: Action too low
summary: Strings sitting too close to the frets buzz, choke on bends and lose sustain. Often it is the weather or a lighter string gauge rather than a bad setup.
symptoms: Buzz on many frets, notes die early
Bends cut out ('choke') high on the neck
Action dropped suddenly in winter (acoustic)
Action fell after switching to lighter strings
Saddle on an acoustic is barely above the bridge

causes.cause: Too little relief or a back-bowed neck
causes.check: Measure relief [dx-measure-relief]. Zero or negative relief lowers the low-fret action and causes buzz near the nut.
causes.fix: Loosen the truss rod a quarter turn at a time [fn-truss-rod-basics].

causes.cause: Dry air (acoustic): the top sinks and the action falls
causes.check: Taylor's dry-guitar signs: unusually low action, a hump where the neck meets the body, the top sunken between bridge and fingerboard, sharp fret ends.
causes.fix: Humidify to 45–55% RH before changing anything else [dx-seasonal-changes].

causes.cause: Saddles set too low
causes.check: Measure 12th/17th-fret action against spec [dx-measure-action].
causes.fix: Electric: raise saddles or posts. Acoustic: shim under the saddle with a hardwood or bone shim, or fit a new, taller saddle (Fender notes acoustic saddles may need shimming when action is too low).

causes.cause: Lighter strings: less pull, less relief
causes.check: Did the problem start with a lighter set?
causes.fix: Loosen the rod slightly to restore relief, re-check action and intonation, and check that the lighter strings are not rattling in wide nut slots [dx-string-gauge-change].

causes.cause: Nut slots worn or cut too deep (open strings only)
causes.check: Fret at the 3rd fret: no gap at all over the 1st fret means the slot is too low.
causes.fix: Fill and re-cut the slot or replace the nut [fn-nut-problems].

specs.label: Relief minimums, Fender electric
specs.value: 7.25 in: 0.012 in; 9.5–12 in: 0.010 in; 15–17 in: 0.008 in (Fender calls these minimum guidelines)

steps.title: Check humidity first (acoustics)
steps.detail: Put a digital hygrometer in the case or room. If it reads well under 45%, humidify for several days and re-measure before making any adjustment.

steps.title: Measure relief
steps.detail: Capo 1st fret, fret at the body joint, gauge at the 8th fret. Add relief if it is below spec.

steps.title: Measure and raise action
steps.detail: Raise saddles in small steps to the factory figure, outer strings first, middle strings following the radius.

steps.title: Shim an acoustic saddle
steps.detail: Slacken strings, lift the saddle out, add a full-length shim of the thickness you need (about twice the rise you want at the 12th fret), keeping the bottom flat. Better: make a new taller saddle.

steps.title: Play-test and re-intonate
steps.detail: Check bends at the top of the neck and finish with [dx-intonation].

models.note: Truss rod adjusts at the headstock behind the nut. US-made Fenders take a 1/8 in hex key; Mexican-made Fenders and recent Squiers are commonly reported to take 4 mm (check that the key seats fully before turning).

The rod nut is at the body end of the neck. On many you must loosen the strings and remove or tilt the neck, or remove the pickguard, to reach it; it takes a large screwdriver. Some modern Fenders have a spoke wheel at the heel turned with a small rod.
Truss rod nut is under the bell-shaped cover on the headstock; it takes a 5/16 in nut driver or box wrench. The wood around a Gibson nut is thin, so never force it.
Shims under the saddle can unbalance the pickup; a new, taller saddle is the better fix.

pro: If the action is low even with correct relief and humidity and the saddle is maxed out, or the guitar has a hump at the body joint, have a luthier check the neck and frets.

title: Bass fret buzz and rattles
summary: Track down whether a bass buzz is the strings hitting frets (relief, height, frets, nut) or something loose vibrating (saddles, rod, tuner, pickup), and fix it in the right order.
symptoms: Buzz on open strings only
Buzz on the first few frets
Buzz in the middle of the neck (around frets 5-12)
Buzz everywhere
Buzz on one fret only
A rattle that continues after the note, or that you hear acoustically but not through the amp

causes.cause: Relief wrong for your playing
causes.check: Capo at 1, hold the low string at the last fret, measure at the 8th (Fender targets .010-.014 in by radius). Music Man: buzz open-5th wants more relief, buzz 5th-12th wants a straighter neck. La Bella: buzz mainly 3rd-9th often means the neck is too flat or back-bowed. These disagree on the middle zone - measure rather than guess.
causes.fix: Adjust the rod in quarter turns. See [bs-fender-bass-setup].

causes.cause: Action too low
causes.check: Buzz all over the neck; measure at the 17th against Fender's 6/64 in bass, 5/64 in treble (9.5-12 in radius).
causes.fix: Raise the saddles.

causes.cause: Nut slot cut too low
causes.check: Buzz only on open strings; fretted notes clean.
causes.fix: Shim or replace the nut, or fill and recut the slot (StewMac Nut Rescue Powder method).

causes.cause: High or uneven fret
causes.check: Buzz on one or two notes only; rock a short straightedge over three frets around the problem - if it rocks, a fret is high.
causes.fix: Reseat or level the fret (tech job).

causes.cause: Loose hardware rattling
causes.check: Mute strings with your hand and tap around: saddles, saddle height screws, bridge plate, tuner bushings and nuts, pickup covers, strap buttons, jack nut. On Rickenbackers a loose truss rod nut or rod can rattle.
causes.fix: Tighten what moves. Saddle buzz: Hipshot's B-style saddles have side walls to cut it. Ric rod rattle: snug the nut, else tape the rods (tech).

causes.cause: String not seated or twisted
causes.check: Ball end not fully home, string twisted on install, or the ball-end wrap sitting on the saddle.
causes.fix: Reinstall the string straight and fully seated. See [bs-ball-end-saddle].

causes.cause: Old strings
causes.check: Dull, uneven, will not intonate.
causes.fix: Restring.

steps.title: Listen through the amp
steps.detail: Some acoustic buzz is normal on bass and disappears through the amp. If you cannot hear it plugged in at playing volume, it may be fine.

steps.title: Map the buzz
steps.detail: Play every string open and at every fret. Note which strings and which frets buzz - the pattern points to the cause.

steps.title: Fix in order
steps.detail: Relief first, then saddle height, then nut, then frets. Each step changes the next.

steps.title: Chase rattles separately
steps.detail: If the noise continues after the note stops or sounds like a buzz from the body, mute the strings and tap hardware to find it.

pro: High frets, worn frets, a low nut that needs replacing, or Rickenbacker rods that must be removed and taped.

title: Bass neck dive
summary: Neck dive is when the headstock sinks toward the floor as soon as you let go, so your fretting hand ends up holding the bass up. It comes from where the strap pulls on the body compared with where the weight sits.
symptoms: Headstock drops when you take your fretting hand off
Aching fretting wrist or shoulder
You keep pushing the neck up between phrases

causes.cause: Strap button position
causes.check: Where is the upper strap button? If it is far back on the body (not out on the upper horn), the pivot point is behind the balance point.
causes.fix: Move the upper strap button further toward the neck (out on the horn or neck heel area).

causes.cause: Heavy headstock hardware
causes.check: Heavy tuners add weight at the far end. Hipshot's HB1 tuner weighs 2.9 oz each; its USA Ultralite bodies are lighter.
causes.fix: Lightweight tuners (for example Hipshot Ultralites).

causes.cause: Body design
causes.check: Long necks with small or offset bodies - reverse Thunderbirds and SG-shaped EB basses are classic examples - tend to dive.
causes.fix: Strap fixes first; headless designs exist largely to cure this (Steinberger moved the tuners to the bridge for this reason).

causes.cause: Slippery strap
causes.check: Nylon or slick leather strap slides on your shirt.
causes.fix: Wide strap with a grippy backing (suede or rubberised).

parts: Wooden toothpick and wood glue (to fill the old hole)

steps.title: Try the strap first
steps.detail: Swap to a wide, grippy strap and check the strap length. Many mild cases stop here.

steps.title: Find a better button spot
steps.detail: Hold the bass on the strap and pinch the strap end at various points along the upper horn to see where it balances level. Mark that spot on masking tape.

steps.title: Drill a pilot hole
steps.detail: Drill a pilot hole the size of the screw's core (not its threads) with a depth stop or tape flag on the bit. Keep the drill square to the surface.
steps.warn: Check for hidden wiring channels or the neck pocket before drilling; drill through masking tape to avoid chipping the finish.

steps.title: Fit the button
steps.detail: Screw the button in snugly with a dab of wax on the threads. Do not overtighten - it strips the wood.

steps.title: Fill the old hole if you want
steps.detail: Glue a toothpick into the old hole, trim flush, touch up.

steps.title: Lighter tuners
steps.detail: If the bass still dives, lightweight tuners reduce headstock weight. Match the post-hole size before buying.

warnings: Drilling a vintage instrument reduces its value - consider a removable strap-button extender instead.
pro: Have a tech drill vintage or finished-in-nitro instruments.

title: Dead spots on a bass neck
summary: A dead spot is one note that dies away much faster than its neighbours, often reported on the G string around the 5th-7th fret on Fender-style bolt-on basses. It is usually the neck itself resonating at that note's pitch and soaking up the string's energy, so fixes work by changing the neck's mass or stiffness.
symptoms: One note (sometimes the same pitch on two strings) has much shorter sustain
The note sounds thin or 'wolfy' even though it is in tune and not buzzing
Clamping or holding the headstock changes how long the note rings

causes.cause: Neck resonance matching that note
causes.check: Play the dead note, then play it again while pressing the headstock firmly against a wall or holding a heavy clamp on it. If the sustain improves, the neck is soaking up energy at that pitch.
causes.fix: Add mass to the headstock (a clamp-on weight such as Fender's Fat Finger, or heavier tuners) or change the neck's stiffness slightly. This works the same way as the wolf-note eliminator a cellist clamps on a string: a mass that shifts or damps the resonance.

causes.cause: Truss rod tension
causes.check: Note whether the dead spot appeared or moved after a rod adjustment.
causes.fix: A tiny rod change in either direction can move the resonance; Rickenbacker owners report a small tweak clearing a dead spot after an adjustment.

causes.cause: Fret problem
causes.check: A dead note that also buzzes slightly or chokes - check with a fret rocker. La Bella lists uneven frets as a cause of dead spots.
causes.fix: Reseat or level the fret (tech).

causes.cause: Loose parts
causes.check: Loose neck screws, tuner bushings or nuts, a loose bridge or saddle can all rob sustain at specific notes.
causes.fix: Tighten everything (neck screws snug, not cranked).

causes.cause: Strings
causes.check: Try a different gauge or brand: the string's mass changes which note lines up with the neck resonance.
causes.fix: Change strings and retest.

steps.title: Confirm it is a dead spot
steps.detail: Play each note up the G and D strings with the same force and count how long it rings. A true dead spot is markedly shorter than notes either side.

steps.title: Clamp test
steps.detail: Put a small padded clamp on the headstock (protect the finish) and replay the dead note. Then try it in different spots on the headstock. If sustain improves, a headstock mass will help.

steps.title: Try a permanent mass
steps.detail: Fit a clamp-on headstock weight, or swap to heavier tuners. Recheck that the bass does not become too neck-heavy - see [bs-neck-dive].

steps.title: Tighten and check frets
steps.detail: Snug the neck screws and all hardware; check the fret under the dead note for rocking.

steps.title: Accept small improvements
steps.detail: You can move or weaken a dead spot but rarely remove it completely; moving it to a note you rarely play is a win.

warnings: Clamps can mark finishes; pad them and do not overtighten.
pro: Graphite reinforcement or a replacement neck are the only cures for a severe dead spot; both are tech decisions.

title: Fix a volume knob (every problem)
summary: Start here for any volume-knob trouble: crackle, cutting out, doing nothing, working backwards, all-or-nothing volume, losing treble when you turn down, a loose or spinning knob, or hum when you touch it. Each cause says how to check it and which fix to follow.
symptoms: Crackles or scratches when you turn it
Sound cuts out or drops at one spot on the dial, or at full
Turning it does nothing (always full, or always silent)
It works backwards: louder as you turn down
Nothing happens until the last bit of travel, then it jumps (all-or-nothing)
Turning down makes the sound dull and muddy
On a two-volume guitar, turning one down silences both in the middle position
Knob is loose, wobbles, slips, won't come off or won't fit the shaft
The whole pot spins round in the body
Hum or buzz that changes when you touch the knob or the pot
Knob is too stiff or too floppy to turn

causes.cause: Dirt or oxidation on the pot's track (the most common cause of crackle)
causes.check: The noise happens only while the knob is moving and changes with speed. Sweep it with a meter as in [ef-test-pots]: flicker or jumps on the reading.
causes.fix: Work the knob end to end 10–20 times, then clean with a small squirt of contact cleaner: [ef-crackling-pots]. If it comes back quickly, replace the pot: [ef-replace-volume-pot].

causes.cause: Worn track or wiper (cuts out at one spot, or at full)
causes.check: Meter sweep from lug 2 to an outer lug shows a dead spot, a sudden OL, or a value that jumps at the same place every time ([ef-test-pots]).
causes.fix: Cleaning rarely cures wear. Replace the pot: [ef-replace-volume-pot].

causes.cause: Broken or cold solder joint on a lug or on the pot casing
causes.check: Wiggle each wire gently with the guitar plugged in at low volume; a crackle or drop when you touch one wire is the joint. Dull, grainy or cracked solder is suspect.
causes.fix: Reflow the joint with fresh solder ([ef-soldering-basics]); for the casing see [ef-soldering-pot-backs].

causes.cause: Wires on the wrong lugs (does nothing, always silent, or works backwards)
causes.check: Read the lugs from the back of the pot, shaft away from you, lugs up: lug 1 left, lug 2 (wiper) middle, lug 3 right. A standard volume pot takes the signal in on lug 3, sends it to the jack (or switch) from lug 2, and has lug 1 grounded. Signal in on lug 1 with lug 3 grounded makes it work backwards; the output on an outer lug makes it do nothing.
causes.fix: Move the wires to the right lugs. Backwards: swap the two outer-lug wires. See the recipe for your guitar under Wiring, e.g. [wr-strat-standard] or [wr-les-paul-modern].

causes.cause: Knob slipping on the shaft (the knob turns but the shaft doesn't)
causes.check: Hold the shaft with the knob off and turn it by hand: if the volume changes normally, the knob isn't gripping.
causes.fix: Spread a split shaft slightly or match the knob to the shaft's spline count (24 fine vs 18 coarse): [ef-knobs].

causes.cause: Wrong taper (all-or-nothing volume)
causes.check: Most of the change happens in the last part of the turn or in the first part. Check the pot's markings and taper with a meter: [ef-identify-pots] and [ef-test-pots]. Volume pots are normally audio/log taper (usually marked A on US/CTS pots; some imports reverse the letters, so measure).
causes.fix: Fit an audio-taper pot of the same value: [ef-replace-volume-pot]. Some players like a linear volume pot for swells; it's a preference, not a fault.

causes.cause: Treble loss when turning down (normal with standard wiring)
causes.check: The sound gets duller as soon as the knob leaves 10, worse with long cables.
causes.fix: Add a treble bleed ([ef-treble-bleed], [wr-treble-bleed]) or use 50s-style wiring on a Les Paul/SG ([wr-les-paul-50s]).

causes.cause: Two-volume guitar silences both pickups in the middle position (normal for standard Gibson-style wiring)
causes.check: With the toggle in the middle, turning either volume fully down kills the whole guitar.
causes.fix: Rewire for independent volumes: [wr-independent-volume].

causes.cause: Pot nut loose (the whole pot turns)
causes.check: Take the knob off: the nut under it is loose, and the pot rotates when you turn the shaft.
causes.fix: Hold the pot from behind, seat any anti-rotation tab in its hole, and tighten the nut with a nut driver (not pliers): see the last step of [ef-knobs].

causes.cause: Pot casing not grounded (hum changes when you touch it)
causes.check: Meter from the pot casing to the jack sleeve should read about 0 ohms; OL means it isn't grounded.
causes.fix: Solder a ground wire to the casing ([ef-soldering-pot-backs]); for hum in general see [ef-hum-buzz].

causes.cause: Active electronics (EMG etc.): crackle from a low battery or DC on the pot
causes.check: The guitar has a battery; crackle also comes with distortion or fading output.
causes.fix: Fit a fresh battery and see [ef-active-noisy] / [ef-active-dead].

causes.cause: Pot too stiff or too loose to turn
causes.check: Feel only — no electrical fault on the meter sweep.
causes.fix: Pots aren't serviceable inside; replace it ([ef-replace-volume-pot]) and choose the same value and taper.

tools: Screwdrivers for the cover or pickguard
Knob puller, a soft cloth or a loop of string
Nut driver to fit the pot nut
Soldering iron and rosin-core solder (for joints and replacements)
Contact cleaner such as DeoxIT (for crackle)
Phone camera to photograph the wiring
parts: Replacement pot of the same value and taper (250k single coils, 500k humbuckers, 1M some Jazzmasters and vintage Teles, 25k EMG actives)
Knobs that match the shaft (24 or 18 spline, split or solid)
Treble-bleed parts if you want them

specs.label: Volume pot lugs (back view, lugs up)
specs.value: Lug 3 = signal in, lug 2 (wiper) = out to jack/switch, lug 1 = ground

specs.label: Usual values
specs.value: 250k single coils · 500k humbuckers · 1M some Jazzmasters/vintage Teles · 25k EMG active

specs.label: Usual taper for volume
specs.value: Audio/log (often marked A); measure to be sure

specs.label: Good ground
specs.value: ≈ 0 Ω from pot casing to the jack sleeve

steps.title: Listen and narrow it down
steps.detail: Plug in at low volume. Turn the knob slowly end to end, then quickly. Note whether the problem is noise while moving, a dead spot, the wrong amount of change, a dull sound, or something mechanical (loose, spinning, slipping). Match what you hear to the symptoms above.

steps.title: Check the knob before opening anything
steps.detail: Pull the knob off with a cloth or puller (never lever it with a screwdriver). Turn the bare shaft: if it works fine, the knob was slipping; if the whole pot turns, the nut is loose. Both are fixed in [ef-knobs].

steps.title: Open up and photograph
steps.detail: Remove the control cover, control plate or pickguard. Take clear photos of every wire on the pot before you touch anything.

steps.title: Try the cheap fixes first
steps.detail: For crackle: work the pot 10–20 times, then a brief squirt of contact cleaner into the opening beside the lugs and work it again ([ef-crackling-pots]). For a cutting-out sound: wiggle each wire to find a bad joint and reflow it.

steps.title: Check the lugs
steps.detail: With the pot seen from the back (shaft away, lugs up), confirm signal in on lug 3, output on lug 2, ground on lug 1, and a ground wire on the casing. Correct anything that's on the wrong lug.

steps.title: Measure the pot
steps.detail: Unsolder one outer lug and sweep the pot with a meter ([ef-test-pots]). Smooth sweep and right value = the pot is fine, look elsewhere. Jumps, dead spots, open circuit or wrong taper = replace it.

steps.title: Replace if needed
steps.detail: Follow [ef-replace-volume-pot].

steps.title: Test before closing up
steps.detail: Plug in, sweep the volume end to end in every pickup position, tap the pickup pole pieces with a screwdriver to confirm sound, and check there's no hum change when you touch the knob or the strings.

models.note: The volume pot is on the pickguard: strings off (or slackened) and the guard lifted to reach it. It's usually the pot nearest the pickups, with the pickup grounds on its casing.
Reached by unscrewing the control plate (two screws); the volume is the pot nearest the switch on a standard plate.
Two volumes; through the rear cover on solid bodies, through the f-hole on a 335 (see [wr-es-335]). Turning one volume down killing both in the middle position is normal: [wr-independent-volume].
Uses 25k pots and a stereo jack; don't fit 250k/500k pots there ([wr-emg-active]).
Stacked shafts can rub and crackle; replacement needs the same stacked type ([wr-jazz-bass]).

warnings: Unplug the guitar from the amp before soldering.
Contact cleaner is flammable: no soldering until it has fully evaporated.
pro: the pot is buried in a hollow-body guitar and you'd have to fish the whole harness out through an f-hole, or the fault is in an active preamp board.

title: Fret buzz
summary: Buzz is a vibrating string touching a fret it should clear. Where on the neck it buzzes points straight at the cause, so map it first and only then reach for a wrench.
symptoms: Open strings buzz but fretted notes are clean
Buzz on the first few frets (roughly 1st–5th or up to the 7th)
Buzz from about the 7th–12th fret upward, or only high up the neck
One note, or two or three notes, buzz while the rest are clean
Buzz almost everywhere on the neck
Buzz only when you pick or strum hard
Buzz you can hear unplugged but not through the amp
Buzz that appeared after a change of season or a new string gauge

causes.cause: Buzz everywhere: action set too low overall
causes.check: Measure string height at the 12th fret (17th on Fender specs) and compare with the factory figure for your guitar [dx-measure-action]. Also measure relief, because a straight neck plus low saddles buzzes everywhere.
causes.fix: Raise the saddles in small steps (about a quarter of a millimetre at a time), retune, and play-test after each step until the buzz clears. Then re-check intonation [dx-intonation].

causes.cause: Buzz on the low frets (open-position to about the 5th–7th) with clean upper frets: too little relief or a back-bowed neck
causes.check: Measure relief [dx-measure-relief]. Zero clearance, or the string touching the 7th–8th fret with capo at 1 and finger at the body joint, means the neck is too straight or bowed backwards.
causes.fix: Loosen the truss rod (anticlockwise, seen from the adjusting end) no more than a quarter turn at a time to add relief, retune and re-measure. See [fn-truss-rod-basics].

causes.cause: Open strings only: nut slots cut too low or worn
causes.check: Fret each string at the 3rd fret and look at the gap over the 1st fret: if the string lies right on the 1st fret, the slot is too low. Shim test: slip a small square of paper (about 1/16 in / 1.5 mm) into the slot under the string and retune; if the open-string buzz stops, the nut is the problem.
causes.fix: Short term: shim or fill the slot. Proper fix: fill and re-cut the slot or fit a new nut [fn-nut-problems].

causes.cause: Buzz from about the 7th fret toward the body: too much relief, or a rising fretboard tongue/high frets past the body joint
causes.check: Measure relief. Frank Ford's rule: buzz only from the 7th fret up suggests too much relief. If relief is normal, lay a short straightedge across three frets at a time in the upper register to look for a rocking (high) fret or a rising 'ski jump' over the body.
causes.fix: Too much relief: tighten the truss rod a little and raise the saddles slightly so 12th-fret action stays about the same. High frets or ski jump: [fn-fret-level-crown-polish].

causes.cause: One note, or a few notes: a high or loose fret
causes.check: Note the buzzing fret: the culprit is usually the next fret toward the bridge, which is sitting high. Rock a fret rocker or short straightedge across three frets there. Press the ends of that fret: if it clicks or a 0.004 in (0.10 mm) feeler slides under the fret end, it has lifted.
causes.fix: Reseat a lifted fret, or spot-level/full-level high frets [fn-fret-level-crown-polish]. Deep string grooves worn into the first frets also cause local buzz and need levelling or a refret.

causes.cause: Only when picked hard: your attack exceeds the clearance
causes.check: Play the same notes at normal strength; if the buzz vanishes and the action and relief are within spec, the setup is not faulty.
causes.fix: Play a little lighter, or add a touch of relief and/or saddle height to suit a heavy attack. Buzz that does not come through the amp is often left alone.

causes.cause: It is not fret buzz: a rattle elsewhere
causes.check: If the buzz has a 'fizzy' or sitar sound, occurs at certain pitches only, or seems to come from the headstock or body, rap the guitar with a knuckle in different spots and listen.
causes.fix: Tighten loose tuner nuts, truss rod nut, strap buttons, spring cover; see [dx-rattle-sitar].

causes.cause: Seasonal change (mostly acoustics): dry air lowers the action and can lift fret ends
causes.check: Did the buzz appear in winter? Look for sharp fret ends and a hump where the neck meets the body.
causes.fix: Bring humidity back to 45–55% RH first, then reassess [dx-seasonal-changes].

causes.cause: Technique: fretting too far behind the fret or with too little pressure
causes.check: Have someone else play the same notes, or fret right behind the fret wire with firm pressure.
causes.fix: Fret close to the fret wire. No adjustment needed.

tools: 6 in steel rule with 1/64 in or 0.5 mm marks
Truss rod wrench for your guitar

specs.label: Fender electric action, 9.5–12 in radius
specs.value: 4/64 in (1.6 mm) bass and treble side, measured at the 17th fret

specs.label: Lifted fret test (MusicNomad)
specs.value: A 0.004 in (0.10 mm) feeler sliding under a fret end means it is not seated

specs.label: Nut shim test (MusicNomad)
specs.value: Paper square about 1/16 x 1/16 in (1.5 x 1.5 mm) under the string in the slot

steps.title: Tune and hold in playing position
steps.detail: Tune all strings to pitch with the strings and gauge you normally use. Sit or stand as you play: a guitar lying flat on a bench lets gravity pull the neck and strings and changes what you hear and measure.

steps.title: Map the buzz
steps.detail: Pick each string open, then at every fret up to the top, at your normal playing strength. Write down string and fret for every buzz. Listen through the amp too: buzz that only you hear acoustically is a lower priority.

steps.title: Match the pattern
steps.detail: Open strings only = nut. Low frets only = too little relief. Upper frets only = too much relief, low saddles or high frets near the body. One note = a high/loose fret one position toward the bridge. Everywhere = action too low. Use the causes list above.

steps.title: Check in this order: relief, action, nut
steps.detail: Relief affects every other measurement, so measure it first [dx-measure-relief], then 12th-fret action [dx-measure-action], then nut height. Compare with the factory specs for your guitar (see the factory spec guides).

steps.title: Change one thing at a time
steps.detail: Truss rod no more than a quarter turn at a time, then retune and re-measure. Saddles in small steps. Re-play the whole neck after each change, so you know which adjustment fixed it.

steps.title: Re-check intonation
steps.detail: Any change of relief or saddle height shifts intonation slightly; finish by checking it [dx-intonation].
steps.warn: Lowering the action and straightening the neck can expose uneven frets that the old, higher setup was hiding. If buzz remains with relief and action at spec, the frets need attention.

models.note: Needs more action than flatter boards: Fender spec is 5/64 in bass, 4/64 in treble at the 17th fret, and 0.012 in relief. Going much lower on a 7.25 in board invites buzz and choked bends.
Action is set with the two thumbwheels on the bridge posts, not per string. Slacken the strings slightly before turning the wheels.
Action is set at the two pivot studs (on Edge bridges release the stud lock first). Changing the height changes the tuning, so retune after each change.
Action is changed by shimming or sanding the bone saddle; dry winter air often lowers the action and causes buzz.
Basses need more relief (Fender 0.010–0.014 in depending on radius) because the strings swing wider.

warnings: Never force a truss rod that is stiff or will not turn; stop and get it checked.
Fret ends can be sharp in dry weather; run a finger along the edge gently before sliding your hand along the neck.
pro: If buzz remains with relief, action and nut at factory spec, the frets need levelling or reseating, or the fretboard has a hump or ski jump. That is bench work for a luthier unless you have levelling tools and practice.

title: Hum when a Jazz Bass pickup is soloed
summary: A Jazz Bass is quiet with both pickups full up but hums when you turn one down. That is normal for two single coils wired to cancel each other's hum - but excess hum can also point to poor shielding or a broken ground.
symptoms: Quiet with both volumes on 10, hum when either pickup is soloed or the blend is uneven
Hum changes as you turn toward or away from the amp, a computer screen or lights
Hum gets quieter when you touch the strings or bridge (normal) - or louder (fault)

causes.cause: Normal single-coil hum
causes.check: Fender's two Jazz pickups are reverse-wound, reverse-polarity (RWRP) to each other, so hum cancels only when both are at full volume. Solo one and you hear ordinary single-coil hum.
causes.fix: Play with both full when hum matters, or fit hum-cancelling J pickups (Fender Noiseless or stacked/split designs).

causes.cause: Interference source nearby
causes.check: Turn on the spot while playing; hum that peaks in one direction is pickup interference from dimmers, screens, power supplies.
causes.fix: Face away from the source or move it.

causes.cause: Missing bridge/string ground
causes.check: Hum gets louder (not quieter) when you touch the strings, or does not change at all.
causes.fix: Check the bridge ground wire under the bridge or in the control cavity. See [wr-jazz-bass].

causes.cause: Poor or no cavity shielding
causes.check: Hum and buzz even with both pickups up; buzz changes as you move your hand near the controls.
causes.fix: Shield the control and pickup cavities with conductive paint or copper foil tied to ground (wiring guides).

causes.cause: Mismatched replacement pickups
causes.check: Both pickups up and still humming loudly after a pickup change - the pair may not be a matched RWRP set, or one is wired backwards.
causes.fix: Use a matched set or reverse one pickup's leads (wiring guides).

steps.title: Both full, then solo
steps.detail: Turn both volumes to 10 - hum should drop. Turn one down and listen. If both-full is quiet, the system is working as designed.

steps.title: Touch test
steps.detail: Touch the strings and bridge. Hum should drop when you touch them. If it rises, suspect a ground fault.

steps.title: Rotate test
steps.detail: Turn slowly through 360 degrees with one pickup soloed to find interference sources.

steps.title: Inspect
steps.detail: With the strings slackened, open the control plate and look for a broken ground wire or loose solder joints. Wiring repairs are covered in [wr-jazz-bass] and [wr-pj-bass].

models.note: RWRP pair; hum-cancelling only when both are at full volume.
The split-coil P pickup (since 1957) is hum-cancelling on its own because its two halves are wired out of phase with reversed magnets. On a PJ, the J pickup soloed will hum.

warnings: Never open an amplifier to chase hum - mains voltages inside can kill.
pro: If you are not comfortable soldering grounds or shielding a cavity, a tech can do it quickly.

title: Intonation sharp or flat (and saddles that run out of travel)
summary: If chords sound sweet in open position but sour up the neck, the vibrating length of one or more strings is wrong. Set it by moving each saddle, and know what to do when a saddle hits the end of its travel.
symptoms: Open strings tune perfectly but chords at the 5th–12th frets sound out
The fretted 12th-fret note reads sharp or flat against the 12th-fret harmonic or the open string
A saddle is already as far back (or forward) as it goes and the note is still off
Notes waver or 'warble' on the low strings high up the neck

causes.cause: Saddle in the wrong place
causes.check: Tune the open string, then play the 12th-fret harmonic and the fretted 12th note. Fretted sharp = string too short. Fretted flat = string too long.
causes.fix: Sharp: move the saddle away from the neck. Flat: move it toward the neck. Slacken the string a little before moving the saddle, retune, re-check.

causes.cause: Old or dead strings
causes.check: Old strings won't intonate reliably whatever you do.
causes.fix: Fit and stretch new strings before intonating [dx-restring-electric].

causes.cause: Action too high or nut slots too high
causes.check: High action stretches the string sharp when you press it down; high nut slots make first-position notes sharp. Measure [dx-measure-action].
causes.fix: Fix relief, action and nut first, then intonate.

causes.cause: Pickups too close to the strings ('Strat-itis')
causes.check: Low-string notes high on the neck warble or beat; lowering the pickup cures it.
causes.fix: Lower the pickup, especially the neck pickup's bass side, then re-check intonation [dx-pickup-height].

causes.cause: Saddle runs out of travel: still sharp with the saddle all the way back
causes.check: Confirm the action and string gauge are normal (an unusually heavy or wound G needs more length) and that the intonation screw is not simply too short.
causes.fix: Options in order: fit a longer intonation screw or remove the saddle spring to gain room (Strat-style); turn tune-o-matic saddles around so the slope faces the other way, or turn the whole bridge round if the saddles are all pushed one way; on a Tele 3-saddle bridge fit compensated barrels. If the bridge itself is in the wrong place, moving it is pro work.

causes.cause: Saddle runs out of travel: still flat with the saddle all the way forward
causes.check: Often action that is very high or a bridge placed slightly too far back.
causes.fix: Lower the action first; then as above. Acoustic saddles cannot move: the slot must be filled and re-cut in a new place (pro).

causes.cause: Floating trem not at its normal angle
causes.check: If the bridge is tilted forward or back from where it was set, every string's length changes.
causes.fix: Set the trem angle first [bt-strat-vintage-trem] [bt-floyd-balance-setup], then intonate.

tools: Screwdriver or hex key for the saddles
parts: Longer intonation screws, compensated Tele saddles or replacement saddles if travel runs out

specs.label: Target
specs.value: Fretted 12th note equals the 12th-fret harmonic (or open string an octave up)

specs.label: Tele 3-saddle bridge
specs.value: Each barrel serves two strings: split the error between them, or fit compensated barrels

steps.title: Do it last
steps.detail: Intonation depends on relief, action, nut height, string gauge and trem angle. Set all of those first.

steps.title: Tune in playing position
steps.detail: Fit new, stretched strings and tune with an accurate tuner with the guitar held as you play it.

steps.title: Compare 12th harmonic and fretted 12th
steps.detail: Play the harmonic lightly over the 12th fret, then fret the 12th normally (no extra pressure). On wound strings the 5th-fret harmonic can be easier to read.

steps.title: Move the saddle
steps.detail: Slacken the string a quarter turn or so. Fretted sharp: lengthen the string (saddle away from the neck). Fretted flat: shorten it (saddle toward the neck). Small moves - often a turn or two of the screw.

steps.title: Retune and re-check
steps.detail: Retune the open string, compare again, and repeat until they match. Then check the 17th fret too if you play high up; split the difference if 12 and 17 disagree.

steps.title: Floyd/Edge bridges
steps.detail: Detune the string until slack, loosen the saddle lock screw, slide the saddle by hand (no adjusting screw on most), lock it, retune and re-check. Repeat per string.
steps.warn: Floyd saddles can be pushed by the string tension when the lock screw is released at pitch; always slacken first.

models.note: Intonation screws at the back of the bridge; a Phillips screwdriver on most (PRS molded trem: #1 or #2 Phillips).
Two strings per barrel: compromise, or fit compensated or 6-saddle hardware.
Screws on the pickup side of the bridge, usually a small flat screwdriver. Saddles can be reversed if one runs out of travel.
Maryland stoptail: 1/16 in hex; SE stoptail: 1.5 mm hex; 2-piece stoptail and plate bridges: #1/#2 Phillips; Floyd: 3 mm hex.
Loosen the string, then the saddle lock bolt; slide, lock, retune.
The saddle is fixed. Small errors can be improved by reshaping the saddle top's contact point; larger errors need the slot filled and re-cut (pro).
Same method; heavy strings need more saddle travel, and bridge springs can be removed to gain room.

pro: Moving an acoustic saddle slot, or relocating an electric bridge.

title: Neck dive and poor balance
summary: If the headstock drops when you let go, your fretting hand ends up holding the guitar up. The fix is usually the strap, the strap button position or the weight of the tuners.
symptoms: Headstock sinks toward the floor when you let go
Fretting hand and wrist tire because they support the neck
Guitar slides along the strap

causes.cause: Slippery strap
causes.check: Nylon or smooth straps let the guitar slide.
causes.fix: A wide leather or suede strap with a grippy back.

causes.cause: Front strap button too far from the guitar's balance point
causes.check: SG-style and long-necked basses often have the button on the neck heel or far back on the horn.
causes.fix: Move the button forward (to the end of the upper horn or the back of the neck heel). Drill a small pilot hole, lubricate the screw and countersink the hole slightly.

causes.cause: Heavy tuners on a light body
causes.check: Common on basses and light electrics.
causes.fix: Lighter tuners (for example open-gear or lightweight bass tuners).

causes.cause: Strap button pulling out
causes.check: Button wobbles.
causes.fix: Fill the screw hole with hardwood and glue, re-drill a pilot hole; consider strap locks.

steps.title: Try a different strap
steps.detail: The cheapest test: a wide leather or suede strap often cures mild dive.

steps.title: Find the balance point
steps.detail: Hang the guitar on the strap and hold the strap end at different points on the upper horn; note where it balances level.

steps.title: Move the button
steps.detail: Mark the new spot, put masking tape over it, drill a pilot hole slightly smaller than the screw core, lubricate the screw and fit the button with its felt washer. Countersink the hole a little to stop finish cracking.
steps.warn: Avoid drilling into the neck joint area, control cavities or the neck screws; check the inside first.

steps.title: Lighten the headstock
steps.detail: If dive remains, lighter tuners reduce it.

models.note: Famous for neck dive; many players move the front button to the back of the neck heel or use a grippy strap.
Heavy bass tuners make dive worse; lightweight tuners help a lot.

pro: If you're unsure what is inside the body where you want to drill, or on vintage guitars where originality matters.

sources.title: StewMac: Wilkinson Vintage S guitar kit instructions (setup section)

title: Sharp fret ends and tuning that drifts with the seasons
summary: Wood shrinks in dry air and swells in humid air; metal frets and strings do not. That is why fret ends stick out in winter, action changes between seasons and tuning drifts with the weather.
symptoms: Fret ends feel sharp along the edge of the fretboard (winter)
Action dropped and the guitar buzzes (dry) or action rose and feels stiff (humid)
A hump where the neck meets the body (dry acoustic)
Top looks sunken behind the bridge (dry) or bulging (humid)
Tuning shifts from day to day or room to room

causes.cause: Dry air: the fretboard shrinks across its width, leaving the frets sticking out
causes.check: Run a finger gently along the fretboard edge. Taylor lists sharp fret ends, low action, a hump at the body joint and a sinking top as dry-guitar signs.
causes.fix: Humidify to 45–55% RH (case humidifier, hygrometer in the case). Once the guitar has recovered, file any fret ends that still stick out [fn-fret-level-crown-polish].

causes.cause: Humid air: the wood swells
causes.check: Taylor's wet-guitar signs: high action, dull tone, the back dipping at the tail block, the neck plane sighting below the bridge. Over-humidifying for weeks at 80–90% or months at 60–70% RH does this.
causes.fix: Dehumidify (room dehumidifier or silica packs in the case); stop using soundhole humidifiers.

causes.cause: Neck relief changes with the season
causes.check: Re-measure relief at the start of winter and summer [dx-measure-relief].
causes.fix: Small truss rod corrections, a quarter turn at a time [fn-truss-rod-basics].

causes.cause: Temperature shock
causes.check: Tuning moves right after taking the guitar from a cold car or into a hot venue.
causes.fix: Leave it in its case in the new room for a few minutes before opening, then retune.

specs.label: Ideal relative humidity (Taylor)
specs.value: 45–55% RH; Taylor's factory runs at 47% RH

specs.label: Over-humidified (Taylor)
specs.value: Several weeks at 80–90% RH or several months at 60–70% RH

specs.label: Seasonal check (Music Street)
specs.value: Twice a year, spring and autumn

steps.title: Measure the room
steps.detail: Put a digital hygrometer where the guitar lives and another in the case. Readings tell you whether to humidify or dry.

steps.title: Store in the case
steps.detail: A case slows moisture changes. Humidifiers work in gig bags too, if they sit in the open case area.

steps.title: Humidify gradually
steps.detail: Check daily. Taylor's example: four days with a case humidifier put back about 25 g of water. Do not overdo it - watch the top's arch return.

steps.title: Re-check the setup
steps.detail: Once humidity is stable, re-measure relief and action and adjust.

steps.title: Deal with fret ends last
steps.detail: Ends that still stick out after the wood recovers need dressing. Until then, a hand moving along the neck can be cut.
steps.warn: Sharp fret ends can cut your hand; until they are dressed, slide your hand carefully.

models.note: Most affected: risk of top and back cracks below about 45% RH.

models.model: Unfinished/oiled necks (many Ibanez, some PRS and Fender)
models.note: Move faster with humidity than lacquered necks; fret-end sprout is common in winter.
A small gap around the fretboard extension appears when dry.
Bodies are stable, but the neck still moves; expect seasonal relief tweaks and occasional fret-end dressing.

pro: Cracks, a lifting bridge, or a top that stays sunk after humidifying need a luthier. Fret-end dressing is bench work if you have no fret files.

title: Sitar buzz and rattles
summary: Not every buzz comes from the frets. A fizzy, sitar-like tone on open strings, or a rattle at certain notes, usually comes from the nut, saddle, tuners or a loose part.
symptoms: Sitar-like 'fizz' on one or more open strings
Rattle that happens only at certain pitches
Buzz that seems to come from the headstock or body rather than the frets
Rattle when you knock on the guitar

causes.cause: String touching the side of a tuner post
causes.check: Look where the string leaves the post: if it almost touches the next post or its own post wraps, it can buzz with a 'fuzzy' tone.
causes.fix: Add or remove a wrap so the string clears the post or sits firmly against it.

causes.cause: Nut or saddle slot not breaking cleanly
causes.check: If the string rests on a flat or rising slot floor instead of leaving from a crisp front edge, it buzzes like a sitar on open strings only. Push down on the string just behind the nut (or saddle): if the fizz stops, that slot is the cause.
causes.fix: Re-shape the slot so it slopes down toward the headstock (nut) or the saddle crown comes to a clean point [fn-nut-problems].

causes.cause: Loose tuner parts
causes.check: Washers and nuts under the tuners loosen as the wood compresses; press-fit bushings ride up; button screws back out.
causes.fix: Snug the nuts and screws; a drop of thin glue holds a loose button collar.

causes.cause: Loose string ends
causes.check: Long tails at the headstock vibrate.
causes.fix: Trim them short.

causes.cause: Truss rod nut, washer or cover
causes.check: A rod nut that is completely slack lets its washer rattle; a cover can be loose.
causes.fix: Snug the nut just enough to stop it turning; tighten the cover screws.

causes.cause: Truss rod rattling in its channel
causes.check: Rap firmly on the back of the neck; a rattle there and a buzz on certain notes suggest the rod.
causes.fix: Luthier fix: thin glue or rubber cement wicked into the channel (never CA glue).

causes.cause: Loose brace (acoustic)
causes.check: Rattle when you rap on the back or top.
causes.fix: Re-glue the brace (pro).

causes.cause: Other loose hardware
causes.check: Strap buttons, output jack nut, pickup covers, trem springs in their cavity, pickguard screws.
causes.fix: Tighten; slip a piece of foam or tubing over trem springs that ring.

steps.title: Isolate the note
steps.detail: Find exactly which strings and notes rattle. Open-string-only fizz points at the nut; all notes on one string at the saddle; certain pitches anywhere at a loose part.

steps.title: Knuckle test
steps.detail: Rap the headstock, neck back, body top, back and sides. Where the rattle is loudest is usually where the loose part is.

steps.title: Mute test
steps.detail: Touch the string between nut and tuner, or between saddle and tailpiece, while it rings. If the fizz stops, the problem is in that part of the string's path.

steps.title: Tighten and trim
steps.detail: Tuner nuts and screws, rod cover, jack, strap buttons; cut long string ends.

steps.title: Re-test
steps.detail: Play again; work through the list until it is gone.

models.note: Trem springs can ring in the back cavity; pickup screws and the pickguard can rattle.
Loose wiring touching the inside of the top, and the pickup ring screws, can rattle.
Check the end-pin jack, the pickup battery holder and loose braces; on classicals a saddle that is not seated flat buzzes.

pro: Loose braces and truss rods rattling in their channel need a luthier.

title: Strings keep breaking
summary: A string that keeps snapping in the same place is telling you where a sharp edge, burr or tight bend is. Look at the broken end, find the spot and smooth it.
symptoms: Breaks at the saddle or near the ball end
Breaks at the tuner post
Breaks at the nut
Breaks mid-string over the frets or pickups
Breaks while tuning up a new string

causes.cause: At the saddle / ball end: a sharp saddle edge or burr
causes.check: Look closely at the saddle where the string crosses it and leaves it toward the tailpiece. Drag a cotton swab or thin cloth over it: snagging fibres reveal burrs.
causes.fix: Smooth the contact point with very fine abrasive (600 then 1000 grit, or abrasive cord) and polish. Graphite or self-lubricating replacement saddles reduce breakage.

causes.cause: At the tuner post: rough edges on the string hole
causes.check: Breaks right where the string enters the post. Look inside the hole for a sharp edge.
causes.fix: Run abrasive cord, a cotton swab, or an old wound string through the hole, back and forth, to round the edges (remove the tuner first if you are working hard on it).

causes.cause: At the nut: dirty, rough or pinching slot
causes.check: The break is at the nut and tuning was also unstable.
causes.fix: Clean the slot, smooth it with a wound string or gauged file, and lubricate [fn-nut-problems].

causes.cause: Too sharp a break angle (acoustic)
causes.check: Strings snap at the saddle edge or bridge pin hole where they bend sharply.
causes.fix: Smooth and slightly round the saddle crown and the edge of the pin holes (a luthier can add ramps to the pin holes).

causes.cause: Mid-string: fret burrs, pick or old strings
causes.check: Feel the fret tops for burrs; look for corrosion on the strings; heavy, sharp picks wear plain strings fast.
causes.fix: Polish frets, change strings more often, try a smoother pick edge. Heavy strummers on acoustic may do better on a medium gauge.

causes.cause: Breaking while tuning up
causes.check: Is the tuner you are turning actually that string's? Is the string going to a higher octave? Is there a kink from a previous winding?
causes.fix: Follow the string from tuner to bridge before turning; tune with an electronic tuner; use a fresh string.

tools: Fine abrasive paper (600, 1000 grit) or abrasive cord
Small vice (if working on tuners off the guitar)

steps.title: Keep the broken string
steps.detail: Find exactly where it parted and match that to a point on the guitar: saddle, nut, tuner, or over a fret.

steps.title: Inspect that point
steps.detail: Use a bright light and magnifier. Swab test the saddle and tuner hole.

steps.title: Smooth and polish
steps.detail: Work only the contact surface with fine abrasive, then polish. Do not change the height or shape of a saddle notch more than needed.
steps.warn: Mask surrounding finish and pickups when using abrasives; steel dust is attracted to pickup magnets.

steps.title: Lubricate
steps.detail: A little graphite or nut lubricant at the nut and saddle notches reduces wear and breakage.

steps.title: Restring and watch
steps.detail: Fit a new string and see whether breakage moves or stops.

models.note: Check the edges of the saddle where the string comes up through the bridge plate and the ferrules on the back.
Check the front and back edge of each saddle notch and the stopbar edges.
Strings often break at the saddle clamp; do not over-tighten the clamp bolts, and replace worn clamp blocks.
The cross-holes in the posts often have sharp edges; abrasive cord fixes them.
Look at the saddle crown and the bridge pin holes.

pro: If a saddle notch is badly worn or cut sharp, a replacement saddle is quicker than re-shaping it.

title: Tremolo won't return to pitch
summary: Track down why strings come back flat or sharp after using the arm. Most of the time the cause is friction at the nut or string trees, or string winding, not the bridge itself.
symptoms: Strings return flat after a dive
Strings return sharp after a pull-up
Pinging sound from the nut when using the arm
One string always ends up out after arm use

causes.cause: String binding in the nut slots
causes.check: Use the arm slowly and listen for a ping or click from the nut. Strings that come back sharp after a dive usually stuck at the nut.
causes.fix: Smooth and lubricate the slots (graphite, PTFE or nut grease); StewMac recommends slots a few thousandths wider than the string with rounded, polished floors. A Graph Tech TUSQ or roller nut helps. See [bt-string-trees-friction].

causes.cause: String trees grabbing the strings
causes.check: Inspect the underside of the trees for grooves, rust or burrs. Watch whether the string hops under the tree when you use the arm.
causes.fix: Clean with abrasive cord, lubricate, swap for Tusq or roller trees, or raise the tree. See [bt-string-trees-friction].

causes.cause: Too many or slipping wraps on the tuner post
causes.check: Look for overlapping or bulging windings, especially on the plain strings.
causes.fix: Rewind neatly in a downward spiral (StewMac: 2–3 wraps on wound strings, 3–5 on plain), or fit locking tuners. See [bt-locking-tuners].

causes.cause: Strings not stretched
causes.check: New strings that keep going flat over the first session.
causes.fix: Stretch each string along its length, retune, repeat 2–3 times.

causes.cause: Pivot screws or studs too tight, worn or notched
causes.check: Rock the bridge by hand with strings slack; feel for notches or grinding. Inspect knife edges and stud collars.
causes.fix: Reset pivot screws (vintage: 1/16 in up then outer two flush). Haze suggests removing the middle four screws as a test. Replace notched studs; dress worn knife edges with a fine file and polish.

causes.cause: Bridge resting lightly on the body
causes.check: A bridge that floats a hair above the body, or sits on it with almost no spring pressure, can come back to a slightly different point each time.
causes.fix: Either float it properly or deck it firmly with extra claw tension. Haze notes a 'hard-to-body' balance is unstable on 2-point bridges.

causes.cause: Block rubbing the cavity wall
causes.check: Look at the sides of the block and cavity for shiny rub marks.
causes.fix: Sound On Sound suggests easing the cavity slightly with sanding; get a tech if much wood must go.

causes.cause: Worn or mixed springs
causes.check: Springs of different brands/types, or a trem that keeps drifting flat over time.
causes.fix: Fit a fresh matched set.

tools: Graphite, PTFE lube or nut grease

steps.title: Find where the string sticks
steps.detail: Tune up. Dive the arm and let it return; note which strings are off and whether flat or sharp. Then pull up and release. Gently push each string down behind the nut and on the headstock side of the tree: if pitch jumps back, the string was stuck there.

steps.title: Fix the cheapest causes first
steps.detail: Lubricate nut slots and string trees, rewind strings neatly, stretch them. Retest.

steps.title: Check the bridge mechanics
steps.detail: Slacken strings, inspect pivots and springs as in the causes list, reset the pivot screws or studs, rebalance.

steps.title: Consider hardware upgrades
steps.detail: Locking tuners, a low-friction or roller nut, roller trees, and Graph Tech saddles each remove a friction point (StewMac). A Hipshot Tremsetter can improve return to centre.

pro: If the nut needs re-slotting or replacing, or the pivot holes need plugging and re-drilling, a tech will do it faster and without damage.

title: Weak or floppy low B string
time: 15 min to diagnose; 1 h with a string change
summary: A low B that feels slack, flaps against the frets, sounds woolly or goes sharp when you dig in. Usually a string choice or setup issue; sometimes the scale length is simply short for that string.
symptoms: B string feels loose compared with the E
Fret rattle or buzz on the B only
Notes on the B go sharp as you pluck hard, then settle
Low notes sound woolly or undefined next to the E
The B is quieter or louder than the other strings through the amp

causes.cause: String with low tension or thin core
causes.check: Look up the set's tension and core. Hipshot notes light-tension strings use thinner cores (it wants at least a .022 in core to drop an E to B with an Xtender) - thin cores feel slacker.
causes.fix: Try a heavier B or a taper-wound B. On a taperwound string the exposed core sits on the saddle without its outer wraps, which many players find helps the B ring clearly. See [bs-choose-bass-strings].

causes.cause: Action or relief too low on the B side
causes.check: Measure: Music Man suggests 7/64 in for the B; Strandberg 1.75 mm at the 19th. Check relief with the B held at the last fret.
causes.fix: Raise the B saddle a little and/or add a touch of relief. See [bs-five-six-string-setup].

causes.cause: Pickup too close to the B
causes.check: Hold the B at the last fret and measure to the pole piece. Strong magnets pull the string and cause warble.
causes.fix: Lower the bass side of each pickup, then balance by ear.

causes.cause: Wrong wound length - silk or taper sitting on the nut, or the ball-end wrap on the saddle
causes.check: The silk/taper must start after the nut (La Bella). At the bridge, look for the thick wrapped section near the ball sitting on the saddle.
causes.fix: Buy the correct scale set (through-body basses often need longer strings). See [bs-ball-end-saddle].

causes.cause: Short scale for the B
causes.check: Standard basses are 34 in; long-scale 35 in is common on 5-strings because it helps the B (Wikipedia). Multiscale basses give the B a longer length - Strandberg's Boden 5 uses 35 in for the B.
causes.fix: Within your bass: a heavier or taper-core B. Otherwise a 35 in or multiscale bass is the long-term answer.

causes.cause: Old or dead string
causes.check: Is the B the oldest string? Does it sound dull and not intonate?
causes.fix: Replace it.

causes.cause: Nut slot too wide or too low
causes.check: Open B buzzes or the string moves sideways in the slot.
causes.fix: Have the slot filled and recut, or replace the nut.

tools: Screwdriver/hex keys for saddles and pickups

steps.title: Compare with the E
steps.detail: Pluck the open B and open E with the same force. If the B feels clearly floppier, note whether it buzzes (setup) or just feels slack (string/scale).

steps.title: Check setup on the B side
steps.detail: Measure B-side relief and B height. Bring them to the targets in the causes list.

steps.title: Check pickup distance
steps.detail: Lower the bass side of the pickups a turn or two and listen for a clearer B.

steps.title: Check the string fit
steps.detail: Confirm the silk/taper position at the nut and that the right part of the string sits on the saddle.

steps.title: Try a different B
steps.detail: Buy a single B of a different construction (heavier, taper-core, or a different brand's tension) and compare. This is the most common real fix.

pro: If the B still buzzes in specific spots after setup, the frets may need levelling.

title: Won't stay in tune (and pinging when tuning)
summary: Tuning that drifts is almost always friction or slippage at the tuners, nut, string trees, trem or ball end, or strings that have not settled. Work through each contact point in order.
symptoms: Strings go flat after a few minutes of playing or after bends
A 'ping' or 'tick' and a jump in pitch while tuning or bending
Guitar returns sharp or flat after using the trem arm
New strings keep dropping flat for the first day
Tuning changes when you move from one room to another
One string (often G or D on angled headstocks) is always the problem

causes.cause: New strings still stretching and seating
causes.check: Strings fitted in the last day or two keep drifting flat.
causes.fix: Stretch them, retune, repeat until they hold [dx-restring-electric].

causes.cause: Nut slot binding or pinching (the 'ping')
causes.check: Tune up slowly and listen at the nut. A ping with a sudden pitch jump means the string is catching in the slot and then letting go. Press the string between nut and tuner: if the pitch jumps, it was stuck.
causes.fix: Lift the string out and rub pencil graphite or a nut lubricant into the slot. If it still binds, the slot is too narrow or pinches at the front: have it opened out and shaped so the back of the slot slopes down toward the headstock [fn-nut-problems].

causes.cause: Slipping at the tuner post
causes.check: Too few wraps, wraps crossing each other, or a vintage slotted post where the end is not tucked in.
causes.fix: Restring with about 2–3 in of slack: StewMac suggests 2–3 wraps on wound and 3–5 on plain strings for non-locking posts (others suggest 3–4 / 5–6), wraps going downward; locking tuners need only ½–1 wrap.

causes.cause: Loose or worn tuners
causes.check: Wiggle each tuner: check the bushing nut on the face, the screw on the back and the button screw.
causes.fix: Snug them (do not over-tighten). Replace tuners only if the gears are worn and have play.

causes.cause: String trees binding
causes.check: Each string should run under its tree; a rough or dry tree catches the string, especially with trem use.
causes.fix: Lubricate the tree, smooth any burr, or fit a low-friction roller/graphite tree.

causes.cause: Trem not returning to pitch
causes.check: Tune, press the arm down and let go, pull up and let go. Compare pitch each time. Check the bridge sits parallel to the top, the springs are even and the anchor/claw screws are solid.
causes.fix: Balance and lubricate the trem [bt-strat-vintage-trem] [bt-floyd-balance-setup], or deck/block it if you never use it.

causes.cause: Ball end not seated
causes.check: Sweetwater lists the tuner, the nut and the ball end as the three points where strings slip; a ball end that is not pulled fully home creeps.
causes.fix: Pull each new string firmly toward the headstock as you tune up, so the ball end seats before stretching.

causes.cause: Temperature and humidity changes
causes.check: Drift happens when moving between hot and cold places or with the seasons.
causes.fix: Let the guitar sit in its case in the new room for a few minutes before tuning. StewMac recommends about 45–50% RH for storage in dry areas [dx-seasonal-changes].

causes.cause: Playing technique or intonation
causes.check: Heavy fretting pushes notes sharp; a guitar with bad intonation sounds out of tune even when the open strings are perfect.
causes.fix: Lighter fretting pressure; check intonation [dx-intonation].

tools: Small wrench/socket for tuner bushings (often 10 mm on modern tuners)

specs.label: Wraps, non-locking (StewMac)
specs.value: 2–3 wraps wound strings, 3–5 plain strings, wound downward

specs.label: Wraps, locking tuners (StewMac)
specs.value: ½–1 wrap

specs.label: Storage humidity (StewMac)
specs.value: About 45–50% RH

steps.title: Always tune up to pitch
steps.detail: If you overshoot, drop below the note and come back up. Tuning down leaves slack trapped behind the nut that pops loose later.

steps.title: Check the tuners
steps.detail: Snug the bushing nuts and back screws, check button screws, and look at how each string is wound.

steps.title: Check the nut
steps.detail: Tune each string up slowly and listen for pings. Lubricate every slot at the next string change.

steps.title: Check string trees and saddles
steps.detail: Look for burrs where the strings touch; polish and lubricate.

steps.title: Check the trem
steps.detail: Do the press-and-release return test. Balance, lubricate or block it.

steps.title: Stretch and settle the strings
steps.detail: Stretch, retune, play for a few minutes, retune. New strings can take a few hours of playing to settle fully.

models.note: String trees on the high strings, the nut and the trem are the usual culprits; balance the springs so the bridge rests where you set it.
The long, angled path of the G and D through the nut makes them prone to binding: lubricate those slots first.
With the nut locked, tuning is done with the fine tuners; centre the fine tuners before locking the nut. If it drifts, check the knife edges and studs.
Rocking bridges and saddles that let strings jump can make the trem return unreliable; check the bridge sits correctly in its posts.
Humidity swings move tuning more than on electrics. Nylon strings take much longer to settle than steel.

pro: Re-cutting or replacing a binding nut is best done with proper gauged nut files.

title: Floyd Rose knife edges, studs and worn parts
summary: Diagnose a locking trem that grinds, clunks or won't return to the same pitch because of worn knife edges, notched studs, chewed clamp blocks or a loose nut, and decide what to replace.
symptoms: Trem returns slightly sharp or flat after dives
Gritty or notchy feel when moving the arm
Clicking from the pivot
Strings slipping out of the saddle clamps
Strings slipping at the nut

causes.cause: Dull or chipped knife edges on the base plate
causes.check: Slacken strings, block the bridge or remove it, and inspect the two sharp edges at the front of the plate under a magnifier. Look for flattening, chips or burrs.
causes.fix: Light burrs can be dressed with a fine file and polished (Gearnews, Haze). Badly worn edges on a licensed bridge usually mean a new bridge or base plate; Diamond Guitars notes licensed Floyds use softer metal that wears faster and recommends genuine Floyd Rose parts.

causes.cause: Notched studs
causes.check: Look for a groove worn into the stud collar where the knife edge sits.
causes.fix: Replace the studs (match thread and type to your bridge). Gearnews: replace notched posts.

causes.cause: Grooved saddle clamp blocks
causes.check: Inspect blocks for deep string grooves; strings that slip or break at the saddle.
causes.fix: Replace the blocks. Remove saddle burrs with a fine file (Seymour Duncan).

causes.cause: Worn nut pads or loose nut
causes.check: Strings drift after locking; nut moves; pads deeply grooved.
causes.fix: Tighten the nut mounting screws; replace grooved pads (LeVan). Don't overtighten pads.

causes.cause: Loose saddle lock bolts or intonation screws
causes.check: Saddles slide when you dive.
causes.fix: Tighten firmly (Diamond Guitars).

tools: Fine needle file and polishing paper
parts: Replacement studs/inserts, clamp blocks, nut pads or a genuine bridge as needed

steps.title: Rule out the easy causes
steps.detail: Check nut tightness, string stretch and fine-tuner travel first. A Floyd that drifts is more often a nut or setup issue than worn steel.

steps.title: Inspect the pivot
steps.detail: Block the bridge, slacken strings, and look closely at the knife edges and stud collars. Rock the bridge by hand and feel for grit.

steps.title: Dress light wear
steps.detail: With the bridge off, run a fine file lightly along a burred edge to restore a clean line, then polish. Remove as little metal as possible. Clean and put a smear of petroleum jelly where edge meets stud.

steps.title: Replace worn parts
steps.detail: Swap notched studs and grooved blocks. Match Original vs licensed parts and metric vs imperial threads; StewMac hosts Floyd's spec sheets for each model.

steps.title: Re-set up
steps.detail: Rebalance, set height and intonation - see [bt-floyd-balance-setup].

models.model: Floyd Rose Original (Germany/USA) vs Special/1000 Series and licensed
models.note: Original uses hardened steel; Special and many licensed units use softer alloys that wear sooner (Diamond Guitars).
Uses a ball-bearing pivot instead of a knife edge, so it doesn't dull the same way (Wikipedia: Ibanez ZR).

pro: Pulling and refitting stud anchors (inserts) in the body, or re-drilling for a different stud size, is best left to a tech - the anchors are a press fit and can split the body.
