title: High E slips off the fretboard edge
summary: If the high or low E falls off the edge when you add vibrato or pull off, the strings are not running centrally down the neck, or the fret ends are bevelled too far. Check the string line before blaming technique.
symptoms: High E slides off the edge during vibrato or pull-offs, especially high up
One outer string sits much closer to its edge than the other
The problem started after a neck was removed or a nut replaced

causes.cause: Bolt-on neck has shifted in its pocket
causes.check: At the last fret, compare the gap from the high E to its edge with the gap from the low E to its edge. Unequal gaps that get worse toward the body mean the neck is angled.
causes.fix: Slacken the strings a little, loosen the neck screws slightly, nudge the neck so both outer strings are equal from the edges, and retighten. Retune and re-check.

causes.cause: Nut slots spaced too close to the edge
causes.check: Measure from each outer string to the fretboard edge at the 1st fret. If the outer strings sit very close to the edge here, the nut is the problem.
causes.fix: A new nut with correct spacing [fn-nut-problems].

causes.cause: Bridge saddles out of line
causes.check: On Strat-style bridges, saddles can drift sideways. Check that the string spacing at the bridge is even and centred on the pickups.
causes.fix: Set the saddles back in line; on Floyds check the saddles are evenly spaced.

causes.cause: Fret ends bevelled too steeply
causes.check: After a fret job, the usable fret top may end well inside the board edge.
causes.fix: Not easily reversed; a refret or a nut with slightly narrower outer spacing (pro).

causes.cause: Worn nut slot lets the string wander
causes.check: Do the Gibson inspector's high-E bend test and watch whether the string stays in its nut slot.
causes.fix: Re-cut or replace the nut [fn-nut-problems].

steps.title: Sight the string line
steps.detail: Look down the neck from the headstock: both outer strings should follow the fretboard edges evenly.

steps.title: Measure at the 1st and last fret
steps.detail: Measure each outer string's distance to its edge at both ends. Equal at the nut but unequal at the body = neck alignment. Unequal at the nut = nut spacing.

steps.title: Re-align a bolt-on neck
steps.detail: Slacken strings, loosen the neck screws a quarter turn each, push the neck gently toward the side that needs it, retighten in a cross pattern, retune.
steps.warn: Do not loosen the screws completely or strip them; they hold the neck under string tension.

steps.title: Check bridge and nut
steps.detail: If alignment is good, look at saddle spacing and the nut.

models.note: Bolt-on necks can shift in the pocket after a knock; easy to correct.
Neck can't move; check nut and bridge spacing instead.

pro: Nut replacement and fret-end rework.

sources.title: Gibson Forum: Setup guide in metric (Gibson Memphis final inspector's numbers)
Premier Guitar (Dave Helmer): How to set up a guitar

title: Low B, F# or baritone string will not intonate
summary: The fretted 12th on the lowest string stays sharp even with the saddle all the way back, or the low string drifts out of tune as you go up the neck. Heavy, stiff strings on a relatively short scale need more compensation than the bridge may offer.
symptoms: Saddle is at the end of its travel and the 12th fret is still sharp
Chords up the neck sound sour on the low string only
The low string goes sharp when picked hard, then settles

causes.cause: Thick, stiff string for the scale
causes.check: Gauge versus scale: heavy low strings on a 25.5 in scale need the most saddle setback. The Wikipedia 8-string article notes bass strings on these guitars often need the saddle pulled back farther.
causes.fix: A slightly lighter or more flexible low string, a taper-core string, or a longer-scale/multiscale instrument.

causes.cause: Action too high on that string
causes.check: Measure the low string's height; high action stretches the string more when fretted, pushing notes sharp.
causes.fix: Lower it to spec (see [bs-extended-range-setup]) then re-intonate.

causes.cause: Pickup pulling the string
causes.check: Lower the bass side of the pickups and retest. Strandberg: if higher notes are consistently sharp, lower the pickups or try lighter strings.
causes.fix: Set pickup height to spec.

causes.cause: Wrong part of the string on the saddle
causes.check: Ball-end wrap or extra winding sitting on the saddle.
causes.fix: Use a longer string or one with a tapered ball end. See [bs-ball-end-saddle].

causes.cause: Old or dead string
causes.check: Intonation random across the fretboard - Strandberg lists worn strings or uneven frets as causes.
causes.fix: New string; check frets.

causes.cause: Bridge placement or saddle range
causes.check: If every string needs the saddle near the back, the bridge may be mounted too far forward.
causes.fix: Flip the saddle (if symmetrical), fit a longer intonation screw or a bridge with more travel; relocating a bridge is a pro job. For reference, Hipshot places its A-style bass bridge screws 3/4 in behind the scale line on a 34 in bass.

steps.title: Fresh string, correct height
steps.detail: Fit a new low string and set its height and the pickup height first - both change intonation.

steps.title: Measure the error
steps.detail: With the saddle all the way back, note how many cents sharp the fretted 12th is versus the harmonic.

steps.title: Try the cheap fixes
steps.detail: Lower pickup, lighter or taper-core low string, correct ball-end position.

steps.title: Then hardware
steps.detail: Flip the saddle, longer intonation screw, or a bridge with more range.

steps.title: Choose your compromise
steps.detail: If it is still slightly sharp, Strandberg's suggestion is to intonate for where you play: compare at the 5th and 17th if you use the whole neck, or favour the open string for low-position riffing.

pro: Moving a bridge or re-routing a bridge pocket is a luthier job.

title: Notes choke out on bends
time: 20 min to diagnose; fret work 2–4 h
summary: A bent note that suddenly dies is hitting a higher fret as it is pushed sideways. Low action, a tightly curved fretboard and high frets up the neck are the usual causes.
symptoms: Bends on the B and high E die above the 12th fret
Bends work on some frets but cut out on others
Unbent notes ring fine
Problem is worse on a vintage-radius (7.25 in) board

causes.cause: Action too low for the bends you play
causes.check: Do the Gibson inspector's test: bend the high E a step and a half at every fret from the 6th to the 22nd. Measure 12th/17th-fret action.
causes.fix: Raise the treble-side saddles a little at a time until every bend rings.

causes.cause: Small fretboard radius (curved board)
causes.check: Check the radius with understring radius gauges. A 7.25 in or 9.5 in board 'frets out' sooner on big bends than a 12–16 in board.
causes.fix: Keep the action at the higher factory figure for that radius (Fender 7.25 in: 5/64 in bass, 4/64 in treble at the 17th). Permanent cure: a compound-radius re-radius and refret (pro).

causes.cause: High frets or lifted fret ends in the upper register
causes.check: Rock a short straightedge across three frets at a time from the 12th up, especially where the bend dies. Look for fret ends that are lifted.
causes.fix: Reseat and level [fn-fret-level-crown-polish].

causes.cause: Neck hump or rising fretboard tongue at the body joint
causes.check: Sight down the neck or lay a straightedge from about the 12th fret to the end. Acoustic necks in dry weather develop a hump here (Taylor).
causes.fix: Humidify an acoustic first. Then level frets or plane the tongue [fn-fret-level-crown-polish].

causes.cause: Too much relief making upper frets relatively high
causes.check: Measure relief; Frank Ford notes buzz from the 7th fret up can mean too much relief.
causes.fix: Tighten the rod slightly and raise the saddles to keep action the same.

specs.label: Bend test (Gibson Memphis final inspection)
specs.value: Bend the high E 1½ steps at every fret from the 6th to the 22nd

specs.label: Fender action for 7.25 in radius
specs.value: 5/64 in (2.0 mm) bass, 4/64 in (1.6 mm) treble at the 17th fret

steps.title: Find the dead frets
steps.detail: Tune up. Bend the B and high E a whole step and a step and a half at every fret from the 6th up. Note where the bend dies.

steps.title: Measure
steps.detail: Measure relief and action [dx-measure-relief] [dx-measure-action] and the board radius.

steps.title: Raise treble saddles first
steps.detail: Raise the B and high E saddles by small amounts and repeat the bend test. If a modest rise cures it, you are done; re-intonate.

steps.title: Inspect the frets where it dies
steps.detail: If you need a lot of height to cure one or two frets, rock a straightedge over those frets: a rocking fret is high and needs levelling.

steps.title: Finish
steps.detail: Re-check intonation [dx-intonation] and pickup height (raising the action lifts the strings away from the pickups).

models.note: The most bend-sensitive layout. Expect to run action slightly higher than modern-radius guitars.
12 in radius; Jim DeCola sets 3/64 in treble and 5/64 in bass at the 12th fret. Raise the treble-side thumbwheel only if the bass side is fine.
Flat or compound boards bend cleanly at low action; choking usually means a high fret rather than radius.

pro: Re-radiusing a fretboard, planing a tongue or levelling frets are bench jobs.

title: Change strings on an acoustic (bridge pins)
summary: Steel-string acoustics anchor the ball end under the top with a bridge pin. The key is making the ball end sit against the bridge plate, not jammed against the bottom of the pin.

specs.label: Wraps on the post (StewMac)
specs.value: 2–3 on wound, 3–5 on plain strings, wound downward

steps.title: Slacken and remove
steps.detail: Detune each string until slack, then cut or unwind it. Lift each bridge pin with the notch of a string winder. If a pin is stuck, push the string into the guitar an inch to free the ball end, then lift the pin.

steps.title: Clean
steps.detail: Wipe the fretboard and bridge; a little lubricant in the nut slots.

steps.title: Fit the ball end and pin
steps.detail: Push the ball end about 2–3 cm into its hole, then press the pin in with its groove facing the neck so the string runs up the groove.

steps.title: Seat the ball against the bridge plate
steps.detail: Hold the pin down with a thumb and pull the string up firmly toward the neck: you will feel the ball end slide up and lock against the bridge plate under the top. Only then tune up. A ball end left against the pin's tip pushes the pin out and makes tuning creep.

steps.title: Wind at the headstock
steps.detail: Pull tight through the post, back off about 2–3 in of slack, kink and wind downward, wraps under each other.

steps.title: Tune and stretch
steps.detail: Tune up, stretch each string gently along its length, retune; repeat until stable. Press each pin down once more after the first tuning.

steps.title: Trim
steps.detail: Clip ends at the posts.

models.note: Martin specifies its MA535T/MK11 (0.011 in) or MA540T/MK12 (0.012 in) strings for the factory setup.

models.model: Pinless or through-body bridges (e.g. some Taylor and Ovation designs)
models.note: Strings feed through holes behind the saddle; no pins to seat, but pull each string home before tuning.
Octave strings are very thin and break easily at the post; take your time tuning up.

warnings: Never pry bridge pins with a screwdriver against the bridge; you will gouge the wood.
pro: If strings break at the pin holes, or pins won't stay seated, have the pin holes and bridge plate checked.

title: Change strings on an electric guitar (every tuner and bridge type)
summary: How to fit strings so they stay in tune: the right amount of slack, neat downward wraps, ball ends seated and strings stretched, with notes for vintage slotted posts, Gibson 3+3 headstocks, locking tuners, string-through bodies and Floyd Rose bridges.
tools: Floyd/Edge: 3 mm hex key (locking nut and saddle clamps on most), string cutter for ball ends

specs.label: Slack, standard posts (StewMac)
specs.value: Pull the string tight past its post, then pull it back to the next post along to make slack (about 2–3 in)

specs.label: Wraps, standard posts
specs.value: StewMac: 2–3 on wound, 3–5 on plain strings; MusicRadar: 3–4 wound, 5–6 plain

specs.label: Vintage slotted posts (StewMac)
specs.value: Pull tight and cut the string two posts beyond its own post

specs.label: Locking tuners (StewMac)
specs.value: ½–1 wrap

steps.title: Loosen before cutting
steps.detail: Detune every string until slack before you cut it, so it cannot whip back. On floating trems and Floyds read [dx-remove-strings-safely] first: change one string at a time, or block the bridge.
steps.warn: Wear eye protection; string ends are sharp and spring back.

steps.title: Remove and clean
steps.detail: Top-loaded strings come out of the top of the bridge; string-through bodies push out from the back. Wipe the fretboard and frets, and add a touch of lubricant to the nut slots and string trees.

steps.title: Seat the ball end
steps.detail: Feed the new string through the bridge (or tailpiece) and pull it firmly toward the headstock so the ball end sits fully home in the block, ferrule or tailpiece.

steps.title: Standard tuners (modern Fender, most guitars)
steps.detail: Thread through the post hole, pull tight, then pull back to the next post to set slack. Kink the string sharply where it leaves the post, then wind so the wraps go downward, each under the last, and the string leaves the post from the inside (toward the centre of the headstock). Downward wraps increase the break angle over the nut.

steps.title: Vintage slotted (split-shaft) tuners
steps.detail: Pull the string straight and cut it about two posts beyond its own post (StewMac; others suggest about three tuner-lengths). Push the cut end straight down into the centre hole, bend it into the slot toward the inside of the headstock, and wind down neatly. No sharp end sticks out, and nothing slips.

steps.title: Gibson-style 3+3 headstocks
steps.detail: Bass-side strings wind anticlockwise and treble-side clockwise (seen from the front), so every string leaves its post on the inside and runs straight to the nut. Keep G and D wraps tidy: these strings have the longest, most angled path through the nut.

steps.title: Locking tuners
steps.detail: Turn the post so the hole points along the string path, pull the string tight through, lock the clamp (thumbwheel on the back or the integrated lock), clip the excess and tune up. Only ½–1 wrap is needed.

steps.title: String-through bodies (Tele, hardtails)
steps.detail: Feed from the back through the ferrules and the bridge plate. Push each string fully home so the ball end seats in its ferrule before tuning.

steps.title: Floyd Rose / Ibanez Edge
steps.detail: Loosen the locking nut pads (3 mm). Cut the ball end off the new string, loosen the saddle's string-clamp bolt, insert the cut end, tighten the clamp firmly, wind onto the tuner and tune. Do one string at a time so the bridge stays balanced. Lock the nut once stretched and tuned, then fine-tune [bt-floyd-balance-setup].

steps.title: String trees
steps.detail: Make sure the strings that need it run under their string tree.

steps.title: Tune and stretch
steps.detail: Tune to pitch. Pull each string up gently from the fretboard along its length (a few cm at a time), retune, and repeat two or three times until it holds. Then play for a while and retune again; a new set fully settles over a few hours of play.

steps.title: Trim
steps.detail: Clip the ends close to the post. Long ends can rattle.

models.note: Changing all strings at once lets the bridge tilt; change one at a time, or wedge the bridge, then rebalance.
With all strings off, the tune-o-matic and stopbar can fall off; change one at a time or tape the bridge in place.
Hooking the ball end on the Bigsby's pins is fiddly; bend the string end around the axle so it holds the ball on the pin while you wind.
Floating bridge rocks on its posts; keep it in place while restringing.
Bass strings are thick: measure so you get about 2–3 wraps, and bend the string sharply at the cut point before cutting so the windings cannot unravel.

warnings: Eye protection when stretching and cutting strings.
Cover the body under the headstock; a loose string end scratches finish.

title: Measure action and nut height
summary: Action is the gap between the top of a fret and the bottom of the string. Measure it at the 12th fret (or the brand's own reference fret) with a steel rule, and check the nut with the 3rd-fret test.
tools: 6 in steel rule whose markings start flush at the end, in 1/64 in or 0.5 mm divisions
Optional: string action gauge, understring radius gauges

specs.label: Reference fret by brand
specs.value: Fender: 17th; Ibanez: 14th; Gibson: 12th (Gibson Memphis inspector used the 15th); PRS, Taylor, Martin: 12th; Fender acoustic: 14th

specs.label: Nut clearance over the 1st fret (StewMac kit guide)
specs.value: Plain strings 0.007–0.012 in; wound 0.013–0.020 in

specs.label: Nut clearance (Gibson Memphis inspector)
specs.value: Low E and A 2/64 in; D and G 1.5/64 in; B and high E 1/64 in

specs.label: Nut clearance (PRS, string height at 1st fret)
specs.value: Treble about 0.2–0.6 mm; bass 0.4–0.8 mm

specs.label: Nut clearance (Dave Helmer)
specs.value: About 0.015 in plain, 0.020 in wound

steps.title: Tune up and hold in playing position
steps.detail: Measurements change with tension and gravity.

steps.title: Use the right rule
steps.detail: A school ruler has a blank margin before zero and a tape measure is too coarse. Use a machinist-style rule whose zero is the end of the blade.

steps.title: Measure the 12th fret
steps.detail: Stand the rule's end on top of the 12th fret (not the wood) beside the low E. Get your eye level with the string and read the mark at the string's underside. Repeat for the high E. Record the result in 64ths or mm.

steps.title: Set the middle strings by radius
steps.detail: Once both E strings are right, rest an understring radius gauge matching your fretboard radius on the saddles' strings or just under the strings near the bridge pickup, and set the middle four to follow the curve.

steps.title: Nut check 1: the 3rd-fret test
steps.detail: Press each string at the 3rd fret and look at the gap between the string and the top of the 1st fret. There should be a very small but visible gap. No gap at all = slot too low (open-string buzz). A large gap = slot too high (stiff first position, sharp chords).

steps.title: Nut check 2: measure the open-string clearance
steps.detail: With the string open, slide feeler blades between the top of the 1st fret and the bottom of each string. Wound strings sit a little higher than plain ones. The fretboard radius makes the blade rock, so hold it level with the string.

steps.title: Nut check 3: StewMac's double-it method
steps.detail: Capo at the 1st fret and measure the gap over the 2nd fret. Double that number: that is a good target for the open-string gap over the 1st fret.

models.note: Factory action figures are taken at the 17th fret.
Factory action figures are taken at the 14th fret.
Taylor and Martin quote the 12th fret; Fender's acoustic chart quotes the 14th.

pro: Lowering nut slots needs gauged nut files; one stroke too many means a new nut. If you have never done it, have it done.

title: Measure neck relief
summary: Relief is the slight forward bow of the neck under string tension. Measure it with the string itself as a straightedge: capo at the 1st fret, finger at the body joint, feeler gauge at the 7th–8th fret.

specs.label: StewMac starting values
specs.value: Electric 0.004–0.008 in; acoustic 0.006–0.012 in; bass 0.008–0.015 in; treble side often 0.001–0.002 in less than bass side

specs.label: Gibson Les Paul (Jim DeCola)
specs.value: 0.010–0.012 in at the 8th fret, capo at 1st

specs.label: PRS
specs.value: 0.005–0.010 in at the 8th fret

specs.label: Ibanez
specs.value: 0.3–0.5 mm at the 8th fret

specs.label: Quick paper gauges (Jim DeCola)
specs.value: Printer paper about 0.004 in; business card about 0.013 in

steps.title: Tune and hold as you play
steps.detail: Tune to pitch with your normal strings. Hold the guitar in playing position (or support it on its side): lying flat on its back lets gravity sag the strings and neck and skews the reading.

steps.title: Capo the 1st fret
steps.detail: This takes the nut out of the measurement and frees a hand. A light capo is better than a heavy clamp.

steps.title: Fret at the body joint
steps.detail: Hold the low E down at the fret where the neck meets the body (acoustics: around the 14th; Strat/Tele often the 17th; Fender's method uses the last fret). Use your picking hand or a second capo.

steps.title: Gauge at the 7th–8th fret
steps.detail: Slide feeler blades between the top of the 8th fret (the fret wire, not the wood) and the bottom of the string. The right blade slips through with a slight drag without lifting the string. If the string moves, that blade is too thick.

steps.title: Repeat on the high E
steps.detail: Check the treble side too; it often runs a little less.

steps.title: Compare with spec using the same method
steps.detail: Brands measure in slightly different places (Fender 8th fret with last fret held; MusicNomad 6th fret with 12th held; Martin SC 5th fret with 12th held), so compare like with like. Adjust with the truss rod a quarter turn at a time, retune and re-measure [fn-truss-rod-basics].

models.note: Truss rod adjusts at the headstock behind the nut. US-made Fenders take a 1/8 in hex key; Mexican-made Fenders and recent Squiers are commonly reported to take 4 mm (check that the key seats fully before turning).

The rod nut is at the body end of the neck. On many you must loosen the strings and remove or tilt the neck, or remove the pickguard, to reach it; it takes a large screwdriver. Some modern Fenders have a spoke wheel at the heel turned with a small rod.
Truss rod nut is under the bell-shaped cover on the headstock; it takes a 5/16 in nut driver or box wrench. The wood around a Gibson nut is thin, so never force it.
Maryland-made (USA) PRS: 5/16 in truss rod wrench at the headstock. PRS SE: 7 mm.

models.model: Ibanez / superstrat with Floyd or Edge
models.note: Most modern Ibanez take a 4 mm hex key at the headstock (Prestige models are commonly reported as 5 mm); use the wrench supplied with the guitar when you have it.
Rod adjusts inside the soundhole at the neck block with a 5 mm hex key (not the SC-13E / Modern Deluxe style models, which differ).
Most Taylors adjust at the headstock with a 1/4 in nut wrench; Big Baby and pre-2012 nylon-string models adjust inside the soundhole.
Martin specifies 0.003–0.005 in at the 5th fret with capo at 1 and the high E held at the 12th, 0.008 in maximum.
MusicNomad's method holds the string at the 1st and 12th and reads 0.006 in at the 6th fret for Gibson and PRS, 0.008 in for Martin and Taylor.

warnings: After a truss rod change, retune and wait a little: wood takes time to settle and the reading can creep.
pro: If the rod is at the end of its travel, very stiff, or the neck has a twist (different relief on bass and treble sides by a lot), see a luthier.

title: Set pickup height (Fender, Gibson, PRS, Seymour Duncan, DiMarzio specs)
summary: Pickup height sets output, balance between pickups and tone. Too close and strong magnets pull the strings, causing warbling notes, buzz and lost sustain; too far and the sound goes thin.
tools: Small hex key or screwdriver for pole pieces

specs.label: How everyone measures
specs.value: Hold the string down at the last fret; measure from the top of the pole piece (or cover) to the bottom of the string, on the high E and the low E

specs.label: Fender single coil, American/Mexican Std
specs.value: Bass 5/64 in (2.0 mm); treble 4/64 in (1.6 mm)

specs.label: Fender vintage-style single coil
specs.value: Bass 6/64 in (2.4 mm); treble 5/64 in (2.0 mm)

specs.label: Fender Texas Special
specs.value: Bass 8/64 in (3.2 mm); treble 6/64 in (2.4 mm)

specs.label: Fender humbucker
specs.value: 4/64 in (1.6 mm) both sides

specs.label: Gibson (Memphis inspector, 22nd fret)
specs.value: High E 3/32 in both pickups; low E neck 1/8 in, bridge about 3/32 in

specs.label: Gibson Les Paul (Jim DeCola)
specs.value: Neck 4/64 in; bridge 3/64 in

specs.label: PRS humbuckers
specs.value: High E 2.5/32 in (2.0 mm); low E 3.5/32 in (2.8 mm)

specs.label: PRS single coils (high E / low E)
specs.value: Bridge 2/32 & 4/32 in; middle 3.5/32 & 4/32 in; neck 2.5/32 & 4/32 in

specs.label: Seymour Duncan
specs.value: Start about 1/8 in from the strings; for balancing, 1/8 in bass side and 1/16 in treble side with strings held at the last fret

specs.label: DiMarzio humbucker, bridge
specs.value: At least 1/16 in (1.5 mm) from the high E and 5/64 in (2 mm) from the low E; neck by ear

specs.label: DiMarzio single coil (Alnico 5 rod magnets)
specs.value: Neck/middle: low E 1/8 in (3.2 mm), high E 3/32 in (2.4 mm). Bridge: low E 3/32 in, high E 1/16 in (1.6 mm)

specs.label: DiMarzio low-pull models
specs.value: Neck/middle: 3/32 & 1/16 in; bridge: 1/16 & 3/64 in (low E & high E); add 1/32 in for a more open sound

specs.label: Fender bass
specs.value: Vintage 8/64 in bass, 6/64 in treble; American/Mexican Std 6/64 & 5/64 in

steps.title: Finish the setup first
steps.detail: Relief, action and intonation must be done, because pickup height is measured from the strings.

steps.title: Measure each pickup
steps.detail: Fret the low E at the last fret, measure pole to string. Repeat with the high E. Do each pickup.

steps.title: Set to the maker's starting figure
steps.detail: Turn the height screws: clockwise raises the pickup on most guitars. Keep both ends moving in small steps.

steps.title: Balance by ear
steps.detail: Play the neck pickup, then the bridge, at the same picking strength. Lower the louder one or raise the quieter one until switching sounds even. Raise the bass side for more bass, the treble side for more treble.

steps.title: Check for magnetic pull
steps.detail: On single coils especially, play the low E at the 12th–17th frets and let it ring. If it warbles, beats or the sustain is short, lower that pickup's bass side (and check the neck pickup in particular).

steps.title: Pole pieces
steps.detail: Adjustable poles fine-tune string-to-string balance; on Gibsons keep the E poles low and raise the inner ones to follow the radius.

steps.title: Re-check after changes
steps.detail: Re-check when you change string gauge, action, playing style or amp.

models.note: Neck and middle pickups set too high cause 'Strat-itis' warble; lower them first if notes waver.
The bridge pickup screws through the bridge plate; springs or tubing under it give height.
Adjust gently; excess pressure can damage the circuit card.
Fender/Jackson: as close as you like while leaving room for the string to vibrate.

title: Change strings on a classical (tie block)
summary: Nylon strings are tied at the bridge and wound onto rollers in a slotted headstock. Done neatly they hold tune; done loosely they slip and creep for days.

steps.title: Remove one string at a time
steps.detail: Slacken each string and untie it. Changing one at a time keeps tension on the neck and lets you copy the tie on the string next to it.

steps.title: Tie at the bridge
steps.detail: Push the string through the bridge hole from the soundhole side toward the tail, leaving about 5–8 cm out the back. Bring the short end back over the top of the tie block, pass it under the main string, then tuck it under itself where it crosses the back edge of the tie block. Trebles (plain nylon) are slippery: wrap the end around itself two or three times before the final tuck, or use beads/tie-block helpers.

steps.title: Wind on the roller
steps.detail: Pass the string through the roller hole, then loop the end back around and under itself so it pinches when tension comes on. Wind so the string comes off the roller on the top and lies neatly toward the outside of the slot, without touching the slot walls.

steps.title: Tune up slowly
steps.detail: Pull the knot at the bridge tight as you bring the string up to pitch, and check the tail end does not stick up and touch the top.

steps.title: Settle
steps.detail: Nylon stretches far more than steel. Stretch gently and retune many times over the first day; expect to retune for two or three days.

steps.title: Trim
steps.detail: Trim the tails at the bridge to about 1 cm, and at the roller.

models.model: Classical with pin bridge or ball-end strings
models.note: Some student and crossover guitars use ball-end nylon strings; fit them like an acoustic or through the tie block with the ball at the back.

warnings: Never fit steel strings to a classical guitar; the neck and bridge are not built for the tension.

title: Change strings on a headless guitar or bass
summary: Headless instruments tune at the bridge and clamp or hook the string at the far end of the neck. Steinberger-style systems use double-ball strings (or an adaptor for single-ball); Strandberg and many others use ordinary single-ball strings clamped in a string lock. The one step people miss is resetting the tuner travel.
tools: Hex keys / T-wrench supplied with the instrument (Strandberg string lock: 3 mm)
parts: Correct strings: double-ball for Steinberger-style headpieces (or single-ball with Steinberger's adaptor), single-ball for Strandberg
Steinberger single-ball adaptor if needed: STADB04 (4-string bass), STADB05 (5-string bass), STADG06 (6-string guitar)

specs.label: Strandberg Rev 7 string lock
specs.value: 3 mm hex; tuner and lock bore 2.5 mm (about .1 in)

specs.label: Strandberg Boden Bass tuner/lock bore
specs.value: 4 mm (.157 in) including any double-wound ball-end section; not compatible with double-ball strings

specs.label: Hipshot headless tuner travel
specs.value: .025 in (0.6 mm) per turn of the knob (about 25:1 guitar, 47:1 bass equivalent)

specs.label: Steinberger factory sets
specs.value: SST-105 standard guitar, SST-102 light baritone (TranScale), SST-108 light 4-string bass, SST-111 5-string low B

steps.title: Change one string at a time if there is a tremolo
steps.detail: Strandberg recommends one at a time on tremolo guitars (and suggests it on fixed bridges too) so the bridge stays balanced.

steps.title: Steinberger / double-ball: remove
steps.detail: Turn the tuning knob counter-clockwise only until the string's ball is fully visible in the tuner jaw - no further. Lift the ball out, then unhook the other end from the headpiece.

steps.title: Steinberger / double-ball: install
steps.detail: Hook one ball into the headpiece first (on basses, the small ball goes in the headpiece), then drop the other ball into the tuner jaw. Tighten the knob to pitch, stretch the string and retune. Steinberger says once stretched you should rarely need to retune until the next string change.

steps.title: Steinberger with single-ball strings
steps.detail: Fit Steinberger's headpiece single-ball adaptor, which lets the headpiece hold ordinary strings; the ball end goes at the bridge tuner and the plain end is clamped at the headpiece.

steps.title: Strandberg: reset the tuner first
steps.detail: Unscrew the tuning bolt completely, screw it back in a few turns, and push the plunger fully forward. This gives full tuning range. If you skip it, the ball end ends up poking out of the back of the tuner.

steps.title: Strandberg: remove the old string
steps.detail: Loosen the string lock screw on the headpiece with the 3 mm key, slide the string out of the lock and out through the back of the tuner.

steps.title: Strandberg: thread the new string
steps.detail: Push the plain end through the back of the tuner (a slight bend at the tip helps), along the neck and through the string lock with the protective washer under the string. Pull out slack without stretching it tight, centre it, and tighten the lock with the key held upright (so you cannot over-tighten).

steps.title: Tune, check, then cut
steps.detail: Tune up at the bridge. Check tuning range and intonation before trimming - an uncut string is easier to adjust. Then cut just above the lock (on EGS Arc, so the end sits between the lock housing's fingers).

steps.title: Troubleshoot
steps.detail: String slips: washer missing or string off-centre. String snaps at the lock: over-tightened, missing washer, or a burred lock screw (polish the burr with fine sandpaper). Ball end sticks out the back: slacken, unlock, reset the plunger as above and reinstall.

models.note: Double-ball system; single-ball adaptors available. Steinberger Spirit manual and TranScale docs on the Steinberger documentation page.

models.model: Strandberg Boden (EGS Rev 7 and EGS Arc)
models.note: Single-ball strings through the tuner, clamped at the headpiece lock (3 mm). Heavy .080 in-plus strings with fat double-wound ball ends may not fit 2.5 mm bores - use tapered ball ends.
Conventional single-ball strings; not double-ball. Buy super-long-scale sets (5-string B speaking length about 37.5-38 in).
Follow Kiesel's Headless Guitar Manual for its specific string retention and tuner layout.

warnings: Cut string ends are sharp - wear eye protection.
Over-tightening a string lock can cut the string.
Do not unwind a Steinberger tuner past the point where the ball is visible.
pro: A worn string lock or stripped tuner should be replaced through the maker's support.

title: Choosing string gauge, and what a gauge change needs
summary: Going up or down a gauge changes the pull on the neck and the fit in the nut. Expect to re-check relief, action, nut slots, trem springs and intonation - and if a new set feels wrong, this is why.
symptoms: After heavier strings: action is higher, bends are harder, strings ping at the nut, a floating trem tilts forward
After lighter strings: buzz, the trem sinks back into the body, strings sound thin or rattle in the nut slots
Intonation is off after the change

causes.cause: Heavier strings pull the neck forward (more relief)
causes.check: Measure relief [dx-measure-relief].
causes.fix: Tighten the truss rod slightly back to spec.

causes.cause: Lighter strings pull less (less relief)
causes.check: Measure relief; low-fret buzz suggests too little.
causes.fix: Loosen the rod slightly.

causes.cause: Nut slots too narrow (heavier) or too wide (lighter)
causes.check: Pinging when tuning means binding; a buzz on open strings with a loose-fitting string means a sloppy slot.
causes.fix: Widen slots with gauged nut files for heavier strings; a new nut if lighter strings rattle [fn-nut-problems].

causes.cause: Floating trem out of balance
causes.check: Heavier set: bridge pulled forward (tilts up). Lighter set: bridge pulled back.
causes.fix: Adjust the claw screws or the number of springs [bt-strat-vintage-trem] [bt-floyd-balance-setup].

causes.cause: Intonation shifted
causes.check: Compare fretted 12th with harmonic.
causes.fix: Re-intonate [dx-intonation].

specs.label: Trem springs vs gauge (Wilkinson/StewMac kit)
specs.value: 2 springs for 0.009–0.042 sets; 3 springs for 0.010–0.046 or heavier; 3 still enough for 0.013–0.060

specs.label: StewMac kit guide springs
specs.value: 3 standard; 5 for a heavier feel

specs.label: Ibanez Edge-Pro II
specs.value: Designed for three springs, equally tensioned, with a 0.009 set

steps.title: Choose the gauge
steps.detail: Lighter sets (0.009s) bend easily and suit low action, but sound thinner and go out of tune more with a heavy hand. Heavier sets (0.010–0.011 and up) give more volume and stability and suit lower tunings and slide, but are harder to bend. Longer scales (Fender 25.5 in) feel tighter than shorter ones (Gibson 24.75 in) with the same set.

steps.title: Fit and tune the new set
steps.detail: Fit the strings, stretch them in and tune to the pitch you'll actually use.

steps.title: Balance the trem (if floating)
steps.detail: Let the bridge find its angle, then adjust the claw screws (or spring count) until it sits where it should, retuning as you go.

steps.title: Re-set relief
steps.detail: Check and correct relief.

steps.title: Re-check action and nut
steps.detail: Measure action; check the nut for binding or rattle.

steps.title: Re-intonate
steps.detail: Always after a gauge change.

models.note: The biggest change: the springs must match the new tension or the bridge angle moves.
A gauge change needs the spring claw readjusted and the fine tuners re-centred.
Usually only relief, nut and intonation need attention.
Do not go above medium gauge on a lightly built guitar unless the maker approves it; extra tension can lift the bridge.
Ibanez notes its guitars are set for a standard gauge and that other gauges may need neck and intonation adjustment.

pro: Nut slot widening and a new nut for a big gauge change.

steps.title: Know your radius
steps.detail: Vintage reissues are usually 7.25 in, most modern Fenders 9.5 in, some 12 in, and compound 15–17 in boards appear on some models. Check the spec sheet or use radius gauges.

steps.title: Relief, Fender's way
steps.detail: Tune, capo the 1st fret, hold the string at the last fret (or the body joint, often the 17th on Strats and Teles), and measure the gap from the top of the 8th fret to the bottom of the string with a feeler gauge, low E and high E.

steps.title: Action at the 17th fret
steps.detail: Measure from the top of the 17th fret to the bottom of each E string and adjust the saddles; set the middle strings to follow the radius.

steps.title: Pickup height
steps.detail: Hold each E string at the last fret and measure from the top of the pole piece to the bottom of the string.

steps.title: Intonate
steps.detail: Finish with intonation [dx-intonation].

models.note: 1/8 in hex key at the headstock.
Commonly reported to take 4 mm at the headstock; check the key fits snugly.
Adjusts at the neck heel with a large screwdriver; often the neck or pickguard must come off to reach it. Some modern models have a spoke wheel at the heel.
Same relief and action table; offsets with vintage bridges are happier with action not set at the very lowest figure, so the strings keep down-pressure on the saddles.
Use the bass rows; relief measured with the G string held at the last fret as well as the E.

pro: If relief cannot be reached or the rod is stiff on a heel-adjust neck, a tech can do it with the neck off.

specs.label: Action (Gibson Memphis inspector, 15th fret)

specs.label: Pickup height (Gibson Memphis inspector, 22nd fret held)

specs.label: Pickup height (Jim DeCola, 22nd fret held)
specs.value: Neck 4/64 in; bridge 3/64 in

specs.label: Fretboard radius
specs.value: 12 in

steps.title: Strings and relief
steps.detail: Fresh strings, tuned. Measure relief and correct with the truss rod under the bell cover (5/16 in), a quarter turn at a time.

steps.title: Nut
steps.detail: Check the slots with the figures above. Lowering slots needs nut files [fn-nut-problems].

steps.title: Bridge height
steps.detail: Slacken the strings slightly and turn the tune-o-matic thumbwheels to set the low and high E at the 12th fret. Retune and re-measure.

steps.title: Pickups and pole pieces
steps.detail: Set pickup heights with the 22nd fret held. Keep the E-string pole screws low and raise the inner four to follow the 12 in radius, adjusting by ear for balance.

steps.title: Stopbar
steps.detail: Lowering the stopbar increases string pressure on the saddles; raising it softens bends. It does not change action. Do not lower it so far that strings touch the back edge of the tune-o-matic.

steps.title: Intonate
steps.detail: Screws face the pickups; turn with a small flat screwdriver [dx-intonation].

models.note: All Gibson headstock truss rods take a 5/16 in nut driver; remove the bell cover's screws first. The wood around the nut is thin: do not force it.
Commonly reported to take a 4 mm hex key rather than the Gibson 5/16 in nut.
Same specs; take care with tools near the f-holes and top.

warnings: Gibson headstocks break easily; lay the guitar on a neck rest and never let it tip over while working.
pro: A stripped or seized Gibson truss rod nut, or a cracked headstock, is pro work.

steps.detail: Remove old strings and clean, new strings, relief, action, bridge angle (trem models), intonation, pickup height, then check the nut and tuning stability, then play-test.

steps.title: Relief

steps.title: Action

steps.title: Check humidity first
steps.detail: Acoustic action moves with humidity. Make sure the guitar has been at 45–55% RH for a while before you cut anything.

steps.title: Relief
steps.detail: Measure with the method your maker uses (they differ, see the specs). Martin's rod is reached through the soundhole; most Taylors at the headstock.

steps.title: Nut
steps.detail: Check open-string clearance over the 1st fret; low slots buzz, high slots make first position stiff and sharp [dx-measure-action].

steps.title: Saddle height
steps.detail: To lower the 12th-fret action by x, take 2x off the BOTTOM of the saddle, kept flat and square. To raise it, shim the saddle or make a new one [dx-action-too-high] [dx-action-too-low].

steps.title: Neck angle check
steps.detail: If the saddle would need to be lower than about the minimum protrusion your maker allows to reach spec, the neck needs a reset (pro). Martin SC models use elevation plates instead.

1/4 in nut at the headstock on most; Big Baby and pre-2012 nylon models adjust in the soundhole. 12-strings run lower action.

title: Complete professional setup, in order
summary: A full setup is strings, relief, action, nut, pickups, trem and intonation, done in an order where each step builds on the last. Doing them out of order means re-doing earlier work.
tools: 6 in steel rule (1/64 in or 0.5 mm marks, zero at the edge)
Truss rod wrench for your guitar
Hex keys and screwdrivers for saddles and pickups
parts: A fresh set of strings in the gauge you will use

specs.label: Relief (StewMac kit guide)
specs.value: 0.004–0.012 in at the 7th–9th fret; some necks play well near 0.000 in

specs.label: Action at 12th (StewMac kit guide)
specs.value: High E 3/64–4/64 in, low E 3/64–5/64 in

specs.label: Nut clearance over 1st fret (StewMac kit guide)
specs.value: Plain strings 0.007–0.012 in, wound 0.013–0.020 in

specs.label: Trem block gap while setting up (StewMac)
specs.value: 3/32 in between back of bridge and body, held by a wedge

steps.title: 1. Inspect, clean and tighten
steps.detail: Note the current measurements so you can go back. Clean the fretboard, check tuner nuts, strap buttons, neck screws and jack are snug, and look for lifted frets or cracks.

steps.title: 2. New strings, tuned to pitch
steps.detail: Fit the gauge you will actually use and stretch it in. Relief, action, nut and intonation all depend on the tension of that particular set, so this has to come first [dx-restring-electric].

steps.title: 3. Take the trem out of the equation
steps.detail: Floating trem: slip a wedge behind the bridge (StewMac uses a 3/32 in gap) so string changes do not tilt it while you work, or set its resting angle roughly now. PRS sets bridge angle after action; either way it is finished before intonation.

steps.title: 4. Set relief
steps.detail: Capo the 1st fret, hold the string at the body joint/last fret, read the feeler gauge at the 7th–8th fret, and adjust the truss rod a quarter turn at a time [dx-measure-relief]. Relief comes before action because changing it raises or lowers every string's height.

steps.title: 5. Set action at the bridge
steps.detail: Set the two outer E strings to spec at the 12th fret (17th for Fender figures), then set the middle strings to follow the fretboard radius using understring radius gauges [dx-measure-action]. StewMac does this with the capo still on at the 1st fret, so nut height does not affect the reading.

steps.title: 6. Set the nut
steps.detail: With the saddle heights fixed, check the clearance over the 1st fret and lower any slot that is too high [fn-nut-problems]. Professionals disagree on where this goes: StewMac and PRS do the nut after the bridge; Jim DeCola and Dave Helmer do it right after relief. Either works if you re-check the action afterwards, because nut and saddle heights interact.

steps.title: 7. Set pickup height
steps.detail: Pickups are measured from the strings, so they wait until the action is final [dx-pickup-height]. Fret each E at the last fret and measure pole to string.

steps.title: 8. Finish the trem
steps.detail: Remove the wedge and balance the springs so the bridge sits at its intended angle with the guitar in tune [bt-strat-vintage-trem] [bt-floyd-balance-setup]. Spring changes move string tension and bridge position, which is why this is done before intonation.

steps.title: 9. Intonation last
steps.detail: Intonation depends on everything before it (string height, relief, trem angle, gauge), so it is always last [dx-intonation]. Tune in playing position.

steps.title: 10. Play-test and repeat
steps.detail: Play every fret on every string, try bends at the top, listen through the amp. If something buzzes or feels stiff, go back to the step that controls it and work forward again. New setups need a re-check after a day or two as everything settles.

models.note: Use the wedge or set the bridge float before step 4; finish springs before intonation.
Unlock the nut for the whole setup; centre the fine tuners before final locking [bt-floyd-balance-setup].
Jim DeCola's order: strings, relief, nut, 12th-fret action, pickup height, pole pieces, then stopbar height.
PRS order: strings, relief, action, bridge angle (trem models), intonation, pickup height, then nut/tuning-stability check.
Relief, then nut, then saddle height by sanding or shimming; intonation is fixed by the saddle position.
Same order, with more relief and higher action (see Fender bass figures in [dx-specs-fender]).

warnings: Wear eye protection when cutting strings and changing trem springs; a released string or spring can whip.
Turn the truss rod in small steps and stop if it gets very stiff.
pro: Fret levelling, nut replacement and acoustic neck resets are separate jobs; if the setup can't reach spec because of them, stop and book them.

steps.title: Unlock and centre
steps.detail: Loosen the locking nut pads (3 mm). Set every fine tuner to the middle of its travel.

steps.title: Trem parallel
steps.detail: Tune with the tuning keys, then adjust the spring claw so the bridge sits roughly parallel to the body. Tighten the claw screws if it tilts forward (back edge up), loosen if it is pulled back. Retune after every change.

steps.title: Relief
steps.detail: Ibanez method: capo at the 1st fret, hold at the neck joint, measure at the 8th fret. Adjust in quarter turns.

steps.title: Action
steps.detail: Raise or lower the whole bridge with the two pivot studs (on Edge bridges release the stud lock first). Measure at the 14th fret (Ibanez) or 17th (Jackson).

steps.title: Intonation
steps.detail: Slacken the string, loosen the saddle lock (and the string clamp on Edge-Pro), slide the saddle, tighten and retune; repeat [dx-intonation].

steps.title: Lock and fine-tune
steps.detail: Stretch strings, tune, lock the nut pads, then fine-tune with the fine tuners.

steps.title: Pickups
steps.detail: Ibanez gives no number: set them so the neck and bridge pickups are almost equally loud with volume full up. Jackson's figures are above.

models.note: Most current models take a 4 mm hex; Prestige models are commonly reported as 5 mm. Use the key supplied with the guitar where possible.
Same steps; PRS lists 3 mm for the locking nut and Floyd intonation, 2.5 mm for saddle locks, 2 mm for the arm set screw.
Skip the trem steps; set action at the individual saddles.

warnings: Changing all strings at once on a floating bridge lets it swing back into the cavity; change one string at a time (Ibanez's advice) or block it.

title: Set up a 7- or 8-string guitar
summary: Seven- and eight-string guitars set up like a 6-string, but the wide neck, the heavy low B or F# and the long scale change the numbers: more height and pickup clearance on the low strings, relief checked on both sides, and gauges that keep tension balanced.
tools: Steel rule or mm action gauge

specs.label: Relief (Strandberg 6/7/8-string)
specs.value: .010-.013 in (0.25-0.30 mm) at the 9th fret, capo at 1, G string held at the last fret

specs.label: Pickup height, neck humbucker (Strandberg)
specs.value: 2.8 mm (7/64 in) bass side, 2.4 mm (6/64 in) treble side

specs.label: Pickup height, bridge humbucker (Strandberg)
specs.value: 2.4 mm (6/64 in) bass side, 2.0 mm (5/64 in) treble side

specs.label: Fender 6-string reference, 9.5-12 in radius
specs.value: Relief .010 in at 8th; action 4/64 in both sides at 17th

specs.label: Fender 6-string reference, 15-17 in radius
specs.value: Relief .008 in; action 4/64 in bass, 3/64 in treble

specs.label: Tunings
specs.value: 7-string B-E-A-D-G-B-E (drop A: A-E-A-D-G-B-E); 8-string F#-B-E-A-D-G-B-E (drop E: E-B-E-A-D-G-B-E)

steps.title: Right strings, tuned
steps.detail: Fit the gauges you will use (see [bs-extended-strings-nut]) and tune to your tuning. Relief depends on the total pull of all strings, so a tuning change usually means a rod change.

steps.title: Relief on both sides
steps.detail: Capo the 1st fret, hold the G at the last fret and measure at the 9th (Strandberg's method). Then repeat with the lowest string. On a wide neck the two sides can differ; set the rod for the average and note any big difference (possible twist).

steps.title: Adjust the rod
steps.detail: Quarter turns, clockwise for less relief, retune after each. The extra tension of 7 or 8 strings means changes can take a while to settle - recheck after an hour.

steps.title: Set action string by string
steps.detail: Measure each string at the 19th fret (or your usual fret) and set saddles toward the figures above. The low strings go higher because they swing wider. Keep each string at or above the height of the thinner string next to it.

steps.title: Nut check
steps.detail: Low B and F# slots must be wide enough not to pinch and deep enough to avoid a stiff first fret. See [bs-extended-strings-nut].

steps.title: Pickup height
steps.detail: Hold the outer strings at the last fret and set each humbucker's bass and treble sides to the figures above. Low strings with big magnets close by can sound flubby or warble: if the B or F# sounds woolly, lower the bass side a little and balance by ear.

steps.title: Intonation
steps.detail: 12th-fret harmonic versus fretted note on every string. Low strings normally need the saddle well back; if a saddle runs out of travel see [bs-low-string-intonation].

steps.title: Play-test across the neck
steps.detail: Palm-muted chugs on the low string expose rattle that light playing does not. Raise the low string a touch if it rattles.

models.note: Multiscale 25.5-26.25 in (7) and 26.5-28 in (8); truss rod at the headstock with the supplied 4 mm T-wrench; zero fret. See [bs-headless-setup].
The Ibanez Universe was the first mass-produced 7-string (Steve Vai, 1990); Ibanez's RG2228 is often cited as the first mass-produced 8-string. Thin, wide necks - small rod turns.
Factory strings 10-46 plus a .056 low B.
Multiscale 25.5-27.8 in (7) and 25.5-28.2 in (8); see [bs-multiscale-setup].
Same procedure; many are multiscale - measure action at the same fret number on every string.

warnings: A sudden big tuning or gauge change shifts relief - recheck before playing hard.
Never force a truss rod on a wide neck.
pro: If the neck twists (bass side and treble side relief very different) or frets buzz with correct relief and height, see a tech.

title: Set up a baritone guitar
time: 1-1.5 h (plus nut work if changing gauges)
summary: A baritone guitar has a longer scale (usually 27-30.5 in) so it can be tuned a fourth or fifth lower than a standard guitar with good string tension. Setup is like a 6-string, but tuning, gauges and nut slots must match.
parts: Baritone string set for your scale and tuning

specs.label: Common baritone scale
specs.value: 27-30.5 in (690-770 mm); standard guitars 24.75-25.5 in

specs.label: C tuning (a major 3rd down)
specs.value: C2-F2-Bb2-Eb3-G3-C4

specs.label: Steinberger TranScale factory
specs.value: Light baritone set SST-102

specs.label: Fender 6-string reference (9.5-12 in radius)
specs.value: Relief .010 in at 8th; action 4/64 in at 17th

steps.title: Decide the tuning and buy the right set
steps.detail: Pick B, A or C tuning and buy a baritone set long enough for the scale. If you change tuning later, change gauge too (Music Man: roughly a gauge step per half step).

steps.title: Check the nut takes the new gauges
steps.detail: Baritone low strings (.060-.068) need wider slots than a standard guitar nut. If strings bind, ping or sit high, the slots need widening - see [bs-extended-strings-nut].

steps.title: Relief
steps.detail: Capo at 1, hold the low string at the last fret and measure at the 8th. Start at Fender's guitar figure for your radius and add a little if the low string rattles - baritone strings swing wider.

steps.title: Action
steps.detail: Measure at the 17th fret. Start at Fender's 4/64 in and raise the bass side a little (Strandberg's long-scale 8-string figures rise to 1.50-1.75 mm on the lowest strings).

steps.title: Pickups
steps.detail: Set the bass side a little further away than on a normal guitar so the low string does not warble; balance by ear.

steps.title: Intonation
steps.detail: 12th-fret harmonic versus fretted note. The longer scale usually gives enough saddle travel; if the low string runs out see [bs-low-string-intonation].

steps.title: Converting a standard guitar
steps.detail: Tuning a 25.5 in guitar down a fourth with heavy strings works but feels slacker than a true baritone; it needs nut slot work and often more relief. An octave-down tuning on a guitar-scale neck behaves like a Bass VI and needs bass-VI strings.

models.model: Fender Bass VI / Squier Bass VI
models.note: Tuned an octave below a guitar (E1-E3); uses dedicated Bass VI strings, not baritone sets.
The model that popularised the electric baritone (1956).
Ships with the SST-102 light baritone double-ball set; integrated capo raises the tuning.
Not called a baritone, but its 28 in F# string and setup figures apply to long-scale low strings.

warnings: Heavy strings carry high tension - detune before cutting.
pro: Nut replacement for a baritone conversion, or a conversion neck, are tech jobs.

title: Set up a guitar for slide
summary: Slide wants strings that sit higher and feel firmer so the slide never clatters on the frets. Raise the action, consider heavier strings, and decide whether the guitar is slide-only or must still play normally.
tools: Nut files or a nut extender/raiser if dedicated
parts: Nut extender / raised nut for a dedicated lap-style setup (optional)

specs.label: Normal fretted range for comparison (Dave Helmer)
specs.value: 3/64–3/32 in at the 17th/15th fret

specs.label: Slide target
specs.value: Toward or above the top of the normal range: high enough that a slide resting lightly across the strings never touches a fret

steps.title: Decide: dual-use or slide-only
steps.detail: If you still want to fret normally, raise the action moderately (toward the top of the normal range). For slide only, you can go much higher, and lap-style players raise the nut too.

steps.title: Go up a gauge
steps.detail: Heavier strings resist being pushed down by the slide and sound fuller. After a gauge change follow [dx-string-gauge-change].

steps.title: Relief
steps.detail: A little more relief than usual is fine; it raises the middle of the neck where slide players work.

steps.title: Raise the saddles
steps.detail: Raise the outer strings first, then match the middle strings to the fretboard radius so the slide touches all strings evenly. Test: lay the slide lightly over the frets at several positions and play; no clicks.

steps.title: Open tunings
steps.detail: Open G, D or E change string tension; retune, re-check relief and trem balance.

steps.title: Pickups and intonation
steps.detail: Raised strings sit further from the pickups; raise them to match. Intonation matters less with slide (you play over the fret wire), but re-check it for fretted playing.

models.note: Heavier strings and open tunings change the trem balance; many slide players block or deck the trem.
Uses a high nut extender and very high action; not playable fretted.
Raise the action with a taller saddle; do not shim excessively.

title: Set up a headless guitar or bass (Strandberg, Steinberger, Kiesel)
summary: Headless instruments set up in the usual order - relief, height, pickups, intonation - but the truss rod access, locked saddles, zero frets and tuner-based intonation work differently from a conventional guitar.
tools: Supplied hex keys / T-wrench (Strandberg truss rod 4 mm; EGS Arc 1.5 mm and 3 mm; Rev 7 tuner 2 mm)
Steel rule or mm action gauge

specs.label: Strandberg zero fret
specs.value: About 0.25 mm (.01 in) taller than the other frets

specs.label: Steinberger Synapse relief
specs.value: About .010 in (0.25 mm) at frets 7-9, capo at 1, low E held at the 17th

specs.label: Steinberger Synapse rod adjustment step
specs.value: 1/16-1/8 turn at a time, let it settle (ideally overnight)

steps.title: Tune with the strings you will use
steps.detail: Relief depends on string tension. On tremolo models (Strandberg EGS trem), shim the bridge level with a few picks under the base plate while setting up.

steps.title: Relief - Strandberg
steps.detail: The rod nut is in the hole at the headpiece end. Use the supplied 4 mm T-wrench: clockwise for less relief, counter-clockwise for more, a quarter turn at a time, retuning after each. Strandberg says to stop and contact support if the rod feels too tight.

steps.title: Relief - Steinberger Synapse
steps.detail: The graphite-channel neck is stiff and rarely needs adjustment; Steinberger advises leaving it to a qualified tech. If you do: capo at 1, hold the low E at the 17th, aim for about .010 in at frets 7-9, turn the larger supplied hex clockwise to reduce relief, 1/16-1/8 turn at a time, and never force it.

steps.title: Action - Steinberger
steps.detail: Loosen the bridge's side set screw (smaller hex) to unlock the saddles, turn each saddle screw clockwise to raise or counter-clockwise to lower, then lock the side set screw again. Steinberger warns an unlocked saddle causes tuning problems and buzz.

steps.title: Action - Strandberg EGS Arc
steps.detail: Loosen the saddle locking grub screw with a 1.5 mm key, detune and move the string aside, raise or lower the saddle with a 3 mm key (clockwise raises), retune and lightly relock.

steps.title: Zero fret
steps.detail: Strandberg uses a zero fret slightly taller than the rest, so open-string height is set by the fret, not by nut slots. Small dents or wear can cause a ping when bending - polish or have it dressed.

steps.title: Pickups
steps.detail: Hold the outer strings at the last fret and set to the maker's figures (Strandberg bass: neck 2.8 / 2.4 mm, bridge 2.4 / 2.0 mm bass/treble side).

steps.title: Intonation
steps.detail: Headless bridges intonate by moving the tuner or saddle. Steinberger: loosen the side set screw, set the two centre strings first, compare at the 24th fret, move saddles back if sharp, forward if flat, keep the saddle base parallel to the bridge front, relock. Strandberg: see [bs-multiscale-setup] for Rev 7 and EGS Arc methods.

steps.title: Tuning range
steps.detail: If a tuner runs out of travel or the ball end sticks out of the back of a Strandberg tuner, the plunger was not reset at the string change - see [bs-headless-string-change].

models.note: 4 mm T-wrench rod at the headpiece; zero fret; EGS Rev 7 or EGS Arc bridge; multiscale.
Graphite-reinforced neck on Synapse; saddles locked by a side set screw; truss rod at the headpiece.
Kiesel's Headless Guitar Manual covers its setup; follow the maker's tool sizes.

models.model: Hipshot headless bridges (aftermarket and on many boutique builds)
models.note: Each knob turn moves the string about .025 in (0.6 mm), giving fine tuning resolution.

warnings: Do not over-tighten small grub screws - they strip or crack saddles.
Steinberger warns improper rod adjustment can cause permanent damage and void the warranty.
pro: If the rod feels tight, a graphite neck needs correction, or tuners/locks are worn, contact the maker's support or a tech.

title: Set up a multiscale (fanned-fret) guitar or bass
summary: On a multiscale instrument every string has its own length, so the frets fan out from one straight 'neutral' fret, the bridge has individual angled saddles or tuners, and pickups are slanted. Setup is the usual relief-height-pickups-intonation, but you measure at fret numbers rather than straight lines.
tools: Steel rule or mm action gauge
Capo that sits squarely on an angled fret (or a helper to hold the string)
Hex keys for saddles/tuners (Strandberg EGS Arc: 1.5 mm and 3 mm; Rev 7: 2 mm)

specs.label: Neutral (perpendicular) fret on Ormsby
specs.value: 9th fret on a typical Ormsby

specs.label: Ormsby scale ranges
specs.value: 6-string 25.5-27.5 in; 7-string 25.5-27.8 in; 8-string 25.5-28.2 in

specs.label: Strandberg Boden Bass 5 scale per string
Ormsby GTR pickup angles
specs.value: Bridge 21.5 degrees, neck 16.5 degrees

specs.label: Pickup height (Strandberg guitar humbuckers)
specs.value: Neck 2.8 mm bass / 2.4 mm treble; bridge 2.4 mm / 2.0 mm

specs.label: Relief (Strandberg)
specs.value: Guitar .010-.013 in; bass .015-.020 in, at the 9th fret

steps.title: Know your scales and neutral fret
steps.detail: Look up each string's scale (makers list them). The fret that is square to the neck - the neutral fret - is where the fan pivots; on Ormsbys it is the 9th. It is also where your fretting hand naturally sits.

steps.title: Relief
steps.detail: Capo the 1st fret (or hold it - many capos will not sit flat on an angled fret), hold a middle string at the last fret and measure at the 9th fret. Check the lowest and highest strings too.

steps.title: Action at fret numbers
steps.detail: Measure every string at the same fret number (Strandberg uses the 19th), not at a straight line across the neck - on a fanned neck the 19th fret is at a different distance from the nut for each string. Set each individual saddle; Strandberg's EGS Arc saddles lock with a 1.5 mm grub screw and move with a 3 mm key (clockwise raises).

steps.title: Pickup height on slanted pickups
steps.detail: Each end of a slanted pickup sits under a different string length. Hold the outer strings at the last fret and measure at the bass-end pole and treble-end pole separately. Start from the maker's figures, then balance by ear.

steps.title: Intonate each string
steps.detail: 12th-fret harmonic versus fretted 12th. On Strandberg Rev 7 hardware, slacken the string, lift it off the saddle screw, loosen the tuner's 2 mm mounting screw and slide the tuner back (fretted note sharp) or forward (flat). On EGS Arc, loosen the tuner lock about half a turn with a 1.5 mm key and turn the rear 1.5 mm adjuster: clockwise moves the tuner back, counter-clockwise forward - this can be done at full tension. On Hipshot or Ormsby individual saddles, slide each saddle along its own angled track.

steps.title: Side dots look 'off'
steps.detail: On some multiscale necks the side dots are placed to line up with your line of sight rather than centred between frets (Strandberg calls this compensated side dots). That is normal.

models.note: Fan with headless EGS hardware; intonation by moving the tuner. See [bs-headless-setup].
Neutral fret at 9; GTR hardware made by Hipshot; pickups slanted 21.5 / 16.5 degrees.
Ibanez publishes an SRMS bridge manual on its manuals page.
Individual saddles; same at-fret-number measurement rule.

warnings: Over-tightening saddle lock screws can damage saddles (Strandberg).
Change strings one at a time if the instrument has a tremolo.
pro: Refretting or levelling a fanned neck is specialist work.

title: Set up for heavy down-tuning (Drop C, B and lower)
summary: Tuning down without heavier strings leaves them floppy, buzzy and sharp when picked. Go up in gauge to restore tension, then re-do the setup for the new tension.
parts: A heavier string set made for low tunings

specs.label: Trem springs with heavy sets (Wilkinson/StewMac kit)
specs.value: 3 springs are still enough for a 0.013–0.060 set

specs.label: Ibanez
specs.value: Guitars are set up for a standard gauge; off-gauge strings may need neck and intonation adjustment

steps.title: Choose heavier strings
steps.detail: Pick a set made for your tuning (makers sell 'drop' and heavy-bottom sets). The heavier the low string, the closer the tension gets to standard tuning.

steps.title: Open the nut slots
steps.detail: Heavier strings bind and ping in standard slots. Widen the wound-string slots with gauged files so each string sits about half its diameter in the slot and moves freely [fn-nut-problems].

steps.title: Tune down and balance the trem
steps.detail: Floating trem: the new tension will change the bridge angle; adjust the claw or springs. Floyd: also re-centre the fine tuners.

steps.title: Re-set relief
steps.detail: Different total tension = different relief. Measure and adjust.

steps.title: Action
steps.detail: Low tunings with heavy strings swing wider; you may need a touch more height on the bass side.

steps.title: Intonation
steps.detail: Heavy wound strings need more saddle length; the low strings' saddles move back. If a saddle runs out of travel see [dx-intonation].

steps.title: Pickups
steps.detail: Heavy strings carry more steel: lower the bass side of the pickups slightly if the low string sounds muddy or the pickups pull on it.

models.model: Short scale (24.75 in) Les Paul style
models.note: Feels floppier when down-tuned than 25.5 in or longer scales; heavier gauges help more.
Longer scales give more tension at low pitch and are made for this.
Very heavy low strings may not fit the saddle clamp or locking nut pad; check before buying.

pro: Nut slot widening if you don't own gauged files.

title: Set up for low action and a light touch
summary: Very low action works only on a neck with level frets, a straight board and a light picking hand. Get each setting to the low end of the published ranges and stop at the first buzz you can hear through the amp.

specs.label: Relief (StewMac)
specs.value: As little as 0.004 in, and some necks play well at 0.000 in if the frets are level

specs.label: Low published action
specs.value: Fender 15–17 in radius: 3/64 in treble, 4/64 in bass at 17th; Jackson: 3/64 in treble; Gibson (DeCola): 3/64 in treble, 5/64 in bass at 12th; StewMac example ~0.040 in (about 3/64 in) on both E strings

specs.label: Low nut (StewMac kit guide)
specs.value: Plain 0.007–0.012 in, wound 0.013–0.020 in over the 1st fret

steps.title: Check the frets first
steps.detail: Rock a fret rocker across every group of three frets along each string path. One high fret will stop you going low. Level first if needed [fn-fret-level-crown-polish].

steps.title: Flatter radius helps
steps.detail: Flat (12 in and up) or compound boards allow lower action without choking bends; 7.25 in boards do not [dx-choke-on-bends].

steps.title: Reduce relief
steps.detail: Bring relief down toward the low end of the StewMac range a quarter turn at a time. Stop if the first frets start to buzz.

steps.title: Lower the action in small steps
steps.detail: Lower the saddles a little at a time, playing every fret after each step, through the amp. Stop at the first buzz that comes through the amp, then go back up a fraction.

steps.title: Lower the nut
steps.detail: With low saddles, a high nut makes first position feel stiff; take the slots toward the low end of the range [fn-nut-problems].

steps.title: Pickups down a little
steps.detail: Lower action brings the strings closer to the pickups; lower them so magnetic pull doesn't cause buzz or warble [dx-pickup-height].

steps.title: Re-intonate
steps.detail: [dx-intonation]

steps.title: Adjust your touch
steps.detail: Low action needs a lighter pick attack; hard picking pushes the string into the frets.

models.note: Not a candidate for very low action; consider a 9.5 in or compound neck.
Built for this; Ibanez factory 1.5–1.7 mm treble, 2.0–2.2 mm bass at the 14th fret.

pro: Fret levelling and crowning to get a neck truly flat enough for very low action.

title: Beginner's setup tool kit, and how to read feeler and radius gauges
summary: The handful of tools that cover nearly every setup, what to buy first and why, and how to read the two gauges beginners find confusing.
tools: Accurate tuner (clip-on is fine; a strobe tuner helps intonation)
Feeler gauge set in thousandths of an inch (and mm)
6 in steel rule with 1/64 in and 0.5 mm marks, zero flush with the end
Truss rod wrench that fits your guitar
Hex key set, inch and metric (0.050 in, 1/16 in, 1.5 mm, 2 mm, 3 mm, 4 mm, 5 mm cover most bridges and rods)
String winder and flush wire cutters

specs.label: Common truss rod sizes
specs.value: Fender USA 1/8 in hex; Gibson and PRS USA 5/16 in nut driver; PRS SE 7 mm; Martin 5 mm hex; Taylor 1/4 in nut; Ibanez mostly 4 mm; Music Man 3/16 in (user-reported)

specs.label: Paper stand-ins (Jim DeCola)
specs.value: Printer paper about 0.004 in; business card about 0.013 in

steps.title: Buy first
steps.detail: Tuner, capo, feeler gauges, steel rule, the correct truss rod wrench and the hex keys/screwdrivers your bridge needs. With these you can measure and adjust relief, action, pickup height and intonation - most of a setup.

steps.title: Buy next
steps.detail: Understring radius gauges (to set saddle heights to the board curve) and a fret rocker (to find high frets). StewMac also sells a string action gauge that reads in thousandths.

steps.title: Leave until later
steps.detail: Nut files, fret files and levelling beams. They are expensive, and a slip costs a nut or a fret job.

steps.title: Why a machinist's rule
steps.detail: School rulers have a blank space before zero, and tape measures are too coarse; you need the zero at the very end of the blade to stand it on a fret.

steps.title: Reading a feeler gauge
steps.detail: Each blade is stamped with its thickness (e.g. .010 = 0.010 in = 0.25 mm). Slide blades into the gap starting thin. The correct reading is the thickest blade that slides through with a slight drag without lifting the string. If you need an in-between value, stack two blades and add their numbers. Keep the blade flat and square to the gap; on a radiused board tilt it to match the string.

steps.title: Reading radius gauges
steps.detail: Each gauge is marked with a radius (7.25, 9.5, 12, 16 in...). Lay them across the frets (or slide understring types under the strings near the bridge). The one that touches evenly with no rocking and no gap in the middle or at the ends is your radius. A smaller number means a rounder board. To set saddle heights, rest the matching gauge under the strings and raise/lower the middle saddles until all strings touch it.

steps.title: Reading the steel rule in 64ths
steps.detail: Count the smallest marks from the end: 4 marks = 4/64 in (1/16 in, 1.6 mm). On the metric side each small mark is 0.5 mm. Read at eye level with the string.

models.note: Truss rod adjusts at the headstock behind the nut. US-made Fenders take a 1/8 in hex key; Mexican-made Fenders and recent Squiers are commonly reported to take 4 mm (check that the key seats fully before turning).

The rod nut is at the body end of the neck. On many you must loosen the strings and remove or tilt the neck, or remove the pickguard, to reach it; it takes a large screwdriver. Some modern Fenders have a spoke wheel at the heel turned with a small rod.
Truss rod nut is under the bell-shaped cover on the headstock; it takes a 5/16 in nut driver or box wrench. The wood around a Gibson nut is thin, so never force it.
Maryland-made (USA) PRS: 5/16 in truss rod wrench at the headstock. PRS SE: 7 mm.

models.model: Ibanez / superstrat with Floyd or Edge
models.note: Most modern Ibanez take a 4 mm hex key at the headstock (Prestige models are commonly reported as 5 mm); use the wrench supplied with the guitar when you have it.
Rod adjusts inside the soundhole at the neck block with a 5 mm hex key (not the SC-13E / Modern Deluxe style models, which differ).
Most Taylors adjust at the headstock with a 1/4 in nut wrench; Big Baby and pre-2012 nylon-string models adjust inside the soundhole.

warnings: A truss rod wrench that only partly fits will round the nut; make sure it seats fully.

title: Loosen and remove strings safely (every bridge type)
summary: Taking all the strings off is sometimes necessary (cleaning, fretwork, hardware swaps) but each bridge reacts differently when tension disappears. Here is how to do it without whipping strings, losing parts or dropping a trem into its cavity.
tools: Wooden wedge or folded card (floating trems)

steps.title: Always slacken before cutting
steps.detail: Unwind every string until it is floppy before you cut it. A string cut at pitch snaps back and can cut skin or eyes.
steps.warn: Wear eye protection; never cut a string at full tension.

steps.title: Slacken evenly
steps.detail: Detune all strings a few turns each, working across the neck, rather than one string fully at a time. This keeps the neck and bridge evenly loaded as tension comes off.

steps.title: Fender-style floating trem
steps.detail: With the strings off, the springs pull the bridge back flat against the body. That is not harmful, but if you only want a string change, change one string at a time, or wedge a block behind the bridge (StewMac uses a wedge holding a 3/32 in gap) so the bridge stays where it was.

steps.title: Floyd Rose / Ibanez Edge
steps.detail: Unlock the nut pads first (3 mm). With all strings off, the springs pull the bridge into the cavity and it can move off its studs. Change one string at a time (Ibanez's advice), or put a block of wood under the back of the bridge in the rear cavity before slackening. Never take the springs off with the bridge under tension.

steps.title: Tune-o-matic and stopbar (Les Paul, SG, ES)
steps.detail: Both parts are held on only by string pressure. Before removing all strings, note the bridge orientation (intonation screws face the pickups) and tape the bridge and stopbar down with low-tack tape.

steps.title: Jazzmaster/Jaguar and Bigsby bridges
steps.detail: Floating bridges lift out of their posts; tape them or keep track of which way they face. Bigsby rollers and pins can drop; keep the tension bar and springs together.

steps.title: Acoustic (pin bridge)
steps.detail: Slacken all strings, then lift pins with the winder's notch. If a ball end has jammed, push the string into the body a little to free it.

steps.title: Classical
steps.detail: Unwind until loose, then untie at the bridge.

steps.title: Truss rod caution
steps.detail: With no strings, a neck that was set with tight relief may back-bow. That's normal and returns with tension; don't 'correct' the rod with strings off.

models.note: Strings come out through the back of the trem block; the block holes can hold broken ball ends.
Push strings out from the bridge toward the back of the body; ferrules stay in place.
Tape the tune-o-matic and stopbar; they fall off and scratch the top.
Block the bridge or change one string at a time.
Heavy strings carry high tension: slacken fully before removing.

warnings: Cut string ends are sharp; collect and dispose of them.
Floating trem springs store a lot of energy; never remove a spring under tension.

title: Multimeter basics for guitar work
summary: The three meter settings you'll actually use on a guitar (resistance, continuity, DC volts), how to read them, and what 'OL', zero and in-between readings mean.

specs.label: Resistance range for pickups
specs.value: 20 kΩ range (or auto) – most passive pickups read 5–17 kΩ

specs.label: Resistance range for pots
specs.value: The range just above the pot's value, e.g. 2 MΩ for 250k/500k/1M pots

specs.label: Good ground connection
specs.value: Reads close to 0.0 Ω

specs.label: Open circuit
specs.value: Shows 'OL' or '1' (over limit)

specs.label: 9 V battery
specs.value: Fresh reads 9 V or a little more; East UK says replace when it reads below 6 V while loaded

steps.title: Know the three settings
steps.detail: Ω (resistance) measures pickups, pots and ground paths. Continuity (the beep/diode symbol) beeps when two points are connected – handy for quick ground checks. DC volts (V with a straight line) checks 9 V batteries in active systems.

steps.title: Zero your leads
steps.detail: On the Ω setting, touch the probes together. You'll see a small reading (often 0.1–0.5 Ω) – that's the leads themselves; ignore it in later readings.

steps.title: Measure out of circuit when you can
steps.detail: Anything wired in parallel changes the reading. For a true value, lift one wire of the part you're testing. Seymour Duncan notes that an installed pickup must be desoldered for an exact reading; in the guitar you'll get a figure close to it.

steps.title: Don't touch both probe tips
steps.detail: Your body adds resistance in parallel, which matters when measuring pots and high-value parts. Use clip leads or hold only the insulated grips.

steps.title: Use resistance, not just the beeper, for grounds
steps.detail: A cracked or cold joint can still beep but read a few ohms or jump about. Fralin recommends checking grounds on the resistance setting: a good connection reads 0.0, an open one OL.

steps.title: Read the result
steps.detail: Near zero = connected (or shorted, if it's meant to be a coil). A sensible mid value = the part is intact. OL = open (broken wire, open coil, dead switch contact, worn pot track).

steps.title: Let things cool before measuring
steps.detail: Pickup resistance rises with temperature; Seymour Duncan warns a hot pickup (just soldered or potted) reads well above its room-temperature value.
