title: Soldering safety: fumes, lead and burns
summary: The short list of habits that keep soldering safe for you, your family and your guitar's finish.
tools: Fume extractor with carbon filter or a fan drawing fumes away

steps.title: Ventilate
steps.detail: The smoke you see is mostly burning rosin flux. It irritates eyes and airways and can cause or worsen asthma. Work with an extractor pulling the smoke away from your face, or a window open with a fan. Don't lean directly over the joint.

steps.title: Treat lead with respect
steps.detail: Leaded solder (60/40, 63/37) is safe to handle with basic hygiene: don't eat, drink or smoke at the bench, don't chew your nails, and wash your hands with soap and water when you finish and before eating. Keep the bench clean and wipe up solder dust and clippings. Lead-free solder avoids lead but needs a hotter iron.

steps.title: Prevent burns
steps.detail: Hold work with hemostats, clips or a holder, not your fingers. Always return the iron to its stand, and switch it off when done. Parts you just soldered stay hot for a while.

steps.title: Protect your eyes
steps.detail: Wear glasses when soldering and when clipping wire ends, which fly off with surprising speed. Solder can spit when a pump fires or flux pops.

steps.title: Protect the guitar
steps.detail: Lay a cloth or mat over the finish around the cavity. Nitrocellulose lacquer softens and marks instantly under a hot iron or molten solder.

steps.title: Batteries in active guitars
steps.detail: Unplug the cable (which disconnects most active systems) or remove the 9 V battery before working. Don't let 9 V terminals touch metal parts or each other; a shorted battery gets hot.

steps.title: Stay away from mains gear
steps.detail: Guitar circuits are low-voltage and safe to work on. Amplifiers and powered gear contain lethal voltages even when unplugged; leave those to a qualified tech.

warnings: Never use an open flame or a gas torch near the guitar or for heat-shrink.
Keep children and pets away from a hot iron and from solder scraps.
pro: Any repair inside an amplifier, powered speaker or other mains-powered device.

title: Desoldering: braid (wick) and pump
summary: How to remove old solder cleanly so you can lift a wire, swap a pot or switch, or redo a bad joint without damaging lugs or plastic parts.
tools: Spring-loaded desoldering pump or rubber bulb with a heat-resistant tip

steps.title: Add fresh solder first
steps.detail: Old joints often refuse to melt evenly because the flux is gone. Touch a little fresh rosin-core solder onto the joint; it melts the old metal faster and transfers heat better.

steps.title: Lift a single wire (quickest method)
steps.detail: When you only need one wire off, heat the joint from underneath the lug, and as soon as it melts, pull the wire out with hemostats while the iron is still on. Premier Guitar's switch-swap method uses exactly this, one wire at a time.

steps.title: Use the pump for bulk solder
steps.detail: Cock the plunger. Melt the whole joint until fully liquid, put the pump nozzle right next to it, and press the release while keeping the iron in place until the suction fires. Repeat if needed; let the part cool between attempts.

steps.title: Use braid to clean up
steps.detail: Lay fresh braid on the remaining solder, press the iron on top of the braid and wait for the solder to wick into the copper. Lift the iron and braid together (don't drag cold braid, it can tear lugs or pads). Snip off the used, solder-filled section before the next go.

steps.title: Clear the lug hole
steps.detail: For a clean re-solder, the hole in the lug should be open. A combination works best on stubborn lugs: pump for the bulk, braid for the last film.

steps.title: Inspect
steps.detail: Check plastic switch bodies and caps for heat damage, and that no stray solder blobs have bridged neighbouring lugs.

warnings: Repeated long heating can loosen lugs in plastic switch bodies and ruin cheap 'box' switches; work in short bursts.
Molten solder can flick when a pump fires; wear glasses.

title: Hook-up wire: cloth push-back, PVC and braided shielded
summary: What wire to use inside a guitar, how to prepare cloth push-back and vintage braided shielded wire, and how to keep a braid from shorting things out.
tools: Awl or a meter probe (to unpick braid)

specs.label: Gauge
specs.value: 22 AWG stranded is the standard guitar hook-up wire

specs.label: Gibson-style braided wire
specs.value: 22 AWG cloth-covered, 7 tinned strands inside a woven overwrap and braided shield

specs.label: Ground buss (optional)
specs.value: Bare solid 19 AWG wire, as used by Premier Guitar's Dirk Wacker

steps.title: Choose the wire
steps.detail: Cloth push-back wire (22 AWG stranded) is what most techs reach for: you simply push the cloth back to expose the conductor, it doesn't melt back from the iron like PVC, and it springs back over the joint. PVC-insulated stranded wire works just as well electrically but needs stripping and can shrink back when heated. Use stranded wire anywhere that moves (pickguard, control plate); solid wire is fine for a fixed ground buss.

steps.title: Use cloth push-back wire
steps.detail: Pinch the cloth about 1/2 in from the end and slide it back to expose 1/8 in or so of conductor. Tin, solder, then slide the cloth forward again so it butts up against the lug.

steps.title: Know when to use shielded wire
steps.detail: Braided shielded wire keeps long signal runs from picking up noise. Gibson used it for runs to and from the pickup selector, and on guitars without a selector for the run to the jack. The longest, most exposed run (for example the Les Paul selector-to-jack run) benefits most. The braid only shields if it is soldered to ground.

steps.title: Prepare braided wire to land on a pot
steps.detail: Roll the wire under light finger pressure on a tile or glass to loosen the braid. Grip the wire about 2 in from the end and work the braid back towards your fingers so it bunches, then push back the cotton insulation to expose the signal conductor. Pre-tin the braid and the pot casing, solder the braid to the casing (about 60 W), let it cool, then solder the conductor to its lug (25–30 W is plenty).

steps.title: Prepare braided wire for a jack or switch
steps.detail: Either unpick the braid strand by strand with an awl, starting at the tip and working down a few inches, then twist and tin the strands into a ground lead; or roll the braid back, expose about 2 in of conductor, and carefully snip the braid to length with small scissors. Vacuum up the fine strands so none fall into the pickup magnets or bridge lugs.

steps.title: Insulate the braid
steps.detail: A bare braid touching a hot lug will kill the signal. Sleeve it with heat-shrink, PVC or cotton tubing wherever it crosses other parts, especially the long switch-to-jack run in a Les Paul.

steps.title: Shielded pickup leads
steps.detail: On modern pickups with a 4-conductor lead plus bare shield, the bare wire must go to ground. Never leave it floating.

models.note: Traditional harnesses use braided shielded wire with the braid soldered to the pot casings as the pickup ground.
Cloth push-back wire is traditional; the pickguard or control-plate shielding does the screening.

warnings: Cotton braided wire absorbs moisture; Premier Guitar notes this raises resistance and dulls highs. Store it sealed; damp wire can be dried in a kitchen oven at moderate heat (never a microwave).

title: Solder a ground wire to the back of a pot
summary: Pot casings are big chunks of metal that soak up heat, so ground joints there are where most cold joints happen. How to prep the casing and get the solder to flow without cooking the pot.
tools: 40–60 W iron with a chisel or 1/8 in flat tip

specs.label: Iron
specs.value: 40 W or more works reliably; a 25 W iron often won't get a casing hot enough (Planet Z). Let a cheap iron warm up about 10 minutes first.

specs.label: Tip
specs.value: 1/8 in flat/chisel tip for casings; fine conical tips are for circuit boards

specs.label: Prep
specs.value: Scuff the plating with 100-grit sandpaper

steps.title: Pick the spot
steps.detail: Choose an area of the casing away from the lugs and away from where the casing folds over the body of the pot, with room for several wires to share the same puddle. If the pot is still installed, cover nearby wires and the finish.

steps.title: Scuff and clean
steps.detail: Rub a small patch about 1/4 in (6 mm) across with 100-grit paper to break through oil and plating, then wipe with alcohol. (Some people say the plating takes solder without sanding; scuffing does no harm and makes it more reliable.)

steps.title: Pre-tin the casing
steps.detail: Put a flat tip and a small bead of solder on the iron (the bead helps heat transfer), press it onto the patch and feed solder into the gap between tip and casing. Within a few seconds it should spread into a flat, shiny puddle. If it sits as a ball, the casing isn't hot enough yet.

steps.title: Add the wire
steps.detail: Tin the wire end, lay it into the puddle (hold it with hemostats), and re-heat until the puddle melts around it. Add a touch of fresh solder if needed. Remove the iron and hold still until it sets.

steps.title: Check it
steps.detail: The solder should be spread out and blended into the casing, not a domed blob sitting on top. Tug the wire. Then check continuity from the wire's other end to the casing with a meter (see [ef-multimeter-basics]).

warnings: Don't hold the iron on for minutes on end. If solder won't melt after 10–15 seconds, your iron is too small or the tip is dirty; fix that rather than cooking the pot.
Too much solder can run down inside the pot through the gaps; heat at an angle and keep the puddle small, removing excess with a pump.

models.note: Braided shield of each pickup lead and the ground buss wire land on the casings. Premier Guitar recommends roughly 60 W for braid-to-casing joints.
Do as much casing soldering as possible with the harness out of the body, before fishing it in through the f-hole.
The volume pot back is the usual central ground point for pickups, switch and trem claw wire.

title: Soldering for guitar electronics
time: 30 min practice, then 2–5 min per joint
summary: How to make shiny, strong solder joints on pots, switches, jacks and pickup leads: which iron and solder to buy, how hot to run it, how to tin, and how to spot and redo a bad joint.
tools: Soldering iron or station, 30–60 W (temperature-controlled is best)
Damp sponge or brass tip cleaner
Hemostats, crocodile clips or a 'helping hands' holder
parts: Rosin-core electronics solder: 60/40 or 63/37 tin/lead, about 0.032 in (0.8 mm); or lead-free (tin/silver/copper)

specs.label: Iron power
specs.value: 25–60 W pencil; 30–40 W is the usual guitar sweet spot (Premier Guitar); StewMac says an inexpensive 40 W pencil is fine. Under ~30 W is slow on pot casings.

specs.label: Tip temperature (leaded)
specs.value: About 350 °C (660 °F) for normal joints; go hotter only for big ground joints on pot casings or trem claws

specs.label: Melting point
specs.value: 63/37: 183 °C, melts and freezes at one temperature. 60/40: about 190 °C with a short 'mushy' range. Lead-free SAC305: 217–220 °C

specs.label: Solder diameter
specs.value: 0.032 in (0.8 mm) is the common choice; StewMac gives 0.032–0.062 in for guitar wiring

specs.label: Wire strip length
specs.value: 1/16–1/8 in (1.5–3 mm) exposed (StewMac)

specs.label: Heat-shrink length
specs.value: About three times the length of the bare section it covers (Premier Guitar)

steps.title: Set up a safe bench
steps.detail: Work at a clear table with good airflow or a small fume extractor, the iron in its stand, a damp (not dripping) sponge, and a fire-proof dish for solder scraps. Cover the guitar's finish with a cloth; a dropped iron or a flick of solder will mark lacquer instantly.
steps.warn: The tip runs at 350–400 °C. Always put the iron back in its stand, never on the bench.

steps.title: Tin a new tip
steps.detail: As soon as a new tip is hot, melt solder onto it so it is fully coated, wait a few seconds, wipe on the sponge and repeat a few times in the first minutes. A tinned tip is shiny and passes heat well. Wipe the tip before every joint and leave a thin film of solder on it when you put it down.

steps.title: Strip and tin the wire
steps.detail: Strip only 1/16–1/8 in of insulation. Twist the strands, touch the iron under them and feed a little solder in until the strands are just wetted. Don't build a blob; a thin coat is all you want. Also pre-tin the lug or the spot on the pot casing with a small amount of solder.

steps.title: Make a mechanical joint first
steps.detail: Hook the tinned wire through the lug hole or bend a small kink in it so it stays put by itself, or clamp it with hemostats. Never hold a wire with your fingers while soldering; you will either get burned or move the joint while it cools. If you need heat-shrink on this wire, slide it on now and park it well away from the iron.

steps.title: Heat the joint, then feed the solder
steps.detail: Put the tip against both the lug and the wire so they heat together. After a second or two, touch the solder to the joint (not to the iron) on the side away from the tip. It should melt and flow over the lug and into the strands. Use just enough to cover the joint and fill the lug hole.
steps.warn: Don't melt solder on the tip and carry it to the joint: the flux burns off on the way and the joint won't wet.

steps.title: Remove heat and keep still
steps.detail: As soon as the solder has flowed, take the solder away, then the iron, and hold the wire still for a few seconds while it freezes. 63/37 freezes at one temperature, which makes it more forgiving of a slight bump than 60/40. Don't blow on the joint to cool it; that can leave voids that corrode or crack later.

steps.title: Inspect every joint
steps.detail: A good joint is smooth, shiny and shaped like a small concave fillet; you can still see the outline of the wire. A cold or disturbed joint looks dull, grey, grainy or lumpy, or sits as a ball on top of the lug. Tug the wire gently. Re-heat any doubtful joint, add a touch of fresh solder (for new flux), and let it set again. Don't reuse old solder: clean it off first if a joint has been redone several times.

steps.title: Protect heat-sensitive parts
steps.detail: On capacitors, small switches and plastic 'box' switches, work quickly and clip a crocodile clip on the lead between the joint and the part as a heat sink. Plastic switches can melt and fail if a prong is cooked, especially after repeated re-soldering.

steps.title: Finish with heat-shrink
steps.detail: Slide the tubing over the joint once it is cool and shrink it with a heat gun, not a lighter or the side of the iron.

steps.title: Clean up
steps.detail: Turn the iron off, wipe and re-tin the tip, wash your hands, and vacuum up wire clippings so none fall into the pickups' magnets.

models.note: Ground joints on the trem claw and on pot casings need more heat; a flat 1/8 in chisel tip and the hotter end of your range help.
Braided shielded leads are soldered to the pot casings; Premier Guitar suggests about 60 W for the braid-to-casing joint and 25–30 W for signal-to-lug joints.
Most EMG systems use solderless plug-in harnesses; you may only need to solder the output jack.

warnings: Never use acid-core (plumbing) solder on electronics; it corrodes the joint.
Never use a soldering gun (transformer type) near pickups: its strong magnetic field can weaken the magnets.
Rosin flux fumes irritate the airways and can trigger asthma; use ventilation or an extractor. See [ef-soldering-safety].

title: Choose fret wire size and material
summary: Fret wire varies in width, height and alloy. The choice changes how the guitar feels (bends, chording, how hard you press), how long frets last, and what wear means for the next fret job.
tools: Digital caliper (to measure your existing frets)

specs.label: Dunlop 6230 (small vintage)
specs.value: 0.078 x 0.043 in; older Fender necks; lutherie.net calls it classic Martin wire

specs.label: Dunlop 6150 / Fender 'Medium Jumbo'
specs.value: Fender support: 0.103 x 0.046 in; Fender article and lutherie.net: 0.102 x 0.042 in

specs.label: Dunlop 6105 / Fender 'Narrow Tall'
specs.value: Fender support: 0.094 x 0.054 in; lutherie.net and Fender article: 0.090 x 0.055 in

specs.label: Tang
specs.value: Most of the above about 0.020–0.021 in tang (lutherie.net); StewMac wire is sized for a 0.023 in slot

steps.title: Measure what you have
steps.detail: Use a caliper to measure crown width across the fret base and height from the board to the top. Compare with the chart. Worn frets will read low; measure in an unworn spot near the board edge or high up the neck.

steps.title: Pick a height
steps.detail: Taller wire (0.050 in and up) makes bends easier and lets you press less, and gives more metal for future leveling, but a heavy hand can push notes sharp. Lower wire (under 0.040 in) feels closer to the wood and suits chordal players and tight fretting hands, but limits vibrato and usually needs a full refret once worn (StewMac). Fender says low frets suit players who like to feel the board; jumbo frets need less pressure.

steps.title: Pick a width
steps.detail: Wider wire wears more slowly and can be crowned rounder; narrow wire feels more precise and suits tight upper frets. StewMac calls medium width and medium height a good all-round default; bass usually gets extra-wide wire; mandolin and banjo get narrow, low wire.

steps.title: Pick an alloy
steps.detail: Nickel silver (usually 18% nickel): traditional, easy to work, wears fastest. Stainless steel: hardest wearing, slightly brighter, slicker for bends, but hard on tools and slower to install and dress; StewMac suggests trying it on one guitar first. EVO gold (Jescar): a gold-coloured nickel-free hypoallergenic alloy, between nickel silver and stainless in hardness; lutherie.net rates EVO 57110 as very durable and easier to work than stainless. Good for nickel allergies.

steps.title: Check slot fit
steps.detail: A refret may need tang thinning or crimping so the new wire fits the old slots without forcing the neck into backbow.

models.note: Vintage (6190-type) or small 6230-type wire.
Medium jumbo (6150-type) or narrow tall (6105-type) depending on series; check your model's spec page.
Medium-jumbo wire typical; StewMac chose its #0141 Cryowire as closest to late-1950s Gibson wire.
Jumbo (6100-type) or extra-jumbo common.
Wide and often taller wire to resist wear from heavy strings.
Narrow/medium wire common; Martin-style small wire (6230-type) on traditional builds.

warnings: Sizes vary slightly batch to batch; sources even disagree on the exact 6105 and 6150 numbers.
Stainless is noticeably harder to file; budget for more labour if a tech does it.

title: Polish frets during a string change
summary: Polishing removes tarnish and fine scratches so bends feel smooth and strings slide cleanly. It removes almost no metal, so it is safe to do whenever the strings are off.
tools: Low-tack tape or a steel/brass fretboard guard
Abrasives: Scotch-Brite pads (fine/medium) or 3M polishing papers, Micro-Mesh, Fret Erasers or 0000 steel wool
Fretboard oil for unfinished boards only
Small vacuum or magnet wrapped in tape

specs.label: Starting grit
specs.value: Light tarnish 1000–1500; heavier scratches 600–800, then finer (StewMac)

specs.label: Micro-Mesh example
specs.value: 2400, 4000, 12000 on a touch-up stick

steps.title: Strings off, pickups covered
steps.detail: Remove the strings. Tape over pickups (or plug the soundhole) if you will use steel wool; its fibres stick to magnets and get into pots.

steps.title: Protect the board
steps.detail: Maple (lacquered) boards always need protection: clean them first so tape sticks, then use low-tack tape between frets or a metal guard. Rosewood/ebony are more forgiving, but if you polish across the frets (not along the grain), protect them too or you leave cross-grain scratches.

steps.title: Polish each fret
steps.detail: Wrap the abrasive around something soft so it follows the crown. Use light pressure and either move along the fret following the string path, or rub across the width of the fret with small curved strokes (StewMac says across-the-fret polishing gives a smoother bend feel). Step through finer grits, wiping between each, until the shine evens out.

steps.title: Optional buff
steps.detail: A little metal polish on a leather or cloth pad gives a mirror finish. Keep it off the wood.

steps.title: Clean and condition
steps.detail: Vacuum or pick up filings with a taped magnet, peel tape slowly, wipe the board with naphtha if grimy, oil an unfinished rosewood/ebony board lightly (see [fn-fretboard-care]) and restring.

models.note: No oil; tape every gap.
Use a metal fret guard rather than tape; tape can lift chippy old lacquer.
Stay shiny far longer; usually need only a wipe.

warnings: Avoid power buffing with a Dremel; it can groove or overheat frets and burn finish.
Do not sand aggressively at every change; it shortens fret life.

title: Nut materials, locking and roller nuts, and zero frets
time: 15 min (reading); 1–2 h to replace a zero fret
summary: Bone, TUSQ, graphite, brass, plastic, roller and locking nuts all behave differently, and some guitars use a zero fret to set open-string height. This guide helps choose, and explains how to replace a zero fret.
tools: For a zero fret: soldering iron with a notched tip, flush-cut end nippers, fret bender, fretting hammer, thin super glue, small flat file, gauged nut files, crowning file, action gauge

specs.label: Zero-fret open-string clearance at the 1st fret
specs.value: About 1/64 in under the high E and 2/64 in under the low E (Premier Guitar)

specs.label: Zero-fret wire example
specs.value: Original Teisco 0.078 x 0.040 in replaced with 0.078 x 0.050 in Jescar to match taller new frets (Premier Guitar)

specs.label: Floyd Rose locking nut screws
specs.value: 3 mm hex (PRS support, locking-nut bridges)

steps.title: Bone
steps.detail: The traditional choice. Hard, dense, good tone, and it can be polished slippery. StewMac prefers unbleached bone. Needs careful lubrication on tremolo guitars.

steps.title: Synthetic (TUSQ and similar)
steps.detail: Consistent, self-lubricating synthetics made to replace bone; pre-slotted versions are what StewMac recommends for beginners. They fit quickly (Dan Erlewine fitted a pre-shaped TUSQ nut in under 30 minutes) and help tuning on tremolo guitars.

steps.title: Graphite
steps.detail: Slippery, good for vibrato guitars; dark colour; softer than bone so slots can wear faster under heavy strings.

steps.title: Brass and other metals
steps.detail: Very hard-wearing and bright-sounding; harder to file and may bind if slots are not polished. Mostly a 1970s/80s look.

steps.title: Plastic
steps.detail: Cheap and quick; soft plastic nuts wear and grip strings, and Gene Imbody's advice is to replace soft plastic rather than reshape it. Fine on budget guitars (StewMac's Dan Erlewine keeps plastic nuts for quick, low-cost jobs).

steps.title: Roller nuts
steps.detail: Small bearings under each string let the string roll rather than slide, reducing tremolo return-to-pitch problems. They need the correct mounting for your neck and add cost.

steps.title: Locking nuts (Floyd Rose type)
steps.detail: Clamp the strings at the nut so a double-locking tremolo stays in tune; height is set with shims under the nut and the strings are fine-tuned at the bridge. Tighten pads just snug with a 3 mm hex key; overtightening crushes strings.

steps.title: Zero fret: what it does
steps.detail: A fret placed where the nut would be. It sets open-string height (like a fretted note), and the nut behind it only spaces the strings. Open strings then sound more like fretted ones.

steps.title: Replacing a zero fret
steps.detail: Tune up and record action and relief, and correct relief first. Remove strings. Heat the zero fret with a soldering iron tip with a notch filed in it, oiling around the fret with a Q-tip; when the oil bubbles, gently pry (do not pull) the fret out with flush cutters while heating. Clean the slot. Bend new wire slightly rounder than the board, cut about 1/4 in long, tap the ends in then the centre, wick thin super glue, trim flush and file the ends.

steps.title: Set zero-fret height
steps.detail: Restring and measure the gap from the top of the 1st fret to the bottom of the open strings: target about 1/64 in high E and 2/64 in low E. If the trebles are too high, cut shallow guide slots in the zero fret with nut files, then file the top down until the slots nearly vanish, and recrown it so every string touches the peak.

models.note: Synthetic, graphite or roller nuts reduce string hang-ups; bone with lubricant also works.
Locking nut; shim to height.

models.model: Gretsch, Teisco, some vintage European guitars
models.note: Zero frets are common.
Brass and bone both popular; slot wear from heavy strings is the main concern.

warnings: Stainless fret wire is very hard on tools if used for a zero fret.

title: Nut problems: binding, buzzing, high action at the nut
summary: The nut sets how high the open strings sit over the 1st fret, spaces the strings, and is where the open string length ends. Most tuning pings, open-string buzz and hard-to-play first-position chords trace back to the nut. Diagnose it, lubricate it, open up slots for heavier strings, or decide it needs replacing.
symptoms: Tuning pings or sticks (a 'ping' as the string jumps through the slot) and drifts sharp after bends
Open strings buzz but fretted notes are clean (slot too low or too wide)
First-position chords feel stiff and play sharp (slots too high)
Sitar-like zing on an open string (string not leaving the slot at the front edge)
Strings rattle side to side or slip out of their slots

causes.cause: Slot too tight for the string gauge
causes.check: Ping when tuning; string binds; new heavier set just fitted
causes.fix: Open the slot with a gauged nut file (steps below).

causes.cause: Slot too high
causes.check: Fret the string between frets 2 and 3: gap over the 1st fret is more than a hair
causes.fix: Lower the slot, see [fn-nut-make-bone] step on slot depth.

causes.cause: Slot too low
causes.check: String touches the 1st fret when fretted between 2 and 3; open string buzzes
causes.fix: See [fn-nut-slot-too-low].

causes.cause: Slot angle wrong / string leaving from the back
causes.check: Sitar buzz; string touches the nut's back edge first
causes.fix: Re-file the slot floor to slope down toward the headstock so the string's contact point is the front edge.

causes.cause: Slot too wide or worn
causes.check: String moves side to side
causes.fix: Small amounts: fill and re-cut ([fn-nut-slot-too-low]); otherwise replace the nut.

causes.cause: Cheap soft plastic nut
causes.check: Slots worn, grooved or crushed
causes.fix: Replace with bone or a synthetic like TUSQ ([fn-nut-make-bone], [fn-zero-fret-nut-types]).

tools: Gauged nut files (or a set matched to your strings)
Nut lubricant (graphite from a soft pencil, a commercial nut lube, or a self-lubricating fill powder)
String lifter or a spare pick to lift strings out of slots

specs.label: Slot width
specs.value: Match the string gauge; up to about 0.004 in oversize is no problem, 1–2 thousandths under is workable but not ideal (StewMac, Gene)

specs.label: Slot depth
specs.value: Wound strings show about half their diameter above the nut; plain strings just barely felt above it (StewMac). Frets.com: a little more than half buried

specs.label: Height at the 1st fret, quick check
specs.value: Capo behind the 1st fret: the gap over the 2nd fret is the reference; with capo off the open-string gap over the 1st fret should be about 1–2 times that (StewMac, Gene)

steps.title: Check nut height string by string
steps.detail: Tune to pitch. Fret each string between the 2nd and 3rd frets and look at the gap over the 1st fret (Frank Ford's method). You want a tiny gap, about the thickness of a hair; tap the string over the 1st fret and you should hear a faint click. No gap means the slot is too low; a big gap means it is too high. Measured with feeler gauges at the 1st fret (open string), StewMac's pro targets are roughly 0.020 in on the low E graduating down to about 0.010 in on the high E; set relief and saddle height first, because both affect this.

steps.title: Check for binding
steps.detail: Tune a string slowly up and down. Pings, jumps, or a note that creeps sharp after a bend mean the slot is grabbing. Look at the slot: it should be smooth, only as wide as the string, and slope down toward the headstock.

steps.title: Lubricate
steps.detail: Loosen the string, lift it out of the slot, and rub graphite from a soft pencil (or a nut lubricant) into the slot. Drop the string back in and retune. Do this at every string change on guitars with tremolos.

steps.title: Opening slots for heavier strings or drop tunings
steps.detail: A heavier set (for example going from 9s to 11s, or a 56 low E for drop tunings) needs wider slots. Lay tape on the headstock and fretboard face next to the nut. Use a nut file the same size as the new string or one size up (not more than about 0.004 in over), and file only the slot WALLS, tilting the file down toward the headstock, without deepening the floor. Check by laying the string in: it should drop to the bottom and slide freely.
steps.warn: A file one size too big that touches the floor will lower the slot and cause buzz; take two strokes, test, repeat.

steps.title: Fix the take-off angle if needed
steps.detail: If a string buzzes like a sitar, the slot floor is probably flat or sloping the wrong way. File the floor from the back toward the front, keeping the front edge untouched, so the floor angles down toward the tuners. Angle the file between the headstock angle and the fretboard plane (Frets.com).

steps.title: Decide whether to replace
steps.detail: Replace the nut if slots are too wide (rattle), cracked, grossly too low on several strings, the nut is soft plastic, or you are changing string spacing.

models.note: Low break angle makes nut binding and string-tree drag common; a shallower slot angle filed to suit each post works best (StewMac). Staggered tuners or a string tree help the angle.
The D and G strings bend toward their posts on 3-a-side heads; file those slots angled toward the post on one edge to stop binding (StewMac).
Bass strings sit gradually higher at the nut than treble; StewMac's bass guide used slot files of 0.042–0.085 in.
Strings tie at the headstock slots; nut slots are usually deeper and more rounded.
Clamping pads set height; shims under the nut adjust it. See [fn-zero-fret-nut-types].

warnings: Filing nut slots is a one-way street: you can always go deeper, never higher without a repair.
pro: If several slots are too low or the nut is cracked, a new nut is usually quicker and better than repairs.

title: Sharp or sprouting fret ends
summary: When a fretboard dries out it shrinks across its width, but the metal frets do not, so the ends poke out past the edge and catch your hand. Rehumidify first, then file the ends flush and round them.
symptoms: Fret ends scratch your hand when sliding up and down the neck
Little ridges you can feel along the edge of the board
Worse in winter or after the heating comes on

causes.cause: Low humidity shrinking the fretboard
causes.check: Hygrometer reads in the 30s or low 40s %RH; problem appeared seasonally
causes.fix: Rehumidify to about 40–50% RH and recheck after a week or two; mild sprout can recede.

causes.cause: Fret ends never beveled properly at the factory
causes.check: Ends are square or sharp even in normal humidity
causes.fix: Bevel and dress (steps below).

causes.cause: Fret end lifting
causes.check: End rises above the board
causes.fix: Glue it down first, see [fn-fret-reseat-replace].

tools: Fret beveling file (a smooth single-cut mill file with safe edges; StewMac's is fixed at 35°) or a large 3-corner/cant file

specs.label: Bevel angle
specs.value: StewMac written guide: 30–35°; StewMac video: 35–45°; never shallower than about 30° or strings fall off the edge

specs.label: Safe humidity
specs.value: 45–55% RH for most instruments; start preparing when readings drop to the mid-to-low 40s

steps.title: Humidify first
steps.detail: Bring the guitar back to about 40–50% relative humidity (room humidifier, or case humidifier for acoustics) and wait. If sprout shrinks back, you may only need light dressing.

steps.title: Protect the guitar
steps.detail: On a bolt-on, removing the neck makes this easier and protects the body. Otherwise mask the body near the neck with index cards and low-tack tape. Masking along the board edge is optional for beveling (tape leaves a tiny edge equal to its thickness) but use it on finished maple if you are nervous.

steps.title: Bevel the ends flush
steps.detail: Hold the beveling file at roughly 35° with its safe edge riding on the board, and push it in long, even strokes along the whole side of the neck (mill files cut on the push stroke only). Stop as soon as you hear the sound change: that is the file reaching the finish. You only want to cut metal. Clean the file often so grit does not scratch frets or finish.
steps.warn: Avoid coarse cross-cut or diamond files here; StewMac says they are too aggressive and damage the finish.

steps.title: Round each end
steps.detail: Tape or guard the board so only the fret end shows. With the end dressing file flat side down, take a few light strokes to soften the sharp corner left by beveling; then with the rounded side, roll along the arch of the fret end. The ends should feel smooth but still look crisp; StewMac's warning is not to overdo it.

steps.title: Polish
steps.detail: Polish the ends with Micro-Mesh (1500 up to 12000) or 0000 steel wool. Tape over pickups or plug the soundhole first if using steel wool.

steps.title: Prevent it coming back
steps.detail: Keep a hygrometer in the room or case; in winter keep the guitar cased when not playing.

models.note: File only the metal; the board edge is lacquered and shows file marks.
Frets usually sit inside the binding, so sprout is rare; if a fret end lifts over binding, glue it rather than filing the binding.
StewMac used a 6 in leveling file then a coarse diamond stone, with a capo at the nut as a safety stop.

warnings: Sharp fret ends can cut you; handle the neck carefully until done.
Steel wool sheds magnetic fibres that cling to pickups.

title: Fix a nut slot cut too low
summary: If one or two slots were filed too deep, the open string buzzes on the 1st fret. You can raise the slot by filling it (bone dust or baking soda with thin super glue, or a commercial nut fill powder) and re-cutting, or raise the whole nut with a shim.
symptoms: One open string buzzes, fretted notes on that string are clean
Fretting between the 2nd and 3rd frets, the string already touches the 1st fret
tools: Bone dust filed from an old nut (or baking soda)
Feather file / smooth file, gauged nut files, razor saw
For a shim: thin hardwood veneer, bone or plastic shim stock

steps.title: Confirm it is the nut
steps.detail: Fret the string between the 2nd and 3rd frets; if it touches the 1st fret, the slot is too low. Check relief first: too little relief can mimic a low nut.

steps.title: Clean the slot
steps.detail: Remove the string from the slot. Clean the slot with acetone and file lightly until you see clean bone; grease and grime stop the repair sticking (StewMac).

steps.title: Mask and fill
steps.detail: Tape around the slot (slip something thin under the other strings to hold the tape down). Pack fine bone dust (or baking soda) into the slot with a spatula, then touch thin super glue to the edge so it wicks in. Add more dust and glue until the slot is overfilled. Let it harden (a minute or two on bone).
steps.warn: Thin super glue runs everywhere; keep the nozzle away from the fretboard and tape.

steps.title: Re-cut
steps.detail: Shape the fill flush with the nut top, press the string into it to mark its position, start the slot with a feather file and saw, then bring it to height with a gauged nut file, checking the 1st-fret gap as in [fn-nut-problems]. Smooth with 320 grit.

steps.title: Or shim the whole nut
steps.detail: If several slots are low, tap the nut out, glue a thin shim of hardwood veneer or bone to its base (sand it flat), refit, and re-dress any slots that are now too high. This raises every string equally.

steps.title: Know the limits
steps.detail: StewMac's Gene Imbody considers the super glue plus dust method temporary and prone to binding; StewMac offers a self-lubricating fill powder with brush-on accelerator as a harder-wearing alternative. If the nut is plastic, cracked, or several slots are bad, replace it.

models.note: The fill method works on some plastics but not all.
Fill adheres less reliably; replacing the nut is usually better.
Low slots on big strings are common after string changes to heavier gauges; shim or replace.

warnings: Ventilate when using super glue and accelerator; spraying accelerator too early can foam the glue white (Premier Guitar).
pro: If more than two slots are low, a new nut costs little and fixes it properly.

title: Reseat a high or loose fret, or replace one fret
summary: A single fret that has lifted (often at one end) causes buzz at one spot. Press it back down and wick in thin super glue. If a fret is badly worn, kinked or damaged, pull just that one and install a new piece of matching wire.
symptoms: Buzz at one fret position only
A fret end you can slide paper under
A fret rocker rocks on one fret
Fret pushes down when pressed, then springs back
tools: Fret press (StewMac Jaws/Jaws2 with radiused brass insert) or radius block and clamp
Thin (water-thin, #10) super glue and pipette or whip tip
Paste wax and Q-tips, paper towels
For replacement: soldering iron, fret puller (flush-ground end nippers), fret bender, fret cutter, fret end file, beveling file
parts: Fret wire matching the original width and height (see [fn-fret-wire-choice])

specs.label: Clamp time with radius block
specs.value: 5–10 min with plain glue cure (StewMac)

specs.label: Clamp time with accelerator
specs.value: About 1 min more after accelerator (StewMac)

specs.label: StewMac fret slot
specs.value: Wire sized for a 0.023 in slot

steps.title: Find the culprit
steps.detail: Slide a fret rocker across each group of three frets. Look closely at the suspect fret under a bright light; you should not be able to fit paper under it. Press it: if it moves down and back up, it is loose. One loose fret usually means others are loose, so check them all.

steps.title: Seat it first, never file it first
steps.detail: Filing a loose fret only lowers it and it pops up again later. A couple of taps with a deadblow hammer may seat it; a fret press is safer because it presses rather than shocks the neck.

steps.title: Wax around the fret
steps.detail: Rub paste wax on the board on both sides of the fret with a Q-tip. Any glue that runs onto the wood will then wipe off.

steps.title: Glue and clamp
steps.detail: Press the fret down with a fret press (or clamp a radius block over it). Run a thin bead of thin super glue along both sides of the fret; capillary action pulls it into the slot. Wipe the excess immediately with a paper towel. Brush or drip accelerator on, and keep it clamped about another minute (or 5–10 minutes without accelerator).
steps.warn: Work quickly and ventilate; super glue fumes are irritating, and heated CA fumes should not be breathed.

steps.title: Check and level
steps.detail: Recheck with the fret rocker. If it is now level with its neighbours you are done; if slightly high, spot-level just that fret with a small file or a short beam and re-crown it.

steps.title: Replacing one fret: remove it
steps.detail: Heat the fret along its length with a soldering iron (protect the board around it) to soften glue, then slide the flush-ground jaws of a fret puller under one end and rock it out gradually, working along the fret. Go slowly; rosewood and ebony chip easily. Glue down any chip immediately.

steps.title: Replacing one fret: install new wire
steps.detail: Clean the slot. Bend the new wire to slightly tighter than the board radius so the ends do not spring up. Cut it a little long, tap the ends in first, then press or hammer it home from the centre outward. Wick in thin glue as above, trim the ends flush, bevel at the same angle as the others, dress the ends, then level it to its neighbours and crown and polish.

models.note: New frets need their tangs nipped back so the crown sits over the binding; see [fn-refret-bound].
Hammering over the soundboard can crack bracing; use a press with a soundhole caul (Jaws2).
Heat and pulling can chip lacquer; score the finish along the fret first.

warnings: Do not hammer with a steel carpenter's hammer; it kinks and dents frets.
Heated CA glue releases irritating fumes; ventilate.
pro: If several frets are loose across the neck, or the slots are worn wide, consider a full refret.

title: Strings, tension and nut slots for low B and F#
time: 30 min to choose; 1 h for nut slot work
summary: Choosing gauges that keep the low B or F# tight without making the high strings stiff, and making sure the nut and hardware actually take the heavy low string.
tools: Nut slot files sized to your strings
parts: Nut Rescue Powder or similar, plus thin super glue (for overcut slots)

specs.label: Music Man Petrucci 7
specs.value: 10-46 plus .056 low B

specs.label: Tuning down (Music Man)
specs.value: About one gauge step heavier per half step down

specs.label: Nut slot width (StewMac)
specs.value: Close fit; up to about .004 in oversize is acceptable

specs.label: Nut slot depth, wound strings (StewMac)
specs.value: About half the string's diameter above the nut

specs.label: Feeler-gauge slot depth method (StewMac)
specs.value: Fret height plus .005-.010 in, stepping up about .002 in toward the bass side

specs.label: Strandberg Rev 7 tuner/string-lock bore
specs.value: 2.5 mm (about .1 in); many .080 in strings have double-wound ball ends that will not fit

steps.title: Match the low string to the scale
steps.detail: A longer scale makes the same gauge tighter. That is why multiscale and 27-28 in instruments can use relatively light low strings (Strandberg's 8-string uses .084 for F# at 28 in), and why Ormsby suggests some players can drop to a lighter set on a multiscale. On a standard 25.5 in 7-string, a .056-.064 low B is typical of factory sets (Music Man .056, Strandberg .064 at 26.25 in).

steps.title: Balance the set
steps.detail: Use a manufacturer's tension calculator or tension chart for your scale and tuning. Aim for the low strings to feel about as firm as the middle strings. Buying the low string singly lets you fine-tune the feel.

steps.title: Check the hardware will take it
steps.detail: Measure the bridge holes, tuner bores and locks. Heavy low strings often have a double-wound section at the ball end that is fatter than the string - Strandberg recommends tapered ball ends (for example NYXL) for its 2.5 mm Rev 7 tuners.

steps.title: Check the nut slots
steps.detail: Fit the strings and tune. Signs of a tight slot: the string pings when tuning, sticks, or the open note is dull. Signs of a too-wide slot: rattle or sideways movement. Music Man advises having slots widened by a tech when you go heavier, to avoid cracking the nut.

steps.title: Widen a slot (careful DIY)
steps.detail: Tape the headstock around the nut. Use a file a few thousandths wider than the string, follow the existing slot's back angle (sloping down toward the headstock), and do not lower the front edge. StewMac's rule: the slot can be up to about .004 in oversize.

steps.title: Check slot depth
steps.detail: StewMac's quick check: capo at the 1st fret and note the gap between the string and the 2nd fret; with the capo off, the gap over the 1st fret should be roughly one to two times that. Or use StewMac's feeler method - fret height plus .005-.010 in, a little more on the bass side. The wound string should sit with roughly half its diameter above the nut.

steps.title: If you overcut
steps.detail: Fill the slot with Nut Rescue Powder and thin super glue, then recut - or replace the nut.

warnings: Wear eye protection when snipping heavy strings.
Super glue and accelerator fumes: ventilate.
pro: Cutting a new nut for an 8-string, or deepening slots by more than a hair, is best left to a tech.

title: Level, crown and polish frets
summary: A fret level takes every fret down to the same plane so no single fret causes buzz, then the flattened tops are re-rounded (crowned) and polished. Do it when frets have worn grooves under the strings, or one or two high frets cause buzz that a setup cannot cure.
symptoms: Dents or flat spots under the strings in the first few frets
A note buzzes or 'frets out' on bends at one spot
Notes sound sour because the string contacts a wide flat fret top
You cannot get low action without buzz even with correct relief
tools: Leveling beam or bar, 18–24 in (aluminium radius beam or StewMac Fretbar)
Self-adhesive sandpaper: 320 and 400 grit for leveling (Premier Guitar used 400 then 1500)
Notched straightedge (reads the board, not the frets)
Fret rocker (short straightedge for checking 3 frets at a time)
Crowning file to suit fret width (Z-file, 3-in-1 file, diamond crowning file or 3-corner file)
Low-tack masking tape or metal fretboard guards
Polishing papers/Micro-Mesh (400 through 1200–12000), 0000 steel wool or Scotch-Brite
Neck rest or sand bag; truss rod wrench

specs.label: Too low to level
specs.value: Frets under about 0.038 in tall are too low to recrown after leveling and need replacing (Premier Guitar)

specs.label: Max material to remove
specs.value: Aim for under about 0.008–0.010 in total, and under roughly 20% of fret height (StewMac); standard frets are about 0.040–0.050 in tall

specs.label: Crown target
specs.value: A thin line of untouched metal along the top of each fret, about the width of a high E string

specs.label: Normal fall-away
specs.value: On acoustics the last 5–8 frets over the body may show no sanding marks, which is normal (Premier Guitar)

steps.title: Check fret height and seating
steps.detail: Remove the strings. Measure fret height with a caliper resting on the board. If the worn frets are already near 0.038 in, plan a refret instead. Under bright light, look for frets lifted at the ends; press or tap them down and glue them first (see [fn-fret-reseat-replace]). Leveling a loose fret is pointless: it pushes down under the beam and springs back.

steps.title: Make the neck straight
steps.detail: Support the neck on a neck rest. Adjust the truss rod until the board is as straight as possible, checked with a notched straightedge (it sits on the wood between the frets). Do not go into backbow. Some pros (StewMac) prefer to level with the guitar in playing position or under string tension using an understring leveler, because necks behave differently with strings on.

steps.title: Mask and mark
steps.detail: Tape off the fretboard between frets (essential on finished maple) and cover the pickups if you will use steel wool later. Colour every fret top with the marker so you can see exactly where the beam touches.

steps.title: Level
steps.detail: With 320 or 400 grit on the beam, make light, even passes along the length of the neck, keeping the beam moving and spread across the frets. Follow the radius by rolling slightly across the board, or use a radiused beam. Stop and look often: when every fret shows a thin shiny line through the marker, they are level. Frets that still show marker in the middle are low; keep going only if a few strokes will catch them.
steps.warn: Do not press down in one spot. Heavy pressure at the ends of the board (where the neck is unsupported) takes more metal there.

steps.title: Check with a fret rocker
steps.detail: Rock a short straightedge across every group of three frets, at the bass side, middle and treble side. If it rocks, the middle fret is high; touch it up.

steps.title: Re-mark and crown
steps.detail: Colour the fret tops again. Using the crowning file that matches your fret width, file from the sides up toward the top so the shiny flat gets narrower, leaving a thin marker line in the centre. Use forward strokes and clean the file with a file brush every few passes. Stop as soon as the flat is a thin line; do not file the very top.

steps.title: Dress the ends
steps.detail: Round over the fret ends lightly with the end dressing file so they are smooth to the hand (see [fn-fret-ends-sprout]).

steps.title: Polish
steps.detail: Work through progressively finer grits, removing the scratches of each before moving on: StewMac's sequence is 400, 600, 800, 1000, 1200 on a foam block; for a mirror finish continue with Micro-Mesh to 8000–12000. Premier Guitar finishes with a pass of 1500 grit on the beam, first along the neck to confirm level and then across to clean up, then 0000 steel wool.

steps.title: Clean up and restring
steps.detail: Lightly scrape any marker or file marks off the board with a razor blade (no pressure), wipe with naphtha, oil a rosewood or ebony board if it is dry, restring and set up.

models.note: Must be masked fret by fret; abrasives cut through the board's lacquer instantly.
Fall-away over the body is normal; if you are only sanding the last frets and not the middle, the rod may be too loose or the board may have a kick-up, which is pro territory (Premier Guitar).
Much harder; wear diamond files quickly and take longer to level and polish.
Same process; a longer beam (24 in) helps on a 34 in scale.

warnings: Fret leveling is irreversible: every pass shortens the frets' life.
Steel wool fibres stick to pickup magnets; tape the pickups and vacuum as you go.
Tools can cost more than paying a pro for one guitar.
pro: If the frets are very low, if one area needs much more removal than the rest (a hump or kick-up in the board), or the neck will not get straight, have a pro do a refret or plane the board instead.

title: Make a bone nut from a blank
summary: A well-cut bone nut improves tuning stability, open-string tone and first-position playability. This walks through removing the old nut, shaping a blank, laying out string spacing, cutting slots to depth, and gluing it in.
tools: Bone nut blank (unbleached preferred) or semi-shaped/slotted blank
Block of hardwood or steel and a small hammer
Flat file, 120–320 grit paper on a flat surface
Nut slotting files for each gauge
Micro-Mesh or 220–1200 grit paper, polishing compound
Titebond, or a drop of shellac
parts: Bone nut blank sized close to your nut slot

specs.label: First slot depth target
specs.value: Slot bottoms 0.030 in above fret height to start, following the board radius (StewMac)

specs.label: Final 1st-fret clearance (pro)
specs.value: About 0.020 in under the low E down to about 0.010 in under the high E, graduated (StewMac)

specs.label: Feeler gauge method
specs.value: Fret height + 0.005–0.010 in, adding about 0.002 in per string toward the bass (StewMac/Erlewine)

specs.label: Alternative example
specs.value: StewMac replacement neck: 0.024 in gap for wound strings, 0.020 in for plain

specs.label: Nut top height
specs.value: About half the diameter of the thickest string above the slot bottom, leave a little extra to start

specs.label: Slot ramp
specs.value: As shallow as 6°, no steeper than 12–15° (or match the headstock angle)

specs.label: String spacing
specs.value: Outer E strings about 1/8 in in from the board edge (StewMac rule) or about 1/16 in in from the bevelled fret ends at the 1st fret; spaces between strings grow by 0.004 in toward the bass (proportional spacing)

specs.label: Common nut widths (factory specs)
specs.value: Many Fenders 1.650 in (42 mm), many American-made Fenders 1.685 in (42.8 mm), Gibson typically about 1.695 in (43 mm): check your model's spec sheet and measure the slot

steps.title: Prepare the neck
steps.detail: Set the neck straight (truss rod) and set saddle height first. Slacken and remove the strings.

steps.title: Remove the old nut
steps.detail: Score the finish around the nut with a sharp knife so lacquer does not chip. Place a hardwood or steel block against the nut and tap gently, alternating from front and back, until it breaks free. A stuck nut can be sawn lengthwise (not to the bottom) and collapsed inward with pliers. On Fenders, StewMac warns that forcing a stubborn nut can break off the end of the fretboard; take it to a shop if it will not come out easily.

steps.title: Clean the slot
steps.detail: Scrape old glue off the slot sides and floor, keeping it square and without removing wood or chipping the finish edge. Note whether the slot floor is flat or curved (Fender vintage and US necks often have a radiused floor; many imports are flat).

steps.title: Fit the blank
steps.detail: Sand the bottom and sides flat on paper laid on a flat surface (120–150 grit, then 220, then 320 for the final slide-in fit). The blank should slide into the slot snugly without force. Leave the ends long for now. If the slot floor is curved, sand the bottom to match (you can stick sandpaper to the fretboard and sand the nut on it).

steps.title: Mark the height
steps.detail: Measure fret height with a straightedge across two frets and feeler gauges. Mark the nut to leave plenty above that (about 0.030 in above fret height for the slot bottoms plus half the thickest string for the top), and file the top down to roughly that line, following the radius.

steps.title: Lay out string spacing
steps.detail: Mark the two E strings first (about 1/8 in in from each fretboard edge, or match the old nut). Use a proportional spacing rule so each space grows by 0.004 in toward the bass; equal centre-to-centre spacing looks uneven because the strings are different thicknesses. Scribe the positions.

steps.title: Start the slots
steps.detail: With the nut in place, start each slot shallow with a 0.010 in saw, angled down toward the headstock.

steps.title: Cut the slots to depth
steps.detail: Use the correct gauged file for each string. Keep the file angled down toward the headstock so the string touches only the front edge. Stack feeler gauges equal to your target (fret height plus clearance), hold them on the fretboard against the nut face, and file until the file just touches the gauges. Then fine-tune each string with the strings on, checking the 1st-fret gap. As slots deepen, file the top of the nut down so the strings sit about half to two-thirds in the slot.
steps.warn: Go slowly near the target. A string can drop suddenly as the slot floor clears, and a slot cut too deep means starting again or a fill repair.

steps.title: Shape and polish
steps.detail: Mark the overhang, remove the nut, trim the ends with a hacksaw and file flush with the neck edges, round the top edges, then sand up through 220 to 1200 grit and buff with polishing compound.

steps.title: Glue it in
steps.detail: Use two or three small drops of Titebond on the floor (or a little shellac so it comes out easily next time). Restring, tune to pitch, slide the nut to align the strings with the fretboard edges while the glue is wet, and leave strings on as the clamp for about an hour.

models.note: Slot floor follows the fretboard radius on vintage and US models (7.25 to 12 in). File slots with a shallow back angle suited to each post. A string tree affects the B/E (and D/G) angle.
Angled headstock (about 17°); follow that angle with the slot floor. Angle the D and G slot exits toward their posts.
PRS uses its own nut material on many models; same layout principles.
Acoustics generally want a little more nut clearance than electrics. Martin nuts can be flat or angled on the bottom; match the old one.
Wider spacing; nut glued lightly; strings break steeply into slotted headstocks.
Bigger files (about 0.045–0.110 in); add clearance for the wider string vibration.

warnings: Bone dust smells and is an irritant; work with a dust mask and ventilation.
Bleached bone is softer than unbleached (StewMac's preference is unbleached).
pro: If you only need one nut, a pre-slotted bone or TUSQ nut fitted carefully is a good middle ground. Pros can cut a nut in under an hour with the right files.

title: Full refret on a rosewood or ebony board
summary: When frets are too low to level again, all of them come out, the board is cleaned up and trued, and new wire goes in. Unfinished rosewood, ebony and similar boards are the easiest case.
tools: Fret slot cleaning saw or hook
Fret slot depth gauge, feeler gauges
Radius blocks or radiused beam, notched straightedge
Fret bender, fret cutter, tang nippers
Fret press (arbor press with radiused cauls, or Jaws) and/or fret hammer
Thin super glue (or Titebond/fish glue), paste wax
Beveling and end dressing files, crowning file, polishing abrasives
parts: Rosewood or ebony dust for chip repair

specs.label: When to refret
specs.value: Frets below about 0.038 in after wear (Premier Guitar), or when leveling would remove more than about 20% of fret height (StewMac)

specs.label: Slot width check
specs.value: StewMac wire suits a 0.023 in slot; test with feeler gauges

specs.label: Overbend
specs.value: Bend wire to a slightly tighter radius than the board

specs.label: Tang adjustment
specs.value: Thin tangs with a Fret Barber (StewMac set it with a 0.032 in gauge for wire about 0.035 in across the barbs); widen with a Fret Crimper

steps.title: Measure and record
steps.detail: Before removing anything, measure neck relief with the rod slack and tight, and note any hump or fall-away with a notched straightedge. Record the old fret wire size.

steps.title: Pull the frets with heat
steps.detail: Slacken and remove strings and the nut if needed. Heat each fret with a soldering iron and work the puller jaws under it from one end, rocking it out gradually. StewMac's experience: frets pulled cold from above caused chips on the Bloomfield Tele; with heat and pullers under the fret there were no chips. Repair any chip immediately with dust and thin glue.

steps.title: Clean the slots
steps.detail: Clear old glue and gunk with a slot saw or cleaning tool, front and back. Check that every slot is at least as deep as the new tang (depth gauge). Lightly bevel the top edges of each slot with a small file; Frets.com notes this helps frets seat and reduces chipping next time.

steps.title: True the board
steps.detail: Set the neck straight with the rod. Sand the board with a radius block of the correct radius, using long straight strokes without twisting the block, checking often with a straightedge. Use 220 grit if little needs removing so you are not chasing 80-grit scratches (StewMac). Clean up, then oil the board lightly if it is very dry.

steps.title: Prepare wire
steps.detail: Degrease the wire with naphtha. Test-fit a short piece in a slot. If tight, thin the tang with a Fret Barber; if loose, widen it with a crimper. StewMac says not to widen slots or rely on glue to hold loose frets; frets should stay seated by themselves. Bend the coil to a slightly tighter radius than the board and cut each fret a little longer than its slot.

steps.title: Install
steps.detail: Tap the ends in, then press with a radiused caul or hammer from the centre outward (one firm dead blow per spot, keep the hammer moving, strike square). Work over a solid support. Many techs run thin super glue along each fret after installation (wax the board first) to fill tang gaps.

steps.title: Trim, bevel, level, crown, polish
steps.detail: Nip ends close (not flush, so you do not pull the fret), bevel all ends at about 35°, then level, crown, dress ends and polish as in [fn-fret-level-crown-polish].

steps.title: Refit nut and set up
steps.detail: New frets are taller, so nut slots may need adjusting or a new nut (see [fn-nut-make-bone]). Restring and set relief, action and intonation.

models.model: Gibson-style set necks with bound boards
models.note: See [fn-refret-bound] for nipping tangs.
Frets over the body need a press with a soundhole caul, or careful hammering with a heavy support under the top.
Slightly wider tangs (compression fretting) put a small backbow into the neck; StewMac suggests it for these necks. See [fn-neck-bow-twist].
Same process; boards are usually flat (no radius).

warnings: Oversize tangs can force a neck into backbow the truss rod cannot correct (StewMac).
Heating frets on bound boards can melt or burn celluloid binding.
Wear eye protection when nipping wire; offcuts fly.
pro: This is a pro job on any guitar you care about. Practise on a junk neck first.

title: Refret a bound fretboard (nipping tangs)
summary: On a bound board the slots stop short of the binding, so each new fret must have its tang trimmed back at both ends so the crown can sit over the binding. Done wrong, frets will not seat or the binding gets damaged.
tools: Fret slot depth gauge (radiused, small enough for bound boards)
Fret tang nipper with anvils for different crown profiles
Nut shaping file or small file (to clean tang stubs)
Thin (#10) super glue, paste wax, accelerator
Fretbar or leveling beam; beveling and end files; Z-file crowning file; polishing papers

specs.label: Tang nip-back
specs.value: About 1/32 in in from the binding edge at each end; on the base side cut halfway between two barbs (StewMac)

specs.label: Slot width example
specs.value: StewMac fit: 0.020 in feeler loose, 0.022 in sloppy, 0.024 in snug

specs.label: Too low to keep
specs.value: Old frets below about 0.030 in are usually too low for most clients (StewMac)

specs.label: Gibson vintage radius
specs.value: Older Gibsons may be 9.5 in rather than the typical 12 in (StewMac)

steps.title: Remove the old frets
steps.detail: Heat with a fret heater and pull. On many Gibsons the binding is shaped over the fret ends ('nibs'); these can be trimmed off flush, but rebuilding nibs is slow and usually reserved for 1950s/60s Gibsons.
steps.warn: Celluloid binding can melt or catch fire with too much heat.

steps.title: Clean slots carefully
steps.detail: Saw out old glue with a pull/push stroke from each side. Do not yank a snagged saw; it can knock the binding off the far side. Clamp a support against delicate binding while you work.

steps.title: Check depth and width
steps.detail: Make sure slots are at least tang-deep (depth gauge) and check width with feeler gauges. Adjust tang thickness (barber or crimper) rather than altering the slot.

steps.title: Bend and cut the wire
steps.detail: Degrease the wire. Bend it to the radius but do not overbend much on a bound board; aim for a very slight gap at the centre with the ends tight. Cut each fret using the barbs as a length reference.

steps.title: Nip the tangs
steps.detail: With the tang nipper and the anvil matching your crown profile, cut the tang back about 1/32 in from the binding edge at each end. Leave the crown overhanging slightly; do not nip flush to the binding or the crown can undercut and fail to seat. File the stub clean under the crown with a fine file, supporting the fret in a grooved block.

steps.title: Press and glue
steps.detail: Wax around each slot, press the fret in (Jaws or arbor press), tap the ends with a deadblow if needed, and confirm the crown sits on both the board and the binding. Run thin super glue under the fret; the binding forms a trough that keeps glue in. Check level every few frets as you go.

steps.title: Trim, bevel, level, crown, polish
steps.detail: Cut the overhang slightly proud, then bevel with a fine file down to the binding (tape protects it), level with a Fretbar, crown, round the ends and polish.

models.model: Gibson Les Paul / ES / SG Standard
models.note: Bound boards with binding nibs on most original and reissue models.
Same technique; check whether frets run over or between the binding.

warnings: Cutting tangs flush leaves the crown unsupported and the fret will not seat.
Gobs of glue can seal the gap under the crown and ooze onto the binding.
pro: Pro job. Binding repair and nib reconstruction add significantly to the work.

title: Refret a finished maple fretboard
summary: Fender-style maple boards are covered in lacquer that runs right up to the frets, so pulling frets tends to chip the finish and the board cannot simply be sanded and oiled afterwards. The job is a normal refret plus careful finish protection and touch-up.
tools: Sharp craft knife (to score the lacquer at each fret)
Low-tack tape and metal fret guards
Thin and medium super glue, accelerator, or clear lacquer for touch-up
Micro-Mesh / fine abrasives and polishing compound

specs.label: Vintage Fender radius
specs.value: 7.25 in; American Standard 9.5 in (StewMac)

specs.label: Original vintage Fender wire
specs.value: Small wire such as Dunlop 6230 (0.078 x 0.043 in) is found on older Fender necks (Fender)

specs.label: Abrasive caution
specs.value: On maple, always mask; abrasives cut through lacquer in seconds

steps.title: Decide on the approach
steps.detail: Two schools: refret through the finish and touch up only the slot edges (keeps the original look), or refret then strip and refinish the board (cleanest result but a big job). For a player guitar, the first is usual.

steps.title: Score the finish at every fret
steps.detail: With a sharp knife, gently score the lacquer along both sides of each fret where it meets the crown, so the finish breaks at the score line rather than flaking off in chunks when the fret lifts. (StewMac uses the same idea when removing a nut: score the finish around it first.)

steps.title: Heat and pull slowly
steps.detail: Heat each fret with a soldering iron and lift it with flush pullers working under the crown, a little at a time from one end. Glue any lacquer chip back down straight away with a drop of thin super glue.

steps.title: Clean slots; do not sand the board
steps.detail: Clean the slots and check depth. Avoid radius-sanding the board unless you plan to refinish; any sanding goes straight through the lacquer and the bare maple will stain grey with use.

steps.title: Install the new frets
steps.detail: Fit, bend, press and glue as in [fn-refret-rosewood-ebony]. In StewMac's Bloomfield Tele refret (7.25–9.5 in radius board) the frets were bent with a Fret Bender, pressed in a drill press with a radiused caul and set in fish glue, with barbs trimmed on a Fret Barber to suit tight slots.

steps.title: Touch up the slot edges
steps.detail: Fill chips along the frets with clear super glue drop-fill or lacquer, let it cure, then scrape and level carefully and polish. StewMac's worn-neck repair used thin then medium super glue in coats, about 15 minutes apart for thin and 30 minutes for medium, then levelled with fine abrasives and buffed.

steps.title: Level, crown and polish with the board fully masked
steps.detail: Tape every space between frets, or use metal fret guards, before leveling and polishing. Then set up.

models.note: Leveling a vintage board is generally avoided to keep its look and feel (StewMac's Bloomfield Tele).

models.model: Satin or oil-finished maple (some modern necks)
models.note: Easier to touch up; can be lightly sanded and re-oiled or re-sealed as the original.

warnings: Never oil a lacquered maple board; oil does nothing on finish and attracts dirt.
Lacquer and super glue fumes: work ventilated.
pro: Recommended pro job, especially on vintage or nitro-finished necks.

title: Clean and oil a fretboard
summary: Unfinished rosewood, ebony, pau ferro and similar boards benefit from cleaning and an occasional light oil to keep them from drying and cracking. Finished (lacquered) maple boards should only be cleaned and polished, never oiled.
tools: Naphtha (lighter fluid) and a clean cotton rag
Soft toothbrush or plastic scraper for gunk at the frets
0000 steel wool or fine Scotch-Brite (unfinished boards only, pickups masked)
Fretboard oil (e.g., ColorTone fretboard finishing oil) or lemon-oil-type conditioner

specs.label: Oil wipe-off
specs.value: Wipe off after several minutes and buff; the ColorTone oil dries fully in 24 h

specs.label: Safe humidity
specs.value: 45–55% RH for most instruments (StewMac)

steps.title: Strings off
steps.detail: Remove the strings (or do half at a time on a guitar with a floating bridge).

steps.title: Clean the grime
steps.detail: Dampen a rag lightly with naphtha and wipe the board; it lifts grease and dirt without harming most finishes. For crusty buildup against the frets, use a soft toothbrush or a plastic scraper along the fret edge. On unfinished boards a pass of 0000 steel wool or fine Scotch-Brite along the grain cleans deeper (tape pickups first).
steps.warn: Naphtha is flammable: no flames or cigarettes, ventilate.

steps.title: Oil unfinished boards lightly
steps.detail: Shake the oil, put a little on a lint-free cloth, and wipe a thin coat on the board. Wait a few minutes, then wipe it completely dry and buff. Leaving puddles can soak into fret slots and soften glue. Once or twice a year is plenty for most players; more in very dry climates.

steps.title: Finished maple: no oil
steps.detail: Lacquered maple boards are sealed; oil cannot soak in and just sits on top. Clean with a damp cloth or naphtha and use a guitar polish if wanted.

steps.title: Keep humidity steady
steps.detail: Dry air shrinks boards (sprouting fret ends, cracks). Keep a hygrometer near your guitars and humidify in winter.

models.note: Clean only; no oil.

models.model: Rosewood, ebony, pau ferro, Richlite-free natural boards
models.note: Clean and lightly oil.
Treat like rosewood; check the maker's advice.
Dries and cracks easily in low humidity; regular light oil and humidity control help (StewMac crack repair finished with lemon oil).

warnings: Oil fumes: ventilate; keep oily rags flat to dry before discarding (some oils can self-heat in a crumpled rag).

title: Adjust a Gibson, Epiphone or PRS truss rod
summary: Gibson-style guitars hide a hex nut under a small cover on the headstock just behind the nut. It is turned with a thin-wall socket (nut driver) or box wrench, usually 5/16 in on Gibson and US PRS.
tools: 5/16 in thin-wall truss rod socket (Gibson, Maryland-made PRS)
Pocket-style short socket for newer Gibsons/PRS with small access cavities (StewMac sells 1/4, 9/32, 5/16 in)
Small screwdriver for the cover screws

specs.label: Gibson
specs.value: 5/16 in hex nut (10-32 rod thread)

specs.label: PRS Maryland (Core, USA)
specs.value: 5/16 in wrench (PRS support)

specs.label: PRS SE
specs.value: 7 mm wrench (PRS support)

specs.label: Washer
specs.value: Gibson nuts bear on a half-moon (D-shaped) steel washer in the wood

specs.label: Healthy nut position
specs.value: Nut snug with rod end roughly flush with its end; lots of bare thread showing beyond the nut is a warning sign (StewMac)

steps.title: Remove the cover
steps.detail: Take out the two or three screws holding the truss rod cover (the bell-shaped plate behind the nut) and keep them safe. Blow out any dust in the cavity.

steps.title: Measure relief
steps.detail: Tune to pitch, capo the 1st fret, hold the low E at the last fret and measure at the 7th–8th fret. Electric targets of roughly 0.004–0.010 in suit most players.

steps.title: Check the nut and threads
steps.detail: Look into the cavity. If you can see a lot of thread past the nut, or the washer sunk into the wood, the rod may be near its limit (see [fn-truss-rod-stuck-maxed]). Slacken the strings a little, back the nut off a fraction to check it moves, and if it comes off easily, clean and grease the threads and the washer face with petroleum jelly (Dan Erlewine's preference).

steps.title: Seat the socket fully
steps.detail: Push the socket straight down over the nut so it grips all six flats. Gibson cavities are narrow; a socket with too thick a wall will not go down and can grip only the top edge.

steps.title: Turn 1/8 turn at a time
steps.detail: Clockwise (facing the nut) tightens and straightens the neck; counter-clockwise loosens and adds relief. Retune between each step.

steps.title: Settle, recheck, refit the cover
steps.detail: Let it sit a few minutes, re-measure, then set action and intonation. Refit the cover without over-tightening its little screws.

models.model: Gibson Les Paul / SG / ES / Explorer
models.note: 5/16 in socket under the bell cover. In StewMac's Les Paul example, Dan clamped a slight backbow in first and then took about 3/4 turn to set the rod, finishing at 0.070 in (low E) and 0.050 in (high E) action at the 12th fret.
Same cover-and-nut layout. Many Epiphones take a hex (Allen) key in the nut rather than a socket, and sizes vary by factory and year; try sizes gently until one fits with zero play.
5/16 in on Maryland-made guitars, 7 mm on SE models. Newer PRS (and some Gibsons) have small access holes that need a short pocket wrench.
Headstock nut under a cover like Gibson; StewMac and MusicNomad list 5/16 in sockets for Gibson, PRS and Gretsch, but check yours fits snugly before turning.
Same headstock nut; Frets.com lists 1/4 in and 5/16 in as the common sizes on Gibson and Taylor.

warnings: Too much force can snap the rod right at the threaded end, which is a major repair on a set-neck guitar.
Do not use a socket that is a loose fit; rounded Gibson nuts are common.
pro: If the nut is tight against the washer with relief still too high, the washer is sunk into the wood, or the nut will not move, stop. These rods can be rescued with spacers or new threads, but it needs special tools.
