title: Adjust a truss rod safely
summary: The truss rod sets neck relief, the slight forward curve of the neck under string tension. Use this when strings buzz in the low positions (too little relief) or action feels high in the middle of the neck (too much relief). It does not set action height or intonation.
symptoms: Buzz on the first few frets that gets better higher up the neck (neck too straight or back-bowed)
Strings feel high and stiff around frets 5–9 even though the saddles are low (too much forward bow)
Relief changed after a change of season, a move, or a different string gauge
tools: Correct truss rod wrench for your guitar (see the model notes)
Marker or a strip of masking tape to mark the nut position

specs.label: Fender relief, 7.25 in radius
specs.value: 0.012 in (0.3 mm) at the 8th fret

specs.label: Fender relief, 9.5–12 in radius
specs.value: 0.010 in (0.25 mm) at the 8th fret

specs.label: Fender relief, 15–17 in radius
specs.value: 0.008 in (0.2 mm) at the 8th fret

specs.label: StewMac typical ranges
specs.value: Electric 0.004–0.008 in; acoustic 0.006–0.012 in; bass 0.008–0.015 in; treble side often 0.001–0.002 in less than bass side

specs.label: Frets.com rule of thumb (acoustic)
specs.value: About the thickness of a 0.013 in string for a regular player; heavy-handed bluegrass players up to about 0.026 in

specs.label: Turn size per step
specs.value: 1/8 turn (1/16 for fine work); rarely more than 1/4 turn at a time

steps.title: Tune up and hold it like you play it
steps.detail: Put on the strings you actually use and tune to your normal pitch. Measure with the guitar in playing position, not lying flat on its back: gravity and the body's weight bend the neck and give a false reading.

steps.title: Measure the relief
steps.detail: Capo the 1st fret. With your right hand, hold the low E string down at the last fret (on a bolt-on, around where the neck meets the body; on an acoustic, at the body joint is enough). Now the string is a straightedge. Slide feeler gauges between the bottom of the string and the top of the 7th or 8th fret. The thickest gauge that slides in with light drag is your relief. Repeat on the high E; if the two sides differ a lot, the neck may be twisted (see [fn-neck-bow-twist]).

steps.title: Decide which way to go
steps.detail: Too much gap: tighten the rod (less relief). Too little or zero gap, or the string touches the middle frets: loosen the rod (more relief). On nearly every rod, facing the adjusting nut, clockwise tightens and counter-clockwise loosens. Be careful with descriptions written from the player's view: Sweetwater's Fender chart says counter-clockwise for a headstock nut because it is viewed from the body end looking up the neck. What matters is: tighten = straighter, loosen = more bow.

steps.title: Find and fit the right tool
steps.detail: Look up your model's wrench size (model notes below). The tool must fit snugly with no wobble. A loose or worn tool rounds the nut, which is the most common way truss rods get damaged. Push the tool all the way in; on L-shaped hex keys, use the long arm in the socket so it seats fully.

steps.title: Mark the start and test the nut
steps.detail: Put a pen mark or tape flag on the nut so you can see how far you turn and can go back. Before tightening, loosen it slightly first to feel that it moves smoothly. If it is removable, you can take it off, clean the threads and add a dab of petroleum jelly (keep it off the wood). If it will not move with firm hand pressure, stop: see [fn-truss-rod-stuck-maxed].

steps.title: Turn in small steps
steps.detail: Turn 1/8 turn (about 45 degrees). StewMac's experience is that a healthy rod rarely needs more than about 1/8 turn either way for a seasonal tweak; bigger corrections may need 1/4 turn steps. Detune slightly before tightening if the nut feels stiff, then retune.
steps.warn: Never force a rod. If resistance climbs sharply, stop. Over-tightening can strip the threads, snap the rod, or crush the wood under the washer.

steps.title: Retune, let it settle, measure again
steps.detail: Retune to pitch, play for a minute, and re-measure. Necks take time to move: allow at least a few minutes (longer on thick or dense necks), and StewMac suggests rechecking after a few hours. Repeat small steps until you hit the target.

steps.title: Then set action and intonation
steps.detail: Relief changes string height, so after the rod is right, reset saddle height and then intonation. Buzz only high up the neck is usually a saddle-height problem, not a rod problem (Frets.com).

models.note: Adjuster at the heel end of the neck; Phillips-head nut on American Vintage and Classic heel-adjust models. See [fn-truss-rod-fender-heel].
Headstock adjuster: 1/8 in hex on American Standard/Deluxe/Special, Highway One and bullet-nut models; 3/16 in hex on '70s-style and some Mexican models. See [fn-truss-rod-fender-modern].
Nut under the cover at the headstock; Gibson and Maryland-made PRS take 5/16 in; PRS SE takes 7 mm. See [fn-truss-rod-gibson-prs].
Usually a hex key at the headstock end, commonly 4 mm; many are two-way rods. See [fn-truss-rod-two-way].
Martin: 5 mm (some 4 mm) hex through the soundhole. Taylor: 1/4 in nut driver. See [fn-truss-rod-acoustic].
Two rods; pre-1984 rods must not be used to pull the neck. See [fn-truss-rod-rickenbacker].

Bass necks need more relief (Fender 0.010–0.014 in) and often 3/16 in wrenches on Fender-style basses (StewMac's Jaguar bass). The rod tends to stop having much effect past roughly the 12th–16th fret.
Many classical guitars have no adjustable rod at all; relief is fixed by the neck and frets.

warnings: Strings put roughly 200 lb (about 90 kg) of tension on a light-gauge guitar neck; a rod working against that needs respect, not force.
Do not use the truss rod to change action height; it only controls the curve of the neck.
If you meet heavy resistance, the rod has no effect, or it needs constant adjustment, Fender's advice is to stop and see a service center.
pro: Take it to a tech if the nut will not turn with moderate hand pressure, the rod is already very tight with relief still too high, the nut spins without doing anything, threads are showing beyond the nut, or tightening does nothing.

title: Adjust an acoustic truss rod (Martin, Taylor, soundhole access)
summary: Acoustic rods adjust either at the headstock (Gibson, Taylor and others) or inside the body through the soundhole (Martin, Collings, Baby Taylor). The procedure is the same as an electric, but tools and access differ.
tools: Martin: 5 mm hex key with a long right-angle reach (some models 4 mm)
Taylor: 1/4 in thin-wall nut driver (Taylor's own wrench)

specs.label: Taylor check
specs.value: Fret 1st and 14th frets together, look at the 6th fret: a gap slightly thinner than a business card

specs.label: Martin wrench reach (StewMac)
specs.value: 5 mm with 2 in reach for pre-August 2007 Martins; 4-1/2 in reach for later ones (rod sits further back)

specs.label: Martin SC series
specs.value: 4 mm Allen, centered on the front block

steps.title: Measure relief
steps.detail: Tune to pitch. Frets.com method: press the 6th string at the 1st fret and around the 14th (body joint) and look at the gap over the 6th fret. Taylor uses the same idea and says a gap slightly thinner than a business card is about right. Or capo the 1st fret and use feeler gauges at the 7th–8th fret.

steps.title: Find the adjuster
steps.detail: Look for a cover on the headstock first. If there is none, shine a light through the soundhole toward the neck: on Martins the hex socket is at the neck block, at the neck end of the soundhole. On Martins since 2006 the two-way rod sits further back and you find the socket by feel rather than sight.

steps.title: Loosen strings if the tool won't fit
steps.detail: Some soundhole nuts sit tight against the neck block and need the strings slackened (or the tool angled) to get the key in (Premier Guitar).

steps.title: Turn in small steps
steps.detail: Facing the nut (from inside the soundhole you are looking toward the headstock), clockwise tightens/reduces relief. Turn 1/8 turn, retune, re-check. Dan Erlewine's example on a double-action acoustic rod needed half a turn to the left to add relief.
steps.warn: Do not confuse Martin SC's intonation set screw (beside the access hole) with the truss rod; Martin warns the wrong screw can cause damage.

steps.title: Then deal with action at the saddle
steps.detail: Truss rods do not fix neck angle. If action is still high with good relief, the saddle or a neck reset is the next step (Frets.com).

models.note: Adjustable rods since 1985 (earlier Martins have non-adjustable reinforcement). 5 mm or 4 mm hex through the soundhole. Martin recommends an authorized service center and notes incorrect adjustment can affect the warranty.

1/4 in thin-wall nut driver at the headstock on most models; Baby Taylor (1997 on) through the soundhole. Taylor says a magnetic-tip screwdriver handle with no bit in it often fits. Older Taylor NS nylon-string models need Taylor's nylon-string wrench.
Headstock nut under the cover, 5/16 in.
Collings: 5/32 in long key inside the body (StewMac). Santa Cruz: access hole hidden high in the neck block (Frets.com).
Hex keys, reached through a hole in the brace (Takamine) or with long bent keys (Ovation, Larrivee); sizes vary 1/8 in to 5 mm.
Many have no adjustable rod; nothing to turn.

warnings: Humidity changes relief on acoustics more than electrics; check again a few weeks after a season change before making big adjustments.
pro: If relief is right but action at the 12th fret is still high and the saddle is already low, the guitar probably needs a neck reset, which is pro work.

title: Fender headstock, bullet and spoke-wheel truss rods
summary: Most modern Fenders and Squiers adjust the rod at the headstock with a hex key, either recessed behind the nut or through an exposed 'bullet' nut; a few use a spoke wheel. No neck removal is needed.
tools: 1/8 in hex key (American Standard/Deluxe/Special, Highway One, bullet nuts)
3/16 in hex key ('70s-style Classic and Deluxe Player models etc.)
A bent 1/8 in key helps clear tuners on 6-in-line headstocks
For a spoke wheel: a small steel rod, an Allen key or a small screwdriver through the wheel holes

specs.label: 1/8 in hex
specs.value: Fender lists it for American Deluxe, American Standard and American Special guitars, Highway One, and guitars/basses with a bullet nut

specs.label: 3/16 in hex
specs.value: Fender's 3/16 in nut fits Deluxe Player Strat, Toronado, Cyclone, '72 Tele Custom, Classic '70s Strat and Jazz Bass, Road Worn Player, Pawn Shop and Lone Star Strat

specs.label: Bullet nut thread
specs.value: 10-32 (as used by Fender after 1971, per StewMac)

specs.label: Bi-Flex
specs.value: Two-way rod; Fender says currently used on American Professional guitars; US basses had it 1982–84 and 1989–95

specs.label: Relief target (9.5–12 in radius)
specs.value: 0.010 in at the 8th fret

steps.title: Identify your adjuster
steps.detail: Look behind the nut at the headstock. A hex socket inside a hole = recessed headstock adjuster. A domed metal nut sticking out of the headstock = bullet nut (takes a hex key in its centre). No access at the headstock = heel adjuster (see [fn-truss-rod-fender-heel]) or a spoke wheel at the body end of the fretboard.

steps.title: Measure relief
steps.detail: Tune to pitch. Capo the 1st fret, hold the low E at the last fret, and measure the gap at the 8th fret with feeler gauges (Fender's method).

steps.title: Fit the key fully
steps.detail: Insert the hex key all the way into the socket. If tuners get in the way, use a bent or ball-end key. The key must not wobble; a 3 mm or 5/32 key in a 1/8 or 3/16 socket will strip it.

steps.title: Turn the right way
steps.detail: Facing the headstock end of the rod (as Fender support describes, sighting from behind the headstock), clockwise reduces relief and counter-clockwise adds relief. Go 1/8 turn at a time.
steps.warn: On a Bi-Flex (two-way) rod, loosening past the neutral point starts pushing the neck forward rather than just relaxing it. See [fn-truss-rod-two-way].

steps.title: Spoke wheel version
steps.detail: The American Elite introduced a double-action adjustment wheel that you turn without removing the neck. Push a rod or key into one hole of the wheel and lever it a quarter of a hole-spacing at a time; move to the next hole and repeat. Premier Guitar says a small metal rod or miniature screwdriver is the tool for spoke wheels (also used by Music Man and Sadowsky).

steps.title: Retune and recheck
steps.detail: Retune, wait a few minutes, re-measure, repeat. Then reset saddle height and intonation.

models.note: Most Squiers use a headstock hex adjuster; size varies by series, so try 1/8 in first, then 3/16 in, then metric (4 or 5 mm) until one fits with no play.
StewMac's bass setup guide used a 3/16 in wrench on a Fender Jaguar bass. Current Fender basses use single-action rods.
Bi-Flex two-way rod at the headstock.
Double-action spoke-wheel adjuster (replaced Bi-Flex on that series).

warnings: If you meet excessive resistance, Fender says to stop and send it to a Fender service center.
A stripped hex socket is easy to cause and annoying to fix: see [fn-truss-rod-stripped-broken].
pro: Stop if the socket is rounding out, the rod will not turn, or relief does not change after a few small adjustments.

title: Sticky neck fix, satin vs gloss
summary: A gloss neck can feel sticky or 'grabby' with warm or sweaty hands. Cleaning and lightly scuffing the back of the neck to a satin feel fixes most cases without refinishing.
tools: Naphtha and a microfiber or cotton cloth
600 grit paper (gloss necks); 400 only with care
Painter's tape and a plastic bag (to protect the body)
Optional: fret beveling and end files to roll fretboard edges

specs.label: Satin/matte necks
specs.value: 0000 steel wool only; 000 or 00 can cut through

specs.label: Gloss necks
specs.value: 600 grit along the grain; avoid 220, which can cut to bare wood

steps.title: Clean it first
steps.detail: Wipe the back of the neck with a cloth lightly dampened with naphtha, turning the cloth often. Sometimes cleaning alone fixes the stickiness. Rub gently; hard rubbing can polish gloss even shinier or wear a relic finish.
steps.warn: Naphtha is flammable.

steps.title: Protect the guitar
steps.detail: Remove a bolt-on neck if you are comfortable, or bag the body and tape the bag closed at the neck joint. Tape the fretboard edges and headstock face.

steps.title: Scuff lightly
steps.detail: Satin necks: 0000 steel wool, one direction along the grain, until smooth. Gloss necks: 600 grit paper along the grain with light pressure, checking with your fingers. Remove as little as possible; you are only dulling the surface, not removing finish.

steps.title: Wipe and play
steps.detail: Wipe off dust. The result is a satin feel. Clean the neck back with naphtha at string changes and wash your hands before playing.

steps.title: Optional: roll the fretboard edges
steps.detail: For a 'played-in' feel, StewMac bevels the fretboard edges and fret ends lightly with a beveling file and dressing files, then cleans and oils the board. This is a refinishing job on lacquered maple boards.

models.note: Nitro is thin; go very gently with 600+ grit.
Tough, but colour coats underneath show quickly if you cut through.
Altering original finish affects value; clean only.

warnings: Over-abrading means a full strip and refinish.
Keep steel wool fibres away from pickups.

title: Two-way vs single-action truss rods
summary: A single-action rod can only pull the neck back against the strings; a two-way (double-action) rod can also push it forward. Knowing which you have tells you what to expect when you loosen it, and what to do if a neck is back-bowed.

specs.label: Single-action
specs.value: Tightening pulls the neck toward backbow; loosening only relaxes it, and string tension supplies the forward bow

specs.label: Two-way
specs.value: Tightening pulls back; loosening passes a neutral (slack) point and then pushes the neck forward

specs.label: Fender Bi-Flex
specs.value: Two-way; a retainer under the 7th-fret inlay; the rod can sit within about 1/8 in of the back of the neck near the 7th fret

specs.label: Martin
specs.value: One-way adjustable rods from 1985, two-way from 2006 (Martin)

specs.label: StewMac Hot Rod (common replacement/kit rod)
specs.value: Clockwise corrects upbow, counter-clockwise corrects backbow

steps.title: Find out which kind you have
steps.detail: Check the manual or spec sheet. Clues: on a two-way rod the nut usually cannot be unscrewed off the end (it is fixed or brazed on), and after a slack spot it gets stiff again when you keep loosening. On a single-action rod, keep loosening and the nut goes completely slack and can often come off. Fender: Bi-Flex on American Professional (and some earlier American Series/Deluxe); Ibanez and many modern Asian-made electrics: commonly two-way with a hex key at the headstock (4 mm is common); Martin since 2006: two-way.

steps.title: Measure relief
steps.detail: As in [fn-truss-rod-basics]: capo the 1st fret, fret the last fret, measure at the 7th–8th fret.

steps.title: Too much relief (both types)
steps.detail: Tighten clockwise in 1/8 turn steps.

steps.title: Too little relief or back-bow on a single-action rod
steps.detail: Loosen until the nut is barely snug. If the neck is still back-bowed with the rod completely slack, the rod cannot help: the neck itself has taken a backbow (heavier strings or a pro fix are the options; see [fn-neck-bow-twist]).

steps.title: Too little relief or back-bow on a two-way rod
steps.detail: Loosen counter-clockwise through the neutral point. You will feel the nut go easy, then start to resist again; that resistance is the rod now pushing the neck forward. Continue in 1/8 turns until you reach the relief you want.
steps.warn: Do not crank hard in the push direction: Fender found in early Bi-Flex testing that too much force could blow the rod through the back of the neck, which is why the retainer was added.

steps.title: Retune and confirm
steps.detail: Retune and re-measure after each step; then set action and intonation.

models.note: Headstock hex, two-way. Fender's Highway One rods look similar but are not Bi-Flex.
Typically a hex key at the headstock under a cover (commonly 4 mm) and often two-way; confirm in your model's manual.
Two-way rod adjusted through the soundhole; see [fn-truss-rod-acoustic].
Traditional Gibson rods are single-action compression rods (Gibson patent from the 1920s).
Fender moved basses back to larger single-action rods because basses rarely need forward push.

warnings: A two-way rod that rattles at the neutral point is normal; one that rattles all the time may be loose in its channel (see [fn-truss-rod-stuck-maxed]).
Never guess on a valuable instrument: if the nut does not behave like either description, stop.
pro: If a single-action neck is back-bowed with the rod slack, or a two-way rod will not move in either direction, see a luthier.

title: Adjust a vintage Fender heel-adjust truss rod
summary: Vintage-style Fenders (American Vintage, Classic Series, many reissues and '50s/'60s originals) adjust the rod at the body end of the neck. On most you must loosen the strings and lift or remove the neck to reach it, so it is a trial-and-error job.
tools: Large Phillips screwdriver that fits the nut cross snugly (or a flat-blade/'Fender' truss rod screwdriver: StewMac's is a 3/8 in flat blade)
Tele truss rod crank (optional, for slotted heel nuts on vintage Teles)

specs.label: Nut type
specs.value: Phillips-head (cross-slotted) nut on Fender American Vintage and Classic heel-adjust models

specs.label: Rod threads (for replacement nuts)
specs.value: About 3/16 in rod pre-1960 is likely 10-24; about 5/32 in rod (c. 1961–64) is 8-32; post mid-'64 rods are typically 10-32 (StewMac)

specs.label: Relief target (Fender, 7.25 in radius)
specs.value: 0.012 in at the 8th fret; 0.010 in on 9.5–12 in radius necks

specs.label: Direction
specs.value: Facing the nut from the body end, clockwise reduces relief, counter-clockwise adds relief

steps.title: Measure first
steps.detail: Tune up and measure relief at the 8th fret with a capo at the 1st fret and the low E held at the last fret. Decide how much you need to change before taking anything apart.

steps.title: Slacken the strings
steps.detail: Loosen all strings well down (no need to remove them). Premier Guitar warns that loosening neck bolts with the strings still tight can bend the screws.
steps.warn: Slack strings before any neck screw comes out.

steps.title: Get to the adjuster
steps.detail: Some guitars have a slot or notch in the pickguard so a heel wrench or crank can reach the nut with the neck in place (StewMac notes this saves the body from screwdriver slips). Otherwise, remove the four neck screws with the guitar face-down on a towel, then lift the neck out of the pocket, or tip the neck up just enough to reach the nut. Premier Guitar advises not to leave a half-loose neck flopping around: either reach it through the pickguard slot or take the neck fully out, so you do not crack the pickguard finish or damage the neck pickup.

steps.title: Turn a small amount
steps.detail: Seat the screwdriver fully in the cross so it cannot cam out and chew the nut. Turn about 1/8 turn (1/4 turn at most) in the needed direction. Mark the nut position first so you know where you started.
steps.warn: A screwdriver that is too small or slips will strip the cross slots; these nuts are cheap but replacing one still means the same fiddly access.

steps.title: Refit, tune, recheck
steps.detail: Seat the neck fully in the pocket, refit the screws snugly in their original holes (do not over-tighten; they thread into wood), tune to pitch and re-measure. Expect to repeat the remove/adjust/refit cycle three or four times to get it right (StewMac).

steps.title: Finish the setup
steps.detail: Set saddle heights and intonation once relief is correct.

models.model: Fender American Vintage / Classic Series heel-adjust
models.note: Phillips-head vintage-style nut at the heel; neck usually has to come out or be tipped up.
Some vintage-style Teles use slotted heel nuts; StewMac sells a short Tele truss rod crank that reaches them.
Same heel adjuster; bass necks are heavy, so support the neck when it is out of the pocket.
Smaller-diameter (8-32) rods; treat them gently because there is less metal.

warnings: Do not lever the neck out of a tight pocket by the fretboard; lift from the heel to avoid chipping finish.
If the nut is at the end of its threads or will not tighten further, stop: see [fn-truss-rod-stuck-maxed].
pro: If the nut spins without tightening, the rod is maxed out, or the neck is a valuable vintage original, have a tech do it; vintage rods often need thread chasing, a spacer or a deeper bore (StewMac's '65 Mustang repair needed the rod bored deeper and a longer nut).

title: Adjust Rickenbacker dual truss rods
summary: Most Rickenbackers have two truss rods, one under each side of the fretboard, adjusted at the headstock under the large cover. Old-style rods (before about September 1984) must not be used to pull a neck straight; you bend the neck by hand and use the rods only to hold it.
tools: Close-fitting wrench or nut driver for the rod nuts (Premier Guitar lists box wrenches in the 1/4 in to 8 mm range for Rickenbacker)
Screwdriver for the truss rod cover
Towel, and a helper for pre-1984 necks

specs.label: Pre-Sept-1984 rods
specs.value: Folded steel bar with an aluminium spacer block; adjust only with the neck held in a slight backbow

specs.label: Post-1984 rods
specs.value: Sturdier conventional rods with a thin steel spacer; can be adjusted under string tension

specs.label: 4001 vs 4003 bass
specs.value: 4001: old-style rods with nuts only at the headstock end; 4003: nuts at both ends (Rickenbacker FAQ)

specs.label: Rod threads
specs.value: Rickenbacker Resource contributors re-cut worn rod ends with a 10-32 die

steps.title: Work out which era you have
steps.detail: Remove the truss rod cover. Haze Guitars' tip for pre-1984 rods: you can see two channels cut in the neck wood behind the aluminium spacer, and the end of the shorter bar shows in the gap before the fretboard. On later rods the channel is not visible and the spacer is a thin steel plate like a long washer.

steps.title: Measure relief on both sides
steps.detail: Tune to pitch and measure relief under the low E and high E separately (capo at 1, fret at the last fret, gauges at the 7th–8th). Because each rod controls one side, the two readings tell you which rod to move.

steps.title: Post-1984: adjust like a normal rod
steps.detail: Turn each nut in small steps (1/8 turn), keeping the two rods at about the same tension so both sides end up with the same relief, which is what Haze Guitars recommends. Retune and re-measure between steps.

steps.title: Pre-1984: move the neck, then snug the rods
steps.detail: Back both nuts off. Lay the guitar face-up on a towel with the headstock over the edge of the bench and a helper holding the body. Gently pull the headstock down to give a slight backbow, and while holding it, snug each nut just until it contacts the bearing plate. Release, tune to pitch, check, and repeat if needed. Rickenbacker Resource describes the same idea using the guitar across your lap, or a padded clamped board for accuracy.
steps.warn: Tightening old rods against string tension can ruin them or pop the fretboard off the neck.

steps.title: Refit the cover
steps.detail: If the neck rattles, a loose nut or a rod rattling in its channel may be the cause; Rickenbacker suggests tightening the nut, or wrapping each rod in masking tape if it still rattles.

models.note: Old-style rods: bend-then-snug method only. Threads on old rods often get damaged; contributors to Rickenbacker Resource recut them with a die.
Conventional rods adjustable under tension; keep both sides balanced.
A Rickenbacker fretboard that lifts along one edge is often caused by the rods pushing on a weak glue joint; StewMac's reglue removes the rods through the peghead first. See [fn-fretboard-repair].

warnings: Pull the headstock gently; too much force could break the neck.
Rickenbacker rods are flat stock with threads and chew up easily; use a tool that fits perfectly.
pro: If a rod will not tighten (spinning nut), the fretboard is lifting, or threads are mangled, take it to a tech familiar with Rickenbackers.

title: Fix fretboard divots, chips, cracks, side dots and a lifting board
summary: Worn divots in front of frets, chips at fret slots, dry cracks, missing side dots and a fretboard edge coming unglued can all be repaired with wood dust, super glue, wood glue and careful sanding.
tools: Matching wood dust (rosewood, ebony, maple) filed from scrap
Thin (#10) and medium (#20) super glue, accelerator, whip tips
Teflon fret dams (to keep glue out of fret slots)
Razor blades, X-Acto knife, micro chisels
Side dots (1/16 in plastic, or glow dots of the same size) and a matching drill bit with depth stop
For a lifting board: Titebond, rubber clamping bands or cauls and clamps, household iron, thin spatula

specs.label: Side dot size
specs.value: 1/16 in (0.0625 in) is a standard side dot (StewMac)

specs.label: Side dot positions
specs.value: 3rd, 5th, 7th, 9th (and 12th, 15th, 17th...) frets; classical guitars traditionally have none

specs.label: Fretboard reglue
specs.value: Titebond, rubber bands, dry overnight (StewMac Rickenbacker)

steps.title: Divots in front of frets
steps.detail: Frank Ford's method: cut deep slices across the bottom of the divot with a razor blade, lift the fibres into a 'web' with a knife, pack in fine sawdust scraped from matching wood (ebony dust or a little lampblack for ebony), protect the fret slot, and wick in thin super glue so it soaks to the bottom. Sand level when cured. Test the colour on a sample first; the dust darkens when glued.

steps.title: Chips at fret slots
steps.detail: With frets out (or protected), slip a Teflon fret dam into the slot. Small chips: pack with dust and a drop of thin glue, then accelerator. Medium: glue in slivers of matching wood. Large: cut a neat trench between slots and glue in a fitted block. Level with a file, then blend with a radius block.

steps.title: Cracks in the board
steps.detail: Clean with naphtha. Run thin glue into the crack from a razor blade, then scrape across the board with a fresh blade so the wood dust mixes into the glue as a filler; repeat until the crack is full and glue sits on top rather than soaking in. Set with brush-on accelerator, scrape lightly, sand 220 then 320, polish and oil. Fix the humidity that caused it.
steps.warn: Do not spray accelerator too early; it sets glue before it wicks deep.

steps.title: Worn edges on finished boards
steps.detail: On lacquered or poly boards, StewMac built up worn edge divots with thin then medium super glue in several coats, filed and sanded flat, and buffed. Abrasives cut through coloured finishes in seconds, so work slowly.

steps.title: Replace or add side dots
steps.detail: Mark positions halfway between frets on the board edge. Drill with a 1/16 in bit fitted with a depth stop (only a little depth is needed), add a dab of wood glue on a toothpick, push in the dot material, and once dry trim it flush (StewMac pushes the strip through a 1/16 in hole in a maple block and pares it flat with a chisel). Glow-in-the-dark dots install the same way; match the drill to their diameter.

steps.title: Lifting fretboard edge
steps.detail: If the board is only slightly open at an edge, clean out dirt with a thin blade, work glue into the gap (Titebond on a thin spatula), clamp with padded cauls or wrap with rubber bands, wipe squeeze-out and leave overnight. If it is loose over a long length, StewMac's approach is to heat the board with a household iron (about 10 minutes) and take it off with a thin knife, clean the old glue, index it with pins in two fret slots, reglue with Titebond and rubber bands overnight. Tape off the truss rod channel so glue cannot lock the rod.
steps.warn: Do not use super glue for board regluing; it can run into the rod channel and seize the rod.

models.note: Use ebony dust; ebony cracks more readily in dry air.
Divot repairs need finish touch-up; clear super glue drop-fill blends well.
Fretboards lifting from the rods are a known issue; remove the rods through the peghead before regluing (StewMac).
Binding can lift with heat; keep heat moderate.

warnings: Super glue and accelerator fumes: ventilate.
Wood dust: wear a mask.
pro: Fully removing and regluing a fretboard, or repairing large cracks through the neck, is luthier work.

title: Shim a bolt-on neck, Micro-Tilt, pocket gaps and loose screws
summary: On bolt-on guitars the neck angle can be changed by putting a shim in the neck pocket, or with Fender's Micro-Tilt screw. Use it when the saddles are bottomed out and action is still high, or when saddles are jacked right up because the angle is too steep. Also fix stripped neck-screw holes and gaps in the pocket.
symptoms: Action too high with the saddles already at their lowest
Saddles raised very high (or tremolo sitting high) to get playable action
Neck shifts in the pocket; screws spin without tightening
A visible gap at the end of the pocket, or a hump/high frets near the neck joint
tools: Shim material: full-pocket tapered shim (e.g., StewMac laser-cut wood shims), or a strip of hardwood veneer/card
For stripped holes: thin (#10) and medium (#20) super glue, or hardwood dowel, glue, drill bits
parts: Full-pocket neck shim (StewMac 1° shim: 0.060 in at the thick end tapering to zero)
Hardwood dowels (3/16 in) for stripped holes

specs.label: Fender small shim
specs.value: A shim about 1/4 in wide, 1-3/4 in long and 0.010 in thick under the butt end of the neck raises action about 1/32 in (0.8 mm)

specs.label: Fender Micro-Tilt
specs.value: Loosen the two neck screws beside the access hole at least four full turns; 1/4 turn of the hex screw (1/8 in key) raises action about 1/32 in

specs.label: StewMac full-pocket shim
specs.value: 1° version: 0.060 in at the thick end tapering to zero

specs.label: Neck screw holes
specs.value: Body holes 3/16 in (clearance); neck pilot holes typically 1/8 in (StewMac)

steps.title: Confirm you need a shim
steps.detail: Set relief first. Then look at the saddles: if they are bottomed out and action is still above spec (Fender: 4/64 in bass and treble at the 17th fret on 9.5–12 in radius), the neck angle needs tilting back (shim at the body end of the pocket). If the saddles are very high, the angle may need reducing (shim at the pickup end, or remove an old shim).

steps.title: Slacken strings and remove the neck
steps.detail: Detune fully. Lay the guitar face-down on a towel, remove the four neck screws (note which hole each came from), and lift the neck out from the heel. Look for an old shim stuck in the pocket and note where it sits.

steps.title: Choose full-pocket over partial
steps.detail: A small strip of card under one end works and is Fender's quick method, but it leaves an air gap under most of the heel. In StewMac's '65 Mustang repair, Dan Erlewine found the factory shim's air gap caused a hump at the heel and high frets, and replaced it with a full-pocket 1° tapered shim that supports the whole heel. Full-pocket shims also help sustain and stability.

steps.title: Fit the shim
steps.detail: Place the thick end toward the body end of the pocket (to tilt the neck back). Trim the shim to the pocket if needed and poke the screw holes through. A dot of glue or double-sided tape holds it in place.

steps.title: Refit the neck
steps.detail: Seat the neck fully into the pocket, start all four screws by hand, then tighten them evenly. Do not overtighten; the threads are cut into maple. Tune and measure action, then reset saddles and intonation.

steps.title: Micro-Tilt guitars
steps.detail: With strings slack, loosen the two screws beside the access hole in the neck plate at least four turns, turn the hex screw 1/4 turn with a 1/8 in key to raise action about 1/32 in, retighten the neck screws, tune and check.

steps.title: Fix stripped neck-screw holes
steps.detail: Quick fix: blow out the holes, protect the area with paste wax, swirl thin (#10) super glue into the hole (do not fill it), let it cure about 20 minutes, add more coats or medium glue for bad holes, then wax the screws and drive them back in to cut new threads. Sure fix: drill the hole slightly (StewMac used a #14 bit) and glue in a 3/16 in hardwood dowel, pare it flush once dry, then re-drill a small pilot and a final hole of about 0.128 in (#30 bit) and wax the screws.

steps.title: Check for pocket gaps
steps.detail: With the neck in, a small gap along the pocket sides is normal; the neck should drop in or be a little snug. Big side gaps let the neck shift; centre the neck (both E strings equally inset from the board edges) before final tightening.

models.model: Fender with Micro-Tilt (some American Standard/Deluxe and 1970s 3-bolt)
models.note: Use the tilt screw instead of shims. Fender says factory pitch rarely needs changing.
Shim method; full-pocket shims are an upgrade over card strips.
Same process; bass neck plates sit 1-5/16 in from the rout versus 5/8 in on guitars (StewMac).
Cannot be shimmed; neck angle problems need a neck reset or bridge changes (pro).

warnings: Never remove neck screws with the strings at pitch; tension can bend the screws and crack finish.
Thin super glue runs; keep it out of the pocket finish.
pro: If the neck needs more than about 1.5° of tilt, the pocket or neck heel itself may need machining.

title: Stuck or maxed-out truss rod
summary: When a rod nut will not turn, or is fully tight and the neck still has too much relief, there are a few safe tricks: clean and lubricate, add a washer or spacer to gain thread, and clamp the neck straight so the rod does not have to do all the work.
symptoms: Nut will not turn with moderate hand pressure
Nut is tight but relief is still too high
Lots of bare (often rusty) thread visible past the nut
Washer has sunk into the wood
A rattle from inside the neck

causes.cause: Dry or corroded threads
causes.check: Nut is stiff from the first movement, or squeaks/grinds
causes.fix: Slacken the strings, back the nut off (it is often easier loosening than tightening), clean the threads with a small stiff brush, add petroleum jelly, refit.

causes.cause: Rod at the end of its thread (maxed out)
causes.check: Nut tight with bare thread beyond it, or the nut bottoms on the rod end
causes.fix: Add one or two washers or a steel spacer behind the nut (steps below).

causes.cause: Washer pressed into the wood / anchor crept forward
causes.check: Washer sunk, or tapping the rod end with a punch moves it back into the neck (StewMac measured about 1/8 in)
causes.fix: Washers plus clamping the neck straight; tech may remove the sunken washer and refit.

causes.cause: Neck has taken a set beyond what the rod can correct
causes.check: Rod tight, relief still high even with washers
causes.fix: Heat/compression work, see [fn-neck-bow-twist].

causes.cause: Loose rod rattling in its channel
causes.check: Rap the back of the neck; a buzz/rattle from inside
causes.fix: Frets.com: wick very thin rubber cement (thinned with naphtha) or water-thinned wood glue into the channel after oiling the threads; never super glue.

tools: Small stiff brush (spray-gun cleaning brush works)
Gibson-style half-moon washers or StewMac truss rod spacers
Small file and vise (to remove washer barbs)
Rigid bar or straightedge, notched spacers, padded clamp(s)
parts: Truss rod washers (Gibson half-moon style) or spacers: 0.040 in, 0.100 in or 0.200 in thick (StewMac #6200/6201/6202)

specs.label: Spacer for Fender heel-adjust
specs.value: 0.040 in (StewMac)

specs.label: Spacer for most Gibsons
specs.value: 0.100 in; some Gibsons 0.200 in (StewMac)

specs.label: Spacer size
specs.value: 0.365 in OD, 0.195 in bore

specs.label: Warning sign (Gibson)
specs.value: About 1/8 in of thread showing past the nut means it has been pulled to its limit

steps.title: Slacken the strings and loosen first
steps.detail: Detune well down. Try to LOOSEN the nut slightly first; StewMac recommends this because a maxed nut can shear if you keep tightening. If it will not move either way with firm hand pressure, stop and see a tech.

steps.title: Clean and lubricate
steps.detail: Remove the nut if it comes off. Brush the exposed threads clean, run a little petroleum jelly on the threads and the face of the nut/washer with a toothpick, and clean inside the nut. StewMac's '65 Mustang and Gibson repairs started with exactly this. If the threads look mangled, a tech can chase them with a matching die (10-32 Gibson; Fender uses 10-24, 8-32 or 10-32 depending on year).

steps.title: Add a washer or spacer
steps.detail: With the nut off, slide one or two washers over the rod, then thread the nut back on. On Gibson-style rods, file the locating barbs off any washer that will sit against the factory washer (hold it in a small vise). Each washer gives the nut more usable thread.
steps.warn: Do not add so many washers that the nut only catches two or three threads; it can strip.

steps.title: Clamp the neck straight first
steps.detail: Loosen the rod completely. Lay a rigid bar along the fretboard on notched spacers (or lay the neck face-down on a padded bar) and use a padded clamp at the middle to push the neck straight or into a very slight backbow. Now tighten the nut until it is snug. Release the clamp and check. The rod now only has to hold the shape, not create it (StewMac).
steps.warn: Pad every clamp contact; a bare clamp will crush the neck.

steps.title: Restring and recheck
steps.detail: Tune up, let it settle overnight, and re-measure. Fine-tune with small turns.

models.note: Classic case: sunken half-moon washer and long exposed thread. Half-moon washers solve most of these.
Use a thin 0.040 in spacer or a longer extension nut; a strike washer may sit at the bottom of the cavity.
Non-adjustable reinforcement; no rod to adjust. See a luthier for relief problems.
Old-style rods: never use force; see [fn-truss-rod-rickenbacker].

warnings: A seized nut that is forced will snap the rod at its threaded end; on a set-neck guitar that can mean removing the fretboard.
Keep grease off bare wood and out of glue joints.
pro: If the nut is seized, the rod still will not hold relief with washers and clamping, or threads are damaged, a tech can bore a deeper pocket and cut fresh thread (StewMac Truss Rod Rescue Tools) or deal with the neck itself.

title: Fit a replacement bolt-on neck
summary: Replacement and licensed necks usually arrive without screw holes and sometimes need pocket and tuner work. The keys are matching heel shape and width, getting the neck centred, and drilling straight, correctly-sized screw holes to the right depth.
tools: Drill press (ideal) or careful hand drill
1/8 in drill bit for neck pilot holes; brad-point bit to mark
Radius block or sanding beam to cradle the neck while drilling
Fishing line or two strings, straightedge
Tuner drill bits (pilot 1/16 in for tuner screws in StewMac's example)
parts: Replacement neck matched to the body (heel shape, width, scale, pocket depth)
Tuners matching the peghole size (StewMac's example: 10.5 mm pegholes for sealed-back tuners)
String tree(s), nut if not fitted

specs.label: Neck pilot holes
specs.value: Most neck screws use a 1/8 in drill (StewMac)

specs.label: Body holes
specs.value: 3/16 in, lightly countersunk at the back (StewMac)

specs.label: Fit
specs.value: Neck should drop into the pocket or be a little snug, never forced

steps.title: Check compatibility before buying
steps.detail: Match heel shape (Strat-style rounded vs Tele-style square), heel width, pocket depth, scale length (Fender 25.5 in, bass 34 in), and fretboard radius to your saddles. Licensed Fender-spec necks generally fit Fender-spec pockets, but StewMac notes pockets vary a little.

steps.title: Test-fit
steps.detail: Drop the neck in with no screws. Too tight: lightly sand the pocket sides (finish buildup often makes them tight) rather than the neck heel. Too loose: thin veneer on a pocket wall can take up slop.

steps.title: Centre the neck
steps.detail: Clamp the neck lightly in the pocket with soft cauls. Run fishing line (or strings) from the outer nut slots to the outer saddles and check both E strings sit equally in from the fretboard edges (StewMac), adjusted to taste for bending room.

steps.title: Mark the holes
steps.detail: From the back, run a brad-point bit (or a neck screw used as a punch) through the body holes to dimple the heel.

steps.title: Drill to depth
steps.detail: Measure how far the screws protrude through the body and mark that depth on a 1/8 in bit with tape, or use a drilled guide block as a stop. Support the neck on a radius block, drill square, and back out often to clear chips in hard maple.
steps.warn: Do not drill through the fretboard. Measure twice.

steps.title: Fit tuners, string tree, nut
steps.detail: Line up tuners with a straightedge, drill small pilot holes (tape depth marks), and wax the screws. Fit the string retainer where the original was.

steps.title: Bolt up and set up
steps.detail: Wax the neck screws, install, then do a full setup: relief, nut slot check (new necks often have high nut slots: StewMac left 0.024 in wound / 0.020 in plain at the 1st fret), fret ends, action and intonation. Shim if the angle is off ([fn-neck-shim]).

models.note: Heel shapes differ (rounded vs square end); they are not interchangeable without pocket work.
Some Squier pockets differ from US Fender dimensions; measure pocket width and depth.
Need a neck with the tilt plate insert, or ignore the tilt hole.
Precision and Jazz necks differ in nut width; pockets are similar but check.

warnings: Wear eye protection when drilling.
Slack strings before removing any neck.
pro: If the pocket needs routing, the heel needs reshaping, or the holes do not line up, a tech can plug and re-drill.

title: Fretboard radius: single, compound and re-radiusing
summary: Radius is the curve across the fretboard. A small radius (7.25 in) is rounder and comfortable for chords; a large one (12–16 in) is flatter and better for low action and bends. A compound radius gets flatter as you go up the neck. Changing a board's radius means removing the frets and sanding the board with radius blocks.
tools: Radius blocks (4 in for spot work, 8 in or 18 in for full length) or a radiused aluminium beam
Fret removal and installation tools if refretting

specs.label: Common radii
specs.value: Vintage Fender 7.25 in; American Standard Fender 9.5 in; typical Gibson 12 in (older Gibsons sometimes 9.5 in)

specs.label: Compound example
specs.value: 10 in at the nut to 16 in or 20 in at the last fret (StewMac)

specs.label: Grits
specs.value: 80–120 to shape; start at 220 if little needs removing; 400 on a block for leveling frets

steps.title: Measure the current radius
steps.detail: Lay understring radius gauges under the strings at the nut, mid-neck and the last fret to see which gauge matches. If the readings get flatter up the neck, it is a compound radius.

steps.title: Understand compound vs single
steps.detail: StewMac explains that because strings spread apart from nut to bridge, a true 'cylindrical' single radius lets some strings sit higher than needed on bends; a conical (compound) board follows the string spread, which allows lower action with less fretting out on bends.

steps.title: Re-radius only with frets out
steps.detail: Pull the frets (see [fn-refret-rosewood-ebony]). Straighten the neck with the truss rod. Note that making a board flatter (larger radius) mainly removes wood at the edges; making it rounder removes wood in the centre and quickly thins the board, so it is usually only done toward flatter.

steps.title: Sand with the block
steps.detail: Stick paper to the block, folding the overhanging ends upward so the edge cannot dig in. Mark the board all over with pencil. Sand with long, straight, even strokes along the board; never twist the block. Check with a straightedge often. When the pencil is gone evenly and the radius gauge fits everywhere, move to finer grit.

steps.title: Compound radius
steps.detail: Work in sections with successive blocks: for example the 10 in block near the nut, then 12 in, 14 in and 16 in further up, blending each zone by rocking the next block side to side. Expect to use several blocks for a smooth transition.

steps.title: Refret and match the nut and saddles
steps.detail: Bend new wire to the new radius, refret, then match the nut slot bottoms and the bridge saddle heights to the new radius (radius gauges under the strings).

models.note: A popular mod is flattening to 9.5 in or more during a refret to allow lower action with bends; it changes the vintage feel and value.
Sand pearl block inlays with narrow strips of paper down their centres before blending the whole board (StewMac).
Usually flat; radius sanding not needed.

warnings: Every sanding thins the board and can expose side-dot holes or inlays.
Wood dust: wear a dust mask; rosewood and ebony dust can be irritants.
pro: Re-radiusing is normally part of a pro refret. Not worth it on a finished maple board unless it will be refinished.

title: Stripped truss rod nut or broken rod
time: 30 min (nut swap) to several days (rod replacement)
summary: A rounded-out socket or worn nut can usually be swapped in half an hour. A rod with stripped threads or one that has snapped is a rescue job with special cutters and dies, or in the worst case a fretboard-off rod replacement.
symptoms: Wrench slips or spins in the socket
Nut turns but nothing happens (spins freely)
Rod end has pulled back below its normal position
A crack or bang while adjusting, then no adjustment at all

causes.cause: Wrong-size or worn tool rounded the socket
causes.check: Correct key slips; socket flats look rounded
causes.fix: Remove nut with a Gripper-style tapered wrench or extractor, fit a new nut (steps below).

causes.cause: Stripped threads on nut or rod
causes.check: Nut spins after a certain point and won't tighten
causes.fix: Tech chases threads with a die, or bores deeper to fresh thread and fits a longer nut (StewMac).

causes.cause: Rod snapped at the threaded end
causes.check: Rod end has disappeared down the hole; no resistance at all
causes.fix: Tech bores around the rod end and cuts new thread (rescue tools); otherwise rod replacement.

causes.cause: Rod broken at the far (anchor) end
causes.check: Nut tightens but neck does not respond; hammering the nut drives the rod backward
causes.fix: Rod replacement or new neck.

tools: Gripper truss rod wrench (tapered tip that bites into a rounded socket)
Canned air, small brush, petroleum jelly
Replacement nut (Gibson-style acorn nut, Fender bullet nut etc.)

specs.label: Fender bullet nut
specs.value: 10-32 thread, 1/8 in hex (StewMac)

specs.label: Gibson
specs.value: 10-32 thread

specs.label: Relief after fitting a new nut
specs.value: About 0.010–0.012 in is usually enough (Premier Guitar)

steps.title: Slacken the strings
steps.detail: Always detune before working on the nut (Premier Guitar).

steps.title: Try the right tool first
steps.detail: Confirm the true size; a metric key in an imperial socket (or the reverse) is what usually caused the damage. If it slips, stop before you make it worse.

steps.title: Get the old nut off
steps.detail: Options in order of risk: a Gripper wrench, whose tip tapers to grab a rounded socket (StewMac); needle-nose pliers on a bullet nut, taking care of the headstock; gently tapping a small flat screwdriver into a bullet socket until it bites, then turning counter-clockwise; and as a last resort a screw extractor turned by hand with a T-handle. StewMac rejects pounding a screwdriver into the nut as a habit. Recessed nuts on some Strats are very hard to extract and can cost more than a new neck.
steps.warn: Do not use a power drill; patience by hand is safer.

steps.title: Clean and fit the new nut
steps.detail: Blow out the cavity with short blasts of canned air, brush the rod threads clean, dab petroleum jelly on the new nut, and thread it on clockwise by hand. Tighten until just snug, tune up, and set relief (about 0.010–0.012 in for most players). On vintage guitars use period-correct parts.

steps.title: If the nut spins without tightening
steps.detail: The threads are stripped. StewMac's '65 Mustang repair first chased the threads (failed), then bored the cavity deeper with a 3/8 in cutter that rides on the rod, reached fresh thread, and fitted a longer nut, with the neck clamped into a slight backbow while tightening. This is tech work.

steps.title: If the rod has broken
steps.detail: When the break is near the nut, a tech can bore around the rod end, cut new threads with a die and use spacers or a longer nut (StewMac Truss Rod Rescue Tools). If the rod broke or pulled loose at the anchor end, the fix is removing the fretboard to replace the rod, or replacing the neck; compare costs first.

models.note: Broken Gibson rods often snap where they meet the washer and retract; StewMac uses a Gibson relief cutter and 10-32 die, then a new acorn nut and washer.
Bullet nuts can be replaced from the headstock without removing the neck (StewMac).
A replacement neck may be cheaper than a fretboard-off rod replacement.

warnings: Do not over-tighten a freshly rescued rod; it has already been weakened.
Rods with welded/brazed nuts (many two-way rods) cannot be unscrewed; a Gripper wrench can still turn them if the socket is rounded.
pro: Anything beyond swapping a removable nut: chasing or recutting threads, boring for a longer nut, broken rods, and rod replacement.

title: Cracked or broken headstock
time: Glue-up 1–2 h; cure 24 h; finish touch-up up to 1–2 weeks
summary: Angled (tilt-back) headstocks, especially Gibson's, break easily when a guitar falls backward because the grain runs out through the thin area behind the nut. Clean breaks with lots of long-grain gluing surface can be glued very strongly; blunt or shattered breaks need reinforcement.
symptoms: Crack running diagonally behind the nut, often from the truss rod cavity
Headstock moves when you push the tuners
Tuning won't hold after a fall
tools: Glue: Titebond (original or III), liquid hide glue, or hot hide glue
Glue syringe with blunt needles, small brushes, thin spatula
Padded cauls shaped to the neck and a flat caul for the face
Small hardwood wedges (to open a crack)
Heat-shrink or tape to protect truss rod threads

specs.label: Gibson headstock angle
specs.value: About 17° (traditional Gibson pitch)

specs.label: Cure before string tension
specs.value: At least 24 h (StewMac)

specs.label: Lacquer touch-up
specs.value: Frets.com let lacquer cure about 10 days before leveling with 320 grit, then 600 and buffing

steps.title: Stop and stabilise
steps.detail: Slacken strings immediately. Remove tuners if the head is fully off (their weight stresses the joint). Save every splinter, especially pieces with finish on them. Do not try to glue it with super glue from the shop counter; StewMac's techs avoid CA for structural joints because it is brittle.

steps.title: Assess the break
steps.detail: A long diagonal break with lots of grain overlapping (the typical Gibson break) has plenty of glue surface and is the easiest. A blunt, straight-across break (a 'decapitation') has little surface and needs reinforcement such as splines, carbon fibre rods or a backstrap.

steps.title: Dry-fit and clean
steps.detail: Pull out crushed fibres and debris with tweezers and a knife so the pieces mate perfectly. Dry-fit and practise the clamping until it is smooth. Protect the truss rod threads from glue.

steps.title: Glue and clamp
steps.detail: Open the crack slightly with wedges if it is still attached, and force glue deep into it (a syringe or even a suction cup helps). Coat both surfaces. Close it, line up the grain, and clamp with padded cauls front and back (wax paper between) or wrap rubber bands to pull it shut. Even squeeze-out all round shows good contact. Wipe squeeze-out with warm water.

steps.title: Cure
steps.detail: Leave at least 24 hours before any string tension.

steps.title: Reinforce if needed
steps.detail: For short or blunt breaks, a pro may add a backstrap veneer over the back, splines across the joint, or (StewMac's top-down method) carbon fibre rods and sheet inlaid under the headstock overlay.

steps.title: Touch up the finish
steps.detail: Drop-fill finish into the crack line, let it cure fully, level and buff. Expect the repair to be visible but strong.

models.model: Gibson Les Paul / SG / ES / Explorer
models.note: 17° headstock and thin wood around the truss rod cavity make these the classic break.
Same design; repair cost may exceed the guitar's value.
Rarely breaks this way; neck cracks happen at the heel or through drops.
Frets.com used hot hide glue for heat resistance on a long D-41 break.
Heavier tuners; reinforcement more often needed.

warnings: Heat guns near finish and binding can burn; StewMac's tech nearly set wood alight shrinking tubing.
Always use a guitar stand that supports the neck, and lay angled-headstock guitars down carefully.
pro: Headstock breaks are structural; a luthier repair is strongly recommended. Ask about reinforcement for short breaks.

title: Scalloping a fretboard (and the risks)
summary: Scalloping removes wood between the frets in a concave dip so only the fret contacts your fingertip. It suits a light touch and wide vibrato, but it is permanent, weakens the board, and makes heavy-handed players play sharp.
tools: Sanding sticks or dowels wrapped in paper (120 to 400 grit)
Masking tape or metal fret guards
Fretboard oil (unfinished boards) or finish for maple

steps.title: Decide carefully
steps.detail: Scalloping cannot be undone except by replacing the board or neck. It changes feel dramatically: pressing too hard pushes notes sharp because the string bends down into the scoop. Try a scalloped guitar first, or scallop only the upper frets (a common compromise).

steps.title: Check board thickness and inlays
steps.detail: Thin boards (many modern rosewood veneers) leave little wood. Side dots and face inlays may be cut into or exposed. Do not scallop near the truss rod channel depth on thin boards.

steps.title: Protect the frets
steps.detail: Cover each fret with tape or a metal guard, leaving only the wood between them exposed. Pencil a line across each space at the planned depth along the board edges, and keep the edges and fret slots fully supported (do not undercut the fret tang area).

steps.title: File evenly
steps.detail: Work each space with a half-round file, then sanding sticks, keeping a smooth concave dish centred between frets and a consistent depth across the radius. Count strokes so every space matches. Leave a small flat margin right at each fret.

steps.title: Finish
steps.detail: Sand through finer grits, clean with naphtha, and oil an unfinished board. Maple boards need refinishing. Then do a fret level and setup.

models.note: Factory scalloped necks exist (a replacement scalloped neck avoids risking your original).
Scalloping breaks through the finish and means a refinish.

warnings: Permanent and value-reducing on collectable guitars.
Wood dust: wear a mask.
pro: Have a luthier do it, or buy a pre-scalloped replacement neck.

title: Twisted neck, back-bow, or bow the truss rod can't fix
time: Diagnosis 20 min; repairs days to weeks
summary: If the neck is bowed more than the rod can correct, back-bowed with the rod slack, or twisted (different relief on the bass and treble sides), the fix is beyond a setup. Here is how to diagnose it and what the repair options are.
symptoms: Relief still too high with the rod tight
Neck back-bowed (strings buzz at the middle frets) with a single-action rod completely loose
Relief under the low E differs noticeably from under the high E
Action measures different on one side at the 12th fret even with saddles matched
A hump where the neck meets the body (ski-jump) that buzzes up high

causes.cause: Neck has taken a forward set over years
causes.check: Rod tight/maxed, relief still high
causes.fix: Washers and clamp (see [fn-truss-rod-stuck-maxed]); else heat-press or compression refret.

causes.cause: Back-bow on a single-action rod
causes.check: Rod slack, neck still back-bowed
causes.fix: Heavier strings, or a pro heat-press; Dan Erlewine notes poorly built factory rods can cause this.

causes.cause: Twist
causes.check: Measure relief on both E strings; difference more than a few thousandths
causes.fix: Small twists: fret leveling with a tapered level; larger: heat treatment, plane the board and refret (pro). Rickenbacker: balance the two rods.

causes.cause: Hump at the neck joint
causes.check: Notched straightedge rocks on the body end of the board
causes.fix: Bolt-on: check for a partial shim leaving an air gap ([fn-neck-shim]); else fret leveling or board planing.

causes.cause: Heat damage
causes.check: Guitar left in a hot car or attic
causes.fix: StewMac measured 175°F on a dashboard; glue joints can creep. Pro assessment.

steps.title: Measure both sides
steps.detail: Measure relief at the 7th–8th fret under the low E and under the high E (capo at 1, fret at the last fret). StewMac notes the treble side is often set 0.001–0.002 in less on purpose, but a larger difference suggests twist. Sight down each edge of the board from the headstock too.

steps.title: Check the rod's range
steps.detail: Back the rod off completely and see where the neck sits, then tighten to the point it feels firm and measure again. This tells you whether the rod can reach the relief you need.

steps.title: Try the simple fixes first
steps.detail: Slight forward bow beyond the rod: washers plus clamping (see [fn-truss-rod-stuck-maxed]). Slight back-bow with a single-action rod: a heavier string gauge adds forward pull. Rickenbacker: adjust the two rods to balance the sides.

steps.title: Fret leveling can hide small errors
steps.detail: A slight twist or hump can often be leveled out in the frets if they are tall enough. Leveling removes metal, so it is a one-time fix per set of frets.

steps.title: Pro options
steps.detail: Heat straightening: the neck is clamped in a corrected shape (often slightly over-corrected) and heated, usually with frets removed or with a heating blanket, then cooled clamped. Compression refretting: new frets with slightly wider tangs push the board into a little backbow; StewMac suggests it for non-adjustable necks such as many older Martins. Planing the fretboard and refretting removes humps and twist in the wood. In bad cases, a new neck or rod replacement is cheaper.

models.note: Compression refret is the classic fix.
A replacement neck is often cheaper than heat-pressing.
Heat-press or board planing; rod work through the headstock.
Long necks twist more readily; store at stable humidity.
Dual rods can correct small twists; old-style rods need the neck moved by hand.

warnings: Do not try heat straightening at home: heat can soften glue joints, lift fretboards and damage finish.
pro: Heat pressing, compression refretting, board planing and rod replacement are all bench work for a luthier.

title: Fix a loose, floppy or stuck tremolo arm
summary: Make the whammy bar stay where you leave it without wobbling, whether it screws in (vintage Strat), pops in (modern Fender, Floyd, Ibanez Edge) or has a tension cap (Ibanez Lo-TRS/ZR).
symptoms: Arm swings down out of reach
Arm wobbles or clicks in its hole
Arm too stiff to swing out of the way
parts: Replacement arm tension spring or bushings if missing/worn

steps.title: Identify your arm type
steps.detail: Screw-in (threaded, vintage and many import Strats), pop-in/push-in (American Professional and many modern Fenders, Floyd Rose with collet or set screw, Ibanez Edge with nylon bushings), or screw-in with a tension cap (Ibanez Lo-TRS, TRS, ZR/Edge-Zero).

steps.title: Screw-in arms: restore the spring or use PTFE
steps.detail: Many screw-in Strat arms rely on a small coil spring in the bottom of the arm hole. Sound On Sound notes it can fall out; if the hole has a closed bottom, put a blob of silicone sealant in, let it cure, then press the spring in on top so it stays put. If no spring will fit, wrap the arm's thread in a couple of turns of PTFE tape and screw it in; renew the tape every so often.

steps.title: Pop-in Fender arms
steps.detail: Modern American Professional-style pop-in arms have adjustable swing tension via small set screws in the bridge (check your model's manual for the exact screw location). Adjust in small steps.

steps.title: Ibanez Edge / Lo-Pro Edge
steps.detail: Push the arm in until it snaps and both bushings are hidden. Ibanez says you can reduce torque by removing bushings, and that if the arm won't stay secure the bushings need replacing.

steps.title: Ibanez Lo-TRS / TRS101 / TRS505 / Edge-Zero / ZR2
steps.detail: Insert and turn clockwise until it stops; turn the torque cap or arm anticlockwise to reduce tension (Lo-TRS/TRS). On Edge-Zero/ZR2, fully loosen the torque adjustment cap before inserting, push the arm in until it snaps, then tighten the cap clockwise for more stiffness.

steps.title: Floyd Rose
steps.detail: Original Floyd arms are held by a collet/nut or a set screw depending on version; snug it so the arm holds position, without overtightening threads in the bridge.

warnings: Do not force an arm into the wrong thread size; Fender, import and Floyd arms vary. Cross-threading the arm hole in a cast block is hard to fix.

title: Deck or block a tremolo
summary: Make a Strat-style or Floyd-style trem rest firmly on the body (decked), stop it moving upward (one-way block) or lock it completely (full block) so bends, broken strings and alternate tunings don't pull the other strings out of tune.
symptoms: Bending one string makes the others go flat
A broken string throws every other string out
You never use the arm or only use dive-downs
Drop tunings throw the whole guitar out
tools: Hardwood offcut, saw and sandpaper (for a block)
Double-sided tape or a little glue (optional)
parts: Extra tremolo springs (up to 5 on a Strat)
Or a commercial stopper: Tremol-No, Hipshot Tremsetter, Floyd Upgrades stopper

specs.label: Fender decked setting
specs.value: Spring tension equal to string tension with the bridge resting on the body, plus an extra 1/2 turn on each claw screw

specs.label: Premier Guitar setup wedge
specs.value: About 1/2 in wide x 1.5 in long, tapering from about 1/8 in to 3/8 in

specs.label: StewMac setup block
specs.value: 1 in wide x 2 in long, tapering from 1/4 in to 1/2 in

steps.title: Choose the option
steps.detail: Decked: bridge sits on the body, arm only lowers pitch; stays usable and keeps tune on bends. One-way block: wood glued or taped in front of the block in the cavity so the bridge can't go past its rest point upward; with a Floyd this lets you keep a floating look but no pull-up. Full block: wood in front and behind the block, turning it into a hardtail. Commercial stoppers (Tremol-No, Hipshot Tremsetter, Floyd stopper) do the same reversibly.

steps.title: Decking a Strat (John LeVan's method)
steps.detail: With the strings at pitch, add springs - LeVan went from two to five. Screw the claw in to put rough tension on, then lower the six pivot screws only until the plate sits flat (overtightening makes it rock on its bevel). Tune, then bend a string while holding a note on another; if the held note goes flat the bridge is still lifting, so tighten the claw further. Repeat until a held note stays put. Fender's shortcut: find the point where the bridge just rests on the body at pitch, then add half a turn to each claw screw. Sound On Sound adds that you can stop at 2–3 springs set so the bridge rests on the body but still dips freely.

steps.title: Making a one-way block
steps.detail: Measure the gap between the front (neck side) of the trem block and the cavity wall with the bridge at its correct rest position. Cut a hardwood piece to fit snugly, fix it to the cavity wall with double-sided tape or a little glue (Bax-shop), then tighten the springs so the bridge always rests against the block. Haze Guitars warns this needs precision - if it's too thin the bridge sits high; too thick and it sits low.

steps.title: Full block
steps.detail: Add a second wedge behind the block (toward the tail) so it can't move either way. This is reversible: remove the wood and rebalance to float again.

steps.title: Temporary block for setups and string changes
steps.detail: A tapered wedge pushed into the gap behind the block (Premier Guitar) or under the back of the bridge (StewMac, Sweetwater) holds the bridge at its normal position while you change strings, set intonation or adjust height. Pad the wedge with cloth so it can't mark the finish. Remove it after tuning and rebalance with the claw.

steps.title: Recheck setup
steps.detail: Decking or blocking changes the bridge angle, which changes saddle height and intonation. Reset action and intonation afterwards.

models.model: Floyd Rose guitars (Jackson, Charvel, ESP, Ibanez, Kramer)
models.note: Blocking or a Tremol-No-style stopper is the usual way to make drop tunings and bends stable; Seymour Duncan's Jay Hale suggests credit-card stock or stacked picks as a DIY wedge for restringing.
Fender's flush (decked) setup: equalise tension with the bridge on the body, then half a turn more on each claw screw.

warnings: Don't overtighten springs to the limit - Fender warns too much tension strains the arm when used.
A wedge that sticks out of the back cavity can be knocked loose; set the guitar down carefully.

title: Fix loose, wobbly or stiff tuners
summary: Stop tuners that wobble, click, slip or feel gritty: tighten hardware correctly, refit loose press-fit bushings, use conversion bushings for oversize holes, and clean and lubricate the gears.
symptoms: Tuner moves in its hole
Buzz or rattle from the headstock
Knob feels gritty or stiff
String slips back flat at the tuner

causes.cause: Loose bushing nut or mounting screw
causes.check: Grip the post and try to rock it; look for a gap under the hex nut or a loose screw on the back.
causes.fix: Snug the nut with a correctly sized nut driver and the screw with a fitting screwdriver - snug, not overtight (StewMac).

causes.cause: Vintage tuners in oversize (10 mm) holes
causes.check: Post rattles even with everything tight; the hole is far bigger than the bushing.
causes.fix: Fit conversion bushings (3/8 in/10 mm or 10.5 mm versions) - StewMac warns vintage machines otherwise move in 10 mm holes.

causes.cause: Loose press-fit bushing
causes.check: Bushing spins or lifts out by hand.
causes.fix: Refit it with a bushing press in small steps; a tiny drop of glue on the outside can help a slightly loose one; a very loose hole needs a larger bushing.

causes.cause: Stripped mounting screw hole
causes.check: Screw turns without tightening.
causes.fix: Plug and redrill (see [bt-strap-buttons-locks] for the plug method) or move up a screw size carefully.

causes.cause: Dirty, dry or worn gears
causes.check: Gritty feel, uneven tension, backlash.
causes.fix: Remove the tuners, flush with naphtha, relubricate (petroleum jelly per StewMac's syringe method, or Tri-Flow on open-gear vintage tuners). Never oil them on the guitar.

causes.cause: Loose button screw (on tuners that have one)
causes.check: Button wobbles on its shaft or the tuner feels slack.
causes.fix: Snug the small screw on the end of the button; on many tuners it sets the turning tension too.

steps.title: Find the loose part
steps.detail: With strings at pitch, play and touch each tuner in turn to find a rattle; then wiggle each post.

steps.title: Tighten hardware
steps.detail: Snug nuts and screws as above. Don't overtighten face nuts: crushing the finish can crack it.

steps.title: Re-seat or convert bushings
steps.detail: Use a press, not a hammer. Add conversion bushings where vintage-style tuners sit in big holes.

steps.title: Clean and lube off the guitar
steps.detail: Take the tuners off, warm them gently, flush the gears with naphtha (or lighter fluid), let dry, then grease or oil and work them back and forth. Keep silicone grease away from finishes.

title: Kahler, headless (Steinberger, Strandberg) and EverTune basics
summary: Orientation for less common bridge systems: Kahler cam-type locking vibratos, headless designs with tuners at the bridge (Steinberger, Strandberg), and EverTune spring-tensioned bridges. Models vary, so the maker's sheet has the exact numbers.
tools: Hex keys supplied by the maker

specs.label: Steinberger gearless tuner (headstock retrofit)
specs.value: 3/8 in (10 mm) post hole; 1/16 in pilot hole 1/8 in deep for the alignment pin

steps.title: Kahler: know what you have
steps.detail: Kahler units use a cam that rotates the strings' anchor point instead of a Floyd-style knife edge rocking on two studs, and many models keep the springs inside the unit rather than in a rear cavity. Identify the model (surface-mount or recessed, with or without fine tuners and string lock) before you start; the factory sheet gives the adjustment points for that model.

steps.title: Kahler: change strings one at a time
steps.detail: As with any floating locking vibrato, swapping one string at a time keeps the unit near balance. Stretch each string well before locking anything.

steps.title: Kahler: balance spring tension
steps.detail: Adjust the unit's spring tension so the arm returns to a stable rest position at pitch. Retune after each adjustment, as with a Floyd.

steps.title: Kahler: set height and intonation
steps.detail: Set action and intonate after the balance is right, using the same 12th-fret harmonic versus fretted note test as any bridge (sharp = lengthen, flat = shorten).

steps.title: Kahler: lock and fine-tune
steps.detail: If your guitar has a locking nut, lock it last and finish with the fine tuners.

steps.title: Headless: identify the string type
steps.detail: Steinberger-style systems traditionally use double-ball-end strings; Strandberg-style systems clamp an ordinary single-ball string at the head piece and cut it at the bridge tuner. Use what the maker specifies.

steps.title: Headless: string changes
steps.detail: Anchor the string at the head end, run it over the zero fret or nut, then through the bridge clamp/tuner. Pull it taut, clamp firmly, then tune with the bridge tuner. Change one string at a time on trem versions.

steps.title: Steinberger gearless tuners (on a headstock)
steps.detail: Turn the large tuning knob fully clockwise to expose the hole, open the small clamp knob anticlockwise, feed the string through, pull tight and clamp the small knob as hard as you can by hand. For the high E, tilt the trem forward slightly and pull the string tight before clamping (it stretches a lot). Cut about 1/4 in from the post. When installing, tighten the hex nut only until the tuner is flush - overtightening breaks the body; tighten knob set screws gradually and alternately.

steps.title: EverTune: how it works
steps.detail: Each saddle has a spring-loaded lever that balances string tension. Bringing a string up to tension moves the module into its working zone, where pitch stays steady even if the string stretches or temperature changes. Once in that zone, final pitch is set with the module's own tension adjustment rather than the headstock tuner. Follow EverTune's manual for which key does what on your version.

steps.title: EverTune: intonation and action
steps.detail: Saddles still need setting for height and intonation, but with EverTune you intonate only after every string sits in the working zone.

warnings: Kahler and Floyd parts are not interchangeable; get parts and the correct manual for your exact model.
Headless guitars often use a zero fret or locking clamp at the head; don't overtighten small clamp screws.
pro: Retrofitting a Kahler, EverTune or headless bridge means routing and bridge-placement calculations - luthier work. Gearnews notes even fitting a Kahler to a PRS Silver Sky needed modifications.

title: Restring a Floyd Rose or Ibanez Edge
summary: Change strings on a double-locking trem without losing the bridge balance: one string at a time, ball ends cut, clamp blocks snug but not crushed, nut locked last.
tools: 3 mm hex key (locking nut pads, Floyd saddle clamp screws)
Thin wooden block or wedge padded with cloth (if removing all strings)
parts: Strings - same brand and gauge as before, or you will need to rebalance

specs.label: Fine-tuner starting position
specs.value: Middle of their travel

specs.label: Bax-shop fine-tuner range
specs.value: Roughly 1.5 to 3 full notes depending on string

steps.title: Unlock the nut
steps.detail: Loosen the three nut clamp screws with a 3 mm key and lift off the pads; keep them in order and note which way they face. Wind all the fine tuners back to the middle of their travel.

steps.title: Change one string at a time
steps.detail: Ibanez, Bax-shop and Seymour Duncan all say: remove and replace a single string, then bring it near pitch, before doing the next. Taking all strings off lets the springs pull the bridge back and you lose the balance. If you must remove all of them (to clean the board), first wedge a padded block under the back of the bridge (or behind the block in the cavity), or use a trem stopper.

steps.title: Remove the old string
steps.detail: Slacken it at the tuner, then loosen the saddle's clamp screw at the back of the bridge (Floyd: 3 mm hex on the long screw; Ibanez Edge: string stopper screw) and pull the end out. Check the clamp for leftover bits of old string, especially after a breakage.

steps.title: Cut the ball end
steps.detail: Snip the ball end off just above the twisted windings, so only straight string goes into the clamp. Seymour Duncan warns not to leave a squashed remnant (flash) that can make the string slip.

steps.title: Clamp the new string
steps.detail: Push the cut end straight into the saddle, between the saddle and the clamp block, so it runs in a straight line. Tighten the clamp screw snug. Bax-shop and Fender both warn against overtightening: it can crack the block, damage the saddle or flatten the string so it breaks there.

steps.title: Wind on and bring up to pitch
steps.detail: Run the string over the nut and under the string retainer bar to its tuner. Wind 3–4 neat downward wraps (American Musical) with no overlaps. Bring it close to pitch, then do the next string.

steps.title: Stretch thoroughly
steps.detail: Seymour Duncan calls this the most important step: grip each string and pull it gently along its full length, retune, and repeat until it stops going flat.

steps.title: Rebalance if needed
steps.detail: If the bridge is no longer parallel to the body at pitch, adjust the claw screws (see [bt-floyd-balance-setup]).

steps.title: Lock the nut and fine-tune
steps.detail: Fit the pads, tune with the headstock tuners as closely as you can, then tighten the nut screws firmly but not hard. Final tuning is done only with the fine tuners. Turning a fine tuner clockwise raises pitch.

models.note: No clamp to cut into: thread the string through the string holder hook, tune, check intonation, then lock the nut (Ibanez manual).
Same cut-ball-end clamp method; 3 mm for pressure pads and string stopper screw.

models.model: Floyd Rose Original vs licensed (Special, 1000 Series)
models.note: Same procedure; the Original uses hardened steel parts, licensed versions are often softer and the clamp blocks wear faster.

warnings: Don't rest a tilted-back headstock on a hard surface while working - Bax-shop warns the pressure can break it.
Cut string ends are sharp; trim them neatly at the tuners and the back of the bridge.
