title: Rickenbacker bridge adjustment basics
summary: General approach to height and intonation on Rickenbacker six-saddle bridges with the separate R tailpiece, and what to check before loosening anything.
tools: Small screwdrivers and hex keys to fit your bridge

steps.title: Identify your bridge
steps.detail: Rickenbacker has used several bridge designs over the years. Before loosening screws, look at how the bridge base is fixed to the body and which screws set height and which set intonation. Change strings one at a time so nothing shifts.

steps.title: Set relief first
steps.detail: Rickenbacker necks have their own truss rod arrangement; get relief right before working on the bridge.

steps.title: Set height
steps.detail: Use the bridge's height adjusters to set the low and high E heights, then bring the middle strings into line with the fretboard radius (understring radius gauge) if the saddles allow individual height changes.

steps.title: Intonate
steps.detail: Compare 12th-fret harmonic with fretted note; move each saddle back if sharp, forward if flat, retuning each time.

steps.title: Check the tailpiece path
steps.detail: Strings should run cleanly from the saddles to the R tailpiece without touching the back of the bridge body.

warnings: Don't strip small screws in the bridge; use the correct driver size and don't force seized screws - penetrating oil and patience, or a tech.
pro: Vintage Rickenbacker hardware is model-specific and some parts are hard to replace; if screws are seized or a bridge needs moving, see a tech familiar with Rickenbackers.

title: Set up a Tune-o-matic bridge (ABR-1 and Nashville)
summary: Height, radius, saddle orientation and intonation on Gibson-style Tune-o-matic bridges, plus the differences between ABR-1 and Nashville, and stopping rattles from the retainer wire and saddles.
symptoms: Saddles run out of travel when intonating
Bridge collapses or the middle strings sit low
Rattling or buzzing from the bridge
Bridge leaning toward the neck
tools: Bridge jack (optional, to turn thumbwheels under tension)
Small flat screwdriver for saddle screws

specs.label: ABR-1
specs.value: Original Tune-o-matic; posts screw directly into the wood (Gibson 6-32 thread); retainer wire holds the saddles

specs.label: Nashville
specs.value: Slightly larger with more saddle travel; posts screw into metal bushings pressed into the top

specs.label: Post thread
specs.value: 6-32 for Gibson, M4 x 0.7 for many imports (ABR-1-style posts)

specs.label: ABR-1 post height
specs.value: About 1/2 in above the top, rest of the 1 in post in the wood

specs.label: Typical TOM radius
specs.value: 12 in

specs.label: Les Paul neck angle
specs.value: About 4 degrees optimum, 3–5 degrees in practice (StewMac)

steps.title: Check saddle orientation
steps.detail: Intonation screw heads should face the neck (pickups), not the tailpiece. Reversed, the screw heads can touch the strings and change the break angle. If the bridge was put on backwards, flip it so this is true while still allowing saddle travel.

steps.title: Check posts are straight and seated
steps.detail: Posts must be perpendicular. Bent posts lean the bridge and hurt intonation - straighten or replace them. ABR-1 posts should stand about 1/2 in proud; if they stick up above the bridge and dig into your hand, they aren't screwed far enough into the body.

steps.title: Set height
steps.detail: Raise or lower each side with the thumbwheel (Nashville) or post (ABR-1), watching 12th-fret action. The bridge base should sit flat on both wheels. A bridge jack lets you turn the wheels without slackening strings; otherwise slacken a little first so the posts don't lean.

steps.title: Check the radius
steps.detail: Measure the fretboard with a radius gauge. Most TOMs are 12 in; if your board is flatter or rounder, the saddle slots must be filed to suit (see [bt-tom-notch-saddles]). A bridge that has sagged in the middle with age has lost its radius and should be replaced.

steps.title: Intonate
steps.detail: Fretted 12th sharp vs harmonic = move saddle back; flat = forward. Retune between moves.

steps.title: Fix rattles
steps.detail: Common rattle sources: a loose ABR-1 retainer wire, loose saddle screws in their threads, or posts loose in their holes. Press on each part while playing to find it. The retainer wire's curve is meant to press down on the saddle screws; if it has lost that tension, re-bend it or replace it with an original-style wire (StewMac shows making one from 0.018 in plain string). Many techs simply remove a buzzing wire, though then saddles fall out when restringing.

steps.title: Check the stopbar relationship
steps.detail: Strings should not touch the back edge of the bridge on their way to the tailpiece. See [bt-stopbar-height-topwrap].

models.model: Gibson Les Paul Standard / Classic / Custom
models.note: Nashville on many modern Les Pauls; ABR-1 on historic and many Classics. StewMac describes converting a Les Paul Classic from Nashville to ABR-1 by pulling bushings, plugging the 17/64 in holes with maple and drilling 1/8 in post holes - a bench job.

models.model: Gibson SG / ES-335 / Explorer / Flying V
models.note: Tune-o-matic with stopbar (or trapeze on some 335s); same procedure.
Usually metric posts and bushings (M4 or larger); check thread before buying replacement posts.

models.model: ESP/LTD, PRS SE and other TOM-equipped guitars
models.note: Same method; many use locking TOM bridges with set screws to lock the bridge to the posts.

warnings: Keep a bridge jack flat on the top - tilting it puts metal on the finish.
pro: Converting between Nashville and ABR-1, or moving a misplaced bridge, involves plugging and redrilling the top; leave that to a luthier.

title: Set up a wraparound bridge (Les Paul Junior, PRS stoptail)
summary: Get the best intonation and action from one-piece wraparound bridges - plain bar, compensated casting, or adjustable versions - and understand their built-in compromises.
symptoms: Some strings intonate, others don't
Bridge tips forward or the studs lean
Bridge rattles on its studs
tools: Stop tailpiece wrench or large flat screwdriver for studs
parts: Locking studs (e.g. TonePros) to stop the bridge rattling or tipping

specs.label: Typical stud spacing
specs.value: 3-1/4 in (StewMac compensated wraparound and Pigtail)

specs.label: StewMac compensated wraparound
specs.value: M8 posts, 14 in radius, compensated for an unwound G

specs.label: StewMac wraparound for PRS
specs.value: Studs 82 mm centre to centre, M8 x 1.25, 12 in radius, adjustable G and B saddles

steps.title: Know the limits
steps.detail: A plain bar wraparound has one fixed witness line for all six strings, so only the overall angle can be set. A compensated casting (the stagger on top) is shaped to suit a particular G string - many are made for an unwound G, so a wound G set won't intonate as well. Adjustable versions add individual saddles or two adjustable saddles.

steps.title: String it correctly
steps.detail: Strings feed through the front of the bridge (pickup side) and wrap over the top toward the neck.

steps.title: Set the overall angle
steps.detail: Most wraparounds have two adjusting screws (or the stud positions) that move the bass and treble ends independently. Intonate the low E with the bass-side adjustment and the high E with the treble-side adjustment, checking the 12th-fret harmonic against the fretted note. Then check the others; on a compensated bridge most should be close.

steps.title: Set the height
steps.detail: Raise or lower both studs evenly to set action; the radius is fixed by the casting. Retune and recheck intonation.

steps.title: Stop rattles and tipping
steps.detail: StewMac's road-ready case replaced the posts with TonePros locking studs so the bridge sat tight and parallel to the body. If the adjustment screws are wound fully out and the bridge still can't intonate, the studs were placed wrong - a wider-range adjustable bridge (e.g. Pigtail) can rescue it.

models.model: Gibson Les Paul Junior / Special / SG Junior / Melody Maker
models.note: Wraparound on two studs; compensated or plain-bar depending on era. Gibson pre-set compensation favours a wound or plain G depending on version; check yours.
StewMac's compensated wraparound fits the factory studs on most imported Juniors and Specials (3-1/4 in spacing).
PRS's one-piece stoptail is compensated; PRS adjustable stoptails and aftermarket copies add adjustable G/B or full saddles. StewMac's PRS-style unit uses 82 mm M8 studs.

title: Set up and upgrade a Telecaster bridge
summary: Height and intonation on vintage 3-barrel-saddle Tele bridges, why they never intonate perfectly, fitting compensated saddles, and the 6-saddle and modern alternatives.
symptoms: G string or B string won't intonate with the 3-saddle bridge
Saddles rattle or rock
Bridge sidewalls get in the way of palm muting
tools: Small hex key for saddle heights (StewMac: 1.5 mm on Tele 3-saddle)

specs.label: Fender string height 7.25 in radius (17th fret)
specs.value: Bass 5/64 in (2 mm), treble 4/64 in (1.6 mm)

specs.label: Fender string height 9.5–12 in radius (17th fret)
Gotoh In-Tune compensated saddles
specs.value: Diameter 0.310 in (7.87 mm); 2-1/8 in string spread; fits vintage-style Tele bridges

specs.label: Wilkinson adjustable compensated Tele bridge
specs.value: 3 brass saddles with a central locking pivot screw; 2-5/32 in string spread; string-through

steps.title: Know the compromise
steps.detail: A 3-saddle bridge puts two strings on each saddle (low E/A, D/G, B/high E). Each pair wants different lengths, so one saddle position is always a compromise. Compensated (angled or grooved) saddles move each string's contact point to reduce the error.

steps.title: Record your current setup
steps.detail: Before swapping saddles, measure each string's height at the 14th fret (top of fret to bottom of string) and keep the same gauge (StewMac).

steps.title: Set saddle heights
steps.detail: Each barrel has two height screws; adjust both so the saddle is level (a tilted barrel rattles and sets the two strings at odd heights). Match your recorded heights or Fender's specs, then check the strings follow the fretboard radius with a radius gauge.

steps.title: Intonate the pairs
steps.detail: Tune open strings. For each saddle, compare 12th-fret fretted note with open/harmonic for both strings. Plain barrels: set the saddle between what the two strings want - StewMac's advice is to intonate low E first, check A, then settle between. Angled compensated saddles: if one string is very sharp and its partner flat, turn the saddle round so its slant goes the other way.

steps.title: Pivoting saddles (Wilkinson)
steps.detail: Loosen the centre pivot screw and angle the saddle so the sharp string gets longer and the flat one shorter; retighten, retune, repeat until both strings are in tune.

steps.title: Upgrades
steps.detail: Six-saddle bridges intonate each string individually and are standard on many modern Teles. Cut-down (ashtray-less) plates or bridges with lower sidewalls make palm muting easier. Swap like for like on string-through bodies (ferrules on the back) or top-loaders.

models.model: Fender American Vintage / Vintera / Classic Vibe Tele
models.note: Vintage 3-barrel bridge with steel or brass barrels; many newer vintage-style models ship with compensated barrels.

models.model: Fender American Professional / Ultra / Player Tele
models.note: Professional II and Ultra use 3 compensated saddles on a cut-down plate; many Player models use 6 saddles - check yours.
Often 6-saddle top-load or string-through; standard 6-saddle method applies.

title: Stopbar tailpiece height and top-wrapping
summary: Set the stop tailpiece high enough that strings clear the back of the Tune-o-matic, low enough for good break angle, and use top-wrapping when you want the tailpiece down with an easier bending feel.
symptoms: Strings touch the back edge of the bridge
Bridge leaning forward
Bends feel stiff
Tailpiece studs turning or bushings loose
tools: Stop tailpiece wrench (fits the 1/2 in stud)

specs.label: Break angle from back of saddle to stopbar
specs.value: About 13–17 degrees (StewMac)

specs.label: Standard stud spacing
specs.value: 3-1/4 in (82.55 mm) centre to centre

specs.label: Stud threads
specs.value: Metric M8 x 1.25 or US 5/16-24 (Gotoh)

specs.label: Stud position (Gotoh spec)
specs.value: 1-1/2 in behind the centre of the bass-side bridge post

steps.title: Check clearance
steps.detail: Sight along each string from the side. It should leave the saddle crown and run to the tailpiece without touching the back edge of the bridge body. If it touches, the tailpiece is too low for this neck angle and bridge height.

steps.title: Adjust the studs
steps.detail: Slacken the strings a little, then turn both studs equally with a stop-tail wrench so you don't slip and scratch the plating or top. Raise them to clear the bridge; lower them for more break angle (more down-pressure). StewMac's target is about 13–17 degrees: shallower eases bending, steeper transfers more energy.

steps.title: Steep neck angle? Raise and lock
steps.detail: StewMac's example Les Paul had a 5 degree neck angle, so the bridge sat high (about 11/16 in to its top) and strings hit the bridge until the tailpiece was raised. They added 5/16 in set-screw jam nuts in the stud bushings so the studs could be locked tight with the tailpiece raised. Locking studs (TonePros) do a similar job.

steps.title: Top-wrap instead
steps.detail: Thread the strings through the tailpiece from the pickup side (front) and wrap them back over the top of the bar toward the bridge. The strings then approach the saddles at a higher angle even with the tailpiece screwed down, keeping the original hardware. Many players say it slackens the feel; StewMac lists it as the alternative to raising the tailpiece.

steps.title: Recheck intonation
steps.detail: Changing the string path changes witness points slightly; recheck intonation afterwards.

models.model: Gibson Les Paul / SG / ES-335 with stopbar
models.note: Neck angles roughly 1.5–4 degrees for TOM guitars (StewMac); a steeper set means a higher bridge and tailpiece.
Often M8 metric studs; Vibramate and many replacement tailpieces need 3-1/4 in non-staggered spacing.

title: String and set up a Bigsby
summary: Load strings onto the Bigsby roller bar without them popping off the pins, keep them seated over the tension bar, and stop the bridge from dragging so the guitar returns to pitch.
tools: Short dowel with a nail in it (pre-bend tool) or a Vibramate Spoiler
Abrasive cord and lubricant for saddles
parts: Strings (some players prefer a slightly heavier set for stability)

steps.title: Pre-bend the ball end
steps.detail: StewMac suggests a dowel with a nail in it to bend the last inch or so of each string into the curve of the roller bar, so the ball end stays on its pin as you wind. Alternatively fit a Vibramate Spoiler - the strings sit in its notches instead of wrapping around the bar and it is held in place by string tension (no drilling).

steps.title: Hold the strings while winding
steps.detail: Wedge a small foam pad under the strings near the bar (StewMac) so they can't spring off the pins while you take up slack at the tuner. Bring each string up enough to stay seated before starting the next.

steps.title: Route under the tension bar
steps.detail: Each string goes from the roller bar, under the tension bar, then over the bridge saddle. Check none has jumped over the tension bar.

steps.title: Make the bridge slick
steps.detail: Inspect Tune-o-matic saddles for cross-grooves and burrs and clean them with abrasive cord. A roller bridge, Graph Tech saddles, or a rocking bar bridge lets the strings move with the bar instead of dragging. Lubricate nut slots too.

steps.title: Stretch and retune
steps.detail: Stretch the strings well, retune, use the arm several times, retune again.

steps.title: Set up the rest
steps.detail: Set action at the bridge and intonate as normal; a Bigsby changes the string's angle over the bridge, so recheck after fitting.

warnings: A floating archtop bridge can be dragged out of position by the vibrato; mark its position with low-tack tape and check it after each restring.

title: Tremolo springs: how many, claw adjustment and spring noise
summary: Choose the number of back springs for your string gauge and feel, adjust the claw safely, and cure ringing or crackling springs on Strat-style and Floyd-style trems.
symptoms: Bridge tips forward after fitting heavier strings
Bridge sits hard on the body after going lighter or tuning down
Arm feels too stiff or too floppy
Springs ring or sing through the pickups
Crackle or pops when you use the arm
tools: Thin foam or soft tubing (for noise)
parts: Matched set of replacement springs (same brand and type)

specs.label: Spring slots on a Strat block
specs.value: Five; most guitars ship with three

specs.label: StewMac kit guide
specs.value: 3 springs standard, 5 for a heavier feel

specs.label: StewMac tremolo tips (floating trems)
specs.value: 3 springs recommended; some players use 2 depending on gauge and style

specs.label: Diamond Guitars (Floyd Rose)
specs.value: 3 springs with heavier strings, 2 with lighter strings

specs.label: Sound On Sound (flatten-only, resting on body)
specs.value: 2 or 3 springs depending on gauge; all 5 for a fully fixed bridge

specs.label: Fender decked setting
specs.value: Balance springs to strings with bridge on the body, then add 1/2 turn to each claw screw

steps.title: Know what the springs do
steps.detail: The springs pull the block toward the neck end of the body; the strings pull the bridge the other way. At pitch the two forces balance. Spring count changes how stiff the arm feels and how much spring tension is available; the claw screws set exactly where the balance lands. Haze Guitars notes that, once balanced, spring count affects feel more than stability.

steps.title: Pick a starting spring count
steps.detail: Typical starting points from the sources: floating with 9s, 2–3 springs; floating with 10s, 3 springs; heavier gauges, lower tunings with heavy strings, or a decked bridge, 4–5 springs. If the springs are almost slack at pitch (claw screwed far out), use fewer. If the claw is screwed nearly to the cavity wall and still can't pull the bridge back, add a spring. Haze Guitars says springs should still be slightly stretched open at rest.

steps.title: Detune before changing springs
steps.detail: Slacken the strings a few turns (or block the bridge, see [bt-deck-or-block-trem]) so the springs are under less load. Unhook each spring from the claw end first using a spring hook. Fit new springs block end first, then hook onto the claw.
steps.warn: A spring that slips under load flies hard enough to chip finish or cut skin. Wear safety glasses and keep fingers out of the line of pull.

steps.title: Arrange springs symmetrically
steps.detail: Use a symmetrical layout (e.g. three straight across, or two outer plus centre). A V or angled layout is fine if symmetrical. Haze Guitars advises not mixing spring brands or types (the black springs on modern 2-point trems and silver vintage springs have different tension); replace the whole set at once (Sweetwater agrees).

steps.title: Adjust the claw
steps.detail: Turn both claw screws by equal amounts - about one turn at a time - then retune and check the bridge angle. In (clockwise) = more spring pull, bridge moves back toward the body. Out = less pull, bridge tips forward. Keep the claw roughly square to the body. Small final tweaks of a quarter or half turn are normal.

steps.title: Cure crackle
steps.detail: The bridge ground wire usually goes to the claw, and the string ground passes through the springs and block. A crackle when using the arm usually means poor contact at the spring ends. Sound On Sound suggests a contact cleaner such as DeoxIT on both ends of each spring. Also check the ground wire solder joint on the claw.

steps.title: Quieten ringing springs
steps.detail: Springs can ring sympathetically and come through the pickups or be heard acoustically. Common fixes are to thread thin foam or soft plastic tubing through the springs, or press a strip of foam lightly against them, so they are damped but still move freely. Make sure no spring touches the cover plate or the wood (Sound On Sound). Replacing tired springs with a fresh set can also change the ring.

steps.title: Recheck everything
steps.detail: After any spring change, retune, recheck float, action and intonation.

models.note: Fender factory float is 1/8 in at the rear of the bridge; most ship with 3 springs.

Same claw principle; the bridge should sit parallel to the body. Ibanez's manual says spring number depends on string gauge and desired angle and gives no fixed chart. Remove the Ibanez Block Lock before changing springs on Edge/Lo-Pro Edge.
Tension is set with a knob on the back of the body rather than claw screws - see [bt-ibanez-edge-zr].

warnings: Never use pliers to stretch springs on - StewMac specifically warns against it.
Keep springs and claw away from the cover plate; contact causes buzz and noise.

title: Balance and set up a Floyd Rose
summary: Get a double-locking trem sitting parallel to the body at pitch, with fine tuners centred, correct action from the studs, and a locking nut and retainer bar that don't pull the tuning when clamped.
symptoms: Bridge tilts forward or back when in tune
Fine tuners run out of travel
Strings go sharp when you lock the nut
Action too high or low and saddles can't be raised individually
tools: 3 mm hex key (nut, studs on modern units)
2.5 mm hex key (saddle lock on many units)
Wooden block the right height to hold the bridge level
parts: Floyd Rose locking nut shims (if nut height needs raising)

specs.label: Bridge attitude at pitch
specs.value: Base plate parallel to the body (Floyd, Ibanez, Fender, PG)

specs.label: MusicRadar medium action (12th fret, top of fret to bottom of string)
specs.value: 1.5 mm 1st string, 2 mm 6th string

specs.label: TC Gakki action (12th fret)
specs.value: 1.5 mm 1st string, 1.5–2.0 mm 6th string

specs.label: John LeVan example finish (12th fret, capo at 1)
specs.value: 2/64 in treble, 3/64 in bass on 0.009–0.042

steps.title: Prepare
steps.detail: Fresh, stretched strings; neck relief set; nut clamps off; fine tuners set to the middle of their travel (Sweetwater, Ibanez).

steps.title: Block method (Sweetwater)
steps.detail: Use the arm to lift the bridge and slide in a block that holds it level with the body. Tighten the claw screws more than you think you need so the bridge stays on the block. Tune to pitch like a hardtail; if the bridge lifts off the block, tighten the claw further or add a spring.

steps.title: Release and level
steps.detail: Dive the bar, remove the block, and let the bridge return. It should tip back and the strings go sharp. Now loosen both claw screws by equal small amounts, retuning each time, until the bridge sits level and the strings are at pitch. Sweetwater's rules: level and flat = tighten claw; level and sharp = loosen claw; in tune but bridge high (tail up) = tighten claw; in tune but bridge low = loosen claw.

steps.title: Without a block (LeVan / Bax-shop)
steps.detail: Tune to pitch, look at the bridge angle, and turn both claw screws equally - about a full turn at a time early on, half or quarter turns near the end - retuning after each. Tuning down makes the bridge sink and tuning up lifts it, so judge only when in tune.

steps.title: Set action at the two studs
steps.detail: Floyd-style saddles have no individual height adjustment; set the whole bridge with the two front studs (3 mm hex on modern studs, a flat screwdriver on older ones). Ibanez Edge and Lo-Pro Edge have stud lock screws you must loosen first and retighten after. Then retune and check the bridge is still level - raising the bridge reduces how far it can travel. Individual string heights are only changed with saddle shims.

steps.title: Check the locking nut
steps.detail: With strings off or slack, make sure the nut is bolted tight to the neck so it can't shift (Haze). The nut's curve must match the fretboard radius or outer/middle strings sit at the wrong heights (LeVan). Nut height is changed with shims under the nut; going lower means removing wood, which is a job for a luthier.

steps.title: Set the string retainer bar
steps.detail: Lower the bar behind the nut just enough that the strings lie flat across the nut and don't change pitch when you clamp the pads (LeVan). Gearnews notes that if strings go sharp when you lock the nut, the bar is often set too high. TC Gakki warns not to overtighten its screws - on some necks they can poke through the back.

steps.title: Lock the nut - snug, not crushed
steps.detail: Tune as accurately as you can at the headstock, then tighten the three clamp screws until snug. LeVan: overtightening strips the bolts and grooves the blocks; Diamond Guitars: overtightening causes tuning problems. Replace pads that show deep string grooves.
steps.warn: Loosen the nut clamps before making big spring or bridge adjustments - Bax-shop warns the screws or saddles can break under high tension otherwise.

steps.title: Fine-tune and recheck
steps.detail: Final tune with the fine tuners. Check the bridge is still parallel; if all strings are slightly off together, a small claw tweak shifts the whole guitar (Gearnews). Then intonate - see [bt-floyd-intonation].

models.model: Jackson / Charvel (Floyd Rose Original or licensed Floyd 1000/Special)
models.note: Same method. Older studs use a slotted screwdriver; modern Floyd studs take a 3 mm hex.
Same method; recessed (routed) Floyds can pull up, surface-mounted ones often only dive.

Should sit parallel to the top when in tune. Loosen stud lock screws (C) before turning the studs (B). MusicRadar notes the Lo-Pro Edge's top profile isn't flat, so judge parallel from the base plate.
Fender: on most free-floating systems the bridge should be parallel to the body; pre-set intonation before stringing and remove the nut pads during setup.
Drop-in for some non-routed guitars; StewMac hosts Floyd's bridge, stud and nut spec sheets for each model.

warnings: Never sand the neck under a locking nut yourself to lower it - the nut screws go through the neck and too little wood weakens it.
Retune after every claw change; judging the angle while out of tune gives wrong results.
pro: Nut height changes needing wood removal, stripped nut or stud threads, or a cracked locking nut block are bench jobs for a luthier.

title: Ibanez Edge, Lo-Pro Edge, Edge-Zero and ZR setup
summary: The Ibanez-specific parts of a locking-trem setup: stud lock screws, the Zero Point System (ZPS) stop rod and sub-spring, the spring knob instead of claw screws, and switching ZPS off to float.
tools: 3 mm hex (stud lock screws, nut pressure pads, string stopper screws)
2 mm hex (Edge-Zero stud lock bolts, ZR2 saddle lock screws)

specs.label: Bridge attitude
specs.value: Parallel to the body when in tune

steps.title: Edge / Lo-Pro Edge: angle with claw screws
steps.detail: Remove the rear cover. If the bridge tips forward (toward the neck), tighten the claw screws; if it's pulled back, loosen them. Retune and recheck until parallel. Remove the Block Lock (if fitted) before changing springs.

steps.title: Edge / Lo-Pro Edge: height
steps.detail: Loosen the stud lock screws (C) on each side first, then turn the studs (B): clockwise lowers, anticlockwise raises. Retighten the lock screws.

steps.title: Edge-Zero / ZR2: angle with the ZPS knob
steps.detail: The spring tension knob is on the back of the body. If the stop rod isn't touching the stopper, or the bridge tips forward, turn the knob clockwise to tighten. If the tremolo block isn't touching the stop rod, or it tilts back, turn anticlockwise. Goal: roughly parallel to the body at pitch, with block and stop rod just touching.

steps.title: Turn ZPS off to float freely
steps.detail: Hold the arm up so the block moves away from the stop rod, remove the stop rod and sub-spring, then set the bridge parallel with the knob. Retune repeatedly - spring changes affect tuning.

steps.title: Edge-Zero stud locks
steps.detail: With the bridge and stud bolts removed, fit the stud lock bolts in the bottom holes with their hex openings facing up; then put a 2 mm key down the top of each stud and turn clockwise until the lock bolt meets the anchor and stops.

steps.title: Intonation
steps.detail: Edge / Lo-Pro Edge: loosen nut pad screw (D) and saddle lock screw (E), move saddle, tighten, retune; use the rear hole for the saddle screw if it needs to go further back. Edge-Zero / ZR2: thread the intonation bolts into the rear saddle holes until they touch the bridge wall, loosen saddle lock screws (2 mm), set with the intonation screws, tighten, then return the bolts. The EJK1000 tool works on Edge, Lo-Pro Edge and Edge-Pro.

steps.title: Fine tuners and nut
steps.detail: Set fine tuners to mid-travel before locking the nut. Lock the nut first, then fine-tune.

models.note: Uses a ball-bearing pivot instead of knife edges plus ZPS springs and a removable stop bar; stable but limits up-bends with ZPS engaged (Wikipedia). First fitted to the S series.
ZR-II succeeded the ZR on S Prestige; Edge-Zero is a knife-edge trem with ZPS3 springs, first on 2008 RG Prestige.
Single-locking trem whose ZPS-FX springs engage only when you pull up (SV Prestige).
Screw-in arm with torque adjustment; arm stop screw under the block (Lo-TRS/TRS).

title: Intonate a Floyd Rose or Edge bridge
summary: Move the saddles on a locking trem to fix sharp or flat fretted notes without the saddle shooting forward under string tension - using slack, a trem stopper, or an intonation tool.
tools: 2.5 mm or 3 mm hex key for the saddle lock bolt (check your bridge)
Optional: Floyd Rose intonation tool ('The Key') or Ibanez EJK1000

steps.title: Finish the rest of the setup first
steps.detail: Balance, action, relief, nut and pickup height all affect intonation (Haze). Fresh strings, stretched and tuned, guitar in playing position.

steps.title: Unlock the nut
steps.detail: Loosen the nut clamps so you can retune with the headstock tuners during the process. Re-lock at the very end.

steps.title: Test each string
steps.detail: Tune the open string (or the 12th-fret harmonic) to pitch and compare with the fretted 12th-fret note. Fretted note sharp: saddle must move back, away from the neck. Fretted note flat: saddle must move forward, toward the neck (LeVan, Gearnews).

steps.title: Move the saddle with the string slack
steps.detail: Detune that string well down so the saddle isn't under pull, loosen the saddle lock bolt on top of the bridge plate, slide the saddle a small amount (Bax-shop suggests starting with about 1 mm), retighten the bolt firmly, retune and recheck. Don't try to shove the string aside under full tension - Haze Guitars explains the tension drags the saddle forward and you lose control.

steps.title: Faster method: hold the bridge down
steps.detail: Push the trem arm down until the strings go slack; then the saddle lock can be loosened without the saddle being pulled. It is awkward because you must hold the arm while moving the saddle.

steps.title: Faster method: the saddle tool trick
steps.detail: Floyd's intonation tool ('The Key', Allparts) hooks between the back of the bridge and the string-lock screw and holds the saddle against string pull, so you can loosen the lock bolt and wind the saddle forward or back under tension without retuning from scratch. Haze notes it only fits Original Floyd Rose and licensed OFR copies and works best moving saddles forward, so start with saddles slightly back. Ibanez's EJK1000 does the same on Edge, Lo-Pro Edge and Edge-Pro: clip it on the fine tuner, hook the saddle, turn the dial - no need to loosen the tuning.

steps.title: When the saddle runs out of slot
steps.detail: Each saddle lock bolt can sit in a front or rear threaded hole. If the saddle can't go back far enough (often after going to heavier strings), take the bolt out - watch for its small washer - and fit it in the other hole (Ibanez, MusicRadar, Bax-shop).

steps.title: Recheck balance and lock up
steps.detail: Big saddle moves shift the bridge balance slightly. Recheck the bridge is parallel, retune, lock the nut, and finish with the fine tuners.

models.note: Ibanez: move the intonation bolts into the rear saddle screw holes until they touch the bridge wall, loosen saddle lock screws (2 mm), set position with the intonation screws, retighten, then return the bolts.

models.model: Fender Floyd Rose and American Deluxe locking trems
models.note: Fender suggests a rough pre-set before stringing: first saddle at scale length (nut to centre of 12th fret, doubled), each next saddle back by its string's gauge, 4th parallel with 2nd, 5th and 6th like 2nd and 3rd.

warnings: Retighten every saddle lock bolt firmly; a loose saddle can slide when you dive and change intonation (Diamond Guitars says keep them very tight).

title: Jazzmaster, Jaguar and Mustang vibratos
summary: Set the offset Fender floating vibrato (with its trem lock) and the rocking bridge so strings stop buzzing and jumping saddles; options include heavier strings, a buzz stop, or a Mastery-style replacement bridge. Includes the Mustang's Dynamic Vibrato.
symptoms: Strings jump out of saddle grooves when strummed hard
Buzz or rattle from the bridge
Guitar won't stay in tune with the trem lock engaged
Bridge leans toward the neck
parts: Replacement bridge such as a Mastery bridge (optional)

specs.label: StewMac Golden Age Jazzmaster/Jaguar bridge
specs.value: Post spacing 2-7/8 in (73.02 mm); string spread 2-3/16 in; body bushing hole 11/32 in dia x 13/16 in deep

steps.title: Understand the parts
steps.detail: The vibrato is a separate tailpiece with a spring adjusted by a screw; the bridge sits on two legs in thimbles (bushings) and is meant to rock as the vibrato moves, which helps it return to pitch. Overall height comes from the two outer adjusting screws; individual saddles fine-tune heights.

steps.title: Set the vibrato with the lock (Fender's method)
steps.detail: Engage the trem lock, tune the guitar, then release the lock. Use the vibrato's tension adjustment screw to bring the strings back to pitch. Tuning should now be the same with the lock on or off. Repeat after any gauge change.

steps.title: Check the bridge rocks freely
steps.detail: With strings at pitch, move the arm and watch the bridge rock with it. If it leans permanently toward the neck or sticks, check the legs are seated in the thimbles and not bent; reset it upright and retune.

steps.title: Stop strings jumping saddles
steps.detail: The Jazzmaster/Jaguar string angle over the bridge is shallow. Options, roughly in order: use a heavier string set (more tension holds strings in place); make sure each saddle groove is the right one for its string and not worn; raise the bridge a little to increase break angle; fit a buzz-stop bar on the vibrato plate to push strings down behind the bridge (it adds friction and reduces vibrato range); or fit a replacement bridge with deeper, better-shaped saddles such as a Mastery bridge. Check whether your thimbles are US or import size before buying a bridge.

steps.title: Set heights and intonation
steps.detail: Use the outer screws for overall action and the saddles for radius. Intonate as usual; on a rocking bridge, intonate with the bridge sitting upright at its rest point.

steps.title: Mustang Dynamic Vibrato
steps.detail: The Mustang uses a floating vibrato with springs under the tailpiece and a separate bridge on two posts in thimbles that rocks with it. The same principles apply: let the bridge sit upright at pitch, set heights at the posts and saddles, and keep strings seated in their grooves; heavier strings or a better saddle design help stability.

models.model: Fender American Vintage / American Original Jazzmaster and Jaguar
models.note: Vintage-correct bridge and trem lock. Fender also sells a Jaguar mute kit for these.
Modern bridges with deeper saddles reduce string-jumping.

models.model: Squier Classic Vibe / Vintera / Japanese-made offsets
models.note: Often use smaller import-size thimbles; aftermarket bridges come in US and import versions.
Dynamic Vibrato with rocking bridge; same setup logic.

title: Notch (slot) Tune-o-matic saddles
summary: Cut string slots in new, unslotted Tune-o-matic saddles so strings stay put, are evenly spaced and follow the fretboard radius.
symptoms: New replacement bridge with blank saddles
Strings slide sideways on the saddles
High E slips off the edge of the fretboard
Strings break at the saddle
tools: Gauged nut-slotting files (string size or a few thousandths larger)

steps.title: Rough-position saddles
steps.detail: Set saddles roughly where intonation will want them, using the old bridge as a reference.

steps.title: Place the outer strings
steps.detail: Fit the bridge and old strings. Put the two E strings where they line up with the outer edges of the bridge pickup's pole pieces and sit correctly on the fretboard edges. Mark this E-to-E spread on a string spacing rule and space the rest proportionally - bass side slightly wider than treble.

steps.title: Mark plain strings by tapping
steps.detail: Hold each plain string in position and give it a light tap with a fretting hammer to leave a small groove, then chase that groove with a nut file just deep enough to hold the string. Recheck spacing after each - taps can shift it. Dan Erlewine notes hammering alone can break strings, so do this with old strings.

steps.title: Scribe wound strings
steps.detail: Tapping doesn't work well on wound strings. Scribe a line each side of the string with a craft knife and file between the lines, checking placement constantly.

steps.title: Set depth and radius
steps.detail: File so roughly half of each wound string sits above the saddle top and plain strings sit just below the top. Middle strings should end up slightly higher to follow the fretboard radius - check with a radius gauge; a 10 in board needs more filing than the bridge's usual 12 in. Slope each slot down toward the tailpiece at roughly the string's angle.

steps.title: Polish
steps.detail: Run abrasive cord through each slot to remove burrs and file marks, which cause breakage and tuning snags.

warnings: Don't use a file wider or deeper than needed - a sloppy slot lets the string wander.
Bad slot placement can push the high E off the edge of the fretboard.
pro: If the saddles are already over-cut, replace them rather than trying to fix the slots.

title: Place and fit a floating archtop bridge (Gretsch and jazz guitars)
summary: A floating bridge is held only by string pressure, so it can move during string changes. Find the right position for intonation, fit its foot to the top's arch, and mark it so you can put it back.
symptoms: Intonation suddenly wrong after a string change
Bridge leaning toward the neck
Bridge rocks or has gaps under the foot
Thin, weak tone or buzz from the bridge

specs.label: Scale length check
specs.value: Measure nut to 12th fret and double it

specs.label: StewMac archtop bridge (ebony/rosewood)
specs.value: 12 in saddle radius; centre height 1-1/16 to 1-1/4 in; compensated for wound G

specs.label: Archtop neck angle
specs.value: Around 3.5 degrees and up (StewMac)

steps.title: Mark before you move it
steps.detail: Before slackening strings, put low-tack drafting tape on the top against each end of the bridge so you can return it exactly. Change strings one at a time so the bridge stays clamped. StewMac warns ordinary masking tape can mark new lacquer if left on; remove tape quickly.

steps.title: Find the rough position
steps.detail: Measure from the nut to the centre of the 12th fret and double it for the scale length. The saddle's crown should sit at about that distance on the treble side, slightly further back on the bass side (compensation). Also check the bridge is centred so the outer strings run evenly along the fretboard edges.

steps.title: Fine-tune position by ear
steps.detail: Tune up and compare the 12th-fret harmonic with the fretted note on both E strings. Both sharp: slide the whole bridge back toward the tail. Both flat: slide it toward the neck. Treble right but bass sharp: angle the bass end back. Slacken slightly before nudging, then retune. Keep the bridge upright.

steps.title: Check the fit of the foot
steps.detail: Slide a thin feeler under the foot edges with strings at pitch; it should not go in anywhere. Gaps rob tone and let the bridge rock.

steps.title: Fit the foot to the top
steps.detail: Remove strings (after marking). Mask the top around the bridge area with low-tack tape, then stick sandpaper over it, grit up. Scribble the underside of the foot with white pencil and slide the bridge back and forth along the string direction on the sandpaper, keeping it upright (a fitting jig helps). The top's arch transfers to the foot. Stop when the pencil marks are gone everywhere. Check with no gaps.

steps.title: Set height
steps.detail: Use the thumbwheels on the posts to set action. Keep both wheels similar so the saddle stays level.

models.model: Gretsch hollowbodies (6120, Country Gentleman, Falcon, Streamliner)
models.note: Many use a floating bar or rocking bar bridge on an ebony or rosewood base, sometimes pinned to the top. If a Bigsby is fitted, the bridge can be pulled forward when you use the arm - check its position often.

models.model: Gibson ES-175, L-5 and jazz archtops
models.note: Floating wooden base with Tune-o-matic or wooden saddle; same placement method.
Same method; many imports ship with a poorly fitted foot that benefits from sanding to fit.

warnings: Never sand a bridge directly on a bare top - always mask the finish first.
Cheap gold plating can tarnish from fumes off new finishes or plastic; StewMac suggests a tiny amount of fine polish and care, because the plating is thin.
pro: If the top has sunk or cracked under the bridge, or the bridge must be shimmed significantly, see a luthier.

title: Set up a 2-point Strat tremolo
summary: Set float, height and intonation on a two-pivot synchronized trem (Fender American Standard, American Professional, American Ultra, Player and similar), which rocks on two knife edges against two height-adjustable studs.
tools: Hex key or screwdriver for the pivot studs (check yours)

specs.label: Fender spec for float
specs.value: 1/8 in (3.2 mm) gap at the rear of the bridge

specs.label: Premier Guitar (George Ellison) for vintage and American Standard trems
specs.value: Front edge down, rear raised about 3/32 in

specs.label: Gearnews view for modern 2-point
specs.value: Baseplate parallel to the body; posts set overall height, saddles fine-tune

specs.label: Fender string height, 9.5–12 in radius (17th fret)
specs.value: 4/64 in (1.6 mm) bass and treble

specs.label: Fender pivot screws (part 0028957049)
specs.value: Pair of threaded steel pivot screws for American, Ultra and American Standard Strats, 1986 to present

steps.title: Strings and neck first
steps.detail: Fit and stretch your chosen gauge, tune to pitch and set relief. Any later gauge or tuning change upsets the spring balance.

steps.title: Inspect the knife edges and studs
steps.detail: Unstring or slacken and look at the two notches in the front edge of the plate and the collars of the two studs. A sharp, clean edge riding in a groove is what you want. Burrs or a flattened edge, or a stud with a notch worn in it, cause sticking and return-to-pitch problems. Gearnews and Haze Guitars suggest filing burrs off worn edges with a fine file and polishing out the file marks; notched studs should be replaced. Smear a little petroleum jelly on the contact points.

steps.title: Seat the plate on the studs
steps.detail: Pull the bridge flush to the body with the arm and adjust the two pivot studs until the plate sits fully flush with no lift at the front or back edge (Fender). Turning a stud raises or lowers that side of the whole bridge, so keep both sides even unless you deliberately want different bass and treble heights.

steps.title: Set the float
steps.detail: Tune to pitch. Adjust both claw screws evenly (in = bridge pulls back toward the body, out = bridge tips forward), retuning after each change, until the rear gap matches the target. Fender's spec is 1/8 in at the rear. Many techs and Gearnews prefer the plate closer to parallel with the body on a 2-point because it returns to pitch more reliably; tilting it forward gives more pull-up range. Pick one and be consistent.

steps.title: Set height at the studs, then fine-tune at the saddles
steps.detail: Use the studs for overall action, then set individual saddles to match the fretboard radius with an understring radius gauge. Raising the studs a lot changes the float slightly, so recheck the rear gap.

steps.title: Intonate
steps.detail: Compare 12th-fret harmonic with fretted note: sharp fretted note = move saddle back; flat = forward. Retune between moves. Recheck the float afterwards.

steps.title: Exercise and verify
steps.detail: Work the arm up and down, retune, play a bend on the G or B while holding a note on another string and note how much it detunes. Some detuning is normal on a floating trem. If it returns flat or sharp, see [bt-trem-wont-return].

models.model: Fender American Standard (1986–2016), American Professional / Professional II, American Ultra
models.note: Two-point trem on threaded pivot studs; American Standard and later use a pop-in or screw-in arm depending on year. Fender sells the pivot screws as part 0028957049.
Two-point trem with bent-steel saddles; same setup method.

models.model: Squier and other imports with 2-point trems
models.note: Same method. Cheaper studs may be softer, so check the stud collars for notches first.
Same principle; many use Gotoh or Wilkinson units with steel blocks. Wilkinson VS-style units are designed to float parallel.

warnings: Do not pry a stud sideways or force a worn one; the stud anchors are pressed into the body and can split the wood if mishandled. If a stud anchor is loose, see a tech.
pro: If the stud anchors are loose or the body wood around them is cracked, or the studs won't turn, take it to a tech - re-seating anchors needs care.

title: Set up a PRS tremolo
summary: PRS Patented and Gen III tremolos rock on six knife-edge screws; the screw heights must be even and the springs balanced so the bridge floats and returns to pitch.
tools: Screwdriver for the six pivot screws

steps.title: Strings and neck first
steps.detail: Fit your gauge, stretch, tune, set relief. PRS trems are sensitive to gauge changes.

steps.title: Set the six pivot screws evenly
steps.detail: Gearnews points out that on PRS-style bridges all six screws must be at the same height, more critically than on a vintage Strat. With strings slackened a little, set each screw so its head just meets the bridge plate without pulling it down; the bridge should rock freely with no screw holding it down more than the others.

steps.title: Balance the springs
steps.detail: Adjust the claw screws evenly, retuning after each change, until the bridge floats at the attitude PRS specifies for your model (Gearnews: the baseplate parallel to the body on PRS-style floating trems). PRS ships its trems floating; check PRS's published setup for your guitar.

steps.title: Set action and intonation
steps.detail: Set the saddles to the fretboard radius and intonate as usual. Recheck the float afterwards.

steps.title: Check return to pitch
steps.detail: Use the arm, retune, repeat. If strings return sharp, look first at the nut and tuners (PRS locking tuners need only part of a wrap).

models.model: PRS core and S2 with PRS Patented or Gen III trem
models.note: Six-screw knife-edge design; PRS Phase locking tuners on many models.
PRS-designed trem on SE models works the same way.
Vintage-style six-screw trem; Gearnews describes the Silver Sky trem as set flush with the body.

title: Set up a vintage 6-screw Strat tremolo
summary: Get a vintage-style synchronized tremolo (six pivot screws, bent-steel saddles) pivoting smoothly, floating at the right angle and returning to pitch. Do this after a string-gauge change, when the bridge sits at an odd angle, or when it grinds, clicks or won't come back in tune.
tools: #2 Phillips screwdriver with a long shank (8 in or more for the claw screws)
0.050 in or 1.5 mm hex key for saddle height (check your saddles)
6 in steel rule with 1/64 in marks
parts: Fresh set of strings in the gauge you will keep using
Spare tremolo springs (only if replacing - replace all at once)

specs.label: Fender factory float (vintage trem)
specs.value: 1/8 in (3.2 mm) gap between the back edge of the bridge plate and the body

specs.label: StewMac kit-assembly float
specs.value: 3/32 in between back of bridge and body

specs.label: Fender pivot-screw method
specs.value: Raise all six screws to about 1/16 in (1.6 mm) above the plate, then lower the two outer screws flush with the plate

specs.label: Fender string height, 7.25 in radius (17th fret)
specs.value: Bass 5/64 in (2 mm), treble 4/64 in (1.6 mm)

specs.label: Fender string height, 9.5–12 in radius (17th fret)
specs.value: Bass and treble 4/64 in (1.6 mm)

steps.title: Decide gauge and tuning first
steps.detail: Spring tension balances string tension, so every later step depends on the strings. Fit the set (and tuning) you will actually use, stretch each string by pulling it gently away from the board along its length, and tune to pitch. Changing gauge or tuning later means rebalancing.

steps.title: Check the neck before the bridge
steps.detail: Set neck relief first (Fender: 0.010 in at the 8th fret for 9.5–12 in radius necks, capo at fret 1, fret the 6th string at the last fret). Bridge height, float and intonation all interact with relief.

steps.title: Free up the pivot
steps.detail: Take off the back cover. Push the bridge down flat to the body with the arm (or slacken strings a little). Loosen all six front-edge screws and raise them to about 1/16 in (1.6 mm) above the plate. Now screw the two OUTER screws down until their heads are just flush with the plate. The bridge rocks on these two; the four inner screws sit slightly high so they steady the plate without binding it. StewMac's alternative is to lower each screw until it just touches the plate, listening for scratching or clicking as you rock the bridge.
steps.warn: Do not crank the screws down onto the plate. A tight screw makes the plate rock on its bevelled edge and stick, so it won't return to pitch.

steps.title: Lubricate the knife edge
steps.detail: Put a tiny dab of lip balm or petroleum jelly where the plate's front edge touches the screw shafts. Fender and StewMac both suggest this. Replace any screw whose shaft is visibly worn or notched.

steps.title: Set the float with the claw
steps.detail: With the guitar tuned and nothing touching the arm, measure the gap between the back of the bridge plate and the body. Turn both claw screws in the cavity equally: clockwise (in) pulls the bridge back toward the body, anticlockwise (out) lets the strings pull it forward. Work about one turn at a time on each screw, then retune all six strings, then measure again. Repeat until you hit Fender's 1/8 in gap (or your preference: Paul White in Sound On Sound suggests about 1/16 in for a gentle wobble and about 3/16 in if you want roughly a tone and a half of up-bend).

steps.title: Speed up the balancing with over-tuning
steps.detail: Each string you tune pulls the bridge forward and flattens the strings already tuned. MusicRadar's tip: when the trem is sitting low, tune the 6th string about 20 percent sharp, then a little less sharp on each string after it, so they all land near pitch together.

steps.title: Set saddle heights to the board radius
steps.detail: Measure fretboard radius (most vintage Strats are 7.25 in, most modern ones 9.5 in). Set the two E strings to height first, then use an understring radius gauge to bring the four middle saddles into the same curve. Keep each saddle level (both grub screws equal) so it doesn't rock. If the grub screws stick up and catch your palm, use shorter screws or contoured saddles.

steps.title: Set intonation
steps.detail: Pickup selector in the middle, volume and tone up. Compare the 12th-fret harmonic with the fretted 12th-fret note on each string. Fretted note sharp: turn the intonation screw to move the saddle back (away from the neck). Fretted note flat: move it forward. Retune after every move. Check intonation again after any float change, because a tilted bridge moves the witness points.

steps.title: Final checks
steps.detail: Dip and pull the arm several times, retune, and check that each string comes back to within a cent or two. If one string keeps returning flat or sharp, see [bt-trem-wont-return]. Refit the back cover; springs must not touch it or the wood.

models.model: Fender American Vintage / Vintera / Classic Vibe Strats
models.note: Vintage 6-screw synchronized trem with bent-steel or stamped saddles; Fender's 1/8 in float spec applies.

models.model: Squier Affinity/Sonic and many import Strats
models.note: Often a 6-screw trem with a thinner, lighter block and pot-metal saddles. StewMac's Squier mods video swaps in steel saddles threaded from below so no screws stick out.
Fender's own setup guide groups these with the vintage synchronized trem procedure.

warnings: Springs store a lot of energy. Detune before removing or fitting springs and use a spring hook, not pliers - StewMac warns pliers slip and send the spring into the finish or your knuckles.
If a pivot-screw hole is misaligned or stripped the bridge will never pivot cleanly; repair the hole (dowel and re-drill) rather than forcing it.
pro: If the pivot holes don't line up with the plate (common on replacement bodies), the screw holes are stripped, or the block binds against the cavity wall, have a tech plug and re-drill or relieve the cavity.

title: Bridge lifting: test and first aid
summary: A gap opening under the back edge of the bridge means the glue joint is failing. Test it with a thin feeler, slacken the strings right away if it is open, and plan a reglue.
symptoms: A dark line or gap under the back (tail-side) edge of the bridge
Action rising quickly
Bridge wings rocking forward
Top rippling just behind the bridge

causes.cause: Heat or big humidity swings softening/stressing the glue
causes.check: Recent hot car, heater, or very dry/wet season
causes.fix: Reglue - see [ac-bridge-reglue].

causes.cause: Bridge glued on top of finish (common on budget guitars)
causes.check: Shiny finish visible in the gap
causes.fix: Reglue onto bare wood.

causes.cause: Worn bridge pins/plate letting ball ends climb and pry the bridge up
causes.check: Pins pushed up, ball ends not seated against the plate (mirror)
causes.fix: See [ac-bridge-plate] and [ac-bridge-pins].

causes.cause: Normal varnish/finish line, not a gap
causes.check: Feeler will not go in
causes.fix: Nothing to do.

tools: Thinnest feeler gauge (0.002-0.004 in) or a sheet of thin paper

steps.title: Look along the back edge
steps.detail: Shine a light from behind and look at the tail-side edge and the corners of the wings at eye level with the top. That edge is where lifting starts because the strings rotate the bridge forward.

steps.title: Feeler test
steps.detail: Try to slide the thinnest feeler gauge or a piece of thin paper under the back edge, with gentle pressure only. If it slips in more than a millimetre or two anywhere, the glue has let go there. Check the wing tips too.

steps.title: Slacken the strings if it is open
steps.detail: If the feeler goes in, tune all strings down until slack. Frank Ford's advice: lower the tension before the top suffers more damage. Do not try to flood glue or super glue into the gap - glue cannot bond to old glue and dirt, and it makes a proper reglue harder.
steps.warn: Do not keep playing a lifting bridge - it can tear spruce out of the top.

steps.title: Check inside
steps.detail: With a mirror and light, look at the bridge plate and the ball ends (should sit tight against the plate) and look for a ripple over the cross brace just behind the bridge, which suggests a loose brace too.

steps.title: Book the reglue
steps.detail: A proper fix removes the bridge, cleans both surfaces to bare wood and reglues it. See [ac-bridge-reglue].

models.note: StewMac notes many budget bridges are glued over finish, so they lift readily.
Tied bridges can come off suddenly rather than creep; slacken at the first sign of a gap.

pro: A reglue involves heat near finish and the top; most players should have a luthier do it, especially on a vintage or valuable guitar.

title: Classical guitar: tie-block knots, rollers and new nylon strings
summary: Nylon strings are tied at the bridge and wound onto slotted-headstock rollers. A correct knot (loop under the back corner of the tie block) stops slipping, and patience - not stretching - gets them stable.
parts: Classical string set (normal, high or low tension)

specs.label: Bridge wraps
specs.value: Bass (wound): 1 loop. Trebles: 2 loops (Frank Ford) to 3 wraps (StewMac); add an extra turn for slippery carbon trebles

specs.label: Free end at bridge
specs.value: Leave about 2-3 in (50-75 mm) before tying

specs.label: Settling time
specs.value: Expect a day before they hold pitch well (Frank Ford)

steps.title: Thread through the tie block
steps.detail: Push the string through its hole from the soundhole side out the back, leaving 2-3 in free. If the bass string's end is floppy, bend a hook in it so it threads easily.

steps.title: Tie the knot
steps.detail: Bring the free end back over the tie block and pass it under the string itself (behind the saddle). For basses, one loop; for trebles, two (or three) loops. Pull tight so the last loop sits over the back corner/edge of the block - Frank Ford's key rule: if the final loop sits on top of the block rather than around its back corner, nylon will slip free.
steps.warn: Keep the knot behind the saddle and low; a knot riding up toward the saddle buzzes and can slip.

steps.title: Thread the roller
steps.detail: Pass the string through the roller hole, bring the end back over the roller and tuck it under itself (two loops under, Frank Ford), then pull tight while winding so the loops lock.

steps.title: Wind outward
steps.detail: Wind so the string coils toward the outside of the roller (away from the middle) to leave room for the inner strings, and so it leaves the roller at the bottom heading to the nut.

steps.title: Tune and let them settle
steps.detail: Tune to pitch and keep retuning. Frank Ford advises against pre-stretching beyond pitch - over-stretching creates thin spots that play out of tune. Gentle pulling away from the fingerboard at pitch is the most anyone should do. Trim ends once stable.
steps.warn: Tie the bridge end with the tension low: a slipping knot under tension can snap back.

steps.title: Tidy option
steps.detail: Traditional players tuck each loose end under the next string's knot at the bridge for a neat look.

models.note: Friction pegs need a firm push in while turning; peg holes can be lined or bushed if they wear.
Some bridges have two holes per string - thread through and back out, no knot.

title: Crack in the top, back or sides: assess it
summary: Before anything else, decide whether the crack is in the finish only or through the wood, whether it is clean or dirty, and whether it is moving. That decides between leaving it, humidifying it closed, a DIY glue-and-cleat, or a trip to the luthier.
symptoms: Visible line in top, back or side
Buzz that appears on some notes
Crack that opens in winter and closes in summer
One side of a crack sitting higher than the other

causes.cause: Low humidity (wood shrank and split along the grain)
causes.check: Hygrometer reading; crack runs along the grain, often near the bridge, fingerboard extension or lower bout
causes.fix: Humidify first, then glue and cleat - see [ac-crack-repair].

causes.cause: Impact (knock or puncture)
causes.check: Crushed finish, fibres pushed inward, often on sides
causes.fix: Usually a luthier job: pieces must be aligned and supported.

causes.cause: Finish check only (lacquer crack from cold shock)
causes.check: Many fine lines, often crossing the grain; nothing visible from inside; no step between the edges
causes.fix: Structurally harmless - see [ac-finish-checks].

tools: Inspection mirror and small light (or phone camera on a stick)

steps.title: Look from outside under raking light
steps.detail: Shine a light low across the surface. A through-crack often has slightly shattered finish along its edges, a step between the two sides, or puckered/lifted wood on a spruce top. A finish-only check is usually one of many fine lines and has no step.

steps.title: Look from inside
steps.detail: Slacken the strings a little, put a mirror and light through the soundhole and look at the underside. If you can see the line inside, it goes through. Frank Ford points out that a crack that looks tight outside can be wide open inside.

steps.title: Press gently either side
steps.detail: With very light finger pressure, see whether the edges move against each other or one side drops. A moving crack needs attention soon.

steps.title: Check for loose braces near the crack
steps.detail: Tap along the crack with a fingertip and listen for a buzz. Cracks often go with a brace end that has let go (see [ac-loose-braces]).

steps.title: Record and decide
steps.detail: Note the length, where it is, whether it is clean, and the room humidity. Small, fresh, clean grain-line cracks from dryness: humidify then DIY glue and cleat. Old dirty cracks, cracks with a step, cracks near the bridge or through a brace, side cracks from impact, archtop and f-hole cracks: take to a pro.

models.note: Carved tops crack along the f-holes and grain; the arch makes clamping and alignment hard - pro work.
Very thin tops; cracks near the bridge are common in dry climates.

warnings: Do not put super glue or wood glue into a crack before it is clean and closed - dried glue in a crack makes a later proper repair much harder.
pro: Anything with a step, missing wood, impact damage, a crack running into the bridge or a loose brace, or on a valuable vintage guitar.

title: Heat, cold and travel: avoiding temperature shock
summary: Heat softens the glue that holds a guitar together and sudden cold cracks lacquer. A few habits prevent lifted bridges, loose braces and finish checking.
symptoms: Bridge lifting after the guitar sat in a car
Wrinkle or bulge in the top right behind the bridge
Fine cracks in the finish after coming in from the cold
Blistered finish near a heater

specs.label: Glue softening (Frets.com)
specs.value: Modern guitar glues begin to let go at around 140 deg F (60 deg C)

specs.label: Parked car in the sun (Frets.com)
specs.value: Can reach about 175 deg F within roughly 15 minutes; 150-175 deg F is enough for string tension to pull the top off the cross brace

specs.label: Martin storage temperature
specs.value: 72-77 deg F (22-25 deg C)

steps.title: Never leave it in a parked car
steps.detail: A sunny car can pass the temperature where glue creeps within minutes, even inside the case. Take the guitar with you. Martin also warns against the trunk, where temperatures swing widely.

steps.title: Let a cold guitar warm up in its case
steps.detail: After exposure to freezing weather, leave the case closed at room temperature until the guitar has warmed through before opening it. Sudden temperature change is what makes nitrocellulose lacquer check (crack).

steps.title: Keep away from heaters and sunny windows
steps.detail: Frank Ford shows a neck that blistered from a nearby heater even though the case looked fine.

steps.title: Flying
steps.detail: Martin advises loosening the strings before packing for air travel and padding the case with soft material. Use the hard case.

steps.title: After a heat event, inspect
steps.detail: Check the bridge edges with a thin feeler/paper (see [ac-bridge-lifting]) and look for a ripple across the top just behind the bridge - that is the classic sign the top has pulled away from the cross brace. Classical bridges can come off all at once rather than creeping.
steps.warn: If the bridge has started to lift, slacken the strings straight away to stop further damage.

models.note: Frank Ford notes classical bridges tend to let go suddenly in heat, while pinned steel-string bridges usually lift gradually.
Most prone to cold-shock finish checking; let them acclimatise in the case.

pro: A top wrinkle behind the bridge after heat means the cross brace has let go; that is a repair for a luthier (see [ac-loose-braces]).

title: Humidity control: target range, hygrometers and humidifiers
time: 15 min to set up, then a daily glance
summary: Solid-wood guitars swell and shrink with the air around them. Keeping the guitar in a steady 45-55% relative humidity (RH) prevents most cracks, lifting bridges, sharp fret ends and seasonal action changes.
tools: Digital hygrometer (one in the room, ideally a small one inside the case)
Hard case or well-fitting gig bag
parts: Two-way humidity packs (Boveda 49% or D'Addario Two-Way ~48%) OR a soundhole/case humidifier (sponge or gel type)
Room humidifier or dehumidifier for seasonal extremes

specs.label: Martin recommended storage
specs.value: 45-55% RH at 72-77 deg F (22-25 deg C)

specs.label: Taylor recommended range
specs.value: 45-55% RH; Taylor builds at about 47% RH, 74-75 deg F

specs.label: How much wood moves (Taylor example)
specs.value: A 16 in wide spruce top sized at 47% RH shrinks to about 15.9 in at 30% RH and grows to about 16.06 in at 60% RH

specs.label: Boveda music packs
specs.value: 49% RH two-way packs; acoustic-guitar kit uses 4 packs in 2 holders; replace about every 3 months (can last up to 6)

specs.label: D'Addario Two-Way system
specs.value: Holds the case at roughly 48% RH, adding or absorbing moisture

steps.title: Measure first
steps.detail: Put a digital hygrometer in the room where the guitar lives and, if you can, a small one inside the case. Read it at different times of day for a week. Heating season and air conditioning are the usual culprits for dry air; humid summers and basements for wet air.

steps.title: Keep the guitar in its case
steps.detail: A closed case is a small, stable climate that is far easier to control than a whole room. Taylor's advice is to store the guitar cased, away from outside doors and high ceilings where warm, dry air collects. Wall hangers are fine only if the room itself is held at 45-55%.

steps.title: Pick a humidifier type
steps.detail: Two-way packs (Boveda 49%, D'Addario Two-Way) both add and remove moisture, so they are the safest choice for most players. Sponge or gel soundhole humidifiers only add water: good in a very dry winter, but a common cause of over-humidifying if left in all year. Room humidifiers protect every instrument at once if you can hold the room near 45-55%.

steps.title: Place it correctly
steps.detail: Two-way packs go in their fabric holders in open space in the case (one set near the headstock, one near the body) where the closed lid will not crush them. A soundhole humidifier hangs between the strings over the soundhole. Never put a humidifier in the sealed accessory pocket - it cannot reach the guitar there.
steps.warn: Wring sponge-type humidifiers until they do not drip when held upright, and wipe them dry. Liquid water on the wood or finish, or on the electronics of an acoustic-electric, does real damage.

steps.title: Check and refill on a schedule
steps.detail: Look at the case hygrometer daily for the first week, then weekly. Re-wet sponge humidifiers when the reading drops; replace two-way packs when they go stiff/crunchy (Boveda says about every three months).

steps.title: Adjust for the season
steps.detail: When the room climbs above about 55-60% RH for weeks, take water-adding humidifiers out and switch to two-way packs or silica gel. When the heating comes on, put them back. Watch the guitar itself too - see [ac-dry-wet-guitar] for what too-dry and too-wet guitars look like.

models.note: Martin states that cracks or warping from dry conditions are not covered by warranty, so humidity control protects the warranty as well as the guitar.
Laminated (plywood) backs and sides move much less than solid wood, but a solid top still needs the same care.
Same 45-55% range. Thin carved archtop tops and light classical tops crack readily when dried out.

warnings: Rubber or vinyl parts of some humidifiers can mark lacquer if they touch the finish (Martin).
Do not chase a number with sudden changes - slow, steady correction is the goal.

title: Acoustic setup: action specs and the right order
summary: Set an acoustic in this order: humidity stable, relief (truss rod), nut height, then saddle height. Here are published factory and pro targets to aim at.
tools: 6 in steel rule in 64ths and/or mm, or a string action gauge

specs.label: Taylor 6-string action at 12th fret
specs.value: 4/64 in (1.6 mm) high E, 6/64 in (2.4 mm) low E (Taylor factory spec, straight neck)

specs.label: Taylor 12-string action at 12th fret
specs.value: 3/64 in (1.2 mm) high E, 5/64 in (2.0 mm) low E

specs.label: StewMac example targets
specs.value: 0.070 in (1.8 mm) treble, 0.090 in (2.3 mm) bass at 12th fret

specs.label: Frank Ford 'reasonable' low E
specs.value: About 3/32-4/32 in (2.4-3.2 mm) at 12th fret

specs.label: Relief (Frank Ford)
specs.value: Fret 1st and about the 14th: gap at the 6th fret about the thickness of a .013 string for an average player; up to about .026 in for hard-hitting bluegrass

specs.label: Relief (MusicNomad Taylor kit)
specs.value: .008 in gauge at the 6th fret, string held at 1st and 12th

specs.label: Nut at 1st fret (StewMac example)
specs.value: 0.020 in E and A, 0.015 in D and G; trebles a little lower

specs.label: Truss rod turns
specs.value: About 1/8 turn at a time, then retune and re-measure (StewMac)

specs.label: Maximum string gauge (Martin)
specs.value: Medium .013-.056 on 6-strings; never heavier

steps.title: Stabilise humidity
steps.detail: Do not set up a guitar that is too dry or too wet - action will move when the climate does. Get it to 45-55% RH first.

steps.title: Fresh strings, tuned to pitch
steps.detail: Put on the gauge you will actually use and tune up. Martin puts medium strings on non-cutaway dreadnoughts and jumbos and lights on most smaller and cutaway models.

steps.title: Set relief
steps.detail: Capo at the 1st fret, press the low E at the fret where the neck joins the body (14th on most steel-strings), and measure the gap at the 6th-8th fret. Tighten the rod (clockwise from the adjusting end) for less relief, loosen for more, 1/8 turn at a time.
steps.warn: If the rod is very stiff, stop - remove the nut and lubricate the threads (Frank Ford) or see a pro. Never force it.

steps.title: Check the nut
steps.detail: Fret each string between the 2nd and 3rd frets and look at the gap over the 1st fret - it should be just visible (Frank Ford: about a hair). Too high makes first-position chords hard and sharp; see [ac-acoustic-nut].

steps.title: Measure action at the 12th
steps.detail: Measure from the top of the 12th fret to the bottom of the low E and high E. Compare to the target for your guitar and playing style.

steps.title: Adjust at the saddle
steps.detail: Change action with saddle height: removing material from the saddle bottom lowers 12th-fret action by about half that amount. See [ac-saddle-height]. If you cannot reach the target without the saddle going very low, check [ac-neck-reset-diagnose].

steps.title: Play and fine tune
steps.detail: Play hard in all positions. Buzz low on the neck: more relief or nut. Buzz high on the neck: Frank Ford says raise the saddle, not the truss rod.

models.note: Adjustable rod since 1985 (two-way since 2006); adjust through the soundhole at the neck block with a 4 or 5 mm hex key depending on model (SC models 4 mm). Martin recommends its service centres for rod and saddle work.
Rod adjusts at the headstock with a 1/4 in nut wrench (Big Baby and pre-2012 nylon models adjust through the soundhole). Factory action 4/64 and 6/64 in.
Rod adjusts at the headstock under the cover (Frank Ford). Gibson's wide saddle slot is 1/8 in.
Lower action targets (Taylor 3/64 and 5/64 in) and lighter strings; see [ac-12-string].

title: Bridge pins: stuck pins, fit, slotting and seating
time: 10 min (removal) to 1 h (ream and slot a new set)
summary: Bridge pins only wedge the ball end against the bridge plate - they do not take the string tension. Pins that are stuck, too tall, too loose, or that let the ball end ride up cause tuning drift, buzzes, worn plates and even split bridges.
symptoms: Pin will not come out
Pins sit high or pop up
A string goes flat for days after restringing
Buzz from inside the guitar near the bridge

causes.cause: Ball end jammed against the pin groove
causes.check: Pin stuck tight after the string is slack
causes.fix: Push the string in to free the ball end, then lift the pin (steps below).

causes.cause: Ball end caught in the pin's groove and slowly sliding up
causes.check: Mirror: ball end not against the plate
causes.fix: Bevel the pin tip (StewMac) and reseat.

causes.cause: Pin taper does not match the hole
causes.check: Pin sits too tall or rocks
causes.fix: Ream lightly with the right taper reamer.

causes.cause: Pin slot too small/large for the string
causes.check: Pin will not seat with string in, or string flops in the slot
causes.fix: Slot the bridge holes or pins to suit the gauge.

tools: Bridge pin puller or the notch on a string winder (padded)
Tapered bridge pin reamer (3 deg or 5 deg)
Bridge pin hole slotting saws and files
Poster board/masking tape to protect the top
parts: Replacement pins (bone, ebony or plastic) matched to the hole taper

specs.label: StewMac 3 deg reamer
specs.value: Approx 0.312-0.150 in, 3 in cutting length - suits many Gibson and Gurian pins

specs.label: StewMac 5 deg reamer
specs.value: Approx 0.312-0.135 in, 2 in cutting length - suits vintage-style and modern Martin pins

specs.label: Slotting saws (StewMac)
specs.value: 0.028 in for holes 1-3 (E, B, G); 0.051 in for holes 4-6 (D, A, E)

steps.title: Removing a stuck pin
steps.detail: Slacken the string fully. Push the string about an inch into the guitar so the ball end drops away from the pin, then lift the pin with a puller or the notch in a string winder, using a cloth under the tool to protect the bridge. If it still will not move, reach inside and push the pin up from below with a finger.
steps.warn: Never pry with pliers on the bare bridge or hammer pins in or out - Martin warns that hammered pins can split the bridge.

steps.title: Seat the ball end every time
steps.detail: Put the ball end in the hole, push the pin in with the slot facing the saddle, then pull the string up gently while pressing the pin down until you feel the ball end lock against the plate. Tune up. A mirror check once will confirm the ball sits beside the pin tip, flat on the plate wood.

steps.title: Stop ball ends riding up the pin
steps.detail: StewMac's trick: bevel the very end of each pin so the ball is pushed outward onto the plate rather than catching in the groove. Plastic pins: trim with a utility knife. Bone/ebony: hold in a block with a 3/16 in hole and file, then smooth the slot edges with a needle file and 400 grit.

steps.title: Fit new pins (ream lightly)
steps.detail: New pins should seat with the collar just above or touching the bridge. If they stand tall, ream each hole with the matching-taper reamer - StewMac's tip is just a twist, not a full turn - then test. Number the pins with small file nicks so each returns to its own hole.

steps.title: Slot the bridge holes if needed
steps.detail: Mask the top with poster board. Saw a slot at the front of each hole with the narrow saw for E-B-G and the wide saw for D-A-E, sawing slowly downwards and straight, then round and ramp the slot toward the saddle with slot files. Unwound E and B ball-end wraps are fatter at the top, so open the top of those slots slightly. Unslotted pins then hold the string in the bridge slot.

steps.title: Or slot the pins
steps.detail: Alternatively, slot each pin to suit its string gauge (StewMac recommends about half the pin's depth) - a slot that fits the low E is sloppy on the high E.

models.note: Modern Martin pins match the 5 deg reamer.
Many Gibson pins match the 3 deg reamer.
Some Taylors and many budget guitars use pinless or different bridges - check before buying pins.
