title: Buzz and rattle hunting in an acoustic
summary: Many acoustic buzzes are not frets at all but something loose: a tuner part, truss rod cover, endpin jack nut, a wire or battery, a ball end, or a brace. Make the noise happen without playing, then narrow it down.
symptoms: Buzz only on certain notes
Buzz that continues when you mute the strings
Rattle when you knock on the body

causes.cause: Tuner nut, washer or press-fit bushing loose; tuner button screw backed out
causes.check: Hold each tuner part while playing the problem note
causes.fix: Snug the nuts gently (do not crush the wood), tighten button screws, reglue loose bushings (thin CA in the hole).

causes.cause: Truss rod cover or the truss rod nut/washer loose
causes.check: Press on the cover/rod nut while playing the note
causes.fix: Tighten cover screws; give a slack rod nut just enough snug to stop it rattling.

causes.cause: String touching another string's post, or long string tail at the headstock
causes.check: Look at string paths and cut ends
causes.fix: Rewind so the string clears neighbouring posts; trim tails short.

causes.cause: Ball end not seated, hanging inside
causes.check: Mirror under the bridge plate
causes.fix: Reseat - see [ac-bridge-pins].

causes.cause: Endpin jack nut, strap button, preamp, battery or loose wires
causes.check: Press on each with the guitar ringing; look inside
causes.fix: Tighten the jack's inner nut; clip wires with stick-on clips; pad the battery with foam or tape.

causes.cause: Loose brace or crack
causes.check: Knuckle tap test, mirror and feeler
causes.fix: See [ac-loose-braces] / [ac-crack-assess].

causes.cause: Dead or damaged string windings
causes.check: Worn or separated winding on old strings
causes.fix: Replace the string.

causes.cause: Truss rod grazing its channel (sings on certain notes)
causes.check: Small change of rod tension stops it
causes.fix: Pro fix: glue injected via a tiny hole.

causes.cause: Genuine fret, nut or saddle buzz
causes.check: Buzz is at the fret and stops when you raise action slightly
causes.fix: See [ac-action-specs].

tools: Screwdrivers and small spanners for tuner nuts

steps.title: Reproduce it
steps.detail: Find the note that buzzes. Then, without playing, knock with a knuckle on the headstock, neck, top, back, sides and near the bridge. Frank Ford's method is to recreate the noise by rapping until you find the area.

steps.title: Mute and touch
steps.detail: Play the bad note and, while it rings, press lightly on suspects one at a time: each tuner button, bushing and nut, the truss rod cover, the strap button and endpin jack, the pickguard edge, the label inside. When the buzz stops, you have found it.

steps.title: Check the headstock first
steps.detail: Tuner hardware is the most common culprit. Tighten hex nuts and button screws snugly. Frank Ford fixes press-fit bushings that ride up by swabbing the hole with thin CA, curing it, and pressing the bushing back.
steps.warn: Keep CA off the headstock face finish.

steps.title: Check inside
steps.detail: With mirror and light: ball ends seated? wires flapping against the top/back? battery bag loose? preamp or jack nut loose? anything rattling free (Frank Ford once found an old wasp nest)? Secure wires with stick-on clips and pad batteries with foam.

steps.title: Then braces and cracks
steps.detail: If the buzz follows knocking the body and nothing else stops it, look for loose braces and cracks.

title: Does my acoustic need a neck reset?
summary: Over years, string tension pulls the neck forward and the action rises. When the saddle has nothing left to lower, the fix is resetting the neck angle. These checks tell you if you are there.
symptoms: High action that the saddle cannot fix
Saddle barely stands above the bridge, or the bridge has been shaved
Straightedge on the frets hits below the top of the bridge

specs.label: Straightedge test (Frank Ford, Haze)
specs.value: Straightedge laid on the frets should just touch the top edge of the bridge (not the saddle). Landing below the bridge top = neck underset

specs.label: String height above top (Frank Ford)
specs.value: Low E about 1/2 in (12.7 mm) above the top just in front of the bridge = angle OK; under 3/8 in (9.5 mm) = angle problem

specs.label: Action check
specs.value: Over 4/32 in at the 12th fret on the low E with a very low saddle suggests a neck-angle problem

specs.label: Heel removal estimate (Haze Guitars)
specs.value: X = (A x B) / C, in mm: A = gap between straightedge and bridge top, B = heel length (fingerboard underside to heel end), C = neck/body joint to middle of saddle. X tapers to zero at the fingerboard

steps.title: Make sure humidity is normal
steps.detail: A dry guitar has a sunken top and low action; a wet one bulges and reads high. Frank Ford notes humidity can mimic or hide a neck angle problem. Get to 45-55% RH first.

steps.title: Straighten the neck
steps.detail: Set the truss rod so the neck is straight (or nearly), otherwise the straightedge reads wrong. The truss rod does not change neck angle.

steps.title: Straightedge test
steps.detail: Lay the straightedge on the fret tops (strings removed, or between strings) and slide it toward the bridge. It should rest on the frets and touch the top of the bridge. If it lands below the bridge top, measure the gap - that is how underset the neck is.
steps.warn: A previously shaved, thin bridge can make this test look fine when the angle is actually shallow.

steps.title: String-height test
steps.detail: With the strings at pitch, measure from the low E to the top just in front of the bridge. About 1/2 in is healthy; under 3/8 in usually means someone has lowered the saddle/bridge to cope with a shallow angle.

steps.title: Saddle check
steps.detail: If the 12th-fret action is still high (over about 4/32 in on the low E) and the saddle is already low, the saddle cannot fix it without killing break angle and tone - a reset is the real fix. A high saddle with OK action means the angle is fine.

steps.title: Decide
steps.detail: Small amounts can be lived with (or handled with a slightly lower saddle). Clear failure of these tests on a good solid-wood guitar justifies a reset: see [ac-neck-reset-dovetail] or [ac-neck-reset-bolt-on].

models.note: Reset needs steam - pro job; see [ac-neck-reset-dovetail].

models.model: Taylor NT, Collings, many modern bolt-ons
models.note: Neck angle can be changed by shims or heel adjustments; see [ac-neck-reset-bolt-on].
No reset possible in the usual sense; see [ac-classical-setup].

pro: Any actual reset is luthier work. Haze Guitars notes a neck may last 50 years or 5 before needing one; a brand-new guitar with an underset neck may be a warranty claim.

title: Dry or wet guitar: symptoms and safe recovery
summary: Most 'my guitar suddenly plays badly' complaints between seasons are humidity. A dry guitar's top sinks and action drops; a wet guitar's top swells and action rises. Fix the climate first, then re-check the setup.
symptoms: DRY: action suddenly lower, buzzing high up the neck
DRY: sharp fret ends sticking out of the fingerboard edges
DRY: top sunken between bridge and soundhole; back looks very flat
DRY: a hump in the fingerboard where the neck meets the body (around the 14th fret)
DRY: on Taylor NT necks, a slight gap around the fingerboard extension
DRY: cracks in top or back, bridge edges lifting
WET: action noticeably higher, harder to play
WET: dull, flat, lifeless tone
WET: top bulging behind the bridge more than usual; back dipping at the tail block
WET: sighting down the neck, the frets point below the top of the bridge

causes.cause: Air below about 40% RH (winter heating, desert climates, air travel)
causes.check: Hygrometer in room and case; sight for sinking top and feel the fret ends along the fingerboard edge
causes.fix: Rehydrate slowly in the closed case with humidifiers (steps below).

causes.cause: Air above about 60% RH for weeks, or a soundhole humidifier left in all summer
causes.check: Hygrometer; Taylor notes several weeks at 80-90% or several months at 60-70% will swell a guitar
causes.fix: Remove water-adding humidifiers, use two-way packs or silica gel, run a dehumidifier in the room.

causes.cause: Normal small belly behind the bridge
causes.check: Some bulge behind the bridge is normal on every flat-top. Look for several symptoms together before blaming humidity.
causes.fix: No action needed if playability is fine; see [ac-top-belly] if it keeps growing.

tools: Soundhole humidifier(s) or two-way humidity packs
Silica gel packs or room dehumidifier (for wet guitars)
Kitchen scale (optional - weighing the guitar shows water gain)

specs.label: Target range
specs.value: 45-55% RH (Martin, Taylor)

specs.label: Taylor dry-guitar example
specs.value: Two sponge humidifiers, three refills over nine days; guitar gained 25 g (about 0.9 oz) of water

specs.label: Typical response time
specs.value: About three days before results show (Taylor)

steps.title: Confirm it is humidity
steps.detail: Read the hygrometer. Then look for a group of symptoms from the list - one alone (for example a little belly behind the bridge) is not proof. Note the action at the 12th fret so you can see it recover.

steps.title: Loosen nothing yet
steps.detail: Keep the strings at pitch unless a bridge is visibly lifting or a crack is opening - then slacken them (see [ac-bridge-lifting]).

steps.title: Rehydrate a dry guitar in its case
steps.detail: Wring out one or two soundhole humidifiers until they will not drip when held upright, wipe them, hang them in the soundhole, close the guitar in its case, and leave it. Taylor recommends two humidifiers for a properly dry guitar. Open the case only to re-wet them and to read the hygrometer once a day.
steps.warn: It is possible to over-humidify. Stop adding water once the case reads 45-55% and the top has come back up.

steps.title: Let the body recover before setup work
steps.detail: The top and back respond first; the neck and fingerboard respond less to a soundhole humidifier. Once the body has recovered (often 3-10 days), re-check relief and adjust the truss rod if needed. Do not lower or raise the saddle until the guitar has been stable for a week or two.

steps.title: Deal with sharp fret ends
steps.detail: If the fingerboard shrank, the fret ends may still stick out after rehydration. They can be filed flush and re-bevelled (a standard fret-end dress) - see the frets guides.

steps.title: Dry out a wet guitar
steps.detail: Remove all water-adding humidifiers. Put two-way packs or several silica-gel packs in the case (replace silica every few months), and run a dehumidifier where the guitar is stored. Taylor's trick for a damp case: take the guitar out and blow-dry the empty case interior for 10-15 minutes now and then.

steps.title: Do not 'fix' swelling with lighter strings
steps.detail: Dropping to extra-light strings hides high action from a wet guitar but does not cure it. Fix the air, then reassess.

models.note: A gap appearing around the fingerboard extension is one of Taylor's listed signs of a dry guitar.
Dryness often shows as a hump around the 14th fret where the fingerboard extension sits on the shrinking top.
Keep sponge humidifiers well wrung out and away from preamp, battery box and wiring.

warnings: Rehydrating too fast can itself stress the wood - slow and monitored is the rule.
Open cracks should be humidified closed BEFORE gluing, not glued open.
pro: If cracks have opened, a bridge is lifting, or the action stays wrong after two weeks at 45-55%, have a tech look before more seasonal damage piles up.

title: Lower (or raise) an acoustic saddle
summary: Most acoustic action changes are made by sanding the bottom of the saddle flat or shimming it up. The key rule: the saddle moves about twice as much as the action at the 12th fret.
tools: Steel rule in 64ths or mm / action gauge
120-220 grit sandpaper taped to a flat surface (glass, granite, worktop)
Pliers with tape on the jaws
parts: Shim stock: wood veneer, thin plastic or hard paper (temporary)
New bone saddle blank if you go too low

specs.label: The 2:1 rule
specs.value: Change the saddle by about twice the change you want at the 12th fret: lower action 1/64 in, remove 1/32 in (Frank Ford); lower 0.5 mm, remove 1 mm

specs.label: Ideal saddle protrusion (Frank Ford)
specs.value: About 3/16 in (4.8 mm) above the bridge wood

specs.label: Abrasive
specs.value: Taylor: 120 or 150 grit; Haze: 150-220 grit; Frank Ford: 150 grit

steps.title: Set relief and nut first
steps.detail: Saddle height is the last step of a setup. Confirm relief and nut height are right ([ac-action-specs]).

steps.title: Measure and calculate
steps.detail: Measure action at the 12th fret on both E strings. Decide the change you want for each, then double it. Example: low E 7/64 to 6/64 in = 1/64 in lower, so remove 2/64 (1/32) in at the bass end of the saddle.

steps.title: Remove the saddle
steps.detail: Slacken the strings (on pin bridges, pull the pins out of the outer holes or just slacken well) and lift the saddle out. If it is snug, grip the middle with taped pliers and lift straight up. Mark the treble end so it goes back the right way round. Note how much stands above the bridge.

steps.title: Mark the line
steps.detail: Mark the amount to remove at each end of the saddle bottom (different amounts for bass and treble if needed) and join the marks with a straight line. Frank Ford's trick: lay the pencil on the rule at the right height and rub the saddle along it.

steps.title: Sand the bottom flat and square
steps.detail: Hold the saddle upright and stroke it along sandpaper on a flat surface, in long strokes, keeping pressure even. Keep the bottom dead flat and at 90 deg to the sides - a rocked or rounded bottom gives poor contact, poor tone and (with a pickup) uneven string volume. Check against a square and a light.
steps.warn: Take off a little at a time and test - you cannot put it back.

steps.title: Refit and test
steps.detail: Refit, tune to pitch, re-measure and play. Stop when it plays well, even if you have not reached the calculated number.

steps.title: Too low? Shim or replace
steps.detail: A thin shim of hardwood veneer under the saddle raises it; StewMac lists paper, plastic or wood. For tone and strength a new full-height saddle is better ([ac-bone-saddle]).

steps.title: Lowering from the top (glued saddles)
steps.detail: On older through-cut glued saddles, Frank Ford protects the top with card, files the saddle top down and re-rounds it with a fret file, then smooths with 320 grit.

models.note: Haze Guitars warns: never sand the bottom of these integrated-pickup saddles. Adjust from the top or have a tech do it.
Saddle bottom flatness is critical for even string volume, and the saddle must still move freely in the slot - see [ac-piezo-string-balance].
ES2 sensors sit behind the saddle rather than under it, so normal saddle work applies; Taylor says if the saddle cannot reach spec the guitar may need a neck adjustment.
Narrow saddle slot (3/32 in); Martin recommends saddle work at its service centres.

warnings: A saddle that is very low (little above the bridge) means a weak string break angle and weak tone - see [ac-neck-reset-diagnose].

title: 12-string setup
summary: A 12-string carries far more tension than a 6, so it gets lighter strings, lower action, careful nut work and close watching of the bridge and neck angle.
tools: Nut files (including small sizes for octave strings)
parts: 12-string set in the gauge the maker specifies (light or extra light)

specs.label: Course order (most guitars)
specs.value: Low E, A, D, G courses are octave pairs; B and high E are unison pairs. Octave string sits on the bass side of its partner on most guitars (Rickenbacker reverses this)

specs.label: Taylor 12-string action at 12th fret
specs.value: 3/64 in high E, 5/64 in low E

specs.label: Strings (Martin)
specs.value: Most 12-strings take extra light gauge

steps.title: String in the right order
steps.detail: On each of the four lower courses, the thin octave string goes on the bass side so your pick hits it first on a downstroke - it sounds brighter. The B and E courses are two identical strings. Some players use a unison G course instead of octave; most prefer octave.

steps.title: Check the bridge and top before anything else
steps.detail: Look for bridge lifting, top bulge and plate wear ([ac-bridge-lifting], [ac-top-belly]). 12-strings show these first.

steps.title: Set relief
steps.detail: Set relief as on a 6-string, in small steps of about 1/8 turn, retuning all twelve strings before each measurement.

steps.title: Nut slots
steps.detail: Check each string at the 1st fret as in [ac-acoustic-nut]. Octave strings are very thin - file their slots with a small file so they do not sit loose. Keep the pair spacing even and the octave slot height similar to its partner so both fret cleanly.

steps.title: Saddle and action
steps.detail: Aim lower than a 6-string (Taylor: 3/64 in treble, 5/64 in bass) and use the saddle 2:1 rule from [ac-saddle-height]. Make sure each paired string bears cleanly on the saddle crown.

steps.title: Tune down if needed
steps.detail: Historically many 12-strings were tuned below standard to ease neck and top stress. If an older or lightly built 12 shows bellying, tuning down a semitone or more is a valid choice.

models.note: Reverse pairing - octave string on the treble side of its partner.
Often shorter scale and heavier plates; tune-down was common practice.

pro: Neck resets and bridge reglues are more common on 12-strings; if the saddle is already low with high action, see [ac-neck-reset-diagnose].

title: Acoustic nut: check slot height and fit a new nut
summary: A nut cut too high makes first-position chords hard and sharp; too low buzzes open strings. Check it with the fret-at-3rd test and file or replace as needed.
symptoms: Open-position chords play sharp
Barre at 1st fret is hard work
Open string buzzes on the 1st fret
Strings ping or stick when tuning
tools: Nut files sized to the strings
Feeler gauges and a short straightedge
150 grit on a flat plate; 320-600 grit

specs.label: Frank Ford check
specs.value: Fret between 2nd and 3rd frets: gap over the 1st fret about the thickness of a hair

specs.label: StewMac example clearances at 1st fret
specs.value: 0.020 in E and A, 0.015 in D and G

specs.label: StewMac feeler method
specs.value: Measured fret height plus 0.005-0.010 in, adding about 0.002 in per string toward the bass

specs.label: Slot depth
specs.value: About 1/3 of the string above the nut top, 2/3 in the slot (StewMac); no more than 1/2-3/4 of the string buried

steps.title: Check each string
steps.detail: Tune up. Fret each string between the 2nd and 3rd frets and look at the gap over the 1st fret. If you see none, tap the string above the 1st fret - a faint click means there is a little gap. A gap you can clearly see means the slot is too high.

steps.title: Lower a high slot
steps.detail: Slacken the string, lift it out, and file the slot bottom with a nut file angled down toward the headstock - Frank Ford angles the slot about halfway between the fingerboard plane and the headstock plane, so the string bears on the front edge. Take a few strokes, retune, recheck. Stacked feeler gauges laid on the fingerboard against the nut make a depth stop (StewMac).
steps.warn: Go slowly - a slot cut too low means a new nut or a filled slot.

steps.title: Slot shape
steps.detail: The slot bottom should be round, just wider than the string. V-shaped or tight slots pinch strings and cause tuning pings; graphite in the slot helps.

steps.title: Fitting a new nut: remove the old one
steps.detail: Score the finish along the back of the nut with a fine saw so the headstock veneer does not chip, then tap the nut out sideways with a wood block and light hammer.

steps.title: Shape the blank
steps.detail: Sand the blank to the slot width on a flat plate, using calipers set to the old nut as a go/no-go gauge. Match the bottom angle: Frank Ford notes pre-1999 Martins have the nut bottom in the headstock plane, most other guitars in the fingerboard plane.

steps.title: Space and slot
steps.detail: Mark string positions, cut tiny starter notches, string up to pitch, then deepen each slot with round-bottom files to height, nudging bass strings sideways if needed so spacing looks even. Finally sand the nut top down so wound strings sit about one-third proud and plain strings just below the top.

models.note: Nut base in the plane of the headstock - match the angle when making a new one.
Octave slots are smaller and the pair spacing must be even; see [ac-12-string].
Wider nut (48-54 mm typical) with large spacing; nylon needs a smooth, rounded slot.

title: Archtop floating bridge: placement, fitting and height
summary: An archtop bridge is held only by string pressure, so it can drift. Place it by scale length and intonation, make sure its foot matches the arch with no gaps, and set height with the thumbwheels.
symptoms: Intonation suddenly off after a string change
Weak, thin tone (foot not contacting the top)
Bridge leaning toward the fingerboard
tools: Low-tack tape (drafting or sign-painter's tape, not regular masking tape on lacquer)
Archtop bridge-fitting jig (or careful hand sanding)

steps.title: Mark the current position
steps.detail: Before taking strings off, put low-tack tape at each end of the bridge foot so you can return it to the same spot. StewMac recommends drafting/sign-painter's tape, since normal masking tape adhesive can react with lacquer.

steps.title: Rough placement by scale
steps.detail: Measure from the nut to the 12th fret and double it: that is the scale length. Set the treble-side saddle point at about that distance from the nut and the bass side a little further back (the bass saddle sits further back on a compensated bridge). Keep the bridge centred so the outer strings run evenly along the fingerboard edges.

steps.title: Fit the foot to the top
steps.detail: Stick sandpaper to the top in the bridge area over protective tape, scribble white pencil on the foot underside, and sand by sliding the foot over the paper (a jig keeps it upright). When the pencil is gone the foot matches the arch. Check under string tension with a light or feeler - there should be no gaps.
steps.warn: Protect the finish; the sandpaper must never be dragged across bare lacquer.

steps.title: Set the height
steps.detail: Slacken the strings a little and turn the thumbwheels on the bass and treble posts to raise or lower each side, then retune and measure action at the 12th. Very high action with wheels bottomed out means a lower bridge base is needed (StewMac's Gibson L-1 job made new, shorter bridges).

steps.title: Intonate
steps.detail: Compare each string's 12th-fret harmonic with the fretted note. If most strings are sharp, slide the whole bridge back; if flat, forward. With a one-piece compensated top, small differences per string are built in. Keep the bridge standing upright - strings drag it forward when tuning, so straighten it each string change.

steps.title: Floating pickups
steps.detail: Floating archtop pickups mount to the fingerboard end or the pickguard edge and do not touch the top. Set the pickup close to the strings without touching them at the highest fret you play, and make sure its bracket and wire do not rattle against the top.

models.note: Fully hollow carved tops have only the bridge feet touching the top - fit matters a lot for tone.
Bridge is usually anchored on the block (tune-o-matic posts) - this guide's floating-bridge steps do not apply.
Bridge rocks with the vibrato; a roller-saddle or rocking bridge helps tuning return.

pro: Carving a new bridge base, making a new saddle top, or fixing f-hole/top cracks.

title: Classical and flamenco setup: action, saddle, nut and neck
summary: Classical guitars have higher action than steel-strings, flamenco guitars lower. Most have no adjustable truss rod and a Spanish-heel neck, so action is set almost entirely at the saddle and nut.
tools: Action gauge or rule in mm

specs.label: Example classical targets (Rodrigo Gomes, StewMac)
specs.value: About 0.6 mm (0.023 in) at the 1st fret and about 2.75 mm (0.108 in) at the 12th fret

specs.label: Saddle rule
specs.value: Remove about twice the action change wanted at the 12th fret (luthier James Lister, Delcamp forum); keep the bottom flat and square

specs.label: Flamenco
specs.value: Lower action than classical; a little buzz is accepted as part of the sound

specs.label: Typical dimensions
specs.value: Scale about 650 mm (range 635-664 mm); nut width 48-54 mm

steps.title: Check the neck
steps.detail: Sight the neck and check relief with a capo at the 1st fret and the string held at the body joint. Many classicals have no adjustable rod, so relief is whatever the neck has. If yours has a rod (some modern and Taylor nylon models), adjust as on a steel-string, gently.

steps.title: Measure action
steps.detail: Measure the 6th and 1st strings at the 12th fret. Note that classical action is normally higher on the bass side; players often taper the saddle top so the treble side is lower.

steps.title: Adjust the saddle
steps.detail: Remove the saddle (classical saddles just lift out once strings are slack), mark twice the action change on each end and sand the bottom flat and square on a flat plate, as in [ac-saddle-height]. Rodrigo Gomes files the saddle top lower and gives the front a ramp.

steps.title: Nut
steps.detail: Check the 1st-fret clearance with the fret-at-3rd test ([ac-acoustic-nut]); nylon needs smooth rounded slots so it does not catch.

steps.title: Flamenco setup
steps.detail: Set the saddle lower than you would for classical, accepting a little buzz for a snappier feel, and fit a clear golpeador (tap plate) if the top lacks one.

steps.title: If the saddle is already very low
steps.detail: A classical with a Spanish heel cannot have a normal neck reset. Frank Ford's fixes include planing a tapered wedge under the fingerboard (about 1/4 in stock tapered from zero at the nut to about 3/16 in at the body, reglued with hide glue), clamping the neck back while regluing the fingerboard, or converting to a bolt-on. These are luthier jobs.

models.note: Neck and block are one piece with the sides slotted into it; neck angle corrections need fingerboard work, not a reset.
Truss rod adjusts through the soundhole.
Lighter build, thinner top, lower action; tops crack readily when dry.

warnings: Never fit steel strings to a classical guitar (Martin) - the tension will damage it.
pro: Any neck-angle correction, fingerboard wedge or bridge reglue on a classical.

title: Finish checking (lacquer cracks)
time: 30 min work spread over about a month (drying)
summary: Fine cracks in nitrocellulose lacquer, usually from sudden cold, are cosmetic. Most players leave them as 'vintage character'; small fresh checks on a new guitar can be filled.
symptoms: Fine lines in the finish, often many, sometimes across the grain
No step and nothing visible from inside

causes.cause: Sudden temperature drop on a nitro finish
causes.check: Guitar recently came in from cold or was opened while cold
causes.fix: Prevent by letting the case warm up before opening - see [ac-heat-cold-travel].

causes.cause: Actually a wood crack
causes.check: Visible from inside, step between edges, shattered edges
causes.fix: See [ac-crack-assess].

tools: Glass slide or razor blade as scraper (edge taped)

specs.label: Cure before levelling (Frets.com)
specs.value: About one month for a deep drop-fill

steps.title: Decide whether to touch it
steps.detail: Checks do not affect structure. Frank Ford mostly leaves them and only fills small ones on new instruments. Confirm first that it is not a wood crack.

steps.title: Soften the lacquer around the check
steps.detail: Run a tiny bead of amalgamator along the line with a fine brush so the old lacquer softens and fuses at the edges. Do not open the check with a knife - Frank Ford shows that it makes the damage bigger.

steps.title: Fill with lacquer
steps.detail: After a few hours, brush a thin line of clear lacquer into the check. The next day add a second line so the fill stands slightly proud of the surrounding finish.

steps.title: Wait
steps.detail: Let the fill cure for about a month; slow solvents and deep fills shrink as they dry.

steps.title: Level and polish
steps.detail: Scrape the bump flush with a glass slide or a blade whose corners are taped, block-sand lightly with 2500 grit, then polish back to gloss.
steps.warn: Lacquer solvents are flammable and harmful - work with ventilation and a respirator suited to organic vapours, no flames.

title: Make a new bone saddle (and compensate it)
summary: A new bone saddle restores height after over-sanding, improves tone over plastic, and lets you fine-tune intonation by moving each string's contact point.
tools: 150 and 220 grit sandpaper on a flat plate, 320 for finishing
Electronic tuner (strobe if you have one)

specs.label: Fit (Frank Ford)
specs.value: Snug along the full length: needs pliers to lift it out but pushes in by hand. Never hammer it in.

specs.label: Compensation maths (Frets.com)
specs.value: Move the contact point by (nut-to-1st-fret distance) x (cents sharp at 12th fret as a percent). Example: 25.25 in scale, 1st fret about 1.43 in; 8 cents sharp: 1.43 x 0.08 = 0.114 in (just over 7/64 in) further back

specs.label: Slot widths
specs.value: Martin narrow 3/32 in; Gibson wide 1/8 in (Fishman)

steps.title: Size the blank
steps.detail: Mark length a little longer than the old saddle and cut with a hacksaw; mark height with plenty to spare.

steps.title: Thickness to the slot
steps.detail: Rub the blank flat on 150 grit on a flat plate, flipping sides and trial-fitting often, until it slides in snugly at both ends and along its length. If it gets loose, start again - a loose saddle rocks and loses tone.

steps.title: Shape the ends
steps.detail: Round the ends to match the slot by wiping them on the sandpaper. Small end gaps are cosmetic only. Final fit: pliers to remove, hand pressure to seat.

steps.title: Set the height
steps.detail: With it in the slot, pencil the target height on the face. Base it on the old saddle and the 2:1 rule from [ac-saddle-height], leaving it slightly tall. Sand from the bottom (keeping it flat and square) or the top to reach the line.

steps.title: Shape the top
steps.detail: Pencil witness marks across the top. Hold the saddle at about 45 deg and sand a facet along each edge, leaving a narrow flat crown, then round it with flexible 220 grit backed by your fingers. Match the top curve to the fingerboard radius - check against a thin rule held to the fingerboard.

steps.title: Intonate
steps.detail: String up, tune, and compare each string's 12th-fret fretted note to its 12th-fret harmonic. If a string is sharp, move its contact point back (toward the tail) by filing the front of the crown so the string bears further back; if flat, move it forward. Use the Frets.com formula to estimate how far. On most steel-strings the B string needs its point set back more than the high E and G.

steps.title: Finish
steps.detail: Smooth with 320 grit and polish if you like a shiny look. Recheck action and intonation after a day of playing.
steps.warn: Bone dust is unpleasant - sand with a mask and good ventilation.

models.note: The saddle bottom must be dead flat; StewMac notes a very wide, heavily compensated saddle may not suit a pickup strip as well.
Classical saddles are usually straight and uncompensated, but the same fitting and height rules apply.

pro: Moving a saddle slot (when intonation cannot be fixed within the saddle width) means routing the bridge - luthier work with a jig and router.

title: Top belly and bridge rotation
summary: String tension rolls the bridge forward and bulges the top behind it. A little is normal and built in; too much raises the action, tilts the bridge, and can mean loose braces, too-heavy strings or a wet guitar.
symptoms: Bulge behind the bridge with a dip in front of it toward the soundhole
Action creeping up
Bridge visibly tilting forward
Ripple directly over the cross brace behind the bridge

causes.cause: High humidity swelling the top
causes.check: Hygrometer above 55-60%; other wet symptoms
causes.fix: See [ac-dry-wet-guitar].

causes.cause: Strings heavier than the guitar is built for
causes.check: Gauge on the packet vs maker's advice
causes.fix: Martin: go back to lighter gauges if the top rises abnormally; never exceed medium .013-.056.

causes.cause: Loose cross brace or bridge plate
causes.check: Ripple/wrinkle behind bridge, rattles when tapped, mirror inspection
causes.fix: See [ac-loose-braces] - pro repair.

causes.cause: Bridge glue failing
causes.check: Feeler under back edge
causes.fix: See [ac-bridge-lifting].

tools: Straightedge (short, to lay across the lower bout)
Top deflection gauge or a dial indicator on a bridge (optional)

steps.title: Know what normal looks like
steps.detail: Taylor notes some bellying behind the bridge is normal. Lay a short straightedge across the lower bout behind the bridge and note the gap at the edges; photograph it so you can compare over time.

steps.title: Measure movement under tension
steps.detail: StewMac's top deflection gauge method: with strings at pitch, rest the gauge feet near the rim with the plunger over the bridge area and zero it; remove the strings and re-place it. The reading is how far string tension pulls the top. Repeat every few months to see whether it is getting worse.

steps.title: Rule out humidity and strings
steps.detail: Get the guitar to 45-55% RH for a couple of weeks and use the gauge the maker recommends. Many bellies shrink back.

steps.title: Check braces and plate
steps.detail: Look inside with a mirror for a gap between the top and the cross brace or bridge plate, and look outside for a wrinkle just behind the bridge. Frank Ford explains heat is a common cause of the top pulling off the cross brace.

steps.title: Restore playability
steps.detail: If the belly is stable but the action is high, Martin's guidance is that the saddle (and if needed the bridge) can be lowered. If the saddle is already low, see [ac-neck-reset-diagnose].

models.note: Martin says its steel-string guitars are tested to handle medium strings, but if the top rises abnormally, switch to lighter gauges.
Very high tension; use the light/extra-light sets 12-string makers specify.

pro: A growing belly with a wrinkle, loose brace or tilting bridge needs a luthier (bracing repair, plate work, sometimes a bridge doctor or JLD-type device).

title: Glue and cleat a top, back or side crack
summary: A clean, fresh crack that has been humidified closed can be glued from outside and reinforced inside with small cross-grain cleats (or a long splint on a side). Done well it is stable for good.
tools: Long-reach magnetic clamps or a crack repair kit (wire + cleat cutter)
Flat acrylic or wood cauls, waxed paper
Palette knife or thinned feeler gauge as glue spatula
parts: Glue: Titebond Liquid Hide Glue, hot hide glue, or Titebond Original (aliphatic)
Cleat stock: quartersawn spruce for tops, wood matching the back/sides for those
Side splint: mahogany about 3/32 in thick x 5/8 in wide

specs.label: Cleat grain
specs.value: StewMac: about 45 deg to the crack. Many luthiers (e.g. Frank Ford's patch) run it at right angles to the top's grain. Never parallel to the crack.

specs.label: Side splint (Frets.com)
specs.value: Mahogany 3/32 x 5/8 in, running the full height of the side between the linings, edges and ends bevelled

specs.label: Glue injection pressure (StewMac kit)
specs.value: About 10 psi is enough to push most glues into a crack

specs.label: Cure
specs.value: Leave 24 h undisturbed before restringing (StewMac)

steps.title: Humidify the crack closed
steps.detail: A dryness crack is the guitar telling you the wood is short. Put the guitar (strings slackened) in a closed environment at about 45-55% RH - StewMac's quick method is a bag with a damp sponge in a bowl and a hygrometer - overnight or for a few days. If it closes flush, proceed. If it will not close at normal humidity, the gap needs a wood splint let into it - pro work.

steps.title: Clean the crack
steps.detail: Blow out dust with compressed air and pick out finish chips. Clean, fresh cracks take hide or Titebond glue well. Frank Ford used ordinary yellow glue on an old, dirty crack because hide glue bonds poorly to contaminated surfaces.

steps.title: Dry clamp first
steps.detail: Rehearse everything without glue: how you will push the crack slightly open from inside, where the cauls go, and how much pressure brings the edges flush. Use a flat caul with waxed paper on the outside so the two sides stay level.

steps.title: Glue the crack
steps.detail: Reach inside and press gently upward next to the crack to open it a hair, work glue in from outside with a palette knife or by finger, then release so it closes onto the glue. Clamp lightly with the flat caul so the edges sit level. Wipe squeeze-out with a rag dampened in hot water.
steps.warn: Do not over-clamp - you want the surfaces flush, not crushed.

steps.title: Make cleats
steps.detail: Cut small cleats (round or diamond) 3/32-1/8 in thick from matching wood, grain across the crack. Bevel the edges so they blend into the top. Space them every few inches along the crack, and add one at each end.

steps.title: Place and glue the cleats
steps.detail: Mark positions from outside. Use a magnet holder on the cleat and another magnet outside on low-tack tape (StewMac/Scott Holyfield method), or a crack-repair wire threaded through the crack. Check alignment with a mirror and light, glue the cleat and pull it up against the crack. Expect a little smear where it first touches; centre it and clean squeeze-out.

steps.title: Side cracks: use one long splint
steps.detail: Frank Ford prefers one long beveled mahogany splint (3/32 x 5/8 in) spanning the side between the linings over a row of small cleats, glued with hot hide glue and clamped with magnet cauls (two 1/2 x 1/4 in neodymium magnets per acrylic block, poles alternating so they self-align).

steps.title: Cure and finish
steps.detail: Leave it 24 hours. Scrape any glue line flush and touch up the finish if needed (drop-fill lacquer or have a pro do it). The crack line usually stays visible - the aim is structural, not invisible.

models.note: Hide glue (hot or liquid) matches the original construction and stays reversible for future repairs.
Laminate rarely cracks from dryness; cracks there are usually impact damage and may need a patch rather than a cleat.

warnings: Never glue a crack that is still open from dryness - when the wood swells back it will buckle or crack next to the repair.
CA (super glue) penetrates finish and wood and is hard to reverse; most luthiers keep it for finish drop-fills, not structural crack gluing.
pro: Cracks with a step, missing wood, impact punctures, cracks under the bridge or along the fingerboard, archtop cracks, and anything on a valuable guitar.

title: Loose braces: tap test and regluing
summary: A brace that has come unglued buzzes or rattles when you tap near it and can let the top or back distort. Find it by tapping and with a mirror, open the gap with wedges, work glue in, and clamp with jacks.
symptoms: Buzz or rattle when tapping the top or back with a knuckle
A buzz on certain notes that is not fret buzz
Wrinkle behind the bridge (cross brace)
A crack beside a brace end
tools: Inspection mirror and small LED light
Thin feeler gauge (0.002-0.004 in) to probe the glue line
Acrylic wedges (StewMac uses 1/2 in acrylic, sawn and filed to a taper)
Thin spatula (a cut-down 0.004 in feeler gauge works)
Scissor/brace jacks or long-reach clamps, wood slats and cauls
Magnets to hold jacks in place
Low-tack tape, curved strips of sandpaper
parts: Titebond Original (StewMac) or hot hide glue

steps.title: Tap test
steps.detail: Hold the guitar by the neck and tap with a knuckle all over the top, back and sides, listening for a buzzy or rattly note. Frank Ford's rule: if the buzz appears only when you rap the back, suspect a back brace; if it sounds from the neck when you knock the body, look at the headstock parts first (see [ac-buzz-rattle]).

steps.title: Find the gap
steps.detail: Put a light and mirror inside and follow each brace along its length, watching for a dark line between brace and top/back. Slide a thin feeler along the glue line: where it goes under, the brace is loose. Mark the ends of the loose section on low-tack tape outside.

steps.title: Clean the gap
steps.detail: Vacuum the inside first - dust under a brace stops glue bonding. Ease thin acrylic wedges under the brace to open the gap slightly, then pull a strip of fine abrasive through to freshen the surfaces and vacuum again.

steps.title: Glue
steps.detail: Mask beside the brace with tape. Pick up glue on a thin spatula and work it fully into the gap, using more than you think you need. Remove the wedges.

steps.title: Clamp
steps.detail: Set scissor jacks or brace clamps against the brace, with a paper-covered slat or flat caul outside to spread the load. Magnets can hold jacks in position. Check with the mirror that the brace is down along its full length.

steps.title: Clean up and cure
steps.detail: Clean squeeze-out (a thin even bead left along the brace is fine). Leave overnight before restringing. Glue one brace at a time - StewMac's back-brace job took one day per brace.

models.note: Two 4 in gaps on top braces and four loose back braces were all reglued this way.

Frank Ford calls the cross brace behind the bridge hard to reglue: small glue area, old glue that cannot be fully removed. If it fails again, options are epoxy or a short auxiliary brace - luthier territory.

warnings: Wood glue does not bond well over old glue; get as much out as you can.
pro: Cross-brace looseness under the bridge, braces in the narrow areas near the neck block, or any job where you cannot see and clamp the full length.

title: Neck reset: Taylor NT and other bolt-on acoustics
summary: Bolt-on acoustic necks are designed to be reset without steam: undo the bolts, change the heel contact or swap shims, and bolt back up. Taylor's NT neck uses matched shim pairs to set the angle.
tools: Hair dryer (to soften an internal label over bolt heads)
Socket/nut driver or hex keys to fit your neck bolts (Frank Ford's Taylor: two 1/4-20 bolts, 7/16 in nut driver)
parts: Taylor NT neck shim set (matched pairs) - via Taylor service

specs.label: Taylor NT shims (Haze Guitars)
specs.value: Wedge-shaped shims in two pockets (heel and fingerboard-extension); each step makes one edge 0.010 in (0.25 mm) thicker. A neutral pair gives a zero set angle; fit a thicker extension shim with a matching thinner heel shim to tilt the neck back

specs.label: Goal
specs.value: Straightedge on frets meets the bridge top; saddle at a healthy height

steps.title: Measure first
steps.detail: Do the straightedge and string-height checks from [ac-neck-reset-diagnose] and note the current saddle height.

steps.title: Find the bolts
steps.detail: Look through the soundhole at the neck block. On many Taylors and older bolt-ons the bolts hide under a label; warm it with a hair dryer and peel it back carefully.

steps.title: Loosen and adjust (older Taylor butt joint)
steps.detail: Frank Ford's method on an older Taylor: remove the two bolts, leave the fingerboard extension glued to the top so side-to-side alignment is kept, and draw sandpaper through the heel joint so the heel sits closer at the bottom, tilting the neck back. Rebolt, string to pitch, check, repeat in small amounts.

steps.title: Taylor NT: change the shims
steps.detail: On NT necks the neck lifts out once the bolts are out (the fingerboard extension is not glued). Swap the shim pair for one giving more back-angle (thicker extension shim, matching thinner heel shim). Shims always change as a matched pair.

steps.title: Reassemble and check
steps.detail: Bolt up snugly, restring, tune and check that the straightedge now meets the bridge top and the action can be set with a normal saddle.

steps.title: Re-label and set up
steps.detail: Stick the label back; finish with a normal setup.

models.note: Taylor advises saddle changes only for small action changes and a neck-angle (shim) change for larger ones, which avoids an overly low saddle. Shim sets go through Taylor's service network.
Also resettable without steam; Frank Ford documents it as a separate procedure.
Not bolt-on - see [ac-neck-reset-dovetail].

pro: Use a Taylor service centre for NT shims (and any warranty guitar); otherwise this is careful DIY at most.

title: Worn bridge plate and ball ends pulling through
time: 30 min (brass overlay) to 3 h (plugging with BridgeSaver)
summary: The bridge plate is the hardwood pad under the top that the string ball ends bear against. When the holes wear oval or chew away, ball ends climb into the holes, strings go out of tune and the bridge gets pried up. Fix with a brass overlay, plug-and-redrill, or replacement.
symptoms: Ball ends visible partly inside the pin holes (mirror)
Strings drift flat while settling
Pins pushed up or hard to seat
Oval, chewed or merged holes on the plate
Bridge starting to lift

causes.cause: Ball ends not seated against the plate at restringing
causes.check: Mirror inside: each ball end should sit tight against the plate wood, beside the pin tip
causes.fix: Reseat correctly; see [ac-bridge-pins].

causes.cause: Soft or thin plate material worn over decades
causes.check: Holes oval or several holes run together
causes.fix: Plug and redrill (BridgeSaver) or brass overlay (Plate Mate).

causes.cause: Wood missing between holes
causes.check: Large void across holes
causes.fix: Plate replacement - pro job.

tools: For plugging: StewMac BridgeSaver (cutter, pilot, shoe), plug cutter, soundhole clamps, 3/16 in long-shank drill bit, bridge pin reamer
parts: Plate Mate brass overlay (StewMac/Mitchel's), sized to your string spacing
Maple or rosewood plug stock about 0.135 in thick

specs.label: Plate Mate
specs.value: 0.032 in brass, self-adhesive and held by the strings; made for 2-1/8 and 2-3/16 in string spreads (other spreads, including 12-string, sold by Mitchel's)

specs.label: Pin hole diameter for redrill
specs.value: 3/16 in, then ream to fit the pins

steps.title: Inspect
steps.detail: Remove the strings, then use a mirror and light through the soundhole to look at each hole in the plate. Healthy holes are round with crisp edges and the ball ends sit flat against wood.

steps.title: Quick fix: brass overlay
steps.detail: A Plate Mate is a thin pre-drilled brass plate that sticks to the underside of the worn plate and is clamped by the ball ends. Choose the version that matches the centre-to-centre spacing of your outer pin holes. Clean the plate, line up the holes with pins pushed through from outside, and press it on. It is quick and reversible; some players report brighter tone. Luthiers such as Haze Guitars prefer a proper patch on a nice guitar.

steps.title: Proper fix: plug and redrill
steps.detail: With the BridgeSaver, thread the pilot through a pin hole from outside, attach the shoe inside and turn until the collar meets the plate, cutting a shallow dish around the hole. Do every other hole, plug those, then do the rest. Plugs are cut from maple or rosewood about 0.135 in thick, grain matched to the plate, glued with a soundhole clamp and sanded flush when dry.

steps.title: Redrill and ream
steps.detail: Back the area with clamped scrap, drill 3/16 in holes through the old pin holes, then ream to fit your pins (see [ac-bridge-pins]). Dan Erlewine's tip: a drop of thin super glue soaked into the new hole walls hardens them.

steps.title: Restring correctly
steps.detail: Each time you restring, push the pin in, pull the string up until the ball end bites against the plate, then tension. Check with the mirror once.

models.note: Bryan Galloup (Premier Guitar) notes later factories used much larger, thicker plates, which dampen tone; replacing with a smaller hard plate is a specialist job.
Extra tension wears plates faster; 12-string Plate Mate versions exist.

pro: Plate replacement (heat, special chisel and caul, top support) is a luthier job; a mistake can crack the top.

title: Neck reset: dovetail joint (Martin, Gibson) - how pros do it
summary: On glued dovetail necks the joint is softened with steam injected through the 15th-fret slot, the neck is pulled, the heel is trimmed to the new angle and the neck is reglued. This is pro work; here is what happens so you can judge quotes and results.
tools: Heat blanket on a timer, contact thermometer
1/16 in drill bit (hex shank) and driver
Steam source with fine needle (Frank Ford: 1/16 in OD stainless tube)

specs.label: Dovetail access (Frank Ford)
specs.value: On most Martins the end of the dovetail pocket lies just under the 15th fret

specs.label: Steam hole
specs.value: 1/16 in hole through the 15th-fret slot into the pocket

specs.label: Target
specs.value: Straightedge on the frets lands on the top of the bridge; then a full setup and often a refret

steps.title: Diagnose and measure
steps.detail: Confirm with [ac-neck-reset-diagnose]. Record how far the straightedge lands below the bridge top; Haze Guitars' formula estimates heel removal.

steps.title: Free the fingerboard extension
steps.detail: Heat the fingerboard over the body (Frank Ford insulates it with a thin wood slip under a heat blanket) and slide a broad knife under to free it from the top.

steps.title: Pull the 15th fret and drill
steps.detail: Remove the 15th fret while warm, then drill a 1/16 in hole down through its slot into the dovetail pocket; probe with a bit of old string to confirm.

steps.title: Steam the joint
steps.detail: Mount a jig that pulls upward on the heel. Inject steam through the hole; mop escaping water and steam, and vacuum steam out of the body. Wiggle the neck - it pops free.
steps.warn: Steam and hot water burn skin and can lift finish and loosen nearby glue joints - pros mask and work fast.

steps.title: Trim the heel
steps.detail: Clean the old glue, then cut back the heel's contact face (Frank Ford leaves about 1/16 in of original surface at the edges) and taper the dovetail so the neck sits back. Fine-fit by pulling 180-grit paper through the joint with the neck seated, which removes more at the heel than near the fingerboard.

steps.title: Check angle and centre line often
steps.detail: After every few pulls, check that the straightedge reaches the top of the bridge and that the strings line up with the centre of the fingerboard.

steps.title: Shim and glue
steps.detail: Shim the dovetail cheeks with veneer for a snug fit and glue with hide glue (brushed on the cheeks only, so a future reset is easier), clamping with a caul shaped to the fingerboard radius.

steps.title: Setup
steps.detail: Restring and check action; a new saddle and often fret work follow.

models.note: Classic dovetail with the pocket end under the 15th fret; Martin's own guidance is to use authorised service centres.
Also a glued dovetail; same steam approach by a pro.

pro: Always a pro job.

title: Remove and reglue an acoustic bridge
time: 2-4 h work + 24 h before string tension
summary: The pro method: heat the bridge with the top masked, slide it off with a thin spatula, clean both surfaces to fresh wood, fit, then glue and clamp with cauls centred over the braces.
tools: Bridge spatula and palette knife (dressed sharp and smooth)
Heat source: 250 W infrared lamp with reflector, or a rubber heat blanket on a timer
Cardboard/foil heat mask, copper or aluminium tape, painter's tape
Sharp chisels and a hooked cabinet scraper
80-grit self-adhesive sandpaper on a block radiused to the top
Bridge clamps (deep-throat), internal caul shaped to the plate, external bridge caul
Locating pins/screws through two pin holes
parts: Titebond Original (StewMac's choice; Titebond III for hard-touring guitars) or hot hide glue (Frank Ford's choice on Martins)

specs.label: Heat target (StewMac)
specs.value: Top surface of the bridge about 200-250 deg F so the glue line reaches roughly 140 deg F

specs.label: Heating time (StewMac demo)
specs.value: About 10 minutes total, reheating as it cools

specs.label: Clamp time
specs.value: Clamps off after about 12 h; no string tension for 24 h (StewMac)

steps.title: Prepare and mark
steps.detail: Remove strings and saddle. Lightly score around the bridge outline with a knife (light pressure so the lacquer does not crack) and tape a border just outside it so you can reposition the bridge exactly.

steps.title: Mask the top
steps.detail: Make a cardboard mask that fits tightly round the bridge, seal it with foil/copper tape and add reflective insulation so only the bridge receives heat.

steps.title: Heat
steps.detail: Aim the lamp at the bridge from a few inches and keep it moving, or use a foil-wrapped heat blanket weighted down, on a timer. Check temperature with the IR thermometer.
steps.warn: Overheating scorches finish and can soften brace glue under the top. Never leave a heater unattended; Frank Ford says burnt instruments from timer-less heaters are common. Keep a fire extinguisher handy.

steps.title: Slide the spatula under
steps.detail: Work a thin, sharp spatula in from the edges and through the pin-hole area, a little at a time. StewMac's rule: never force the knife - if it resists, heat more. Lift the bridge off while it is still warm.

steps.title: Clean both surfaces
steps.detail: While warm, scrape old glue and fibres from the bridge underside without taking ebony/rosewood away. On the top, scrape inside the scored line to bare wood, removing any finish (thick finish may need stripper or a router). Frank Ford scrapes lightly even where it looks clean to remove oxidised wood.

steps.title: True the fit
steps.detail: Sand both surfaces with 80 grit on a block radiused to the top so they match. Lightly crosshatch both so glue keys in and the bridge cannot skate. If the bridge itself warped, Frank Ford soaks it a few minutes in boiling water and it often relaxes back to shape.

steps.title: Dry clamp
steps.detail: Locate the bridge with screws or pins through two pin holes, clamp with one centre clamp and lighter clamps on the wings. The inside caul must bear on the bridge plate and not on the X-braces. Check with a mirror. Confirm the outline matches the tape.

steps.title: Glue and clamp
steps.detail: Spread glue slightly generously, locate, and tighten evenly until there is a thin even bead of squeeze-out. Do not crank down - too much pressure starves the joint. Press on the bridge: if it springs back there is trapped air. Clean squeeze-out and swab the pin holes with a damp cotton bud.

steps.title: Cure and restring
steps.detail: Clamps off after about 12 hours, strings on after 24. Check pin fit and ball-end seating and re-set the action.

models.note: Originally hide glue; Frank Ford reglues with hot hide glue to match and for heat resistance.
Higher tension makes bridges lift more often; check the plate condition at the same time.

warnings: Heat and solvent near a lacquer finish can damage it; ventilation needed if stripping finish.
A cracked plate or loose cross brace found during the job must be fixed before the bridge goes back on.
pro: This is pro-level work. Get a luthier to do it on any valuable guitar, any guitar with a pickup under the saddle, or if you do not have proper clamps and cauls.

title: Active bass batteries and active/passive switching
summary: Active basses run their preamp from a 9 V battery (or two for 18 V). This covers when to change it, how to do it safely, why the jack drains it, and what the active/passive switch does when the battery dies.
tools: Small Phillips screwdriver (if no snap-open battery box)
parts: PP3 9 V alkaline battery (two for 18 V systems, same brand)

specs.label: Systems (Fender)
specs.value: 9 V (one battery) or 18 V (two batteries)

specs.label: Battery life (Fender)
specs.value: About 600 hours of playing

specs.label: Battery life (Music Man)
specs.value: About 6 months average with alkaline

specs.label: Battery type (Fender)
specs.value: PP3 9 V of the same or equivalent type; Fender says not to use rechargeables

steps.title: Know the signs
steps.detail: Distortion, crackle, unwanted noise or a weak, thin sound mean the battery voltage has dropped (Fender and Music Man).

steps.title: Unplug first
steps.detail: Many active basses use a switching (stereo/TRS) output jack that connects the battery only when a cable is plugged in. Unplug before changing the battery - and always unplug after playing, or the battery drains.

steps.title: Open the battery box or control cavity
steps.detail: Snap-open boxes lift with a fingernail or latch; others need the control plate or a cover unscrewed.

steps.title: Swap the battery
steps.detail: Pull the old battery from its snap, fit the new one with correct polarity, and tuck the wires so they will not be pinched by the cover. On 18 V systems replace both batteries at the same time with the same brand; never mix old and new or different types.

steps.title: Test
steps.detail: Plug in and play through every control. If an EQ knob or the whole bass is still distorted, recheck the snap connection.

steps.title: Use the active/passive switch when stuck
steps.detail: Many active basses have a switch (often a push/pull knob or mini toggle) that bypasses the preamp and runs the pickups passively. That keeps you playing if the battery dies on stage. Fender notes that active basses without such a switch will not work at all on a dead battery.

steps.title: Storage
steps.detail: Remove the batteries if the bass will sit unused for a long time.

models.model: Fender active basses (Deluxe, Elite, Ultra, etc.)
models.note: Some Deluxe Jazz models run 18 V; check how many batteries your bass has.
Single 9 V; Music Man recommends Duracell because battery sizes vary and some will not fit the compartment.

warnings: A 9 V battery's terminals can short across keys or coins in a pocket and get hot - keep spares in their packaging or with a terminal cover.
Fender advises against rechargeable batteries in its basses.
Dispose of old batteries properly.
pro: If a fresh battery does not fix the noise, the preamp, jack or wiring has a fault - see the wiring guides or a tech.

title: Identify a pot: value, taper and date codes
summary: Read the markings on a pot to find its value (250k, 500k, 1M, 25k), taper (audio/log or linear) and maker/date code – and confirm with a meter.
tools: Cotton bud and alcohol (to clean grime)

specs.label: Taper letters
specs.value: A = audio/log, B = linear on most US/CTS and Asian pots – but some imports reverse them, so check with a meter

specs.label: EIA maker codes
specs.value: 137 CTS, 134 Centralab, 304 Stackpole, 106 Allen-Bradley, 140 Clarostat, 381 Bourns

specs.label: Date code (US)
specs.value: After the maker code: year (2 digits, sometimes 1 on 1950s pots) then week. 1377624 = CTS, 1976, week 24

specs.label: Newer CTS pots
specs.value: May drop the 137 and show a 4-digit year+week code, e.g. 1407 = week 7 of 2014

specs.label: Typical uses
specs.value: 250k single coils; 500k humbuckers; 1M Jazzmaster and some vintage Teles; 25k actives

steps.title: Find the markings
steps.detail: Clean grime or solder flux off the casing. Look for the value and taper (e.g. 'A500K', '250K B', '500 Aud', '250K Lin').

steps.title: Read the source/date code
steps.detail: On US pots, find a 6–7 digit number starting with the maker code. Split it: maker (3 digits), year, week. Remember guitar makers bought pots in bulk, so the pot date only tells you the guitar was made after that date – usually within a year or two.

steps.title: Confirm value with a meter
steps.detail: Measure across the outer lugs (see [ef-test-pots]).

steps.title: Confirm taper with a meter
steps.detail: At half rotation, an outer lug to the wiper reads about half the total on a linear pot, much less (from one side) on an audio pot.

steps.title: Choose replacements
steps.detail: Match value, taper, shaft type (split/solid, 24 or 18 spline – see [ef-knobs]), shaft length and bushing size. US CTS-style and metric import pots differ in size and may need a larger mounting hole.

models.note: Usually 250k (some Teles 1M). Import Fenders often use metric pots with no useful date code.
500k; CTS 137-coded pots in vintage US guitars help with dating.
1M lead pots; Jaguar rhythm circuit 1M linear volume, 50k linear tone.

title: Knobs loose, stuck or won't fit
summary: Remove stuck knobs without marking the finish, make loose push-on knobs grip again, and match knobs to split-shaft or solid-shaft pots.
symptoms: Knob spins without turning the pot
Knob falls off
Knob won't come off
New knobs don't fit new pots
tools: Knob puller (e.g. StewMac Pullit) or a soft cloth/string loop
Small flat screwdriver or knife blade

specs.label: Fine spline
specs.value: 24 splines – US CTS-style pots (most American guitars)

specs.label: Coarse spline
specs.value: 18 splines – Alpha and many import pots

specs.label: Shaft types
specs.value: Split, knurled shaft (push-on knobs) or solid shaft (set-screw knobs)

steps.title: Removing a stuck knob
steps.detail: Don't lever it off with a screwdriver blade – that dents the knob and the finish. Slide a knob puller underneath, or loop a soft cloth or a length of string under the knob, and pull straight up evenly. Turn the knob slightly as you pull.

steps.title: Loose push-on knob (split shaft)
steps.detail: Remove the knob and gently open the split in the shaft with a thin blade so the two halves spread a little; then push the knob back on. Go easy: too much spread and the shaft cracks or the knob binds partway down.

steps.title: Tight push-on knob
steps.detail: If a knob binds, close the split slightly by squeezing the shaft halves together. Squeezing too much (as one Warmoth forum user found) can make the knob stick halfway – adjust in small steps.

steps.title: Set-screw knobs
steps.detail: Line the set screw up with the shaft's split, or with a solid shaft's flat, so it grips without crushing the shaft or tilting the knob. On split shafts, a small spacer in the slot gives the screw something solid to bite.

steps.title: Match spline counts
steps.detail: Knobs made for 24-spline (fine) CTS shafts won't fit 18-spline (coarse) import shafts and vice versa. Check the pot maker's datasheet when ordering; many knob sellers don't say.

steps.title: Pot shaft spinning in the body
steps.detail: If the whole pot turns, the pot nut under the knob is loose. Remove the knob, hold the pot from behind if you can, and tighten the nut with a nut driver. Check the anti-rotation tab sits in its hole if the pot has one.

models.note: Bell/top-hat/speed knobs are push-on; they often stick hard. Use a cloth loop or puller, never a screwdriver near a nitro top.
Push-on knobs on split shafts; easy to spread or close the split.
Many Tele knobs use a set screw (or push-on 'dome' knobs). Align the set screw with the flat or split.
Stacked/concentric pots need matching stacked knob sets; inner and outer shafts have different diameters.

title: Set pickup height (and cure 'Stratitis' wolf tones)
summary: Set each pickup to a starting height measured at the last fret, balance them by ear, and lower any pickup whose magnets pull on the strings and cause warble, false notes or lost sustain.
symptoms: Warbling, chorus-like 'wolf' notes on the wound strings high up the neck
Notes won't sustain or sound out of tune
One pickup much louder than the others
Strings hit the pole pieces when strummed hard
tools: 6 in steel ruler in 64ths or a string-action gauge

specs.label: How to measure
specs.value: Fret the string at the LAST fret; measure from the top of the pole piece to the bottom of the string, on the bass E and treble E

specs.label: Fender Texas Special
specs.value: Bass side 8/64 in (3.2 mm), treble side 6/64 in (2.4 mm)

specs.label: Fender vintage style
specs.value: Bass 6/64 in (2.4 mm), treble 5/64 in (2.0 mm)

specs.label: Fender American/Mexican Standard
specs.value: Bass 5/64 in (2.0 mm), treble 4/64 in (1.6 mm)

specs.label: Fender humbuckers
specs.value: Bass and treble 4/64 in (1.6 mm)

specs.label: Fender bass, vintage
specs.value: Bass 8/64 in (3.2 mm), treble 6/64 in (2.4 mm)

specs.label: Fender bass, American/Mexican Standard
specs.value: Bass 6/64 in (2.4 mm), treble 5/64 in (2.0 mm)

specs.label: Gibson humbuckers (current, per Premier Guitar)
specs.value: Bridge 1/16 in (1.6 mm); neck 3/32 in (2.4 mm). 1950s: 1/16 in both

specs.label: Premier Guitar humbucker starting point
specs.value: 3/32 in (2.4 mm) bass side, 1/16 in (1.6 mm) treble side

specs.label: Lace Sensors
specs.value: Fender: as close as you like, allowing for string movement

steps.title: Tune up and mark the old height
steps.detail: Tune to pitch. Put a strip of masking tape by each pickup and note the current measurements so you can go back.

steps.title: Measure at the last fret
steps.detail: Fret the low E at the highest fret (or use a capo there) and measure from the top of the pole piece under it to the underside of the string. Repeat on the high E. This is the closest the string ever gets to the pickup.

steps.title: Set to the starting spec
steps.detail: Turn the height screws: clockwise raises the pickup on most guitars, anti-clockwise lowers it. Bring each pickup to its spec on both sides. A quarter turn is audible, so go in small steps.

steps.title: Check for magnetic pull (Stratitis)
steps.detail: Play the low E and A strings around the 12th–17th frets with the neck pickup selected and listen for warble, beating, or a note that won't settle. It's worst on the neck pickup (strings swing most there), on wound strings, and high up the neck. If you hear it, lower that pickup – especially its bass side – until it disappears. Strong Alnico-magnet vintage single coils are the usual culprits.

steps.title: Adjust poles if fitted
steps.detail: On humbuckers with screw poles, set the poles to follow the fretboard radius, then fine-tune by ear.

steps.title: Balance by ear
steps.detail: Stand about 10 ft from the amp, volume on full. Switch through all positions and listen for even volume. If one pickup is louder, lower it rather than raising the quiet one – and don't go above the spec heights.

steps.title: Recheck
steps.detail: Make sure strings don't hit the poles when you dig in hard, then re-check tuning and intonation.

models.note: Neck pickup is the most likely to cause Stratitis; set it lower on the bass side.
Bridge pickup height is set by three screws through the bridge plate; the neck pickup by two screws from the top or through the pickguard.
Humbuckers' bar magnets sit under the coils, so they pull the strings less and can sit closer. Neck usually set a little lower than bridge.
Large, wide single coils – watch for magnetic pull on the wound strings.
Weak magnets; EMG recommends setting them as close to the strings as possible – pull isn't usually an issue.
Use Fender's bass figures; bass strings move a lot, so leave enough room on the low string.

title: Acoustic preamp problems and feedback control
summary: Most onboard-preamp faults are batteries, jacks and cables. Feedback is tamed with a soundhole cover, the phase switch, less bass and a sensible input impedance.
symptoms: No sound or crackling output
Sound cuts out when the plug or strap is moved
Distorted, fading sound (battery)
Low boomy howl at volume (feedback)
Amp cutting out on bass notes

causes.cause: Weak or dead 9 V battery (or battery clip worn)
causes.check: Fresh battery; inspect clip and wires
causes.fix: Replace battery; replace a worn clip.

causes.cause: Battery drain from a cable left in the jack
causes.check: Most jack preamps switch on when a plug is inserted
causes.fix: Unplug when not playing.

causes.cause: Worn stereo endpin jack or loose strap button/nut
causes.check: Signal crackles when wiggling the plug; K&K notes a strap button not screwed fully on can break the circuit
causes.fix: Screw the strap cap fully home; tighten the jack's inner nut; replace a worn jack.

causes.cause: Feedback at the body's resonance
causes.check: Howl at one low note, worse near the amp
causes.fix: Soundhole cover, phase switch, cut bass/notch, move away from the speaker.

causes.cause: High-impedance input with piezo/contact pickups
causes.check: Plugging straight into a 5-10 Mohm acoustic amp input
causes.fix: Use a preamp or a lower-impedance input (K&K: about 500 kohm-1 Mohm).

specs.label: K&K phase-switch claim
specs.value: Correct phase gives about 30-40% more volume before feedback

specs.label: Recommended input impedance for passive contact pickups (K&K)
specs.value: About 500 kohm-1 Mohm

steps.title: Battery first
steps.detail: Fit a fresh 9 V battery (or the type the system uses) even if the old one 'seems fine'. Check the clip is not cracked and the wires are not pulling off.

steps.title: Cable and jack
steps.detail: Swap in a known-good cable. Wiggle the plug in the endpin jack; crackle means a worn jack or loose connection. Make sure the strap button/cap is screwed fully home and the jack's inner nut is tight.

steps.title: Isolate pickups in a dual system
steps.detail: With a stereo jack, a mono cable plays the tip pickup only; K&K's trick is to pull the plug out about 1/4 in to hear the ring pickup. This shows which source is faulty.

steps.title: Tame feedback
steps.detail: In order: fit a soundhole cover (the biggest single help), try the phase switch at the volume you play, turn bass down on the preamp or amp, use any notch filter to cut the howling frequency, and stand to the side of or in front of your speaker rather than behind it.

steps.title: Fix the input
steps.detail: Passive contact pickups can make an amp's protection circuit cut out on bass bursts when plugged into very high-impedance inputs. Use a preamp or line input, and turn the bass down.

steps.title: Stop rattles from electronics
steps.detail: Loose preamps, battery boxes and wires rattle; secure them with clips and foam (see [ac-buzz-rattle]).

models.note: Preamp sits in the endpin jack with a battery clip mounted inside on the neck block (Frank Ford); no onboard controls, so tone is set at the amp/PA or an outboard unit.
Preamp is built into the endpin jack and runs from a 9 V battery in a bag inside the body; the volume (and on Anthem, mic trim) control sticks to the soundhole edge.

warnings: Never open amps or mains-powered gear; this guide covers only the battery-powered guitar side.
pro: Intermittent faults inside a sealed preamp, or broken wires at the pickup strip, are best handled by the maker's service or a tech.

title: Active pickups or preamp dead or distorting
summary: Active pickups (EMG, Fishman Fluence, Seymour Duncan Blackouts) and onboard preamps need a 9 V battery and a stereo jack that switches it on. Most 'dead' actives are a flat battery, the wrong cable, or the jack's battery switch.
symptoms: No sound, or very weak sound
Fuzzy, farty distortion on hard notes
Crackle that repeats
Battery dies quickly
tools: Fresh 9 V alkaline or lithium battery

specs.label: Replace battery when
specs.value: Below 6 V measured with the cable plugged in (under load) – East UK

specs.label: EMG 81 current draw
specs.value: About 80 µA at 9 V; EMG quotes 3000 h battery life

specs.label: Battery capacity (Sweetwater)
specs.value: Standard 9 V alkaline ≈ 580 mAh; life = 580,000 µAh ÷ total draw in µA

specs.label: Preamp draws
specs.value: Simple bass preamps ~2–2.5 mA; feature-rich ones ~5 mA (East UK) – so batteries last weeks to months, not years

specs.label: Stereo jack wiring (EMG)
specs.value: Tip = signal (white), sleeve = ground (black), ring = battery negative (black battery lead)

specs.label: Pots for EMG
specs.value: 25k – required

causes.cause: Flat or weak battery
causes.check: Measure with the cable plugged in. A battery can read 7–8 V unloaded and collapse under load.
causes.fix: Fit a fresh, sealed name-brand battery.

causes.cause: Cable left plugged in
causes.check: Battery dies within days or weeks.
causes.fix: Always unplug when not playing – the jack's ring contact is the power switch.

causes.cause: Stereo (TRS) cable used
causes.check: East UK notes a TRS plug can stop the battery circuit closing.
causes.fix: Use a normal mono instrument cable.

causes.cause: Battery clip or jack ring connection broken
causes.check: Continuity from battery black lead to jack ring lug; from battery red to the pickups' + supply.
causes.fix: Re-solder or replace the clip/jack.

causes.cause: Ground or shield touching the ring lug
causes.check: The black battery wire should be alone on the ring terminal.
causes.fix: Re-route; a ground on the ring leaves the battery always on (drains it).

causes.cause: Jack touching other wiring
causes.check: Battery drains even when unplugged.
causes.fix: Insulate and re-route.

steps.title: Fresh battery first
steps.detail: Fit a known-new 9 V battery. Check the clip snaps on firmly.

steps.title: Measure under load
steps.detail: Plug in a mono cable (this switches the power on), then measure the battery terminals on DC volts. Below 6 V = replace.

steps.title: Use the right cable
steps.detail: Mono TS cable only. Try a different cable.

steps.title: Inspect the stereo jack
steps.detail: Tip lug = signal, sleeve = ground, ring = battery negative. Make sure nothing else touches the ring lug and the jack isn't touching other wires.

steps.title: Check solderless connectors
steps.detail: On EMG solderless systems, push each pickup's plug fully into its socket on the pot/harness and check none have crept out.

steps.title: Isolate the preamp (bass)
steps.detail: East UK's test: disconnect the pickups from the preamp inputs, short each input's hot to cold, turn the treble up. Only a slight even hiss should remain; if it's still noisy, the preamp itself is faulty.

models.note: Don't connect a bridge ground wire (EMG cites a shock hazard). Use 25k pots. Unplug after playing.
Passive/active switches usually still draw some current while plugged in, by design, to avoid a thump. 18 V (two 9 V in series) adds headroom only, not gain.
Endpin jacks on Fishman/LR Baggs systems switch the battery the same way; unplug after playing. Weak batteries cause distortion on strums.

warnings: Don't short 9 V battery terminals on pot casings or foil – they get hot quickly.
Remove the battery if the guitar is going into storage, to avoid leaks.
pro: If a fresh battery and correct cable don't help and the wiring checks out, the preamp may be faulty – contact the maker or a tech.

Sweetwater SweetCare – How long will a battery last in EMG pickups?

title: Crackling or scratchy volume/tone knob
summary: A pot that crackles as you turn it has dirt or wear on its track or wiper. Clean it first with contact cleaner; replace it if the noise comes back or the sweep is uneven.
symptoms: Scratchy noise through the amp when turning a knob
Volume jumps or drops at certain points
Noise even when the knob is still
tools: Contact cleaner (e.g. CAIG DeoxIT D-series, or similar)
parts: Replacement pot of the same value, taper and shaft type (see [ef-identify-pots])

steps.title: Exercise it first
steps.detail: Turn the knob end to end 10–20 times. Fender notes this alone sometimes clears light oxidation.

steps.title: Get access
steps.detail: Remove the knobs and the pickguard, control plate or back cover so you can see the pot body. Pots have a small opening at the side where the lugs come out.

steps.title: Protect the guitar
steps.detail: Tuck paper towel around the pot to catch overspray. Don't breathe the spray.

steps.title: Spray a small amount
steps.detail: Give one brief squirt into the opening beside the lugs, turn the shaft end to end several times, then give one more brief squirt and turn again. CAIG suggests a fast-evaporating D-series product (their DN5) because the standard D5 evaporates slowly and can drip. More is not better.

steps.title: Test
steps.detail: Plug in and sweep the knob. Then do the meter sweep in [ef-test-pots].

steps.title: Replace if needed
steps.detail: If the crackle returns quickly, the sweep jumps on the meter, or the pot is sealed, replace it. Seymour Duncan's view is that cleaning sometimes helps but replacing worn pots is generally better. Transfer wires one at a time to the same lugs on the new pot.

causes.cause: Dirt/oxidation on the track or wiper
causes.check: Crackle only when turning.
causes.fix: Clean as above.

causes.cause: Worn carbon track
causes.check: Meter sweep shows jumps or dead spots after cleaning.
causes.fix: Replace the pot.

causes.cause: Cold joint on the pot's wiper or casing
causes.check: Noise when you push the knob sideways without turning.
causes.fix: Re-solder.

causes.cause: Stacked/concentric pot (bass) shafts rubbing
causes.check: East UK notes that crackle when turning a stacked control is usually the shafts, not dirt.
causes.fix: Don't clean sealed pots; check alignment or replace.

causes.cause: DC voltage on the pot in an active circuit
causes.check: Crackle on an active bass/guitar knob even after cleaning.
causes.fix: Preamp issue – contact the maker or a tech.

models.note: All pots on the pickguard; lift the guard (strings slackened) to reach them.
Remove the two control-plate screws; the plate lifts out with pots and switch attached.
Pots are reached through the rear control cavity cover.
No back cavity – you can spray through the f-holes only with great care; replacement means pulling the harness through the f-hole (see a pro if unsure).
Onboard preamp sliders/pots are often sealed; check the maker's advice before spraying.

warnings: Contact cleaner can mark some finishes and soften some plastics; keep overspray off the guitar.
pro: Pot replacement on a fully hollow or semi-hollow guitar (335 style) is fiddly; a tech has the tools to pull and re-fit the harness through the f-holes.
