title: Hum and buzz: single-coil hum vs a ground fault
summary: Work out whether the noise is the normal mains hum single coils pick up, interference from the room, or a real grounding fault in the guitar – using the touch-the-strings test and a meter.
symptoms: Steady hum that changes as you turn your body
Buzz that goes away when you touch the strings or bridge
Buzz that gets louder when you touch the strings
Noise only in positions 1, 3 and 5 on a Strat

specs.label: Mains hum frequency
specs.value: 60 Hz (North America), 50 Hz (Europe/most other regions) plus harmonics

specs.label: Good ground path
specs.value: ≈0 Ω from strings/bridge to jack sleeve on a passive guitar

causes.cause: Normal single-coil hum
causes.check: Hum rises and falls as you rotate the guitar; quieter in Strat positions 2 and 4 (with an RWRP middle pickup). Touching strings reduces it a little.
causes.fix: Turn away from the source, move away from dimmers/monitors/lights, shield the cavities ([ef-shielding]), or fit noiseless pickups.

causes.cause: Room interference (dimmers, fluorescent/LED lights, computer monitors, transformers)
causes.check: Noise changes as you walk around the room; disappears in another room.
causes.fix: Switch off or move away from the source; find the quietest angle.

causes.cause: Missing or broken bridge/string ground
causes.check: Meter from a string to the jack sleeve reads OL. Buzz is unchanged when you touch the strings.
causes.fix: Re-solder or replace the bridge ground wire.

causes.cause: Broken ground elsewhere (pot back, jack sleeve, pickup ground)
causes.check: Loud buzz, sometimes louder when touching strings. Meter from the volume pot back to every metal part.
causes.fix: Re-solder the broken ground.

causes.cause: Shielding not connected to ground
causes.check: Meter from cavity foil/paint to pot back reads OL.
causes.fix: Add a ground connection (see [ef-shielding]).

causes.cause: Amp, power or cable problem
causes.check: Noise remains with the guitar's volume at zero, or with another guitar.
causes.fix: Change one thing at a time: cable, outlet, pedal power. Fluorescent lights and poorly grounded outlets are common (Seymour Duncan).

steps.title: Volume to zero
steps.detail: Turn the guitar's volume off. If the noise stays, it isn't coming from the pickups – check cable, pedals and amp.

steps.title: Rotate test
steps.detail: Volume up, hands off the strings. Slowly turn on the spot. Single coils are directional; if the hum swells and fades with angle, it's interference being picked up by the coils – normal for single coils.

steps.title: Touch-the-strings test
steps.detail: Touch the strings or bridge. On a correctly grounded passive guitar, the noise should drop a little (your body is grounded through the strings and stops acting as an antenna). If it drops a LOT, you are in a noisy spot or the cavity shielding is poor. If it gets LOUDER, or doesn't change at all, suspect a ground fault.

steps.title: Check the bridge ground
steps.detail: Meter (Ω) from any string to the cable sleeve. It should read close to 0 Ω. OL means the bridge ground wire is broken or missing.

steps.title: Check every ground
steps.detail: With the cavity open, put one probe on the volume pot casing and touch every metal part: other pot casings, switch ground lug, jack sleeve lug, bridge/claw, pickup covers/baseplates, shielding. Fralin recommends the resistance setting: 0.0 = good, OL = broken connection.

steps.title: Fix what you find
steps.detail: Re-solder broken grounds; add a jumper where there's no connection. Then repeat the touch test.

models.note: The bridge ground wire runs from the trem spring claw to the volume pot back. Positions 2 and 4 are hum-cancelling only if the middle pickup is RWRP.
Bridge ground is under the bridge plate; the bridge pickup's screws into a grounded plate also ground the strings. The control plate grounds the pots.
Bridge ground wire comes up into the bridge (stud) bushing hole from the control cavity.
No shielding plate – every metal part needs a ground wire; the bridge ground comes via a stud.
Large single coils; Jaguars have metal side plates that help reject interference.
EMG says do NOT connect the bridge ground wire with active pickups (they cite a shock hazard). Some buzz with active pickups is a battery or wiring fault, not the bridge.

warnings: If you get a tingle or shock touching the strings, stop playing and have the amp and the building's power checked – this is not a guitar wiring fault to live with.
pro: Noise that persists after the guitar checks out (all grounds 0 Ω, shielding grounded) is usually in the amp or the building's power – that's for an amp tech or electrician.

title: Measure pickup DC resistance (find an open or shorted coil)
summary: Check whether a pickup is alive, find an open or partly shorted coil, and identify unknown pickups by measuring DC resistance – plus the typical readings for common designs.
symptoms: One pickup silent or much weaker than it should be
You don't know what pickups are in a used guitar
Checking a pickup before installing it
tools: Multimeter on Ω (20 kΩ range or auto)
Soldering iron (to lift leads for an exact reading)

specs.label: Fender Tele neck (rhythm)
specs.value: 7.6 kΩ

specs.label: Gibson PAF humbucker
specs.value: 8.4 kΩ

specs.label: Gibson mini humbucker
specs.value: 6.8 kΩ

specs.label: Gibson P-90
specs.value: 8.6 kΩ

specs.label: Fender Jazz Bass
specs.value: 8.5 kΩ

specs.label: Tolerance
specs.value: Expect small differences from pickup to pickup, even on the same guitar; compare to the maker's published figure

specs.label: Humbucker, one coil
specs.value: About half the full-pickup figure

causes.cause: Open coil (broken winding or a lead broken off at the eyelet)
causes.check: Reads OL across the pickup's leads.
causes.fix: Check the lead-to-coil joint under the pickup (often repairable); if the break is inside the winding, the pickup needs rewinding or replacing.

causes.cause: Short across the leads (solder blob, pinched lead, hot touching a grounded cover or baseplate)
causes.check: Reads near 0 Ω instead of several kΩ.
causes.fix: Look for solder bridging the lead tabs and for insulation crushed under a mounting screw; reroute or re-insulate.

causes.cause: Partly shorted turns inside the coil
causes.check: Reads clearly lower than the published figure and sounds weak.
causes.fix: Rewind or replace – not a DIY repair.

causes.cause: Measuring through the guitar's wiring
causes.check: Reading slightly lower than spec but plausible.
causes.fix: Normal – the pots are in parallel. Lift one lead for an exact figure.

steps.title: Unplug and let it cool
steps.detail: Unplug the guitar. If you've just been soldering near the pickup, wait – a warm coil reads high.

steps.title: Single-coil or 2-conductor pickup
steps.detail: Desolder one of the two leads (usually the hot) so the rest of the circuit is out of the way, then put one probe on each lead. Compare with the specs table or the maker's figure.

steps.title: 4-conductor humbucker – whole pickup
steps.detail: For Seymour Duncan colours: join red and white together, join green and bare together, then measure from black to green/bare. That's the full series reading. Other makers use other colours for the same roles – check their chart.

steps.title: 4-conductor humbucker – each coil
steps.detail: Seymour Duncan: the north (slug/fixed pole) coil is white-to-black; the south (adjustable screw) coil is red-to-green. Each should read about half the full figure. If the total is wrong, this tells you which coil is faulty.

steps.title: Read the result
steps.detail: Within a few hundred ohms of spec: pickup fine – look for wiring, joint or switch faults instead. OL: open coil or broken lead. Near zero: short. Way low: shorted turns. If the total is right but the guitar still won't work, the fault is elsewhere – often a cold joint.

steps.title: Inspect the lead joints
steps.detail: On Fender-style single coils, the coil wire ends are soldered to eyelets in the bottom flatwork. A fine wire broken right at the eyelet is a common cause of an 'open' reading and can sometimes be re-soldered by a careful hand with a fine tip; a break deeper in the coil cannot.

models.note: Middle pickup is often RWRP but reads the same resistance; resistance doesn't tell you polarity (see [ef-pickup-phase-polarity]).
The neck pickup normally reads higher than the bridge (about 7.6k vs 6.2–6.6k vintage). A bridge pickup reading zero is often its hot lead touching the grounded baseplate.
Braided single-conductor leads: the braid is ground, the inner wire is hot – measure between them with the lead lifted off the switch or pot.
Active pickups contain a preamp; a resistance reading across their output means nothing useful. Check battery voltage and the connections instead (see [ef-active-dead]).
P-Bass pickups are two coils in series; measure the pair and each half.

warnings: Resistance only tells you how much wire is on a coil, not how good it sounds; use it to find faults and identify pickups, not to judge tone.
pro: Open or shorted coils deep inside the winding need a pickup maker to rewind them.

title: No sound at all
summary: The guitar makes no sound in any position. Work from the outside in: cable and amp, battery (if active), output jack, then wiring.
symptoms: Silence in every pickup position
Only a faint hum or nothing when you tap the pickups
Worked yesterday, dead today

causes.cause: Cable or amp (not the guitar)
causes.check: Try another cable, and another guitar in the same amp/channel. Check amp standby, volume and pedals.
causes.fix: Replace the faulty cable; bypass the pedalboard.

causes.cause: Dead battery in an active guitar
causes.check: Measure the 9 V battery with the cable plugged in. Below 6 V under load = dead.
causes.fix: Fit a fresh battery; see [ef-active-dead].

causes.cause: Output jack: hot wire broken off, tip contact bent away, or tip shorted to sleeve
causes.check: Look at the jack: is the hot wire still soldered? Does the plug's tip touch the springy tip contact? Meter tip-to-sleeve reads 0 Ω?
causes.fix: Re-solder, re-tension or replace the jack – see [ef-output-jack].

causes.cause: Short from hot to ground
causes.check: Tip-to-sleeve reads near 0 Ω in every position with volume up.
causes.fix: Look for stray wire strands, a shield braid or copper foil touching a hot lug, or a solder blob bridging volume pot lugs.

causes.cause: Volume pot fault (open track, wiper joint broken, output wire off)
causes.check: Meter across the pot as in [ef-test-pots]; check the wire from the pot's middle lug to the jack.
causes.fix: Re-solder or replace the pot.

causes.cause: Selector switch common/output connection broken
causes.check: Switch output lug wire to volume pot intact? Continuity from each pickup hot through the switch?
causes.fix: Re-solder or replace the switch – see [ef-replace-selector-switch].

causes.cause: Kill switch, coil-split or mode switch stuck
causes.check: Toggle every switch on the guitar.
causes.fix: Clean or replace the faulty switch.

steps.title: Rule out cable and amp
steps.detail: Plug a different guitar into the same cable and amp. If that's silent too, the guitar isn't the problem.

steps.title: Active guitar? Check the battery
steps.detail: Plug the cable in (the jack switches the battery on), then measure the battery terminals on DC volts. Replace below 6 V. See [ef-active-dead].

steps.title: Meter from the jack
steps.detail: Do the tip-to-sleeve test in [ef-test-at-jack]. OL in every position = open circuit (jack or volume pot output wire). Near 0 in every position = short. Correct readings but still silent = jack contact or cable.

steps.title: Inspect the jack
steps.detail: Remove the jack plate or control plate. Check the tip (hot) and sleeve (ground) wires are soldered, and that the springy tip contact still presses firmly onto a plugged-in cable's tip.

steps.title: Inspect the wiring
steps.detail: Look for broken wires at the volume pot, switch output lug, and jack. Look for any stray strand, foil or braid touching a hot lug. Gently tug each wire.

steps.title: Repair and retest
steps.detail: Re-solder or replace the faulty part, then repeat the jack test before closing up.

models.note: The cup jack's wires get twisted when the jack spins in a loose cup – a frequent cause of sudden silence. Check here first.
Jack is in a recessed plate; short leads from the volume pot to the jack can snap if the jack rotates.
Long braided lead from the switch to the jack: a braid touching the jack's tip lug kills the output.
Wiring is reached through the f-holes; a dead jack is common and is fixed through the f-hole with a jack installation tool.
Stereo jack: ring switches the battery. A mono cable is required; a TRS cable may leave the system off.
Check the preamp battery and mute switch; endpin jacks loosen and twist their wires inside the body.

pro: If wiring looks perfect, the jack tests good and a known-good pickup still gives nothing, have a tech check it – there may be a hidden short in a pickup or harness.

title: One pickup dead or one switch position silent
summary: Everything works except one pickup or one position. Decide whether the pickup, its wiring or the switch is at fault.
symptoms: Silence in one switch position
Tapping one pickup gives nothing
Combination positions sound like a single pickup

causes.cause: Broken pickup lead at the switch or volume pot
causes.check: Look for a wire hanging loose or a dull, cracked joint at the switch lug.
causes.fix: Re-solder (see [ef-soldering-basics]).

causes.cause: Pickup's ground lead off
causes.check: A pickup with its ground/return lead disconnected makes no sound. Check its ground at the pot back.
causes.fix: Re-solder to ground.

causes.cause: Open coil
causes.check: Meter across the pickup leads reads OL.
causes.fix: See [ef-measure-pickup-dcr]; usually rewind or replace.

causes.cause: Hot lead shorted to ground (e.g. Tele bridge baseplate, crushed under a screw, touching foil)
causes.check: Pickup reads near 0 Ω.
causes.fix: Re-route the lead, insulate it, or free it from the screw.

causes.cause: Dirty or worn switch contact
causes.check: Position works intermittently or after wiggling the lever.
causes.fix: Clean or replace – see [ef-scratchy-switch].

causes.cause: Individual volume pot (Gibson) wiper or output broken
causes.check: On a two-volume guitar, does the pickup's own volume pot sweep correctly?
causes.fix: Re-solder or replace that pot.

steps.title: Confirm which pickup
steps.detail: Plug in at low volume and tap each pickup's poles with a screwdriver in every switch position. Note which pickup is silent and in which positions.

steps.title: Meter at the jack
steps.detail: In the dead position, tip-to-sleeve should read about the pickup's DC resistance. If it reads the volume pot's value (≈250k/500k), the pickup circuit is open. Near 0 = shorted.

steps.title: Measure the pickup itself
steps.detail: Open up and lift the pickup's hot lead. Measure across its leads (see [ef-measure-pickup-dcr]). Good reading = pickup fine, fault is in wiring or switch.

steps.title: Trace the wiring
steps.detail: Follow the hot lead to its switch lug and the ground lead to the pot back or ground buss. Check continuity from the pickup lead to the switch lug, and through the switch to its output lug in that position.

steps.title: Fix and retest
steps.detail: Re-solder, re-insulate or replace the faulty part, then tap-test every position.

models.note: If the middle pickup is dead in position 3 but positions 2 and 4 still sound different from 1 and 5, suspect the switch rather than the pickup.
Bridge pickups with a grounded baseplate: if the hot lead's insulation is worn where it passes the plate, the pickup shorts out.
Each pickup has its own volume pot; a dead pickup in one position only can be a pot or switch leaf. Check the toggle's contacts.
The rhythm circuit only uses the neck pickup; if the bridge pickup seems dead, check the lead/rhythm slide switch is set to lead.

title: Output jack problems: loose, intermittent or cable falls out
summary: Tighten a loose jack without twisting its wires, restore a weak tip contact, replace a worn jack, and fix the special mounts on Teles, Strats, hollowbodies and acoustics.
symptoms: Jack spins when you plug in
Crackle or cut-out when the cable moves
Cable slips out too easily
Tele cup jack wobbles or pulls out of the body
tools: 1/2 in nut driver or deep socket (most US jacks)
Jack-holding tool (e.g. StewMac Jack The Gripper, Bullet jack tightener) or a scribe through the jack
For Tele: StewMac Tele Jack Installation Tool or an Electrosocket
parts: Switchcraft-style mono jack (Switchcraft #11 type) or stereo jack for actives
Tele cup retaining clip or Electrosocket

specs.label: Jack nut (US Switchcraft style)
specs.value: 1/2 in; StewMac's jack wrench has 1/2 in and 14 mm ends

specs.label: Endpin jack hole
specs.value: 1/2 in (12.7 mm), reamed

specs.label: Electrosocket pilot holes
specs.value: 3/32 in bit, about 3/8 in deep, angled to match the mount's holes

specs.label: Wiring
specs.value: Tip lug = hot (signal), sleeve lug = ground

steps.title: Never just finger-tighten the nut
steps.detail: Turning the outside nut by hand or with pliers usually turns the whole jack inside the guitar, twisting the wires until a joint breaks. Hold the jack still from the inside while you turn the nut: use a jack tool that locks into the jack, or push a scribe through it (StewMac). Fender recommends a dedicated jack tightener.

steps.title: Check for twisted wires first
steps.detail: If the jack has been spinning, remove the plate and look. Untwist the leads, and re-solder any fatigued joint. Inspect for corrosion.

steps.title: Check the tip contact
steps.detail: With the jack out, plug in a cable not connected to an amp. The springy tip contact should snap firmly onto the plug tip and the plug should 'click'. If the plug is loose or falls out, the spring has lost tension. You can carefully bend the tip contact back towards the centre a little with pliers, but a worn jack is cheap – replacement is the more reliable fix.

steps.title: Replace the jack
steps.detail: Note which wire goes where: hot to the tip lug (the one connected to the long springy arm), ground to the sleeve lug (connected to the threaded barrel). Desolder, fit the new jack, tin and hook each wire through its lug, solder. Meter tip-to-sleeve with a cable plugged in to confirm a pickup reading, not 0 Ω.

steps.title: Tighten correctly
steps.detail: Fit the lock washer, thread the nut on, hold the jack from inside with the tool and tighten with the nut driver until snug. Don't over-tighten; it can cut into the wires underneath (iFixit).

steps.title: Tele cup jack: retaining clip method
steps.detail: If the cup wobbles, the clip that wedges it in the hole has lost its bite. Collapse and remove the old clip, rebuild a chewed-up hole wall with epoxy and sawdust if needed, then install a new clip and expand its corners with a Tele jack installation tool so they bite into the wood (StewMac).

steps.title: Tele cup jack: Electrosocket
steps.detail: Remove the cup and clip. Set the Electrosocket over the hole, mark the two screw holes and drill with a 3/32 in bit about 3/8 in deep, following the angle of the mount's holes. Thread the jack into the Electrosocket (avoid twisting the wires), then screw it down. Premier Guitar notes that for a right-angle plug you should remove the lock washer between jack and Electrosocket so the plug seats fully.

steps.title: Strat recessed jack plate
steps.detail: Remove the two plate screws and lift the plate gently (leads are short). Check both solder joints and the tip contact, re-tension or replace, then tighten the nut while holding the jack with a tool that fits in the recess.

steps.title: Hollowbody and endpin jacks
steps.detail: Loosen and remove the outer nut, let the jack drop inside, then use a pull-through jack installation tool fed through the f-hole or soundhole to draw the jack back into its hole and hold it while you tighten. For acoustic endpin jacks, hold the jack with a scribe through it and tighten the hex nut with a thin jack wrench; then tighten the strap button.

models.note: Jack sits in a recessed 'boat' plate on the top; a jack tool that fits the recess is the easiest way to hold it.
Side-mounted cup jack held by a friction clip – loosens over time. New clip or an Electrosocket is the permanent fix.
Jack on a plastic plate on the rim (Les Paul) or top (SG). Stripped plate screw holes are common; fill and re-drill if the plate is loose.
Jack on the top; work through the f-hole with a pull-through tool.
Uses a stereo (TRS) jack: tip = signal, sleeve = ground, ring = battery negative. The ring switches the battery on when a mono plug is inserted.
Endpin jack in a 1/2 in hole through the tail block. Fishman says finger-tighten the strap button, though StewMac finds these loosen and snugs them with wire strippers in the strap recess.

pro: A Tele jack hole that has been chewed or split, or an endpin hole that needs reaming, may be best left to a tech.

title: Scratchy or intermittent pickup selector
summary: Crackles, drop-outs or the wrong pickup in some positions usually means dirty contacts. Clean open switches first; closed 'box' switches that keep failing should be replaced.
symptoms: Noise when flicking the selector
A position cuts out unless you hold the lever
Sound changes if you press the lever sideways

steps.title: Work the switch
steps.detail: Flick it through every position 20–30 times. Fender notes this sometimes clears the contacts, and regular use helps keep them clean.

steps.title: Open up
steps.detail: Remove the pickguard (Strat), control plate (Tele) or rear switch cover (Les Paul) so you can see the switch.

steps.title: Spray and work
steps.detail: Shield the area with paper towel. Give a short spray onto the contacts (open switches: directly on the wipers; Gibson-style toggle: onto the leaf contacts), then flick through all positions many times.

steps.title: Gibson toggle: check the leaves
steps.detail: The Switchcraft-style toggle has two springy outer leaves (pickup inputs) and two centre leaves (output). If one outer leaf no longer touches its centre contact in the middle position, or doesn't separate in the end positions, it may be bent; careful re-forming with small pliers can restore it, but if in doubt replace the switch.

steps.title: Test with the meter
steps.detail: Do the jack test in each position (see [ef-test-at-jack]) while pressing the lever lightly in each direction. A stable reading means the switch is good.

steps.title: Replace if it persists
steps.detail: Closed plastic import switches are prone to failure and often get damaged by heat when re-soldered. If cleaning doesn't hold, replace – see [ef-replace-selector-switch].

models.note: Open CRL-type blade switches can be cleaned easily; closed import switches often can't be reached.
3-way blade switch on the control plate; same cleaning approach.
Toggle switch; spray from the rear cavity. On a 335 the switch is reached through the f-hole.
Slide switches on the upper horn plates collect dirt; clean the same way with the plate removed.

title: Sound cuts in and out (intermittent signal)
summary: Signal drops out or crackles when you move, touch the cable, or flick the switch. Almost always a jack, a cold solder joint, or a worn switch.
symptoms: Signal drops when you move or step on the cable
Crackle or cut-out when you wiggle the plug
Pickup position cuts out at certain lever positions
Fine at home, cuts out at gigs
tools: Wooden chopstick or plastic spudger (for poking)

causes.cause: Faulty cable
causes.check: Swap cables; wiggle each end of the cable while playing another guitar.
causes.fix: Replace or re-solder the cable plug.

causes.cause: Output jack tip contact weak or nut loose
causes.check: Plug feels loose or falls out; cut-outs happen when you touch the plug.
causes.fix: See [ef-output-jack].

causes.cause: Cold or cracked solder joint
causes.check: With the guitar plugged in at low volume, gently prod each joint with a chopstick and listen.
causes.fix: Re-heat and re-solder the joint (see [ef-soldering-basics]).

causes.cause: Dirty or worn switch
causes.check: Cut-outs only in certain positions or when the lever is pushed.
causes.fix: See [ef-scratchy-switch].

causes.cause: Worn pot track (only at certain knob positions)
causes.check: Sweep test the pot (see [ef-test-pots]).
causes.fix: Clean or replace.

causes.cause: Active guitar with failing battery
causes.check: Battery under 6 V under load; noise repeats as the preamp powers up and down.
causes.fix: Fresh battery – see [ef-active-dead].

steps.title: Swap the cable first
steps.detail: Most intermittent faults are cables. Try a known-good one.

steps.title: Wiggle-test with the meter
steps.detail: Clip the meter to the cable tip and sleeve (see [ef-test-at-jack]), then wiggle the plug, each knob and the switch. Watch for the reading jumping to OL or 0.

steps.title: Open up and prod
steps.detail: Plug into an amp at low volume. With a non-metallic stick, push gently on each wire and solder joint – jack, switch, pots, pickup leads. The joint that makes it crackle is your culprit.

steps.title: Re-solder suspects
steps.detail: Re-heat dull or cracked joints with a little fresh solder. Pay special attention to the jack's tip and sleeve lugs: wires there get flexed each time the jack turns.

steps.title: Tighten the jack properly
steps.detail: If the jack nut was loose and the jack has been spinning, its wires are probably twisted and fatigued. Re-solder them, then tighten the nut while holding the jack still (see [ef-output-jack]).

models.note: Classic cause: cup jack loose in its hole; the retaining clip has lost its grip.
Recessed 'boat' jack plate: the nut loosens and the jack rotates, twisting the two leads until one breaks.
Jack on the top/side, reachable only through the f-hole; loose jacks here are common.
Endpin jacks loosen and the strap button nut backs off; tighten while holding the jack (see [ef-output-jack]).

title: Test a pot (value, taper, worn track)
summary: Check a volume or tone pot's real value, whether it's audio or linear taper, and whether the track is worn, dirty or open.
symptoms: Volume jumps or drops out at part of the rotation
Knob does nothing for most of its travel
Unknown pot from a parts box
tools: Multimeter on Ω (2 MΩ range or auto)

specs.label: Common values
specs.value: 250k (single coils), 500k (humbuckers), 1M (Jazzmaster, some vintage Teles, Wide Range humbucker guitars), 25k (active systems such as EMG)

specs.label: Acceptable tolerance
specs.value: Usually within about ±10 % of the marking; StewMac notes ±10–20 % is common

specs.label: Taper check at half rotation
specs.value: Linear: about 50 % of total between an outer lug and the wiper. Audio/log: much less than 50 %

steps.title: Identify the lugs
steps.detail: The two outer lugs are the ends of the resistive track; the middle lug is the wiper that slides along it.

steps.title: Lift a lug
steps.detail: If the pot is installed, desolder at least one outer lug so other parts don't skew the reading.

steps.title: Measure end to end
steps.detail: Put the probes on the two outer lugs. This is the total value and shouldn't change as you turn the shaft. 230–270k on a '250k' pot is normal.

steps.title: Check the sweep
steps.detail: Clip one probe to an outer lug and the other to the middle lug. Turn the shaft slowly from one end to the other. The reading should change smoothly from near 0 to near the full value. Repeat using the other outer lug. Jumps, flicker, sudden OL, or a dead spot mean a dirty or worn track or wiper.

steps.title: Check the taper
steps.detail: Set the shaft at exactly half rotation and measure from an outer lug to the wiper. About half the total means linear (B on most US/CTS pots). Much less than half from one side means audio/log (A). Check from both outer lugs – a log pot reads low from one end and high from the other.

steps.title: Decide
steps.detail: A smooth sweep and correct value = good pot; look elsewhere for the fault. Scratchy sweep = try cleaning (see [ef-crackling-pots]). Open or wildly wrong value = replace.

models.note: 250k standard; many players use a 250k audio pot for volume.
500k standard for humbuckers.
Lead circuit uses 1M pots; the rhythm circuit uses a 1M linear volume and 50k linear tone thumbwheel (Jaguar, per Premier Guitar).
Must use 25k pots – EMG states this value is required.
Stacked (concentric) pots on many basses contain two tracks; test each track separately.

title: Test the whole guitar from the output jack
summary: Without opening the guitar, a meter on the cable tip and sleeve tells you whether each pickup position is connected, open or shorted – the fastest way to narrow down an electronics fault.
symptoms: No sound
One position dead
Not sure whether the fault is guitar, cable or amp
tools: Multimeter on Ω (20 kΩ, then 2 MΩ)

specs.label: Single pickup selected, volume full
specs.value: Close to that pickup's DC resistance (e.g. ~6k for a vintage Strat pickup, ~8k PAF, ~16k hot humbucker) – slightly lower because the pots sit in parallel

specs.label: Two similar pickups in parallel (Strat positions 2 and 4, Les Paul middle)
specs.value: Roughly half of one pickup (two 6k coils ≈ 3k)

specs.label: Reading equals roughly the volume pot value (≈250k/500k)
specs.value: Selected pickup or its lead is open – you're reading straight through the volume pot track

specs.label: Reading near 0 Ω
specs.value: Short from hot to ground (or volume on zero)

causes.cause: Cable fault
causes.check: Plug a known-good cable into a known-good guitar or test the cable tip-to-tip and sleeve-to-sleeve for continuity.
causes.fix: Replace the cable.

causes.cause: Open pickup or broken pickup lead
causes.check: One position reads about the volume pot's value instead of a few kΩ.
causes.fix: See [ef-measure-pickup-dcr] and [ef-one-pickup-dead].

causes.cause: Short hot-to-ground
causes.check: All positions read near 0 with volume up.
causes.fix: Look for a jack tip lug touching the sleeve or shielding, a stray strand, or a braid touching a hot lug. See [ef-no-sound].

causes.cause: Bad volume pot wiper
causes.check: Readings jump as you roll volume up and down.
causes.fix: See [ef-crackling-pots].

steps.title: Set up
steps.detail: Plug a cable into the guitar, leave the other end free. Turn volume and tone controls fully up. Put one probe on the free plug's tip and the other on its sleeve (clip leads make this easy).

steps.title: Step through every switch position
steps.detail: Write down the reading for each position. Compare with the expected figures: one pickup ≈ its DC resistance; two equal pickups in parallel ≈ half; series combinations (e.g. Tele 4-way or series switch) ≈ the sum.

steps.title: Roll the volume
steps.detail: With one pickup selected, slowly turn the volume down. The reading should fall smoothly towards zero. Jumps point to a worn pot or bad wiper joint.

steps.title: Wiggle test
steps.detail: Watching the meter, gently wiggle the plug, the switch and each knob. A reading that flickers to OL or 0 finds intermittent faults quicker than listening.

steps.title: Check the ground path
steps.detail: Switch to continuity or low Ω. Probe the plug sleeve and touch a string, then the bridge, then each pickup cover. All should read near 0 Ω on a passive guitar. No reading = broken string/bridge ground (see [ef-hum-buzz]).

steps.title: Tap test
steps.detail: Plug into an amp at low volume and tap each pickup's poles gently with a screwdriver or hemostats in each switch position. Every pickup that should be on should 'clunk'.

models.note: Positions 2 and 4 are two pickups in parallel and read roughly half a single pickup.
With two volume pots, turning down the unselected pickup's volume can also change the middle-position reading – keep all volumes on 10.
Resistance readings at the jack are meaningless for active pickups; check the battery voltage under load and continuity of the harness instead.
Piezo pickups and preamps can't be checked this way; test the battery and the endpin jack connection instead.

title: Tone capacitors: values, types and codes
summary: What the tone cap does, how .022, .047 and .1 µF compare, how to read the code on a cap, and what the ceramic vs film vs paper-in-oil debate really means.
parts: Tone capacitor of chosen value (any voltage rating is fine for a passive guitar)

specs.label: .022 µF (code 223)
specs.value: Typical humbucker/Gibson value

specs.label: .047 µF (code 473)
specs.value: Typical single-coil/Fender value; many basses

specs.label: .1 µF (code 104)
specs.value: Basses and some eras of vintage Fender guitars

specs.label: .001 µF (code 102)
specs.value: Common treble-bleed value

specs.label: 180 pF (code 181)
specs.value: PRS-style treble bleed

specs.label: Reading codes
specs.value: First two digits, then number of zeros, in picofarads: 223 = 22,000 pF = .022 µF; 473 = .047 µF; 104 = 100,000 pF = .1 µF

steps.title: Understand what it does
steps.detail: The tone pot and cap form a path to ground for treble. As you turn the tone down, more highs leak away. A bigger cap reaches down into lower frequencies, so the knob goes darker and acts more like an on/off switch; a smaller cap trims only the very top and gives a longer, more usable sweep.

steps.title: Pick a value
steps.detail: Stock values (.022 for humbuckers, .047 for single coils) are a fine default. If the tone control does nothing until the last few numbers and then goes muddy, try a smaller value. Premier Guitar's Dirk Wacker prefers 3300–6800 pF; Lollar uses .015 µF on everything.

steps.title: Don't worry about voltage
steps.detail: A passive guitar signal is well under a volt, so any cap's voltage rating is more than enough. High-voltage tube-amp caps (e.g. Orange Drops) work but the rating doesn't change the sound.

steps.title: Swap the cap
steps.detail: The cap usually runs from the tone pot's middle lug (or an outer lug) to ground (pot back), or from the pot to the switch. Note the exact lugs, desolder, fit the new cap with short leads, solder quickly with a crocodile clip on the lead as a heat sink. Film and ceramic tone caps aren't polarised – either way round.

steps.title: About cap 'types'
steps.detail: Sources disagree. Lollar tested caps of different materials at the same value and concluded value matters far more than material; expensive caps mainly buy tighter tolerances and reliability. Premier Guitar's Wacker hears clear differences. Practical advice: choose by value first; buy paper-in-oil or vintage-style caps if you enjoy them, but don't expect them to fix a tone problem.

steps.title: Avoid electrolytics
steps.detail: Polarised electrolytic caps aren't suitable as tone caps; use film, ceramic, mica or paper-in-oil.

models.note: Typically .047 µF (vintage examples .1 µF or .05 µF).
Typically .022 µF; late-50s guitars used Sprague Black Beauty / Bumblebee paper caps.
Jaguar lead tone .01 µF; rhythm tone .01 µF; strangle switch .003 µF (Premier Guitar).
.047 or .1 µF are common.

title: Treble bleed: keep the highs when you turn down
summary: Why a guitar goes muddy when you roll the volume back, and how a small cap (often with a resistor) across the volume pot keeps it bright. Choose values to suit your pickups and cable length.
symptoms: Tone gets dull and muffled as you turn the volume down
Can't clean up a crunchy amp with the volume knob without losing clarity
parts: Small cap (180 pF – 2.5 nF) and optional resistor (80k–300k) – see specs

specs.label: Simple cap only
specs.value: PRS: 180 pF; G&L: 200 pF – simplest but can sound very bright

specs.label: Cap + parallel resistor (common)
specs.value: 1 nF + 150k ('golden age' standard); Seymour Duncan 1 nF + 100k; DiMarzio 560 pF + 300k; Suhr 680 pF + 150k

specs.label: Fender (modern)
specs.value: 1.2 nF + 130k parallel with a 20k series resistor ('Version 4')

specs.label: Kinman (series)
specs.value: 1.2 nF in series with 130k

specs.label: Cable rule of thumb
specs.value: Short cable (~10 ft): smaller values (DiMarzio/Suhr). Long cable (~30 ft): larger values (Fender, Seymour Duncan, TV Jones 1–1.2 nF)

steps.title: Why it's needed
steps.detail: Turning the volume down puts the volume pot's resistance in series with the signal, and together with the cable's capacitance that forms a treble-cut filter. A small cap across the pot lets high frequencies bypass the resistance.

steps.title: Pick a circuit
steps.detail: Start with 1 nF + 150k in parallel – a balanced, widely used choice. If it sounds too bright when turned down, use a smaller cap; if it still darkens, a larger one.

steps.title: Prepare the parts
steps.detail: For a parallel network, twist the cap and resistor leads together at both ends and solder them so they sit side by side. For a series network (Kinman), solder them end to end.

steps.title: Fit it
steps.detail: Solder one end to the volume pot's input lug (the outer lug that receives the signal from the switch or pickup) and the other end to the pot's middle (output/wiper) lug. Keep leads short and clear of the casing.

steps.title: Test
steps.detail: Play at full volume (no change expected), then roll back to 7, 5, 3 and listen. Swap values if needed.

models.note: Some Fenders come with a treble bleed fitted; look for a small cap (and resistor) across the volume pot before adding one.
Fit on each volume pot. With independent volumes and the toggle in the middle, the effect interacts; test both pickups.
Not used on active pickups or guitars with a buffer – their low output impedance doesn't lose highs this way.

warnings: Some players dislike treble bleeds on bright vintage single coils (it can get harsh); it's easy to remove if you don't like it.

title: Check pickup phase and magnetic polarity (and why RWRP cancels hum)
summary: Find a pickup's magnetic polarity with a compass, check electrical phase, and understand why a reverse-wound/reverse-polarity middle pickup makes Strat positions 2 and 4 quiet.
symptoms: Combination positions thin and quiet
Positions 2 and 4 hum as much as 1, 3, 5
Mixing pickups from different makers
tools: Multimeter with polarity indication (or a meter with a polarity test)

specs.label: Polarity
specs.value: Which magnetic pole faces the strings: north or south

specs.label: Phase / wind
specs.value: Direction the coil is wound relative to its hot and ground leads

specs.label: Hum-cancelling pair
specs.value: Opposite wind AND opposite polarity (RWRP)

specs.label: Gibson/Seymour Duncan humbuckers
specs.value: Adjustable-pole (screw) coil is south; black line on the bar magnet marks north

steps.title: Know the four combinations
steps.detail: Same wind + same polarity: in phase, no hum cancelling. Opposite wind + opposite polarity (RWRP): in phase AND hum-cancelling. Same wind + opposite polarity, or opposite wind + same polarity: out of phase – thin, hollow and weak when combined.

steps.title: Compass test for polarity
steps.detail: Hold a compass on its side close to the poles. Opposites attract: if the compass's north-pointing end swings toward the pickup, the pickup is south-up; if it swings away, it's north-up. Check each pickup.

steps.title: Check wind direction / phase
steps.detail: Premier Guitar's method uses a meter with a polarity indicator: hot to +, ground to –, then quickly bring a steel screwdriver toward a pole piece without touching it and note the + or – kick. Do every pickup the same way (same motion, same probe leads) and compare: pickups that kick the same way with the same magnet polarity are in phase. (PG warns not to use an ordinary analog meter without a polarity function – it can be damaged.)

steps.title: Use the maker's information
steps.detail: Most makers publish wind and polarity (and RWRP versions). Fralin notes lead colours usually go black = start (ground), white = finish (hot) on single coils, but always check the maker's chart.

steps.title: Fix an out-of-phase pair
steps.detail: Swap the hot and ground leads on one pickup. That reverses its phase but can bring problems: on a single coil with a cover/shield, the 'ground' end becomes hot. On humbuckers with a separate shield wire, swapping is easy; braided single-conductor Gibson leads usually can't be reversed, so flip the magnet instead (pickup maker or careful DIY).

steps.title: Why RWRP works in Strat 2 and 4
steps.detail: Hum from the room induces the same voltage in both coils regardless of magnet direction. String signal depends on magnet polarity. With the middle pickup wound AND magnetised the opposite way, the hum in the two coils is opposite and cancels when they're combined, while the string signal stays in phase and adds. Positions 1, 3 and 5 (single pickups) still hum.

models.note: Standard set: neck and bridge one way, middle RWRP. A non-RWRP middle still works but positions 2 and 4 won't be quiet.
Fralin notes the same RWRP principle applies to Teles: with a matched RWRP pair the middle position is hum-cancelling. Check your set's spec.
Mixing brands can put the middle position out of phase; swap hot and ground on one pickup (4-conductor) or flip a magnet.
Same principle (Fralin): an RWRP pair gives a quiet combined position.
The RWRP principle applies to Jazz Bass pairs too. On a P/J, Fralin's usual phase fix is reversing the P pickup's white and black leads.

title: Grounding layout: star ground and ground loops
summary: How to organise ground wires so every metal part is connected once to a single point – and what the experts actually agree on about 'ground loops' inside a guitar.
parts: 22 AWG wire or 19 AWG bare buss wire

steps.title: What must be grounded
steps.detail: Pot casings, the switch ground, the jack sleeve, pickup grounds and shields, cavity shielding, the bridge/strings, and any metal plate or pickguard shield. Neck plates and screws into grounded plates don't need extra wires.

steps.title: Star grounding
steps.detail: Run every ground wire to one point – usually the volume pot casing, which in turn connects to the jack sleeve. Fralin likes this because it makes it hard to create a loop and every ground ends up at the jack anyway.

steps.title: Ground buss alternative
steps.detail: Gibson-style guitars often run a bare wire from pot to pot with grounds landing on the nearest pot. Premier Guitar's Dirk Wacker uses bare 19 AWG buss wire; he notes the wire thickness doesn't improve grounding, and fewer solder joints mean less risk of overheating pots.

steps.title: Don't close the ring
steps.detail: Avoid wiring the grounds in a full circle (for example pot 1 → pot 2 → pot 3 → pot 4 → back to pot 1). Wacker warns a closed ring on Les Paul/335 harnesses can pick up radio/CB interference, and Fralin describes a ring of ground wires as a one-turn coil that can pick up noise.

steps.title: Where experts disagree
steps.detail: Wacker says there's 'no such thing' as over-grounding and double-grounding a part does no harm; Fralin says a part only needs grounding once and extra paths can create loops. Some engineers say star grounding makes no measurable difference in a passive guitar. Sensible middle ground: connect each part once, avoid closed rings, and check with a meter.

steps.title: Verify
steps.detail: Put one probe on the volume pot casing and touch every metal part. All should read ≈0 Ω on the resistance setting. Then check strings-to-jack-sleeve.

models.note: Volume pot back is the natural star point; pickguard shield ties pots together; trem claw wire lands on the volume pot.
Control plate connects pot casings mechanically; land grounds on the volume pot.
Pots are grounded by buss wire and braid; keep the chain open (no closed ring).
Follow EMG's diagram; no bridge ground.

title: Noisy active preamp (hiss, crackle, motorboating)
summary: Separate the hiss every preamp makes from real faults: weak battery, scratchy stacked controls, intermittent wiring, or a failing preamp.
symptoms: Hiss that rises with treble boost
Repeating pop or 'putt-putt' noise
Crackle when turning EQ knobs
Noise only in active mode

causes.cause: Weak battery: preamp powers up and down
causes.check: Repeating noise or distortion; battery below 6 V under load.
causes.fix: Fresh sealed battery.

causes.cause: Normal preamp hiss
causes.check: Steady, smooth hiss that rises with treble boost.
causes.fix: Normal; reduce treble boost or use more pickup output.

causes.cause: Stacked/concentric control shafts touching
causes.check: Crackle when turning one half of a stacked pot.
causes.fix: Check alignment; East UK says sealed pots should not be cleaned. Replace if needed.

causes.cause: Loose jack, twisted wiring or dirty contacts
causes.check: Noise when moving the cable.
causes.fix: See [ef-output-jack].

causes.cause: Pickup or wiring fault
causes.check: Noise disappears when pickup inputs are disconnected and shorted.
causes.fix: Look at pickup grounds and shielding.

causes.cause: Faulty preamp
causes.check: Noise persists with inputs shorted and a fresh battery.
causes.fix: Repair/replace the preamp.

steps.title: Fresh battery
steps.detail: Rule this out first; batteries can read fine unloaded and sag under load.

steps.title: Passive vs active
steps.detail: If the bass/guitar has a passive mode, compare. Noise only in active mode points at the preamp or battery.

steps.title: Isolate the preamp
steps.detail: Disconnect the pickups from the preamp inputs, short each input's hot and cold together with a jumper, turn the treble up. A slight even hiss is normal; crackle or loud noise means the preamp is faulty.

steps.title: Check the jack ring
steps.detail: The black battery lead must be alone on the ring lug; no ground or shield wires there.

steps.title: Check grounds and shielding
steps.detail: With the pickups reconnected, make sure pickup grounds and cavity shielding all reach the preamp's ground.

models.note: Most active basses with 2- or 3-band EQ; treble boost brings up hiss – that's normal.
Low-noise by design; if noisy, check battery and the solderless plugs.
Feedback and boom are EQ/placement issues, not preamp faults; hiss rising with battery age means replace the battery.

pro: Preamp board repair.

title: Replace a pickup selector switch
summary: Swap a worn Strat 5-way, Tele 3-way or Gibson-style toggle for a quality part – and how CRL, Oak Grigsby and import switches differ.
symptoms: Positions cut out even after cleaning
Broken lever or detent
Plastic import switch melted or lugs loose
tools: Soldering iron 30–40 W with small tapered tip
Deep-well socket or toggle-switch collar wrench (Gibson)
parts: CRL, Oak Grigsby or Switchcraft switch of the right type

steps.title: Photograph and draw the old wiring
steps.detail: Before touching anything, take clear photos and draw which wire goes to which lug. If you're changing switch brand, draw the old switch's internal connections too.

steps.title: Get access
steps.detail: Strat: slacken strings and lift the pickguard. Tele: remove the control plate. Les Paul: remove the rear switch cavity cover. 335: work through the f-hole (often a pro job).

steps.title: Remove wires one at a time
steps.detail: Heat the underside of each lug and lift the wire out with hemostats while the solder is molten. Label each wire.

steps.title: Fit the new switch
steps.detail: Strat/Tele: screw it in with the spring side facing away from the pickups (Premier Guitar). Gibson toggle: tighten the knurled collar or hex nut only finger-tight-plus with the proper wrench or a deep socket – not pliers, which mar it and can slip into the top.

steps.title: Map lugs between brands
steps.detail: A CRL 5-way has two rows (stages) of four lugs. Oak Grigsby is similar inside but its lugs are oriented a little differently; budget closed switches may have one row of lugs that still forms two stages. Transfer connections by function, not by physical position: each stage has a common lug plus one lug per pickup.

steps.title: Solder
steps.detail: Tin each wire, hook it through its lug, apply a small amount of solder. Work quickly on plastic switches. On a CRL Strat switch, a jumper joins the two common lugs if the wiring needs it.

steps.title: Test every position
steps.detail: Plug into an amp at low volume and tap each pickup with hemostats in each position, then check the tone controls by rubbing the pickups while turning the knobs. On a Gibson toggle: up = rhythm/neck, down = treble/bridge, middle = both (as seen from the playing position). If reversed, swap the outer lug wires.

specs.label: Iron
specs.value: 30–40 W, small tapered tip (Premier Guitar)

specs.label: Solder
specs.value: 60/40 rosin-core, 0.032 in

specs.label: Gibson toggle styles
specs.value: Short straight, tall straight (Les Paul), right-angle (SG, thin ES-style bodies)

models.note: CRL is the reference open switch most diagrams use; Oak Grigsby is equally good but lug orientation differs. Cheap closed switches in imports often fail when re-soldered.
3-way blade switch on the control plate; replace with the same layout or follow the new switch's diagram.
Tall straight Switchcraft-type toggle. Two outer prongs = pickup inputs, two centre prongs = output (crimped together), one ground prong on the frame.
Right-angle toggle for shallow cavities; check cavity dimensions before buying.

warnings: Never use a soldering gun near pickups (it can weaken magnets).
Over-tightening a toggle collar strips its threads.
pro: Switches inside a 335 or other hollowbody – fishing the harness through the f-hole takes practice.

title: Replace a volume pot
summary: Swap a worn, crackly or wrong-taper volume pot for a new one, wire for wire, and test it before closing the guitar up.
tools: Soldering iron (temperature-controlled if possible) with stand and damp sponge or brass wool
Desoldering braid or a solder sucker
Nut driver or box spanner for the pot nut
Fine file or sandpaper to scuff the pot casing
Phone camera, masking tape and a pen for labels
parts: New pot: same value (250k / 500k / 1M / 25k active), audio taper for volume, same shaft type (split or solid, 24 or 18 spline), same bushing (US 3/8 in style or metric) and a bushing long enough for the top (long-bushing pots for carved tops)
Short length of hook-up wire, if any wire is too short
Knob that fits the new shaft

specs.label: Lug numbering (back view)
specs.value: Shaft pointing away, lugs up: lug 1 left, lug 2 (wiper) middle, lug 3 right; clockwise moves the wiper towards lug 3

specs.label: Volume pot connections
specs.value: Lug 3 = signal in (pickup or switch) · lug 2 = out to jack tip (or switch) · lug 1 = ground (casing)

specs.label: Typical values
specs.value: 250k single coils · 500k humbuckers · 1M some Jazzmasters/vintage Teles · 25k EMG

specs.label: Pot tolerance
specs.value: About ±10 % (230–270k on a 250k pot is normal)

specs.label: Knob fit
specs.value: 24-spline (fine) for US CTS-style shafts, 18-spline (coarse) for many import pots

steps.title: Unplug and get at the pot
steps.detail: Unplug the cable. Pull the knob straight up with a puller or a cloth looped underneath. Open the control cavity (remove the back cover, control plate or pickguard; on a Strat slacken the strings first). Lay a towel under the guitar.

steps.title: Photograph and label
steps.detail: Take sharp photos of the pot from several angles. Put a masking-tape flag on each wire saying where it goes: 'lug 3 – from switch', 'lug 2 – to jack', 'casing – pickup ground', 'casing – bridge ground', and note any capacitor or treble-bleed parts.

steps.title: Check the replacement matches
steps.detail: Compare the new pot with the old one: value and taper marking (confirm with a meter, see [ef-identify-pots]), shaft type and spline count (so your knob fits, see [ef-knobs]), bushing thread and length, and body size. A metric import pot may need the mounting hole opened slightly, or a US pot may not fit a small import cavity — find out before you unsolder anything.

steps.title: Desolder the wires
steps.detail: Heat each lug joint and lift the wire away as the solder melts; clear old solder with braid or a sucker. Do the casing joints last: they need more heat, so hold the iron there only until the solder flows. Keep track of which wire came from where.
steps.warn: The iron tip is several hundred degrees: park it in its stand every time, and keep it off the finish and the pickup leads' insulation.

steps.title: Remove the old pot
steps.detail: Undo the nut and washer from the top side with a nut driver while holding the pot from behind so it can't spin and twist the wires. Lift it out.

steps.title: Fit the new pot
steps.detail: Put any inner lock washer on the shaft, push the pot up through the hole with the lugs facing the same way as the old one (so the wires reach), seat the anti-rotation tab if it has one, then fit the outer washer and nut. Tighten the nut snugly with the nut driver; hold the pot from behind so it stays square.

steps.title: Prepare the pot for soldering
steps.detail: Lightly scuff a small patch on the casing where the ground wires go and tin it with a little solder; tin each lug you'll use. Tin each wire end too (see [ef-soldering-pot-backs] and [ef-soldering-basics]).

steps.title: Solder the signal wires
steps.detail: Wire from the pickup or switch to lug 3. Wire to the jack tip (or on to the switch) from lug 2. Use your photos and labels: if the original had them differently, copy the original unless it worked backwards.

steps.title: Ground lug 1 and the casing
steps.detail: Bend lug 1 over to touch the casing and solder it, or run a short wire from lug 1 to the casing. Re-solder every ground wire that was on the old casing (pickup grounds, bridge ground, jack sleeve, other pots) to the new casing.

steps.title: Move any other parts across
steps.detail: If the old pot carried a treble bleed (a small cap, or cap + resistor, across lugs 3 and 2 — see [ef-treble-bleed]) or a tone cap, solder it to the same lugs on the new pot. Let joints near capacitors cool; don't cook them.

steps.title: Test before closing up
steps.detail: Plug into an amp at low volume. Sweep the volume end to end: it should go from silent to full smoothly and get louder clockwise. Tap the pole pieces in every pickup position. Then check about 0 ohms from the pot casing to the jack sleeve, and from the strings to the jack sleeve.

steps.title: Close up and fit the knob
steps.detail: Tuck the wires so nothing gets pinched, refit the cover, plate or pickguard (and restring and tune a Strat). Turn the shaft fully clockwise and push the knob on so its '10' sits where you want it.

models.note: Usually 250k; the volume casing often carries the pickup grounds and the trem-claw ground: move all of them across. Pickguard-mounted pots need a short bushing.
Usually 250k (some vintage-style Teles use 1M). The control plate holds the pot; the switch and jack wires are short, so work with the plate turned over beside the body.
500k. Carved tops need long-bushing pots so the nut reaches the thread. The braided shield wires from the switch and pickups ground to the casing.
Everything comes out through the f-hole; see [wr-es-335] before starting.
The lead-circuit volume is 1M on many models; match the old value.
25k pots with solderless connectors on EMG harnesses: [wr-emg-active].

warnings: Soldering fumes: work in a ventilated room and wash your hands after handling solder.
Unplug the guitar before you start.
Don't spray contact cleaner near a hot iron.
pro: the pot is inside a hollow-body or semi-hollow and you're not comfortable fishing the harness out through the f-hole, or the guitar has an active preamp board on the pot.

title: Shield the cavities: copper foil or conductive paint
summary: Lining the control and pickup cavities with a grounded conductive layer reduces buzz from lights, dimmers and screens. It can't stop single-coil hum from the pickups themselves.
symptoms: Buzz drops a lot when you touch the strings
Noise from stage lights and screens
Single-coil guitar much noisier than others in the same room
parts: Self-adhesive copper foil tape (conductive adhesive preferred)
Small brass solder lug and wood screw

steps.title: Decide foil or paint
steps.detail: Copper foil can be soldered to directly and is easy to check; it's best on flat walls and pickguard backs. Conductive paint is easier in irregular routes, wire channels and drilled holes. Both need a ground connection, and both will short a hot lug if they touch one.

steps.title: Strip out the electronics
steps.detail: Photograph everything, then remove or fold back the pickups and control harness.

steps.title: Line the cavity
steps.detail: Foil: cut pieces to fit the floor and walls, overlapping each piece so the surface is continuous. Burnish it flat. If the adhesive isn't conductive, put a dab of solder across each overlap. Paint: apply two or three coats, letting each dry fully.

steps.title: Bring it to the top
steps.detail: Carry the foil or paint up over the edge of the cavity under where the pickguard or control plate screws down, so a shielded pickguard or metal plate makes contact. StewMac suggests near the pickguard screw by the lower tone pot on a Strat.

steps.title: Shield the pickguard
steps.detail: Line the back of the pickguard with foil (many Strats have an aluminium shield already). Trim it clear of pot and switch holes so no hot lug touches it.

steps.title: Ground it
steps.detail: Connect the shielding to ground once: solder a wire from the foil to the volume pot back, or fasten a brass solder lug into a painted cavity with a small wood screw and wire that to the pot. Fralin cautions against wiring the same foil to ground in several places in a loop.

steps.title: Check before reassembly
steps.detail: Meter from various points of the shielding to the volume pot back: ≈0 Ω on foil, a low reading on paint. Then refit the electronics and check no hot lug or jack tip touches the shielding: tip-to-sleeve at the jack should still read your pickup's resistance.

models.note: Shield the control cavity, pickup route and pickguard back; the pickguard foil contacts the cavity at the top edge.
The metal control plate grounds through the pots; bring cavity shielding up to meet it. Shield the neck pickup route too.
Foil or paint the rear control cavity and line the cover plate with foil.
Can't practically be shielded; relies on humbuckers and grounding.
Large cavities under the pickguard; shield routes and pickguard back.

warnings: Shielding can short the output if it touches a hot lug or the jack tip – check with the meter before closing up.

title: Uneven string volume on an acoustic pickup
summary: With undersaddle pickups, one or two strings that are weak or too loud nearly always trace back to the saddle and slot - not the electronics. With contact pickups, it is usually glue coverage or placement.
symptoms: One string almost silent through the amp but fine acoustically
Outer strings weak, middle strings loud
Balance changes when you retune or push on the saddle

causes.cause: Saddle bottom not flat, or slot bottom has ridges/humps
causes.check: Hold the saddle bottom against a straightedge and light; inspect slot with a light and a small mirror
causes.fix: Sand saddle flat; have the slot cleaned or routed flat.

causes.cause: Saddle too tight in the slot (often at the ends)
causes.check: Saddle needs force to remove; measure thickness at ends vs middle
causes.fix: Thin the tight areas so the saddle moves freely.

causes.cause: Saddle too tall and leaning forward
causes.check: Saddle over about 3/16 in proud, tipped toward the neck under tension
causes.fix: Lower it or have the slot recut leaning slightly back.

causes.cause: Slot was flat at rest but bends when the top deflects under tension
causes.check: Measure top deflection (StewMac saw about 0.010 in)
causes.fix: Pro: rout the slot with the top jacked up to its strung position.

causes.cause: Contact pickup not fully glued or misplaced (K&K)
causes.check: Mirror: glue fillet all round each transducer?
causes.fix: Reinstall the transducer with full glue coverage.

causes.cause: String gauge/winding differences
causes.check: Wound G loud vs plain G
causes.fix: Try a different set or gauge on the weak string.

steps.title: Confirm it is the pickup
steps.detail: Plug into a clean amp/PA with tone flat and pick each string equally. Note which are weak or loud.

steps.title: Pressure test
steps.detail: Slacken a little and press down on the saddle directly above the weak string while plucking - if the string jumps in volume, it is a contact problem at the saddle.

steps.title: Flatten the saddle bottom
steps.detail: Remove the saddle and sand the bottom on a dead-flat plate, keeping it square. Check against a straightedge and strong light.

steps.title: Free the fit
steps.detail: Measure thickness along the saddle. StewMac found a saddle .127 in at the ends and .123 in in the middle that bound at the ends; they thinned the ends until the saddle dropped in freely. The saddle should lift out by hand.

steps.title: Clean the slot
steps.detail: Look for glue lumps or ridges in the slot bottom. A micro chisel can remove small ridges; uneven slots need routing flat with a jig (pro).

steps.title: Check saddle height and lean
steps.detail: Saddles 3/16 in or taller tend to lean forward and lose contact. Lowering the saddle (and string angle) often brings a dead string back.

steps.title: Last resorts
steps.detail: A slightly rounded saddle bottom is a 'plan B' that can even out strings but may lose bass. Some techs replace a stubborn factory element with a Fishman Matrix.

models.note: Uneven output almost always means not enough glue; a weak high E on tightly X-braced tops can be helped by moving the E-B transducer toward the brace or adding a fourth transducer.
Do not sand the bottom; see a tech.

pro: Routing the saddle slot flat (with the top jacked to strung position) or recutting it at an angle is pro work.

title: Volume drop or thin, hollow sound
summary: The guitar works but sounds quacky, thin, hollow or much quieter than it should. Common causes: pickups out of phase, a coil split stuck on, a broken ground, or a partly shorted pickup.
symptoms: Two-pickup position sounds thin and nasal, quieter than either pickup alone
Humbucker sounds like a weak single coil
Output much lower than before a repair
Sound gets thinner after a pickup swap

causes.cause: Pickups out of phase with each other
causes.check: Only combination positions sound thin and quiet; each pickup alone sounds normal.
causes.fix: Swap the hot and ground leads on one pickup (or flip a humbucker's magnet). See [ef-pickup-phase-polarity].

causes.cause: Coil split or series/parallel switch stuck on
causes.check: Push-pull or mini switch: does the sound change when you operate it? Meter at the jack reads about half the humbucker's value.
causes.fix: Clean or replace the push-pull pot/mini toggle; check its wiring.

causes.cause: Humbucker series-link wires (Seymour Duncan red + white) touching ground
causes.check: Pickup reads about half its rated resistance and sounds thin.
causes.fix: Insulate the link pair with tape or heat-shrink so it can't touch anything (Seymour Duncan).

causes.cause: Partly shorted coil
causes.check: Pickup DCR clearly lower than spec.
causes.fix: Rewind or replace.

causes.cause: Tone pot not reaching 'full' or wrong cap
causes.check: Does the problem disappear with the tone wire lifted?
causes.fix: Replace the tone pot or cap.

causes.cause: Wrong pot value (e.g. 250k with humbuckers)
causes.check: Muddy, dark rather than thin.
causes.fix: Seymour Duncan suggests trying 500k for muddy humbuckers.

causes.cause: Pickups set too low
causes.check: Measure height (see [ef-pickup-height]).
causes.fix: Raise to spec.

steps.title: Isolate the symptom
steps.detail: Play each pickup alone, then each combination. Thin only in combinations = phase. Thin on one pickup alone = that pickup's coil split, wiring or the pickup itself.

steps.title: Meter at the jack
steps.detail: Compare readings to the expected values (see [ef-test-at-jack]). A humbucker reading about half its value is running on one coil.

steps.title: Check any switches and push-pulls
steps.detail: Work them several times; measure at the jack in both settings. If the reading doesn't change, the switch is stuck or mis-wired.

steps.title: Check phase
steps.detail: If combination positions are thin, follow [ef-pickup-phase-polarity] to find which pickup is reversed, then swap that pickup's hot and ground.

steps.title: Check the link and ground wires
steps.detail: On 4-conductor humbuckers, confirm the series-link pair is joined and insulated, and that bare/shield goes to ground.

models.note: A single pickup with its leads reversed makes positions 2 or 4 thin. RWRP middle pickups mean the middle must be wired as the maker shows.
After swapping one humbucker for a different brand, the middle position is often out of phase. Fixing this on Gibson-style braided leads may require flipping the magnet.
On a P/J bass, Fralin's usual fix for phase is to reverse the P pickup's white and black leads.

title: Squealing or microphonic pickup (wax potting)
summary: A pickup that squeals or howls at high gain, even with the strings muted, has loose windings or a loose cover that vibrate. Wax potting locks them in place.
symptoms: High-pitched squeal at high gain that doesn't follow the note you play
Squeal continues with strings muted
Tapping on the pickup cover comes through the amp loudly
Tele neck pickup howls even at modest volume
tools: Double boiler (old pan inside a larger pan of water)
Electric hotplate (no gas, no open flame)

specs.label: Wax temperature
specs.value: About 160 °F (71 °C) – never higher (Seymour Duncan)

specs.label: Soak time
specs.value: Until bubbles stop; typically a few minutes. Tele lead pickups with metal baseplates about 1–3 min (SD); Premier Guitar's humbuckers took 1–2 min

specs.label: Cooling
specs.value: About 30 min before handling

causes.cause: Normal amp feedback
causes.check: Feedback follows the notes being played and stops when strings are muted.
causes.fix: Not a pickup fault – change position/volume.

causes.cause: Loose metal cover or Tele baseplate
causes.check: Squeal with strings muted; tapping the cover sounds through the amp.
causes.fix: Pot the pickup; secure the plate.

causes.cause: Unpotted or under-potted coil
causes.check: Squeal at high gain, typically on vintage-style or uncovered pickups.
causes.fix: Wax-pot.

steps.title: Confirm it's the pickup
steps.detail: At your usual high-gain volume, mute the strings with your hand and select each pickup. If one squeals with the strings muted, or tapping its cover with a fingernail is very loud through the amp, that pickup is microphonic.

steps.title: Remove the pickup
steps.detail: Mark lead positions, then desolder or cut the leads (Premier Guitar's author cut them midway and spliced them back with solder and heat-shrink). Note the pickup's height setting.

steps.title: Prepare the pickup
steps.detail: Take plastic covers off single coils – hot wax can warp them. For a metal-covered humbucker you may either pot it with the cover on (bottom-up) or remove the cover by desoldering its two joints; Premier Guitar's author removed the cover and later put thin rubber between cover and coils to stop cover rattle.

steps.title: Heat the wax safely
steps.detail: Melt paraffin in the inner pan of a double boiler on an electric plate, with the water below a boil. Hold the wax at about 160 °F and never higher.
steps.warn: Wax is flammable. No gas flame. Never leave it unattended. Wear gloves and glasses.

steps.title: Soak
steps.detail: Lower the pickup in with pliers (never by its lead – the insulation can melt) and agitate gently. Air bubbles will rise; when they stop, the coil is saturated. Watch plastic-bobbin pickups the whole time – bobbins can distort if they get too hot.

steps.title: Cool
steps.detail: Lift out, blot off excess wax, and cool in front of a fan. Don't squeeze the coil. Let it sit about half an hour.

steps.title: Reassemble and test
steps.detail: Wipe wax from covers so they seat flat, re-solder covers, reinstall and reconnect. Measure DCR once cool to confirm the coil is intact, then test at high gain.

models.note: Loose bottom plates on bridge pickups and the metal-covered neck pickup are classic squealers; SD pots the neck pickup with its cover on.
Vintage-style unpotted PAF types can squeal at high gain; covered pickups are potted bottom-up.
Exposed windings: a single broken turn ruins the pickup. Agitate gently.
Epoxy-filled; can't be wax-potted.

warnings: Beeswax is not recommended by Seymour Duncan (too soft and sticky); many hobbyists mix it in anyway, but plain paraffin is the safe choice.
Epoxy-potted pickups won't take wax.
Potting changes the pickup slightly and voids some warranties.
pro: Expensive or vintage pickups – a pickup maker will pot (or rewind) them with a vacuum chamber and controlled heat.

title: How to read a wiring diagram
summary: Learn the symbols, the views and the colour translation step so any maker's wiring diagram can be followed safely, even when it was drawn for a different pickup brand.
tools: The diagram (printed, so you can tick off joints)

specs.label: Pot lug numbering (this app)
specs.value: Back view, shaft away, lugs up: lug 1 left, lug 2 wiper, lug 3 right

specs.label: Typical pot values
specs.value: 250k audio for single coils, 500k audio for humbuckers and P90s, 1M for Jazzmaster lead circuits (Seymour Duncan)

specs.label: Metric pot taper codes
specs.value: A = audio (log), B = linear, C = reverse audio (Mojotone)

steps.title: Find out which side you are looking at
steps.detail: Almost all guitar diagrams draw pots and switches from the BACK, the way you see them in the cavity. Check the drawing: if you can see the lugs and the pot casing, it is a back view. This app always uses the back view with the shaft pointing away and lugs facing up (lug 1 left, lug 2 wiper, lug 3 right). If a diagram is drawn with lugs pointing down, rotate the page before you start.

steps.title: Learn the symbols
steps.detail: A solid dot where two lines cross means they are joined; lines that cross with no dot (or with a little hop) are NOT connected. The ground symbol (a stack of shrinking lines) means 'solder to the shared ground', usually the back of the volume pot. A capacitor is two short parallel lines (one may be curved); a resistor is a zig-zag or small box. A pot is drawn as a circle or arc with three lugs; the middle one is the wiper.

steps.title: Read the switch lug map
steps.detail: Lever switches (Strat 5-way, Tele 3-way, 4-pole 'Super Switch' types) and toggles are drawn as rows of lugs. Diagrams often show a specific brand of switch; if yours is a different brand the lugs can be in a different order. Use the maker's lug map (StewMac publishes one for common lever switches) or, better, map your own switch with a meter - every recipe in this guide starts with that step.

steps.title: Translate the wire colours
steps.detail: Diagrams are drawn for the maker's own colour code. If your pickup is another brand, translate role by role, not colour by colour: find the hot (north coil start), the ground (south coil start), the series-link pair and the bare shield in BOTH codes, then substitute. In this app the steps use roles - {hot}, {ground}, {link}, {nFinish}, {sFinish}, {bare} for humbuckers and {scHot}, {scGround} for single coils - and show the colours for the brand you pick.

steps.title: Trace the signal, then the grounds
steps.detail: With a highlighter, follow each pickup's hot lead from the pickup through the switch, into the volume pot (lug 3), out of the wiper (lug 2) and on to the jack tip. Then use a second colour for every ground: pickup grounds and bare shields, pot lug 1s, the tone caps' far ends, the switch ground, the jack sleeve and the bridge/trem claw ground wire. Anything not highlighted when you finish is either unused or a mistake.

steps.title: Make a joint checklist
steps.detail: Number every solder joint on the printed diagram. As you solder, tick each one. Most 'it doesn't work' repairs come from a single joint that was missed or landed on the neighbouring lug.

warnings: Never assume two brands use the same colours - Seymour Duncan, DiMarzio and Gibson all use different wires for hot and ground.

title: EMG active pickups (solderless, battery, stereo jack, 25k pots)
summary: EMG actives plug together with connectors, run from a 9 V battery switched by a stereo jack, and need the low-value 25k pots they ship with.
tools: Soldering iron only for long panel jacks or some switches
parts: Stereo (TRS) jack, e.g. Switchcraft 152B for a long panel jack
EMG solderless buss (B245 for 2 pickups) if using a selector

specs.label: Pots
specs.value: 25k volume and tone (EMG kit)

specs.label: Jack wiring
specs.value: White to tip, black to sleeve, battery negative (black) to ring (EMG)

specs.label: Battery
specs.value: 9 V; about 400 uA draw, rated about 600 hours (EMG H instructions); EMG FAQ quotes about 1000 h average per set

specs.label: Supply limits
specs.value: Maximum 27 V; 18 V suggested for bass or extra headroom (EMG)

specs.label: EMG toggle harness (BNOG)
specs.value: B bridge input white, N neck input red, O output black, G ground bare (EMG)

steps.title: Learn the lug convention and lay out the parts
steps.detail: Pot lug convention used throughout: hold the pot from the BACK, shaft pointing away from you, lugs facing up. Lug 1 is on the left, lug 2 (the wiper) in the middle, lug 3 on the right. Turning the knob clockwise moves the wiper towards lug 3, so a volume pot takes the signal in on lug 3, sends it out on lug 2 and has lug 1 grounded. 'Ground' in these steps means the shared ground: the back (casing) of a pot, normally the volume pot. Scuff the casing with fine abrasive first so solder takes, and keep the iron on it only as long as needed. EMG's kit uses plug-in connectors rather than pot lugs; the pot convention matters only if you hard-wire it.

steps.title: Remove the old parts and the string ground
steps.detail: Take out the old pickups, pots and switch, noting what each did. EMG says the bridge (string) ground wire is NOT reconnected for EMG actives.

steps.title: Plug in the pickups
steps.detail: Push each pickup cable onto the pickup's header following the arrow; route the cables to the control cavity and store spare cable under the pickup.

steps.title: Controls and selector
steps.detail: Plug the cables into the volume and tone pots. With two pickups on the B245 buss: bridge to position 1, neck to position 2, buss output to the master volume and tone. If you use your own switch, strip its wires and push them into the green terminal block: bridge to BR, neck to NK, output to O, switch ground to a black terminal.

steps.title: Output jack
steps.detail: Output cable to the jack: white to tip, black to sleeve, battery negative to ring - the ring connection means plugging in a mono cable switches the pickups on, so unplug when you stop playing.

steps.title: Power
steps.detail: Push the red wires from the pickups and the battery into the red V+ buss. Put the battery in the supplied foam and secure it so it cannot short against controls.

steps.title: Test before closing up
steps.detail: Before the pickguard/back plate goes on: plug into an amp at low volume. In EVERY switch position (and every push-pull/mini-switch setting) tap the pole pieces of each pickup with a steel screwdriver - only the pickups (or coils) that position should select may give a loud, clear 'tock'. Roll every volume and tone through its range and listen for dead spots or crackle. Then unplug the amp, plug a cable into the guitar and measure tip-to-sleeve at the far end of the cable with a multimeter on the 20k (or auto) ohms range, volume on full: each position should read close to the selected pickup's DC resistance (a little lower because the pots sit in parallel; two pickups in parallel read roughly half; series combinations read the sum). An open/very high reading means a broken joint or wrong lug; near 0 ohms means a short to ground. Finally check about 0 ohms between the strings/bridge and the jack sleeve. EMGs are low impedance, so the tip-to-sleeve resistance test is not meaningful; rely on the screwdriver tap test and a fresh battery.

warnings: Never leave a 9 V battery loose in a cavity - its terminals can short on pot lugs.
Lithium 9 V batteries can get dangerously hot if shorted; insulate and secure them.

title: Independent volume fix (one volume no longer kills both pickups)
summary: On two-volume guitars, turning one volume to 0 in the middle position grounds the output and silences both pickups. Swapping two connections on each volume pot fixes it.
symptoms: Middle position: one volume on 0 mutes the whole guitar
Volumes interact strongly when both pickups are on
tools: Nut driver/socket for pot and jack nuts

steps.title: Learn the lug convention and lay out the parts
steps.detail: Pot lug convention used throughout: hold the pot from the BACK, shaft pointing away from you, lugs facing up. Lug 1 is on the left, lug 2 (the wiper) in the middle, lug 3 on the right. Turning the knob clockwise moves the wiper towards lug 3, so a volume pot takes the signal in on lug 3, sends it out on lug 2 and has lug 1 grounded. 'Ground' in these steps means the shared ground: the back (casing) of a pot, normally the volume pot. Scuff the casing with fine abrasive first so solder takes, and keep the iron on it only as long as needed. Why it happens: with standard wiring the output (toggle) is on the wiper, and at 0 the wiper sits on grounded lug 1 - so the shared output is grounded.

steps.title: Swap input and output on each volume
steps.detail: For each volume pot: move the pickup's {hot} (and, on 'modern' wiring, the tone cap leg that sat with it) from lug 3 to lug 2, and move the wire to the switch from lug 2 to lug 3. Lug 1 stays grounded.

steps.title: What changes
steps.detail: Now turning a volume to 0 grounds only that pickup; the output still sees the full pot value to ground instead of a short, so the other pickup keeps playing. The taper feels different and there is slightly more treble loss when both are on - try it and listen.

steps.title: Test before closing up

An open/very high reading means a broken joint or wrong lug; near 0 ohms means a short to ground. Finally check about 0 ohms between the strings/bridge and the jack sleeve. Middle position: take each volume to 0 in turn - the other pickup must keep sounding when tapped.

warnings: Solder fumes and flux smoke are harmful: work in a ventilated room, ideally with a fume extractor, and wash hands after handling solder.
A soldering iron tip runs at several hundred degrees; always park it in its stand and keep the cable clear of your guitar's finish.
Unplug the guitar from any amp before soldering, and never open an amp or anything mains-powered.
