title: Strat with a tone control on the bridge pickup
summary: Rewire tone 2 so it works on the bridge pickup (alone or together with the middle) - the most common Strat mod to tame an ice-picky bridge.
tools: Nut driver/socket for pot and jack nuts
parts: No new parts if starting from standard Strat wiring

specs.label: Pots
specs.value: 250k audio (Seymour Duncan)

specs.label: Tone cap
specs.value: .047 uF; .022/.033 uF for less cut (Seymour Duncan)

steps.title: Learn the lug convention and lay out the parts
steps.detail: Pot lug convention used throughout: hold the pot from the BACK, shaft pointing away from you, lugs facing up. Lug 1 is on the left, lug 2 (the wiper) in the middle, lug 3 on the right. Turning the knob clockwise moves the wiper towards lug 3, so a volume pot takes the signal in on lug 3, sends it out on lug 2 and has lug 1 grounded. 'Ground' in these steps means the shared ground: the back (casing) of a pot, normally the volume pot. Scuff the casing with fine abrasive first so solder takes, and keep the iron on it only as long as needed. Map the 5-way lever switch with your meter (lug layouts differ between brands - StewMac publishes lug maps). It has two identical rows (decks A and B), each with one common lug and three pickup lugs. On deck A, put the lever in position 1 (towards the bridge) and find the lug that beeps to the common: label it 'B'. Position 3 (middle): label that lug 'M'. Position 5 (neck): 'N'. Confirm that position 2 joins B and M together and position 4 joins M and N. Repeat on deck B. This mod assumes the standard Strat layout from [wr-strat-standard], where deck B lug N feeds tone 1 and deck B lug M feeds tone 2.

steps.title: Option A - tone 2 on middle AND bridge
steps.detail: Solder a short jumper from deck B lug M to deck B lug B. Tone 2 now acts in positions 1, 2, 3 and 4; tone 1 still acts on the neck pickup (positions 4 and 5).

steps.title: Option B - tone 2 on bridge only
steps.detail: Unsolder the wire on deck B lug M and move it to deck B lug B. Tone 2 now acts on positions 1 and 2 (bridge and bridge+middle); the middle pickup alone (position 3) has no tone control.

steps.title: Option C - master tone
steps.detail: If you prefer one tone for everything, connect tone 1 lug 2 to volume lug 3 instead of to the switch, cap from tone 1 lug 1 to ground, and use the spare pot for something else (e.g. a blender, see [wr-strat-blender]).

steps.title: Test before closing up
steps.detail: Before the pickguard/back plate goes on: plug into an amp at low volume. In EVERY switch position (and every push-pull/mini-switch setting) tap the pole pieces of each pickup with a steel screwdriver - only the pickups (or coils) that position should select may give a loud, clear 'tock'. Roll every volume and tone through its range and listen for dead spots or crackle. Then unplug the amp, plug a cable into the guitar and measure tip-to-sleeve at the far end of the cable with a multimeter on the 20k (or auto) ohms range, volume on full: each position should read close to the selected pickup's DC resistance (a little lower because the pots sit in parallel; two pickups in parallel read roughly half; series combinations read the sum). An open/very high reading means a broken joint or wrong lug; near 0 ohms means a short to ground. Finally check about 0 ohms between the strings/bridge and the jack sleeve. Check each tone knob in each position matches the option you chose.

warnings: Solder fumes and flux smoke are harmful: work in a ventilated room, ideally with a fume extractor, and wash hands after handling solder.
A soldering iron tip runs at several hundred degrees; always park it in its stand and keep the cable clear of your guitar's finish.
Unplug the guitar from any amp before soldering, and never open an amp or anything mains-powered.

title: Treble bleed (keep highs when turning the volume down)
summary: A small capacitor (alone or with a resistor) across the volume pot's input and output lets treble pass as you roll back, so the guitar stays clear instead of muddy.
tools: Nut driver/socket for pot and jack nuts

specs.label: Cap only
specs.value: 470-500 pF from volume input to output (Mojotone); Mojotone says not to add a resistor

specs.label: Cap + resistor
specs.value: 0.001 uF (1 nF) with 150k, 1/4 W - from a Fender tech bulletin via StewMac

specs.label: Mojotone diagrams
specs.value: 470 pF with 220k

specs.label: Fender American Professional Tele
specs.value: 1200 pF cap and 20k resistor in its treble-bleed parts

steps.title: Learn the lug convention and lay out the parts
steps.detail: Pot lug convention used throughout: hold the pot from the BACK, shaft pointing away from you, lugs facing up. Lug 1 is on the left, lug 2 (the wiper) in the middle, lug 3 on the right. Turning the knob clockwise moves the wiper towards lug 3, so a volume pot takes the signal in on lug 3, sends it out on lug 2 and has lug 1 grounded. 'Ground' in these steps means the shared ground: the back (casing) of a pot, normally the volume pot. Scuff the casing with fine abrasive first so solder takes, and keep the iron on it only as long as needed.

steps.title: Cap only
steps.detail: Solder the capacitor directly between volume lug 3 (input) and volume lug 2 (output). Keep the legs short and away from the casing.

steps.title: Cap + resistor in parallel
steps.detail: Lay the cap and the resistor side by side, twist the legs together at each end, and solder one end to lug 3 and the other to lug 2. The resistor smooths the taper so the knob doesn't just get brighter as it goes down - this is the common layout for the 1 nF + 150k combination.

steps.title: Cap + resistor in series
steps.detail: Solder the cap to lug 3, the resistor to lug 2, and join their free legs to each other. In series the resistor limits how much the cap bleeds; sources don't agree on one value set, so start with the same parts as the parallel version and judge by ear.

steps.title: Audition first
steps.detail: Clip the network on temporarily (StewMac's tech does this so the player can hear it), roll the volume from 10 to 3 and decide before soldering. Lollar prefers a smaller tone cap instead of a bleed, so try both ideas.

steps.title: Test before closing up
steps.detail: Before the pickguard/back plate goes on: plug into an amp at low volume. In EVERY switch position (and every push-pull/mini-switch setting) tap the pole pieces of each pickup with a steel screwdriver - only the pickups (or coils) that position should select may give a loud, clear 'tock'. Roll every volume and tone through its range and listen for dead spots or crackle. Then unplug the amp, plug a cable into the guitar and measure tip-to-sleeve at the far end of the cable with a multimeter on the 20k (or auto) ohms range, volume on full: each position should read close to the selected pickup's DC resistance (a little lower because the pots sit in parallel; two pickups in parallel read roughly half; series combinations read the sum). An open/very high reading means a broken joint or wrong lug; near 0 ohms means a short to ground. Finally check about 0 ohms between the strings/bridge and the jack sleeve. At 10 the sound must be unchanged; at 5-7 it should be brighter than before.

title: Coil split with a push-pull pot (per humbucker)
summary: Ground the humbucker's series link through a push-pull switch: pushed = full humbucker, pulled = one coil. Needs a 4-conductor (or 3-conductor tapped) pickup.
tools: Nut driver/socket for pot and jack nuts
parts: 500k audio push-pull pot (replaces the volume or tone)

specs.label: Which coil stays
specs.value: Grounding the link keeps the north coil; Seymour Duncan: on Gibson-style humbuckers the non-adjustable (stud/slug) side stays. Bare Knuckle: slug coil = north

specs.label: Other coil
specs.value: Tie the link to the hot instead of ground to keep the south (screw) coil (Bare Knuckle 'screw coil only')

specs.label: Coil split vs coil tap
specs.value: A split switches off one coil of a humbucker; a tap uses an extra lead part-way through one coil's winding (Seymour Duncan)

steps.title: Learn the lug convention and lay out the parts
steps.detail: Pot lug convention used throughout: hold the pot from the BACK, shaft pointing away from you, lugs facing up. Lug 1 is on the left, lug 2 (the wiper) in the middle, lug 3 on the right. Turning the knob clockwise moves the wiper towards lug 3, so a volume pot takes the signal in on lug 3, sends it out on lug 2 and has lug 1 grounded. 'Ground' in these steps means the shared ground: the back (casing) of a pot, normally the volume pot. Scuff the casing with fine abrasive first so solder takes, and keep the iron on it only as long as needed. Push-pull DPDT: two rows of three lugs; the middle lug of each row is that pole's common. Find with the meter which outer lug connects to the common when PULLED.

steps.title: Wire the pot section
steps.detail: Wire the push-pull's pot lugs exactly as the pot it replaces (volume: {hot} to lug 3, lug 2 out, lug 1 ground; tone: signal to lug 2, cap from lug 1 to ground).

steps.title: Split connection
steps.detail: Unsolder/untape the humbucker's {link} pair, solder the two wires together (keep them joined) and run one wire from that joint to the common of one switch row. Solder that row's pulled lug to the pot casing (ground).

steps.title: Optional: choose the other coil
steps.detail: To keep the south coil instead, wire the pulled lug to the pickup's {hot} (the same lug the hot lands on) rather than to ground.

steps.title: Two pickups, two splits
steps.detail: Use the second row of the same push-pull for the other humbucker's {link} pair to split both at once, or a second push-pull to split them separately (Bare Knuckle publishes both layouts).

steps.title: Test before closing up
steps.detail: Before the pickguard/back plate goes on: plug into an amp at low volume. In EVERY switch position (and every push-pull/mini-switch setting) tap the pole pieces of each pickup with a steel screwdriver - only the pickups (or coils) that position should select may give a loud, clear 'tock'. Roll every volume and tone through its range and listen for dead spots or crackle. Then unplug the amp, plug a cable into the guitar and measure tip-to-sleeve at the far end of the cable with a multimeter on the 20k (or auto) ohms range, volume on full: each position should read close to the selected pickup's DC resistance (a little lower because the pots sit in parallel; two pickups in parallel read roughly half; series combinations read the sum). An open/very high reading means a broken joint or wrong lug; near 0 ohms means a short to ground. Finally check about 0 ohms between the strings/bridge and the jack sleeve. Pulled: tap both rows of poles; one row should go almost silent. Pushed: both rows equally loud.

warnings: Solder fumes and flux smoke are harmful: work in a ventilated room, ideally with a fume extractor, and wash hands after handling solder.
A soldering iron tip runs at several hundred degrees; always park it in its stand and keep the cable clear of your guitar's finish.
Unplug the guitar from any amp before soldering, and never open an amp or anything mains-powered.
Insulate the link joint - if it touches ground the pickup is stuck on one coil and gets noisy (Seymour Duncan).

steps.title: Plan the controls
steps.detail: Decide which voices you want switchable and how: push-pull, mini toggle, multi-pole selector, or a permanent jumper/solder joint for a fixed voice. Test-fit the parts and drill nothing until they all fit.

steps.title: Signal and pots
steps.detail: Each pickup's OUTPUT to the selector as for passive pickups (or to its own volume), master/individual volumes and tone with the 25k pots, the 0.22 uF cap from tone to ground, volume output to the jack tip.

steps.title: Voice switching
steps.detail: Wire each voice-select wire to a switch lug whose common goes to ground: grounded = that voice on. On the Mick Thomson set the Voice-2 pin carries no signal and can share a switch contact with other voice wires, but the HFT pad carries signal and must not share a contact with other HFT or voice wires.

steps.title: Power through the jack
steps.detail: Supply + to the pickups' +9-18V pins; supply negative through the stereo jack as on the diagram, so a plugged-in cable switches the power on. Unplug after playing to save the battery.

steps.title: Test before closing up
steps.detail: Before the pickguard/back plate goes on: plug into an amp at low volume. In EVERY switch position (and every push-pull/mini-switch setting) tap the pole pieces of each pickup with a steel screwdriver - only the pickups (or coils) that position should select may give a loud, clear 'tock'. Roll every volume and tone through its range and listen for dead spots or crackle. An open/very high reading means a broken joint or wrong lug; near 0 ohms means a short to ground. Finally check about 0 ohms between the strings/bridge and the jack sleeve. warnings: Fishman recommends professional installation and warns that wrong wiring can damage the pickups.
Secure the battery so it cannot short across control lugs.

parts: Volume pot: 500k audio (Fender American Professional HSS) or 250k
2 tone pots: 250k audio (Fender) or 500k (Mojotone HSS diagram)

specs.label: Fender American Professional HSS
specs.value: 500k volume, 250k tones, 5-way (service manual)

specs.label: Mojotone HSS diagram
specs.value: 500k log volume and tones, .047 and .022 uF caps

specs.label: Split behaviour
specs.value: Grounding the link pair silences the south coil and keeps the north coil (Seymour Duncan: on Gibson-style humbuckers the non-adjustable/stud coil stays)

steps.title: Learn the lug convention and lay out the parts
steps.detail: Pot lug convention used throughout: hold the pot from the BACK, shaft pointing away from you, lugs facing up. Lug 1 is on the left, lug 2 (the wiper) in the middle, lug 3 on the right. Turning the knob clockwise moves the wiper towards lug 3, so a volume pot takes the signal in on lug 3, sends it out on lug 2 and has lug 1 grounded. 'Ground' in these steps means the shared ground: the back (casing) of a pot, normally the volume pot. Scuff the casing with fine abrasive first so solder takes, and keep the iron on it only as long as needed. Map the 5-way lever switch with your meter (lug layouts differ between brands - StewMac publishes lug maps). It has two identical rows (decks A and B), each with one common lug and three pickup lugs. On deck A, put the lever in position 1 (towards the bridge) and find the lug that beeps to the common: label it 'B'. Position 3 (middle): label that lug 'M'. Position 5 (neck): 'N'. Confirm that position 2 joins B and M together and position 4 joins M and N. Repeat on deck B.

steps.title: Humbucker leads
steps.detail: Bridge humbucker {hot} to deck A lug B. Bridge humbucker {ground} and {bare} to the volume casing.

steps.title: Version 1 - no split
steps.detail: Solder the bridge humbucker's {link} pair together, insulate with heat-shrink and tuck it away. Seymour Duncan warns that an uninsulated link touching ground leaves the pickup on one coil and noisy.

steps.title: Version 2 - auto split in position 2
steps.detail: Solder the bridge humbucker's {link} pair together and to deck B lug M. Solder deck B common to ground. Deck B now grounds the link whenever the lever touches lug M (positions 2, 3, 4); the humbucker is only switched on in positions 1 and 2, so it splits in position 2 only. In this version deck B is busy, so the tone pots must be fed from deck A instead (next step).

steps.title: Single coils
steps.detail: Middle {scHot} to deck A lug M, neck {scHot} to deck A lug N; both {scGround} to the volume casing.

steps.title: Volume, tones and jack
steps.detail: Deck A common to volume lug 3. Volume lug 1 to ground, volume lug 2 to jack tip, jack sleeve to ground. Tones: Version 1 can use deck B like a standard Strat ([wr-strat-standard]). Version 2: run tone 1 lug 2 from deck A lug N (neck tone) and tone 2 lug 2 from volume lug 3 (master tone for bridge and middle), each with a cap from its lug 1 to ground.

steps.title: Grounds
steps.detail: Tie the pot casings together and solder the trem claw ground wire to the volume casing.

steps.title: Test before closing up
steps.detail: Before the pickguard/back plate goes on: plug into an amp at low volume. In EVERY switch position (and every push-pull/mini-switch setting) tap the pole pieces of each pickup with a steel screwdriver - only the pickups (or coils) that position should select may give a loud, clear 'tock'. Roll every volume and tone through its range and listen for dead spots or crackle. Then unplug the amp, plug a cable into the guitar and measure tip-to-sleeve at the far end of the cable with a multimeter on the 20k (or auto) ohms range, volume on full: each position should read close to the selected pickup's DC resistance (a little lower because the pots sit in parallel; two pickups in parallel read roughly half; series combinations read the sum). An open/very high reading means a broken joint or wrong lug; near 0 ohms means a short to ground. Finally check about 0 ohms between the strings/bridge and the jack sleeve. Position 2 (Version 2): tap both rows of the humbucker - only one row should stay loud.

warnings: Solder fumes and flux smoke are harmful: work in a ventilated room, ideally with a fume extractor, and wash hands after handling solder.
A soldering iron tip runs at several hundred degrees; always park it in its stand and keep the cable clear of your guitar's finish.
Unplug the guitar from any amp before soldering, and never open an amp or anything mains-powered.

steps.detail: Pot lug convention used throughout: hold the pot from the BACK, shaft pointing away from you, lugs facing up. Lug 1 is on the left, lug 2 (the wiper) in the middle, lug 3 on the right. steps.detail: Neck humbucker: solder the {link} pair together and insulate. {hot} to neck volume lug 3; {ground} and {bare} to the neck volume casing.

steps.title: Toggle to jack
steps.detail: Shielded wire from the toggle's joined output lugs to the jack tip; its braid to the jack sleeve and to the toggle's ground lug.

steps.title: Ground everything
steps.detail: Run a ground wire linking all four pot casings. Solder the bridge/tailpiece ground wire to a volume casing. StewMac's tech gets one ground lead per pickup by wrapping a short push-back wire round the braid.

steps.title: Test before closing up

In EVERY switch position (and every push-pull/mini-switch setting) tap the pole pieces of each pickup with a steel screwdriver - only the pickups (or coils) that position should select may give a loud, clear 'tock'. An open/very high reading means a broken joint or wrong lug; near 0 ohms means a short to ground. Finally check about 0 ohms between the strings/bridge and the jack sleeve. Middle toggle position: both pickups. Turn one volume fully down - with this standard wiring the whole guitar goes silent in the middle position; if that bothers you see [wr-independent-volume].

title: Planning a custom wiring
summary: Turn 'I want these sounds' into a switch table, a parts list and a diagram before you buy parts or pick up the iron.
parts: Pots of the right value/taper and shaft type
Push-pull pots or mini toggles as needed

specs.label: Single coils
specs.value: 250k audio (Seymour Duncan, Mojotone)

specs.label: Humbuckers/P90s
specs.value: 500k audio (Seymour Duncan)

specs.label: Active pickups (EMG, Fishman Fluence)
specs.value: 25k (EMG kit; Fishman: 25k audio)

specs.label: Common tone caps
specs.value: .047 uF single coils (Seymour Duncan Strat/Tele); .022 uF typical with humbuckers (Mojotone LP diagram)

steps.title: Write the sound table
steps.detail: Pot lug convention used throughout: hold the pot from the BACK, shaft pointing away from you, lugs facing up. Lug 1 is on the left, lug 2 (the wiper) in the middle, lug 3 on the right. Turning the knob clockwise moves the wiper towards lug 3, so a volume pot takes the signal in on lug 3, sends it out on lug 2 and has lug 1 grounded. Now make a table with one row per switch position (and per push-pull up/down). For each row write which pickups or coils must be on, whether they combine in series or parallel, and which tone control should act. This table is the real design; everything else follows from it.

steps.title: Count the poles you need
steps.detail: Each independent thing that has to change between positions needs its own switch pole: one pole per output feed that must be selected separately, one pole per coil-split ground, two poles for a series/parallel change, two poles for a phase flip. A Strat 5-way has 2 poles, a 'Super Switch' style 5-way has 4, a push-pull pot or a mini toggle adds 2 (DPDT). If you run out of poles, simplify the table or choose a bigger switch.

steps.title: Choose pot values and tapers
steps.detail: Pick values for the pickups that will be on that pot: higher values sound brighter (Seymour Duncan). Use audio taper for volume and tone in passive guitars. If one pot serves both single coils and a humbucker, choose by ear - 500k brightens the single coils, 250k darkens the humbucker. Active pickups need the low values their maker supplies.

steps.title: Check the space
steps.detail: Push-pull pots are deeper than standard pots and some imported guitars use metric-size pots that will not fit US-size (CTS) parts without opening the holes (Mojotone notes this). Measure cavity depth and hole size before ordering.

steps.title: Draw the diagram in roles
steps.detail: Draw each pickup with role labels ({hot}, {ground}, {link}/{nFinish}/{sFinish}, {bare}, or {scHot}/{scGround}), not colours. Draw each switch pole as a common plus the lug(s) that connect in each position. Draw every ground to one point. Only then translate to your brand's colours. Pot lug convention used throughout: hold the pot from the BACK, shaft pointing away from you, lugs facing up. Lug 1 is on the left, lug 2 (the wiper) in the middle, lug 3 on the right. Turning the knob clockwise moves the wiper towards lug 3, so a volume pot takes the signal in on lug 3, sends it out on lug 2 and has lug 1 grounded.

steps.title: Dry-run with clip leads
steps.detail: Before soldering a complicated layout, connect it temporarily with alligator clips (StewMac's treble-bleed article uses the same trick to audition a change). Plug in and do the screwdriver tap test for each position. It is far quicker to move a clip than to desolder a lug.

steps.title: Label and leave slack
steps.detail: Mark both ends of each pickup's leads (StewMac's tech marks neck leads red and bridge leads blue) and keep pickup leads long until everything is fitted - trim last.

steps.title: Test before closing up
steps.detail: Before the pickguard/back plate goes on: plug into an amp at low volume. In EVERY switch position (and every push-pull/mini-switch setting) tap the pole pieces of each pickup with a steel screwdriver - only the pickups (or coils) that position should select may give a loud, clear 'tock'. Roll every volume and tone through its range and listen for dead spots or crackle. Then unplug the amp, plug a cable into the guitar and measure tip-to-sleeve at the far end of the cable with a multimeter on the 20k (or auto) ohms range, volume on full: each position should read close to the selected pickup's DC resistance (a little lower because the pots sit in parallel; two pickups in parallel read roughly half; series combinations read the sum). An open/very high reading means a broken joint or wrong lug; near 0 ohms means a short to ground. Finally check about 0 ohms between the strings/bridge and the jack sleeve.

title: Series / parallel humbucker switching (push-pull)

tools: Nut driver/socket for pot and jack nuts
parts: Push-pull pot (DPDT), same value as the pot it replaces

specs.label: Series
specs.value: North finish joined to south finish (the normal {link})

specs.label: Parallel
specs.value: North start + south finish to output; north finish + south start to ground (Bare Knuckle: red + white to output; black, green + bare to ground)

specs.label: Pickup needed
specs.value: 4-conductor with separate {nFinish} and {sFinish}

steps.title: Learn the lug convention and lay out the parts
steps.detail: Pot lug convention used throughout: hold the pot from the BACK, shaft pointing away from you, lugs facing up. Lug 1 is on the left, lug 2 (the wiper) in the middle, lug 3 on the right. Turning the knob clockwise moves the wiper towards lug 3, so a volume pot takes the signal in on lug 3, sends it out on lug 2 and has lug 1 grounded. 'Ground' in these steps means the shared ground: the back (casing) of a pot, normally the volume pot. Scuff the casing with fine abrasive first so solder takes, and keep the iron on it only as long as needed. Push-pull rows: call them row A and row B; middle lug of each row = common. Find the 'pushed' and 'pulled' outer lug of each row with the meter.

steps.title: Separate the link pair
steps.detail: Unsolder the humbucker's {link} so {nFinish} and {sFinish} are separate wires. Keep the {hot} on its usual lug (volume lug 3 or switch) and {ground} + {bare} on ground.

steps.title: Row A
steps.detail: Solder {nFinish} to row A common. Row A pushed lug: wire it to row B common. Row A pulled lug: wire it to ground.

steps.title: Row B
steps.detail: Solder {sFinish} to row B common. Row B pushed lug: leave empty. Row B pulled lug: wire it to the pickup's {hot} (same lug the hot lands on).

steps.title: Check the logic
steps.detail: Pushed: {nFinish} meets {sFinish} through row A = series. Pulled: {nFinish} to ground, {sFinish} to hot = parallel.

steps.title: Test before closing up
steps.detail: Before the pickguard/back plate goes on: plug into an amp at low volume. In EVERY switch position (and every push-pull/mini-switch setting) tap the pole pieces of each pickup with a steel screwdriver - only the pickups (or coils) that position should select may give a loud, clear 'tock'. Roll every volume and tone through its range and listen for dead spots or crackle. Then unplug the amp, plug a cable into the guitar and measure tip-to-sleeve at the far end of the cable with a multimeter on the 20k (or auto) ohms range, volume on full: each position should read close to the selected pickup's DC resistance (a little lower because the pots sit in parallel; two pickups in parallel read roughly half; series combinations read the sum). An open/very high reading means a broken joint or wrong lug; near 0 ohms means a short to ground. Finally check about 0 ohms between the strings/bridge and the jack sleeve. Pulled should be clearly brighter and a bit quieter but NOT thin and hollow. Hollow and very weak means a coil is reversed - swap the two finish wires on the rows. Meter: parallel reads about a quarter of the series resistance.

warnings: Solder fumes and flux smoke are harmful: work in a ventilated room, ideally with a fume extractor, and wash hands after handling solder.
A soldering iron tip runs at several hundred degrees; always park it in its stand and keep the cable clear of your guitar's finish.

specs.value: 250k audio, DPDT (two rows of three lugs, middle lug of each row is that pole's common)

steps.title: Learn the lug convention and lay out the parts
steps.detail: Pot lug convention used throughout: hold the pot from the BACK, shaft pointing away from you, lugs facing up. Lug 1 is on the left, lug 2 (the wiper) in the middle, lug 3 on the right. Turning the knob clockwise moves the wiper towards lug 3, so a volume pot takes the signal in on lug 3, sends it out on lug 2 and has lug 1 grounded. On deck A, put the lever in position 1 (towards the bridge) and find the lug that beeps to the common: label it 'B'. Position 3 (middle): label that lug 'M'. Position 5 (neck): 'N'. Confirm that position 2 joins B and M together and position 4 joins M and N. Repeat on deck B. Push-pull pot: the DPDT switch on the back has two rows of three lugs. steps.detail: Wire its pot section exactly like the old tone 2 (deck B lug M to pot lug 2, pot lug 1 to the tone cap).

steps.title: Add the neck feed
steps.detail: Solder a wire from deck A lug N (where the neck pickup's {scHot} is) to the common lug of one row of the push-pull switch. Solder a wire from that row's pulled lug to deck A common (or to volume lug 3, which is the same node).

steps.title: Leave the other row empty
steps.detail: The second pole is not needed. Make sure no stray strands touch it.

steps.title: Test before closing up
steps.detail: Before the pickguard/back plate goes on: plug into an amp at low volume. In EVERY switch position (and every push-pull/mini-switch setting) tap the pole pieces of each pickup with a steel screwdriver - only the pickups (or coils) that position should select may give a loud, clear 'tock'. Roll every volume and tone through its range and listen for dead spots or crackle. An open/very high reading means a broken joint or wrong lug; near 0 ohms means a short to ground. Finally check about 0 ohms between the strings/bridge and the jack sleeve. With the knob pulled, tap the neck pickup in position 1: it must now sound together with the bridge. Push the knob down and confirm the normal five sounds return.

steps.detail: Bend volume lug 1 to the pot casing and solder it (ground). Solder a wire from volume lug 2 to the jack's tip lug and a wire from the jack's sleeve lug to the volume casing.

steps.detail: Run a ground wire across the backs of all three pots so they are tied together (or rely on a shielded pickguard, but a wire is surer). Solder the trem claw/bridge ground wire to the volume casing - Fender's service manuals show this black wire running to the trem claw.

steps.title: Test before closing up
steps.detail: Before the pickguard/back plate goes on: plug into an amp at low volume. In EVERY switch position (and every push-pull/mini-switch setting) tap the pole pieces of each pickup with a steel screwdriver - only the pickups (or coils) that position should select may give a loud, clear 'tock'. Roll every volume and tone through its range and listen for dead spots or crackle. Then unplug the amp, plug a cable into the guitar and measure tip-to-sleeve at the far end of the cable with a multimeter on the 20k (or auto) ohms range, volume on full: each position should read close to the selected pickup's DC resistance (a little lower because the pots sit in parallel; two pickups in parallel read roughly half; series combinations read the sum). An open/very high reading means a broken joint or wrong lug; near 0 ohms means a short to ground. Finally check about 0 ohms between the strings/bridge and the jack sleeve. Position 3 should give only the middle pickup; positions 2 and 4 should sound quieter of hum if the middle pickup is reverse wound/reverse polarity (RWRP).

models.note: Fender's American Vintage '57 reissue manual lists a 3-way switch and a 0.1 uF cap with three 250k pots - use a 3-way switch and skip the in-between positions if you want it fully vintage.
Service manual lists 250k pots and a .022 uF cap.

warnings: Solder fumes and flux smoke are harmful: work in a ventilated room, ideally with a fume extractor, and wash hands after handling solder.
A soldering iron tip runs at several hundred degrees; always park it in its stand and keep the cable clear of your guitar's finish.
Unplug the guitar from any amp before soldering, and never open an amp or anything mains-powered.

title: Telecaster standard 3-way (and reverse control plate)

tools: Nut driver/socket for pot and jack nuts
parts: Tele control plate and jack cup

specs.label: Pots
specs.value: 250k audio for volume and tone (Seymour Duncan; Mojotone 250k log)

specs.label: Tone cap
specs.value: .047 uF (Seymour Duncan); Fender American Professional Tele lists .022 uF

specs.label: Fender American Professional Tele treble bleed
specs.value: Parts list shows a 1200 pF cap and a 20k resistor

specs.label: Positions
specs.value: 1 bridge, 2 both, 3 neck (Fender)

steps.title: Learn the lug convention and lay out the parts
steps.detail: Pot lug convention used throughout: hold the pot from the BACK, shaft pointing away from you, lugs facing up. Lug 1 is on the left, lug 2 (the wiper) in the middle, lug 3 on the right. Turning the knob clockwise moves the wiper towards lug 3, so a volume pot takes the signal in on lug 3, sends it out on lug 2 and has lug 1 grounded. 'Ground' in these steps means the shared ground: the back (casing) of a pot, normally the volume pot. Scuff the casing with fine abrasive first so solder takes, and keep the iron on it only as long as needed. Map the Tele 3-way lever switch with your meter. It has two rows (decks A and B), each with a common and three lugs. On each deck note which lug connects to the common in position 1 (lever towards the bridge), 2 and 3.

steps.title: Bridge pickup
steps.detail: On deck A, jumper the position-1 lug to the position-2 lug and solder the bridge pickup's {scHot} there. Solder the bridge {scGround} to the volume casing. On a Tele bridge pickup the ground lead is also tied to the metal base plate, which grounds the strings (Lollar).

steps.title: Neck pickup
steps.detail: On deck B, jumper the position-2 lug to the position-3 lug and solder the neck pickup's {scHot} there. Neck {scGround} to the volume casing (on Teles this lead also grounds the neck pickup's metal cover).

steps.title: If your switch is different
steps.detail: If your meter showed that position 2 already connects two lugs of one deck at once, you only need deck A: bridge {scHot} to the lug that is live in 1 and 2, neck {scHot} to the lug live in 2 and 3. The goal is always: bridge live in positions 1-2, neck live in 2-3.

steps.title: Volume, tone and jack
steps.detail: Join deck A and deck B commons to volume lug 3. Volume lug 1 to ground. Volume lug 2 to the jack tip. Tone: volume lug 3 to tone lug 2, .047 uF cap from tone lug 1 to the tone casing. Jack sleeve to the volume casing; tie the pot casings together.

steps.title: Reverse control plate
steps.detail: A reversed plate puts the switch behind the volume knob. The circuit is identical: keep the lever's position 1 towards the bridge so positions keep their meaning, and lengthen the pickup leads and jack wires as needed (both Lollar and Mojotone publish reversed versions of this same circuit).

steps.title: Test before closing up
steps.detail: Before the pickguard/back plate goes on: plug into an amp at low volume. In EVERY switch position (and every push-pull/mini-switch setting) tap the pole pieces of each pickup with a steel screwdriver - only the pickups (or coils) that position should select may give a loud, clear 'tock'. Roll every volume and tone through its range and listen for dead spots or crackle. Then unplug the amp, plug a cable into the guitar and measure tip-to-sleeve at the far end of the cable with a multimeter on the 20k (or auto) ohms range, volume on full: each position should read close to the selected pickup's DC resistance (a little lower because the pots sit in parallel; two pickups in parallel read roughly half; series combinations read the sum). An open/very high reading means a broken joint or wrong lug; near 0 ohms means a short to ground. Finally check about 0 ohms between the strings/bridge and the jack sleeve.

warnings: Solder fumes and flux smoke are harmful: work in a ventilated room, ideally with a fume extractor, and wash hands after handling solder.
A soldering iron tip runs at several hundred degrees; always park it in its stand and keep the cable clear of your guitar's finish.

title: ES-335 / semi-hollow wiring through the f-holes
summary: Same 2-volume, 2-tone, 3-way circuit as a Les Paul, but every part goes in and out through the f-holes, so the harness is built outside the guitar and fished in.
tools: Nut driver/socket for pot and jack nuts

specs.label: Pots/caps
specs.value: As Les Paul: 500k audio, .022 uF (Mojotone, Seymour Duncan)

specs.label: Mojotone 335 harness grounds
specs.value: Bridge ground taken from the tailpiece

steps.title: Learn the lug convention and lay out the parts
steps.detail: Pot lug convention used throughout: hold the pot from the BACK, shaft pointing away from you, lugs facing up. Lug 1 is on the left, lug 2 (the wiper) in the middle, lug 3 on the right. Turning the knob clockwise moves the wiper towards lug 3, so a volume pot takes the signal in on lug 3, sends it out on lug 2 and has lug 1 grounded. 'Ground' in these steps means the shared ground: the back (casing) of a pot, normally the volume pot. Scuff the casing with fine abrasive first so solder takes, and keep the iron on it only as long as needed. Gibson/Switchcraft 3-way toggle: seen from the back, the two outer lugs on the long spring leaves are the pickup inputs (one for the neck/'rhythm' side, one for the bridge/'treble' side), the two inner lugs are the output and are joined together, and the lug on the frame is ground. Confirm with the meter: rhythm position connects the rhythm leaf to the output.

steps.title: Build the harness outside
steps.detail: Punch holes in cardboard at the same spacing as the control holes and build the complete circuit from [wr-les-paul-modern] or [wr-les-paul-50s] on it, with leads long enough to reach the pickups, toggle and jack through the f-holes. Label each pickup lead.

steps.title: Tether each part
steps.detail: Slip a looped rubber band or a string over each pot shaft, the toggle and the jack before they go in (StewMac). The tether lets you pull each part up into its hole and stops it falling inside.

steps.title: Fish it in
steps.detail: Protect the top with felt. Feed the parts in through the nearer f-hole one at a time and pull each up through its hole with its tether; slide the washer and nut down the tether onto the shaft and tighten finger-tight, then fully with a spanner.

steps.title: Connect the pickups
steps.detail: Pass the pickup leads through their holes and solder: each {hot} to its volume lug 3, {ground} and {bare} to its volume casing, {link} pair joined and insulated. StewMac's tech avoids soldering through the f-holes where possible - pull wire out for slack, solder outside, then feed it back.

steps.title: Bridge ground
steps.detail: Make sure the tailpiece/bridge ground wire reaches a volume casing.

steps.title: Test before closing up
steps.detail: Before the pickguard/back plate goes on: plug into an amp at low volume. In EVERY switch position (and every push-pull/mini-switch setting) tap the pole pieces of each pickup with a steel screwdriver - only the pickups (or coils) that position should select may give a loud, clear 'tock'. Roll every volume and tone through its range and listen for dead spots or crackle. Then unplug the amp, plug a cable into the guitar and measure tip-to-sleeve at the far end of the cable with a multimeter on the 20k (or auto) ohms range, volume on full: each position should read close to the selected pickup's DC resistance (a little lower because the pots sit in parallel; two pickups in parallel read roughly half; series combinations read the sum). An open/very high reading means a broken joint or wrong lug; near 0 ohms means a short to ground. Finally check about 0 ohms between the strings/bridge and the jack sleeve. Check with an inspection mirror that no bare lug touches another before tightening everything.

warnings: Solder fumes and flux smoke are harmful: work in a ventilated room, ideally with a fume extractor, and wash hands after handling solder.
A soldering iron tip runs at several hundred degrees; always park it in its stand and keep the cable clear of your guitar's finish.
Unplug the guitar from any amp before soldering, and never open an amp or anything mains-powered.
Hot iron near a lacquered top: keep a heat shield/cloth between the iron and the guitar.
pro: If a pot has to be replaced but the harness is otherwise fine, StewMac shows a single pot being fished out and resoldered; a full harness swap on a valuable hollowbody is a good job for a tech.

title: HH superstrat 5-way (split in 2 & 4, or inside/outside coils)
summary: Two humbuckers on a 4-pole 5-way. Choose variant A (each humbucker split on its own in 2 and 4) or variant B (inner coils of both in 2, outer coils of both in 4).
tools: Nut driver/socket for pot and jack nuts

specs.label: Variant A
specs.value: 1 bridge HB, 2 bridge single coil, 3 both HBs, 4 neck single coil, 5 neck HB

specs.label: Variant B
specs.value: 1 bridge HB, 2 inner coils of both, 3 both HBs, 4 outer coils of both, 5 neck HB

specs.label: Keep north coil
specs.value: Ground the link pair (Seymour Duncan / Bare Knuckle 'slug coil only')

specs.label: Keep south coil
specs.value: Tie the link pair to the pickup's hot (Bare Knuckle 'screw coil only': red, green and white to output)

steps.title: Learn the lug convention and lay out the parts
steps.detail: Pot lug convention used throughout: hold the pot from the BACK, shaft pointing away from you, lugs facing up. Lug 1 is on the left, lug 2 (the wiper) in the middle, lug 3 on the right. Turning the knob clockwise moves the wiper towards lug 3, so a volume pot takes the signal in on lug 3, sends it out on lug 2 and has lug 1 grounded. steps.title: Find each pickup's north coil
steps.detail: Variant B needs this, and it helps for A. Connect each humbucker temporarily as a normal series pickup, then clip its {link} pair to ground: tap both rows of pole pieces - the row that still sounds loud is the north coil. Note whether it is the INNER coil (nearest the middle of the guitar) or the OUTER coil for each pickup.

steps.title: Hots and grounds
steps.detail: Both humbuckers: {ground} and {bare} to ground. Variant A: bridge {hot} to P1 lugs 1, 2 and 3 (jumpered); neck {hot} to P2 lugs 3, 4 and 5. Variant B: bridge {hot} to P1 lugs 1-4; neck {hot} to P2 lugs 2-5. Join P1 and P2 commons to volume lug 3.

steps.title: Variant A - splits
steps.detail: P3 common to ground. Bridge {link} pair to P3 lug 2; neck {link} pair to P3 lug 4. Position 2 leaves the bridge's north coil, position 4 the neck's north coil. P4 is spare.

steps.title: Variant B - coil choice, bridge pickup on P3
steps.detail: Solder the bridge {link} pair to P3's COMMON. To P3 lug 2 (inner coil wanted): if the bridge's inner coil is its north coil, wire lug 2 to ground; if it is the south coil, wire lug 2 to the bridge {hot}. To P3 lug 4 (outer coil wanted) wire the opposite. Leave lugs 1, 3 and 5 empty so the pickup stays a full humbucker there.

steps.title: Variant B - coil choice, neck pickup on P4
steps.detail: Same idea on P4 with the neck {link} pair on the common: lug 2 keeps the neck's inner coil, lug 4 its outer coil, using ground (to keep north) or the neck {hot} (to keep south).

steps.title: Volume, tone, jack
steps.detail: Volume lug 1 to ground, lug 2 to jack tip; master tone from volume lug 3 to tone lug 2 with the cap from tone lug 1 to ground; jack sleeve and bridge ground to the volume casing.

steps.title: Test before closing up
steps.detail: Before the pickguard/back plate goes on: plug into an amp at low volume. In EVERY switch position (and every push-pull/mini-switch setting) tap the pole pieces of each pickup with a steel screwdriver - only the pickups (or coils) that position should select may give a loud, clear 'tock'. Roll every volume and tone through its range and listen for dead spots or crackle. Then unplug the amp, plug a cable into the guitar and measure tip-to-sleeve at the far end of the cable with a multimeter on the 20k (or auto) ohms range, volume on full: each position should read close to the selected pickup's DC resistance (a little lower because the pots sit in parallel; two pickups in parallel read roughly half; series combinations read the sum). An open/very high reading means a broken joint or wrong lug; near 0 ohms means a short to ground. Finally check about 0 ohms between the strings/bridge and the jack sleeve. In 2 and 4 tap all four coil rows: exactly the coils from your chosen variant should respond.

title: Jaguar wiring (on/off switches, strangle switch, rhythm circuit)
summary: The Jaguar lead circuit uses three slide switches - neck on/off, bridge on/off and a 'strangle' high-pass filter - plus volume and tone; a rhythm circuit like the Jazzmaster's runs the neck pickup through roller controls.
tools: Nut driver/socket for pot and jack nuts
parts: Lead volume and tone pots and rhythm roller pots - replace like-for-like using the stamped values
3 slide switches on the lower plate, 1 on the upper plate
Strangle-switch capacitor (value as on your original part)

specs.label: Lead switches
specs.value: Switch 1 neck on/off, switch 2 bridge on/off, switch 3 strangle (cap acting as a high-pass filter) (Bacon, 50 Years of Fender, via Wikipedia)

specs.label: Rhythm circuit
specs.value: Upper slide switch; neck pickup only with its own roller volume and tone

steps.title: Learn the lug convention and lay out the parts
steps.detail: Pot lug convention used throughout: hold the pot from the BACK, shaft pointing away from you, lugs facing up. Lug 1 is on the left, lug 2 (the wiper) in the middle, lug 3 on the right. Turning the knob clockwise moves the wiper towards lug 3, so a volume pot takes the signal in on lug 3, sends it out on lug 2 and has lug 1 grounded. 'Ground' in these steps means the shared ground: the back (casing) of a pot, normally the volume pot. Scuff the casing with fine abrasive first so solder takes, and keep the iron on it only as long as needed. Slide switches: each is a small SPDT/DPDT; map with the meter which lugs join in each slider position before you solder anything.

steps.title: Pickup on/off switches
steps.detail: Neck {scHot} to the common of switch 1; its 'on' lug goes to the lead volume input (lug 3). Bridge {scHot} to switch 2's common; its 'on' lug to the same lead volume input. Both pickups on = parallel. Both {scGround} to ground.

steps.title: Strangle switch
steps.detail: Switch 3 decides whether the signal passes straight through or through the small strangle capacitor in series: wire the cap between the two signal points and use the switch to short across it when the strangle is off. With the strangle on, the series cap cuts lows.

steps.title: Lead volume, tone and the rhythm circuit
steps.detail: Lead volume lug 1 to ground, lug 2 to the upper slide switch's 'lead' throw; lead tone from volume lug 3 to tone lug 2, cap from tone lug 1 to ground. Rhythm: neck {scHot} also to rhythm volume lug 3; rhythm volume lug 2 to the 'rhythm' throw; rhythm tone as for the Jazzmaster. Upper slide switch common to the jack tip.

steps.title: Grounds and shielding
steps.detail: Tie all casings and the bridge ground together. Original US Jaguars use brass shielding plates in the cavities; keep them grounded.

steps.title: Test before closing up
steps.detail: Before the pickguard/back plate goes on: plug into an amp at low volume. In EVERY switch position (and every push-pull/mini-switch setting) tap the pole pieces of each pickup with a steel screwdriver - only the pickups (or coils) that position should select may give a loud, clear 'tock'. Roll every volume and tone through its range and listen for dead spots or crackle. Then unplug the amp, plug a cable into the guitar and measure tip-to-sleeve at the far end of the cable with a multimeter on the 20k (or auto) ohms range, volume on full: each position should read close to the selected pickup's DC resistance (a little lower because the pots sit in parallel; two pickups in parallel read roughly half; series combinations read the sum). An open/very high reading means a broken joint or wrong lug; near 0 ohms means a short to ground. Finally check about 0 ohms between the strings/bridge and the jack sleeve. Check every combination of the three lower switches, then the rhythm switch.

warnings: Solder fumes and flux smoke are harmful: work in a ventilated room, ideally with a fume extractor, and wash hands after handling solder.
A soldering iron tip runs at several hundred degrees; always park it in its stand and keep the cable clear of your guitar's finish.
Unplug the guitar from any amp before soldering, and never open an amp or anything mains-powered.
pro: The strangle cap value and pot values were not something we could confirm from a maker's published text; copy them from your guitar's original parts or Fender's diagram for your model, or have a specialist do it.

steps.detail: Pot lug convention used throughout: hold the pot from the BACK, shaft pointing away from you, lugs facing up. Lug 1 is on the left, lug 2 (the wiper) in the middle, lug 3 on the right. steps.title: Understand the loading problem
steps.detail: A passive pickup sees the pot as a load to ground: a 25k pot pulls a passive pickup's highs and output right down. An active pickup has a low-impedance buffered output and works with low-value pots. EMG and Fishman both state their pickups are designed around 25k pots.

Feed the two volume wipers (lug 2) to the selector's two inputs, like a Les Paul ([wr-les-paul-modern]). Avoid a master tone shared between both, or use one sized for the passive pickup.

steps.title: Power
steps.detail: Run the active pickup's power through a stereo jack exactly as its maker shows; the passive pickup needs no power.

steps.title: Middle position
steps.detail: With both on, the passive pickup still sees the active pickup's 25k volume in parallel through the switch and will lose highs. Accept it, avoid the middle position, or ask the active maker about a buffered solution.

steps.detail: Pot lug convention used throughout: hold the pot from the BACK, shaft pointing away from you, lugs facing up. Lug 1 is on the left, lug 2 (the wiper) in the middle, lug 3 on the right. steps.title: Separate the neck cover
steps.detail: The neck pickup's cover is normally tied to its ground lead. steps.detail: Position 1: bridge {scHot} to output, neck {scGround} to ground. Position 2: bridge and neck {scHot} both to output, neck {scGround} to ground. steps.title: Wire the series pole
steps.detail: Use the second pole with the neck {scGround} on its common: the lug(s) live in positions 1-3 go to ground, the lug live in position 4 goes to the bridge {scHot}.

steps.title: Volume, tone, jack
steps.detail: Volume lug 1 to ground, lug 2 to jack tip; tone from volume lug 3 to tone lug 2 with the cap from tone lug 1 to ground; jack sleeve to ground.

Roll every volume and tone through its range and listen for dead spots or crackle. Then unplug the amp, plug a cable into the guitar and measure tip-to-sleeve at the far end of the cable with a multimeter on the 20k (or auto) ohms range, volume on full: each position should read close to the selected pickup's DC resistance (a little lower because the pots sit in parallel; two pickups in parallel read roughly half; series combinations read the sum). An open/very high reading means a broken joint or wrong lug; near 0 ohms means a short to ground. Finally check about 0 ohms between the strings/bridge and the jack sleeve. title: Conversions that aren't practical: 7-string, changing scale length
summary: Some popular 'can I convert it?' ideas don't work on an existing guitar. Here's why a 6-string can't become a 7-string and why you can't change scale length, plus what to do instead. Scalloping is possible — see the Frets & Nut guides.

steps.title: Six-string to seven-string: not possible
steps.detail: A 7-string needs a wider neck and fretboard, a wider nut, a 7-string bridge, 7-string pickups, a headstock with seven tuners and usually different routing. Converting would mean replacing the neck, bridge and pickups and re-routing the body — effectively building a new guitar. Buy a 7-string (or a 7-string replacement neck and body as a project).

steps.title: Changing scale length: not practical
steps.detail: Scale length is set by where the fret slots are cut. Every fret position is calculated from the scale, so moving the bridge alone just ruins intonation. Changing scale would need a new fretboard slotted for the new scale and the bridge relocated. Common scales for reference: Fender 25-1/2 in, Gibson 24-3/4 in, PRS 25 in, Fender bass 34 in. Instead: change string gauge and tuning to get the tension feel you want, or fit a replacement neck that matches your body's bridge position.

steps.title: Want baritone range?
steps.detail: Use heavier strings and a setup for low tuning (md-baritone-drop-tuning). A true baritone feel needs a longer-scale neck designed for it.

steps.title: Multiscale (fanned frets)
steps.detail: Fanned frets use different scales on bass and treble sides (StewMac quotes roughly 27–26.5 in bass side and 25.5–24.75 in treble side). They can't be added to an existing neck.

steps.title: Scalloped fretboard
steps.detail: This one is possible on an existing neck but is skilled file work between the frets — see the scalloping guide in Frets & Nut.

models.note: Replacement necks make many 'conversions' possible without touching the original neck — as long as the neck's scale matches the bridge position.
Neck replacement is major surgery; practically, buy the guitar you want.

summary: Switch the low string between E and D quickly: on a Floyd Rose use the fine-tuner reserve, a stopper or an EVH D-Tuna; on non-locking guitars fit a lever-type drop tuner key (Hipshot Xtender / D-Tuner style) in place of the low-E tuner.

parts: Tremol-No, Hipshot Tremsetter or Floyd Upgrades stopper (optional)

steps.title: Understand the problem
steps.detail: On a floating trem, slackening one string lets the springs pull the bridge back, so every other string goes sharp. Any quick-drop method needs the bridge stopped from moving upward.

steps.title: Simple method: reserve the fine tuner
steps.detail: Bax-shop: wind the low-E fine tuner fully down (loosened) before you set standard tuning, so you can later turn it back up after dropping. On a floating bridge you will still need to retouch the other strings, so this works best with a block.

steps.title: Stop the bridge
steps.detail: Fit a one-way block or a commercial stopper so the bridge rests against it at pitch and can't lift when tension is removed. See [bt-deck-or-block-trem].

steps.title: Fit a D-Tuna
steps.detail: Remove the long string-locking screw from the low-E saddle, fit one of the two long replacement screws supplied, then install the spring assembly and the D-Tuna. It works through the fine tuner, which presses on the locking screw. It can stay on during string changes.

steps.title: Set the two pitches
steps.detail: With the bridge blocked or stopped, set the low string to E in one D-Tuna position, lock the nut, then switch positions and adjust the D-Tuna's own fine tuner until the string reads D. Follow the included sheet for which position is which. For E-flat tuning the same unit gives D-flat and E-flat.

steps.title: Troubleshoot
steps.detail: If the full step won't reach D, check the screw length - if the screw head sticks out past the D-Tuna, use the shorter screw. If other strings go flat when you engage it with the bridge stopped, increase spring tension slightly (claw further out from the block).

steps.title: Drop tuner key: measure the peghole and check layout
steps.detail: Measure the low-E peghole and note whether the guitar has vintage press-fit holes or modern 10 mm-type holes, and which side of the headstock the tuner sits. Buy the version made for that hole (or use the maker's bushing/adaptor). See [bt-replace-tuners] for hole sizes.

steps.title: Drop tuner key: remove the old low-E tuner
steps.detail: Slacken and remove the string, then remove the tuner and its bushing (press-fit bushings come out with a press, not pliers).

steps.title: Drop tuner key: fit the drop tuner
steps.detail: Install it like any tuner: align with its neighbours, mark and pilot-drill any new screw hole with a depth stop, then tighten bushing and screw snug.

steps.title: Drop tuner key: set the upper pitch
steps.detail: String up, lever in the upper position, and tune to E with the tuner knob as normal.

steps.title: Drop tuner key: set the lower pitch
steps.detail: Flip the lever to the lower position and adjust the lower-stop screw until the string reads D (or your target). Flip back and forth, stretching the string, and repeat until both stops are accurate.

steps.title: Drop tuner key: trem guitars
steps.detail: On a floating trem, dropping one string pulls the others sharp. Deck or block the trem first (see [bt-deck-or-block-trem]).

models.model: Original Floyd Rose and licensed units with the long locking screw
models.note: D-Tuna fits these.

models.model: Low-profile Floyds (e.g. Floyd 1000 Pro / low-profile) and Ibanez Lo-Pro Edge
models.note: The D-Tuna listing says it won't work with low-profile Floyd Rose units; other low-profile bridges may work depending on cavity depth and may need minor routing.

warnings: Without stabilising the bridge, the D-Tuna will throw the other strings out of tune - the maker says so explicitly.

title: Fit strap locks (including flush-mount)
summary: Replace strap buttons with locking ones so the strap can't slip off. Button-type locks use the existing screw hole; flush-mount systems need a larger hole drilled for a receiver — measure carefully and follow the maker's sizes.
tools: Drill with brad-point or Forstner bit (flush-mount only), tape depth stop
parts: Strap lock set (button and strap-side halves)
Wood glue/hardwood dowel if the existing hole is worn

steps.title: Choose the type
steps.detail: Button-type locks (e.g. Schaller-type, Dunlop button-type) replace your strap buttons and usually use the same screw hole. Flush-mount systems put a receiver into the body so nothing sticks out; they need a larger hole.

steps.title: Check the existing holes
steps.detail: Remove the old buttons. If a screw was loose, repair the hole first with a glued dowel (md-stripped-screw-holes) — a strap lock is only as secure as its screw.

steps.title: Button-type install
steps.detail: Fit the felt washer if supplied, drive the new screw into the existing hole until the button is firm (wax the threads), and stop — don't keep turning once it's tight. Assemble the strap-side parts on the strap, with the strap's hole tight around the lock body.

steps.title: Flush-mount install
steps.detail: Measure the receiver with calipers and use the drill size and depth given in the maker's instructions. Mark the center with an awl, put a tape flag at the depth, and drill straight with a sharp brad-point or Forstner bit; on finished guitars, score around the hole first to stop chipping. Install the receiver as instructed and test the lock repeatedly.
steps.warn: Drill dead straight and only as deep as specified — the end of a neck heel or a thin horn has little wood to spare.

steps.title: Test
steps.detail: Lock and unlock several times and tug firmly. Check the lock screws periodically — they can work loose.

models.note: The end pin is a tapered peg in a tapered hole; strap lock end pins and endpin jacks need the right adapters. A heel button on an acoustic should be placed and drilled by someone experienced.
The upper button location differs (back of the neck heel on Les Pauls, top horn on SGs) — keep it where it is for balance.

warnings: A loose lock is worse than no lock — check the screws regularly.
pro: Flush-mount systems on acoustic guitars or valuable instruments.

title: Install a Hipshot bass Xtender (drop-D key)
summary: A Hipshot Xtender replaces your E-string tuner with one that has a lever: flip it and the E drops to D (or further) instantly, flip back for E. This guide covers picking the right model, swapping it in, and setting both pitches.
tools: Screwdrivers to fit the old and new mount screws
Wrench or socket for the bushing nut (if your tuners use one)
Hex key supplied with the Xtender
Drill with 1/16 in or 5/64 in bit (only if a new screw hole is needed)
parts: Hipshot Xtender matched to your bass (mounting hardware is included)

specs.label: Standard drop
specs.value: Major 2nd (E to D); up to a 4th (E to B) with normal-core strings

specs.label: Core needed to drop E to B (Hipshot)
specs.value: At least .022 in core diameter; possible with standard .105 strings

specs.label: Headstock hole, BT7
specs.value: 18 mm

specs.label: Pilot hole for #3 wood screw (Hipshot guitar tuner FAQ)
specs.value: 5/64 in bit in hardwood, 1/16 in in softwood

steps.title: Identify your tuner and pick the model
steps.detail: Look at the back of the E-string tuner. Trapezoid-shaped Schaller BMFL (1967-82 Fenders and many reissues): BT2. Kluson reverse-wind (pre-CBS Fenders and reissues): BT3. Fender 'Highway One' tuner with a D-shaped body (American Special, American Player, many MIM, Squier VM): BT7. Schaller BM on Music Man and G&L: BT1 (short key for most Music Man). Gotoh GB10/GB1 (Fender Aerodyne): BT10. Warwick: GB7. Thunderbird: GB7 (Gotoh-style tuners) or 3/8 in Ultralite (mini clover / Y key). If unsure, Hipshot suggests printing its 1:1 dimension drawing and laying it over your headstock, or emailing them photos of the front and back.

steps.title: Remove the E string and old tuner
steps.detail: Detune and remove the E string. Unscrew the tuner's mount screw(s) and, if fitted, the bushing nut on the face of the headstock. Lift the tuner out. Keep the old parts for resale or restoration.

steps.title: Check the hole
steps.detail: Make sure the post hole is clean - one buyer found a lump of finish resin inside that stopped the post turning freely and had to sand it out.

steps.title: Fit the Xtender
steps.detail: Drop it in, align it parallel with the other tuners, and fit the supplied bushing/nut and mount screw. If the screw holes line up, you are done drilling.

steps.title: Only if needed: drill a new screw hole
steps.detail: Mark the new hole through the tuner's screw hole, wrap tape on the bit as a depth flag, and drill straight. Hipshot's guitar-tuner FAQ gives 5/64 in for hardwood and 1/16 in for softwood for its #3 screws - check the screw supplied with your Xtender matches before drilling.
steps.warn: New holes on a vintage bass reduce its value; consider a model that is a direct fit.

steps.title: Restring and tune the upper pitch
steps.detail: Fit the E string (see [bs-string-change]), lever in the up position, and tune to E with the key as normal.

steps.title: Set the lower pitch
steps.detail: Flip the lever down. Using the supplied hex key, turn the drop-adjustment screw shown on Hipshot's instruction sheet until the open string reads D on your tuner. Flip up and down several times and fine-tune both: the key sets E, the screw sets D.

steps.title: Stretch and repeat
steps.detail: New strings stretch, which moves both pitches. Recheck over the first few days. A DoubleStop lever adds a third position between the high and low settings.

steps.title: Accept a small intonation compromise
steps.detail: The bass is intonated for E; dropped notes may be a few cents off up the neck. One buyer noted it took practice to get E and D both right.

models.note: BT2 (replaces Schaller BMFL).
BT3 (replaces Kluson reverse-wind); one buyer fitted it to a Vintera '60s Jazz with no drilling.

models.model: Fender American Special / American Player / Squier VM
models.note: BT7 (Highway One replacement, 18 mm holes); one buyer on a cheap bass had to drill one screw hole.
BT1 (Schaller BM replacement); Bongo needs BT13.
GB7 is a direct fit but usually cannot drop a full step because the lever hits the next tuner, unless the tuners are remounted.
GB7 or 3/8 in Ultralite Xtender depending on key style.
3/8 in Ultralite Xtender or GB7.

warnings: Detune before removing the string.
Drilling a vintage headstock lowers its value.
pro: If your headstock needs holes plugged and redrilled, or the bass is vintage, have a tech fit it.

title: Install and string locking tuners
summary: Locking tuners clamp the string inside the post so you need less than one wrap, which speeds string changes and removes winding slip - a common upgrade for trem guitars.
tools: Drill with pilot bits and depth stop (if new screw/pin holes)
parts: Locking tuners matched to your peghole size and layout (staggered posts can remove the need for string trees)

specs.label: StewMac wraps target
specs.value: 1 wrap or less; about 1/4 to 1/2 wrap on thumbwheel models

specs.label: Clamp tightness
specs.value: Snug plus a final 1/8 turn on thumbwheels/caps - don't overtighten

specs.label: Slack before clamping
specs.value: No more than about 1.5 in

steps.title: Fit the tuners
steps.detail: Follow [bt-replace-tuners] for hole size and alignment. Dan Erlewine's Squier upgrade used Gotoh Magnum Lock-Trads, which covered the old screw holes; he aligned them with a shop rule, piloted then drilled for the screw thread with tape as a depth stop, and tightened with a #00 Phillips.

steps.title: Thumbwheel type (Sperzel/Schaller style, Hipshot Grip-Lock, Gotoh Magnum Lock-Trad)
steps.detail: Turn the rear thumbwheel anticlockwise to open. Point the post hole toward the nut, feed the string through and pull it taut, then hold it taut and turn the thumbwheel clockwise until snug plus about 1/8 turn.

steps.title: Top-cap type (PRS style)
steps.detail: Unscrew the cap a few turns, align the hole toward the nut, pull taut and finger-tighten the cap just enough to bite the string core.

steps.title: Auto-lock type (Gotoh Magnum Lock Auto-Lock)
steps.detail: Pull the string hand-tight with no slack and simply tune up; an internal cam grips as tension builds. To release, push the string slightly into the post to free the cam.

steps.title: Tune and stretch
steps.detail: Tune up, stretch each string 3–4 times, retune over 2–3 rounds. You should end with well under one wrap.

steps.title: Trim
steps.detail: Cut excess close to the post with flush cutters, angled so the sharp end points away from the headstock finish.

models.model: Fender American Deluxe / Elite and modern Fender locking sets
models.note: Dual guide pins, 10 mm holes, 18:1, staggered posts (taller for wound strings).
StewMac's Squier mod: Gotoh Magnum Lock-Trad staggered tuners; seven new holes drilled; old holes hidden.
On 3+3 the treble-side posts often loosen clockwise and bass-side anticlockwise (StewMac).

title: Nashville (high-strung) tuning setup
summary: Replace the four wound strings with lighter strings an octave higher so normal chord shapes give a bright, chiming '12-string top half' sound. Mostly a restring, but the thin strings sit loosely in wide nut slots.
tools: Nut files (if cutting a dedicated nut)
parts: Nashville/high-strung string set, or the octave strings from a 12-string set
Optional second nut cut for high-strung gauges

specs.label: Strings replaced
specs.value: 6th, 5th, 4th and 3rd (the normally wound strings) — tuned an octave above standard

specs.label: Strings kept
specs.value: 2nd and 1st stay as normal

steps.title: Get the strings
steps.detail: Buy a set packaged for Nashville tuning or use the thinner octave strings from the four lower courses of a 12-string set, plus normal 1st and 2nd strings.

steps.title: Restring and tune
steps.detail: Tune E, A, D and G an octave above normal; B and E stay where they are. Chord shapes don't change.

steps.title: Check the nut
steps.detail: The much thinner strings may wander or rattle in slots cut for wound strings. If they do, the clean fix is a second nut cut for these gauges, swapped in when you use this guitar for high-strung (keep the original for standard stringing).

steps.title: Adjust the neck
steps.detail: Total string tension drops a lot, so the neck will pull back toward straight or back-bow. Loosen the truss rod a little at a time until relief is back where you like it.

steps.title: Intonate
steps.detail: Thin plain strings need less compensation than the wound strings they replace — re-intonate on an electric. On an acoustic with a fixed saddle, check the 12th-fret octaves; a compensated saddle for the set may help.

models.note: The classic recording use — a cheap second acoustic dedicated to high-strung is common.
Works too; adjustable saddles make intonation easy.

warnings: Thin high-tuned strings break easily — tune up slowly and check you're in the right octave.

sources.title: Wikipedia — Nashville tuning (high strung)
StewMac — 5 things your guitar nut must get right

title: Set up a guitar for slide (raised action / nut extender)
summary: Raise string height so a slide doesn't clatter on the frets. For occasional slide, raise the saddles and go up a string gauge; for lap-style playing, a nut extender (raiser) lifts the strings high above the frets without permanent changes.
tools: For acoustics: saddle shims or a taller saddle blank

steps.title: Decide how you'll play
steps.detail: Bottleneck slide mixed with normal fretting needs only a moderate action increase. Dedicated slide or lap-style playing needs the strings well clear of the frets everywhere.

steps.title: Go heavier on strings
steps.detail: Heavier strings resist being pushed down onto the frets by the slide and sound fuller. Many slide players also use open tunings (open G, open D, open E).

steps.title: Raise the action
steps.detail: Electric: raise the saddles evenly (keep the radius) until the slide no longer clicks on frets when you play with light pressure. Acoustic: shim the saddle or make a taller one. Re-check intonation if you'll still fret notes.

steps.title: Lap style: fit a nut extender
steps.detail: A nut extender slips over the existing nut and lifts the strings far above the frets, turning the guitar into a lap-style slide instrument. It holds by string tension — no glue — so it removes cleanly. Raise the saddle end to match so the strings run parallel to the board.

steps.title: Check pickups
steps.detail: Raised strings sit farther from the pickups; raise pickups to rebalance output.

models.note: Classic slide instruments; many already have high action. Square-neck resonators are made for lap playing.
Moderate action raise plus heavier strings is usual for bottleneck players.

warnings: Raising action a lot on a fretted acoustic increases load on the bridge — don't exceed what the saddle and bridge can support.

sources.title: StewMac — Guitar strings guide (heavier strings for slide)

title: Soundhole pickups and battery/jack options
summary: A magnetic soundhole pickup clamps across the soundhole and needs no drilling. It only works with steel strings. You can run its cable out the soundhole or fit an endpin jack, and combine it with an undersaddle system.
parts: Optional endpin jack (stereo for dual systems)

specs.label: Strings
specs.value: Magnetic pickups need steel (ferrous) strings - they will not work with nylon (Fishman)

specs.label: Single coil vs humbucking
specs.value: Single coil: brighter but more hum; humbucking: much quieter, slightly less articulation (Fishman)

specs.label: Dual system wiring (Fishman)
specs.value: Soundhole pickup signal to the stereo jack's ring, ground to sleeve; for an active pickup sharing the preamp's 9 V battery, jumper its battery terminals and connect its battery lead to the jack's switch lug

steps.title: Choose
steps.detail: Passive pickups (e.g. Fishman Neo-D) need no battery. Active ones (e.g. Rare Earth) carry a battery. Humbucking types reject 60-cycle hum.

steps.title: Fit
steps.detail: Unscrew or open the wings/clamp, slide the pickup into the soundhole under the strings with the poles under the strings, and tighten evenly. Pad the clamps so they do not mark the soundhole edge.

steps.title: Route the cable
steps.detail: Quick option: run the cable out of the soundhole and tape it to the pickguard. Permanent option: fit an endpin jack ([ac-endpin-jack]).

steps.title: Find the quiet spot
steps.detail: Single-coil pickups pick up hum; StewMac's tech found a 'sweet spot' by rotating/positioning the guitar relative to the amp and lights.

steps.title: Balance the strings
steps.detail: If the pickup has adjustable pole pieces or height, set them so all strings sound even when picked equally.

steps.title: Combine with an undersaddle
steps.detail: Use a stereo jack and follow Fishman's wiring (ring = soundhole pickup) to blend in an external stereo preamp or a dual-channel system.

models.note: Not usable - choose an undersaddle or contact pickup instead.

title: Strap buttons, strap locks and stripped strap-button holes
time: 20 min (locks); overnight if repairing a hole
summary: Fit strap locks (Schaller S-Lock, Dunlop Straplok and others), add a strap button, and permanently fix a strap-button screw that has stripped out and keeps pulling loose.
symptoms: Strap button wobbles or the screw spins
Guitar has fallen off the strap
Strap slips off the button
tools: Screwdriver to fit the button screw
Drill and 7/64 in bit (StewMac buttons) with depth stop
3/16 in drill bit and plug cutter (or 3/16 in hardwood dowel)
parts: Strap lock set (buttons plus strap-end locks)

specs.label: StewMac/Gotoh strap button
specs.value: 0.550 in (14 mm) dia, 0.355 in (9 mm) high; 7/64 in pilot hole

specs.label: StewMac screw rescue plug
specs.value: 3/16 in hole and 3/16 in plug, water-based glue

specs.label: Schaller S-Lock buttons
specs.value: One-piece button and screw with slightly enlarged thread for oversized holes; 3 mm hex

specs.label: Dunlop Straplok
specs.value: Case-hardened, 4-ball lock, recessed plunger

steps.title: Fit strap locks
steps.detail: Remove the old buttons. Fit the new lock buttons in the same holes with a felt washer underneath to protect the finish. Schaller's one-piece S-Lock buttons drive in with a 3 mm hex and their slightly fatter thread bites into worn holes. Then fit the lock parts to the strap: pass the threaded part through the strap hole and tighten its nut or collar (the S-Lock collar has a set screw to keep it from loosening). Check each lock clicks on firmly and releases only with its release action.

steps.title: Add a new strap button
steps.detail: Mark the spot (on a Strat-style body the heel or upper horn; on acoustics StewMac discusses heel and side positions and says to check inside for neck bolts first). Drill a pilot with the size recommended for your button (StewMac: 7/64 in for its buttons) and a depth stop. Use a felt washer where the flat button meets a curved surface.

steps.title: Fix a stripped hole - permanent method
steps.detail: Drill the worn hole out to 3/16 in, square to the surface. Cut or buy a 3/16 in hardwood plug, put water-based glue (Titebond or hide glue) on it and tap it in; moisture swells it for a tight fit. Let it dry, trim flush with a sharp chisel (trim when dry - if trimmed wet it shrinks below the surface). Then drill a new pilot hole in the centre and refit the button.

steps.title: Quick fix
steps.detail: Many players pack a lightly stripped hole with wood glue and a couple of wooden toothpicks or matchsticks, let it dry, trim flush and redrill the pilot. It works, but a proper hardwood plug is stronger for a heavy guitar.

steps.title: Test
steps.detail: Hang the guitar on the strap and pull firmly at the button before you trust it on stage.

models.note: The SG's upper button sits near the neck heel rather than on a horn. Gibson-style buttons differ from Fender's; StewMac sells Gotoh buttons for Gibson separately.
StewMac notes you can mount a button on the neck plate.

warnings: Don't drill into a neck bolt or truss rod area on acoustics - check inside first.
StewMac notes super glue also works for plugs but may leave a visible witness line; it prefers water-based glue (Titebond or hide glue), which swells the plug for a tight fit.

title: String trees, roller nuts and low-friction saddles
summary: Reduce the friction points that make trem guitars come back out of tune: adjust, smooth, add or replace string trees, consider roller or Tusq parts, and fit Graph Tech String Saver saddles.
symptoms: Strings ping when tuning or using the arm
Tuning returns sharp after dives
Weak open strings or buzz at the nut (too little break angle)
Strings break at the saddle
tools: Drill with No. 44 (Gotoh trees) or 5/64 in (roller trees) bit and depth stop
Wax or soap for screw threads
parts: Gotoh/Fender-style string trees with short and tall spacers
Roller string trees or Graph Tech TUSQ XL trees
StewMac Three String Tree (adds G-string angle using an existing hole)

specs.label: Gotoh string retainers
specs.value: 2 strings each; short spacer for E and B; No. 44 bit for pilot hole in hard maple

specs.label: Roller string retainers (StewMac)
specs.value: 5/64 in pilot bit

specs.label: Graph Tech String Saver saddles
specs.value: Strat/Tele, 2-3/16 in or 2-1/16 in spread versions; TUSQ polymer with PTFE

steps.title: Smooth what you have
steps.detail: Clean the underside of every tree with abrasive cord (StewMac does this even on new trees), check for rust or grooves, and add a touch of lubricant. Lubricate nut slots; Paul White (Sound On Sound) found most trem tuning problems come from the nut and trees, not the bridge.

steps.title: Get the height right
steps.detail: A tree should hold the string down just enough for a clean break over the nut. Too low and the string is pinched and binds; too high and the string buzzes or rings behind the nut. Change height with the spacer under the tree (Gotoh sets include short and tall; use the short one for E and B).

steps.title: Add a tree or angle another string
steps.detail: If the G or D string lacks break angle, you can add a second tree or swap to a Three String Tree, which reaches over the G using the existing hole and spacer (StewMac's Squier mod used one to reduce a steep D-string angle). Drill new holes with a pilot bit (No. 44 for Gotoh trees) and a depth stop; wax the screw threads so the delicate screw doesn't snap in hard maple.

steps.title: Low-friction alternatives
steps.detail: Roller trees and Graph Tech TUSQ XL trees reduce friction; staggered-height or locking tuners can let you remove trees altogether (Sperzel staggered, Hipshot Grip-Lock staggered). A low-friction (TUSQ) nut, or a roller nut such as Fender's LSR on American Deluxe Strats, lets strings slide when you use the arm.

steps.title: Low-friction saddles
steps.detail: Graph Tech String Saver saddles replace Strat/Tele saddles; Graph Tech says they reduce breakage at the saddle and stay slippery. Measure your saddle spacing (2-3/16 or 2-1/16 in sets) before ordering. Fit one saddle at a time, keeping its position, then reset heights and intonation.
