title: Swap a pickguard (and make it fit)
summary: Replace a pickguard for looks or a new pickup layout (SSS to HSS), and deal with the usual fit problems: 11-hole vs 8-hole Strat patterns, USA vs import sizing, screw holes that don't line up, and smaller import pot holes.
tools: Phillips screwdriver; soldering iron (to move electronics)
Drill with small bits (5/64 in pilot) and a countersink
Step drill or 3/8 in bit / tapered reamer (to open pot holes)
File, scraper or sanding block for trimming
parts: Replacement pickguard in the right hole pattern and pickup layout
Shielding foil if the new guard isn't shielded
Hardwood dowel and glue for plugging old holes (md-stripped-screw-holes)

specs.label: Modern Strat pattern (Fender)
specs.value: 11 screws, including one near the middle pickup

specs.label: Vintage Strat pattern
specs.value: 8 screws

specs.label: Fender 11-hole modern guard fits (Fender listing)
specs.value: American Series/Standard/Deluxe/Special, Highway 1; Mexican Standard, Deluxe, Road Worn, Blacktop, '70s; Squier Standard Series 2004–on; China Modern Player

specs.label: Typical guard thickness (Allparts)
specs.value: 3-ply 0.090 in; 4-ply pearloid/tortoise 0.100 in; 1-ply 0.080 in

specs.label: Pot hole: import vs CTS (StewMac)
specs.value: Imports often 5/16 in; CTS/USA-size pots need 3/8 in

specs.label: Pickguard screw pilot (Premier Guitar)
specs.value: 5/64 in, about 3/8 in deep

steps.title: Identify your pattern and layout
steps.detail: Count the screws and note their positions, the pickup layout (SSS, HSS, HH) and the control positions. Check what the body is routed for under the old guard (see md-route-humbucker-hss). Buy a guard listed for your exact model — even 'Strat' guards differ between USA, Mexican, Japanese and Squier models, and Allparts warns its USA-spec 11-hole guard won't fit Squiers.

steps.title: Test-fit before moving any parts
steps.detail: Lay the new guard over the old one (or on the body with the neck on) and check: neck pocket edge fit, pickup cutouts over the routs, control holes over the cavity, and how many screw holes line up. Small misalignments of one or two holes are common.

steps.title: Transfer the electronics
steps.detail: Unsolder or transfer the pickups, switch and pots. On an unshielded guard, add shielding foil on the back and connect it to ground. If you're moving from import to CTS-size pots or the new guard has smaller holes, open the holes to 3/8 in with a step bit or reamer from the top side so the plastic doesn't chip.

steps.title: Deal with holes that don't line up
steps.detail: Where a new hole sits close to an old one, plug the old hole in the body with a glued hardwood dowel, trim flush, then drill a fresh pilot through the new guard hole. Never force a screw at an angle into a half-overlapping old hole — it will pull the guard sideways and crack it.

steps.title: Drill new holes neatly
steps.detail: Clamp or tape the guard in position with the neck fitted. Mark through each hole with an awl, drill 5/64 in pilots about 3/8 in deep, and if you drilled extra holes in the guard, countersink them so the screw heads sit flush.

steps.title: Trim if needed
steps.detail: If the guard binds at the neck pocket or a cavity edge, file or scrape the guard edge a little at a time; re-bevel the edge with a scraper held at a slight angle.

steps.title: Assemble and check
steps.detail: Screw the guard down snug — not tight — test all pickup/switch positions, then string up and set pickup heights.

models.note: Modern models use the 11-hole pattern; vintage reissues use 8 holes. Fender lists its modern 11-hole SSS guard for American Standard-era, Highway 1 and Mexican Standard/Deluxe/Road Worn models.

Fender lists Squier Standard Series (2004–on) for its modern guard, but other Squier lines (Bullet, Affinity, Classic Vibe) vary in size, hole spots and neck pocket — buy a Squier-specific guard or expect to drill and trim.
Dimensions and screw positions often differ slightly from USA spec. Test-fit before buying multiples.
Tele guards also come in vintage and modern hole patterns — match your body.

warnings: Celluloid and tortoise-look guards are brittle when cold — warm the material slightly before drilling or trimming.
Over-tightened screws crack pickguards at the holes.
pro: Vintage guitars — don't drill original bodies; get a guard made to the original holes.

title: Swap or fit humbucker rings (carved vs flat tops)
summary: Choose the right humbucker mounting rings and make them sit flat on a carved (arched) top without cracking or warping. Ring height and taper set how high the pickup can go.
tools: Felt or soft cloth to protect the top
parts: Humbucker mounting rings (neck and bridge height), curved-bottom or flat-bottom

specs.label: Ring shape
specs.value: Rings are tapered (taller at one end) so the pickup face follows the strings; neck and bridge rings differ in height

specs.label: Fitting to a curve (Erlewine)
specs.value: Sand on stick-on paper taped to the top: 80 grit, then 120

steps.title: Measure what you have
steps.detail: Measure the existing rings at both ends and note which is neck and which is bridge. New rings must match those heights (or be lower if your pickup is sitting too high even with the springs compressed, higher if it can't get close enough to the strings).

steps.title: Choose curved or flat bottom
steps.detail: Flat-top guitars (SG, many Explorers/Vs, flat-top superstrats) use flat-bottom rings. Carved tops (Les Paul, PRS-style, many archtops) need rings whose underside follows the arch — buy curved-bottom rings or fit flat ones by sanding. Screwing a flat ring down on a curve warps and wrinkles it, and can crack it.

steps.title: Mark the curve
steps.detail: Hold the ring in place with two screws so it can't twist, press lightly in the center, and run a pencil (half a pencil with tape under it works) around the top to scribe the gap onto the ring.

steps.title: Remove the bulk
steps.detail: Stick the ring to a flat board with double-stick tape. Nibble the plastic down toward the line with end nippers, then scrape and file smooth. Don't use a bandsaw — it tends to crack the plastic.

steps.title: Sand to fit on the guitar
steps.detail: Protect the top around the pickup with low-tack tape, stick sandpaper onto the tape (abrasive up), and rub the ring on it with short back-and-forth strokes until it sits flat: 80 grit then 120. A Les Paul top is flat in the middle and curved toward the edges (not a true radius), so sand in the direction the curve runs. Scrape the burr off the bottom edge.

steps.title: Install
steps.detail: Put felt on the top while you work. Fit the pickup into the ring with its springs and screws (StewMac makes small clips to hold the stack together), screw the ring down snug, then set pickup height.

models.model: Gibson Les Paul / Epiphone Les Paul
models.note: Carved top — rings need a curved underside. Epiphone ring heights vary by model and year; measure before ordering.
Flat top with a neck angle — flat-bottom tapered rings. StewMac trimmed a too-tall Flying V ring by about 3/32 in.
Carved tops on Custom/McCarty-type models; many PRS models mount pickups directly into the body without rings — check before buying.

warnings: Don't over-tighten ring screws on a carved top; the plastic will crack at the corners.
Protect the finish with tape and felt — scratches around pickups are very easy to make.

sources.title: StewMac — How to fit a Les Paul pickup ring to the curved top
StewMac — Tricks for installing humbuckers

title: Add a Bigsby to a guitar that doesn't have one
summary: Choose the right Bigsby for your body shape and fit it so it stays in tune. This is a planning guide — follow the Bigsby instructions for your model and the Bridges & Trems guides for the bridge and setup work.
tools: Drill with small pilot bits; masking tape
parts: Bigsby vibrato for your guitar type
Nut lubricant (graphite or a product such as Big Bends Nut Sauce)

specs.label: Pitch range (Bigsby)
specs.value: Designed for gentle bends of 'a couple of steps', not dive-bombs

steps.title: Pick the model
steps.detail: Bigsby makes different models for flat-top solid bodies, carved/arched tops and hollow archtops, and kits with matching bridges for some guitars. Check Bigsby's model pages and choose the one listed for your guitar shape — the mounting screws and tension bar height differ.

steps.title: Plan the bridge
steps.detail: A Bigsby moves the strings over the bridge, so a roller bridge or a well-lubricated saddle is strongly recommended. Some kits (e.g. B500) include a bridge. See the Bridges & Trems guides for bridge fitting.

steps.title: Position and drill
steps.detail: Center the unit on the body centerline, positioned per Bigsby's instructions for your model, tape it, mark the screw holes, and drill pilots straight with a depth stop. On a guitar with a stop tailpiece, Bigsby offers models and adapters that use the existing studs — check before drilling.

steps.title: String and set up
steps.detail: Restring following Bigsby's stringing guide, lubricate every nut slot, and fit locking tuners if tuning stability is a problem. Check for burrs: pings, creaks or sudden pitch jumps while tuning mean something is catching.

models.note: Use the flat-top model and a compatible Tele bridge; many players also fit a roller or compensated saddles.
Use the carved-top model; some versions mount on the existing stop-tailpiece studs.
Use the archtop models that anchor at the end of the body.

warnings: Drilling a vintage guitar for a Bigsby lowers its value; stud-mount options avoid new holes.
pro: If you need to relocate a bridge or plug old holes, or on a carved-top or valuable guitar.

sources.title: Bigsby — Install instructions
Bigsby — Setup tips
Bigsby — Home / model range

title: Add a switch or pot (drilling and hole sizes)
summary: Drill a clean hole in a pickguard, control plate or top to add a mini toggle, a push-pull or an extra pot — including opening up small import pot holes for full-size CTS pots and checking that the parts will fit in the cavity.
tools: Drill (drill press for pickguards/plates), sharp brad-point bits or a step drill
Tapered peghole reamer (for finished solid tops)
Calipers; bent string as a depth probe
Center punch or awl; masking tape
Deep socket/nut driver for pot and switch nuts
parts: Pot (CTS-type 3/8 in bushing, or a metric import pot) or push-pull pot

specs.label: Full-size (CTS) pot hole (StewMac)
specs.value: 3/8 in

specs.label: Typical import pot hole (StewMac)
specs.value: 5/16 in — too small for CTS pots

specs.label: Pot shafts and knobs (StewMac)
specs.value: CTS 1/4 in shaft, 24 splines; imported pots often 6 mm or 18-spline — knobs aren't interchangeable

specs.label: Mini toggle switch
specs.value: 1/4 in threaded bushing (1/4-40) — drill 1/4 in

specs.label: Pot values (StewMac)
specs.value: 250k for single coils; 500k for humbuckers and P-90s; 1M for Jazzmaster-type pickups; 25k for active electronics

steps.title: Plan the location
steps.detail: Choose a spot that is over the control cavity (with room for the part's body and lugs below), that won't be hit by your picking hand, strap or other knobs, and that keeps clear of cavity edges and screw holes. Check from inside the cavity with a ruler. On a carved top, measure the wood thickness at the spot by hooking a bent string or wire through the cavity.

steps.title: Check depth and bushing length
steps.detail: A standard CTS pot fits tops up to about 1/4 in thick (StewMac's example). Thicker tops need a long-bushing pot. Push-pull pots are taller than normal pots — check the cavity depth below the top.

steps.title: Mark and protect
steps.detail: Put masking tape over the spot, mark the center, and center-punch so the bit can't wander.

steps.title: Drill a plastic guard or metal plate
steps.detail: Use a drill press if you can: pilot first, then step up to final size (3/8 in for CTS pots, 1/4 in for mini toggles). A step bit gives the cleanest hole in plastic. Back the guard with scrap wood and don't force it — bits can suddenly grab plastic.

steps.title: Drill a finished solid top
steps.detail: Don't use a big twist bit straight into a finished top — it can chip the wood and finish. Drill a small pilot, then open the hole with a tapered reamer turned by hand from the top, marking the reamer at the 3/8 in point (set with calipers) and stopping there.
steps.warn: Keep away from carved-top binding and the edges of the cavity; wood near the edge can split.

steps.title: Anti-rotation tab
steps.detail: Most pots and some switches have a small tab beside the bushing. Either snip it off or drill a small blind hole for it so the part can't turn.

steps.title: Mount and wire
steps.detail: Fit the part from inside with its washer and nut, tighten the nut with a deep socket (not pliers), and wire it in using the wiring guides. Push knobs on while supporting the back of the pot with your thumb — don't pry them off with a screwdriver against the finish.

models.note: Easiest: drill the pickguard off the guitar on a drill press. Squier/import guards often have 5/16 in pot holes — open to 3/8 in for CTS pots.
Top thickness varies over the carve; check the bushing length you'll need. Use a reamer, not a drill press, on the finished top.
Metal plates need sharp bits, cutting oil and a clamp; deburr the holes.

warnings: Plastic and metal can grab a drill bit and spin — clamp the part.
Measure twice: an extra hole in a body can't be undone neatly.
pro: Drilling the top of a valuable or carved-top guitar.

title: Fit an endpin jack (reaming the endpin hole)
summary: Most acoustic pickups exit through a jack that replaces the strap endpin. The tapered endpin hole has to be opened to a clean cylinder of the jack's size - with a reamer, not a wood drill.
tools: Endpin jack reamer (StewMac: 5 deg taper to 1/4 in, then 15/32 in and 1/2 in sections, 3/8 in shank) or step-up metal-working drill bits
Diagonal cutters with a cork pad

specs.label: Common jack sizes
specs.value: 15/32 in or 1/2 in (12 mm) hole - measure your jack

specs.label: K&K
specs.value: Ream/drill to 1/2 in (12 mm); stepping up through at least 3/8 in (10 mm) then 1/2 in; use self-centring metal bits, not single-point wood bits

specs.label: Thread exposure (StewMac example)
specs.value: Adjust the inner nut so a little more than 1/4 in of thread shows outside before fitting the washer and outer nut

steps.title: Remove the endpin
steps.detail: Pull the old endpin - Frank Ford grips it with diagonal cutters over a cork pad to protect the finish, rocking it out of its tapered hole.

steps.title: Protect the finish
steps.detail: Tape the area around the hole generously with masking tape.

steps.title: Ream to size
steps.detail: Ream slowly by hand or with a slow drill, keeping the reamer straight in line with the guitar's centreline. Stop when the straight section reaches the size your jack needs (15/32 or 1/2 in). StewMac and Frank Ford both prefer a reamer because a drill can grab and chip the wood or finish.
steps.warn: Glued-in endpins are hard to remove cleanly - K&K recommends a pro for those.

steps.title: Pull the jack in
steps.detail: Push a pencil in through the hole from outside, catch the jack inside (with an arm through the soundhole) and draw it out through the hole.

steps.title: Set depth
steps.detail: Adjust the inside nut so the jack's shoulder sits just below the outside surface and enough thread shows for the washer, outer nut and strap cap. Trial fit a couple of times. Twist the jack a turn before final tightening if the cables need a slack loop off the top and back (K&K).

steps.title: Wire and tighten
steps.detail: If soldering: hot lead to the tip lug, ground to the sleeve lug, pre-tinned and covered with heat shrink. Tighten the outer nut, screw on the strap cap fully (grip it in its groove with padded pliers), and clip loose wires inside.

models.note: Frank Ford shows end-block cracks and oversize holes on old Martins; if the end block is cracked, fix it first.
Fill the 1/2 in hole with a glued dowel and redrill for a normal endpin, or fit an oversize endpin.

warnings: Solder fumes and hot iron: ventilate and protect the finish with towels.

title: Install a Bigsby vibrato
summary: Choose the right Bigsby for your body (flat top, carved top, thin or thick archtop, Tele), fit it with or without drilling (Vibramate), and pair it with a bridge that lets strings slide.
tools: 1/8 in hex key and 5/16 in socket for the B7 arm
Drill with depth-stop bits (if screwing to the top)
Masking tape, centre line and square
Stop tailpiece wrench (if removing a stopbar)

specs.label: Bigsby B5 (flat-face solidbody)
specs.value: Base 4-1/4 in x 3-5/8 in; rear screw spread 2-1/16 in; front screw spread 2-3/4 in; 4 top screws

specs.label: Bigsby B7 (thin archtops 1-1/2 to 2-1/4 in thick, carved-top solidbodies)
specs.value: Upper screw spread 1-5/16 in; lower 15/16 in; hinge centre to tension bar 7 in; 6 screws, 2 into the top

specs.label: Bigsby B70 (licensed, archtop/Les Paul)
specs.value: Bodies 1-1/2 to 2-1/4 in; plate extends 1-5/16 in past body end; mounting hole spacing 1-9/32 in; about 6-5/16 in plate to tension bar

specs.label: Vibramate V5 / V7-LP
specs.value: Uses existing stop-tailpiece bushings with 3-1/4 in (82.55 mm) non-staggered spacing - no drilling

specs.label: StewMac locking roller bridge
specs.value: 14 in saddle radius; M8 x 1.25 studs; 2 in string spread

steps.title: Pick the model
steps.detail: Flat-face solidbodies (SG, Les Paul Junior, Tele, Rickenbacker 325): B5, or the licensed B50. Carved tops like the Les Paul: B7 (or B70), ideally with a Vibramate V7-LP; StewMac notes a B5 can go on a carved top or 335 but sits slightly raised. Thin hollow/semi-hollow: B3 or licensed B30 (CE Distribution). Thin archtops: B7/B70; 335-size archtops: B7 with V7-335. Large hollowbodies: B6. Telecaster: B5 Tele kits, or the B16 which combines vibrato and bridge. Large-pickguard SG: B5 with the short-tail V5-ST.

steps.title: No-drill option
steps.detail: If your guitar has a stop tailpiece on standard 3-1/4 in bushings, a Vibramate bolts into those bushings and the Bigsby screws to the Vibramate. Install needs only a screwdriver and the felt pads protect the finish. The V7-LP does not fit the licensed B70.

steps.title: Position a screw-on unit
steps.detail: Without an adapter, align the Bigsby on the body centre line (string from nut through the middle of the bridge). Check that the strings will pass over the tension bar and onto the bridge without hitting pickups or the bridge back edge. Tape the outline and mark screw holes.

steps.title: Drill pilot holes
steps.detail: Use a bit sized to the screw's core with a depth stop so you can't drill too deep; drill square to the surface. On a B7 the end screws go into the tail block/end of the body and two go into the top.

steps.title: Fit the unit and arm
steps.detail: Screw on the frame, fit the spring and arm (B7 arm uses a 1/8 in hex and 5/16 in socket). Check the arm moves freely.

steps.title: Pair it with a sliding bridge
steps.detail: A Tune-o-matic with burred or cross-grooved saddles will make the strings hang up. StewMac recommends checking saddles for burrs; a roller bridge (StewMac's locking roller bridge: 14 in radius, M8 studs, slotted holes for overall intonation) lets the strings roll as the bar moves.

steps.title: String up and set up
steps.detail: See [bt-bigsby-stringing-setup].

models.note: B7 with Vibramate V7-LP or V7-335 avoids drilling a carved top. Gibson factory Bigsby models use B7-type units.
Gretsch is an original-equipment Bigsby user; large hollowbodies take the B6, thinner bodies B3/B7 depending on depth. Many Gretsch use a rocking bar bridge to cope with the movement.
B5 kits with a matching Tele bridge plate, the B16 vibrato/bridge, or Vibramate V5-TEV / V5-TEAS for no-drill fits.
Check whether stop-tail bushings are 3-1/4 in non-staggered before buying a Vibramate.
Not covered by the sources checked for this guide - confirm fit with Bigsby's chart.

warnings: Drilling a vintage guitar reduces its value; use a Vibramate if possible.
Measure body thickness before choosing a B7/B70: they are made for 1-1/2 to 2-1/4 in bodies.
pro: Have a tech drill a carved or arched top, a thin archtop, or any vintage instrument.

title: Install a K&K Pure Mini (bridge-plate contact pickups)
summary: The Pure Mini uses three small transducers glued to the bridge plate inside the guitar. It needs no battery and no saddle work - just accurate placement, full glue coverage, and a reamed endpin hole.
tools: K&K placement jig with pin and golf tee
Putty (supplied) to hold pickups on the jig
Endpin reamer or 3/8 in then 1/2 in metal-working bits

specs.label: Glue
specs.value: Gel CA covering the whole gold underside - hold 30 s, leave the jig 5-10 min. Peel-and-stick tape loses about 30% volume/tone (K&K)

specs.label: Overlap on tiny bridge plates
specs.value: Up to 1/16 in (1.5 mm) allowed on the cable side; none preferred

specs.label: Amp input
specs.value: Sounds best into about 500 kohm-1 Mohm (mixer line input or K&K preamp) rather than 5-10 Mohm acoustic-amp inputs

steps.title: Prepare the endpin
steps.detail: Ream the endpin hole to 1/2 in as in [ac-endpin-jack].

steps.title: Plan positions
steps.detail: Pin bridges: the high-E transducer goes directly under the high E string; the other two sit between G and D and between A and low E. They go on the bridge plate only - K&K says never anywhere else. Pinless bridges: drill tiny 1/16 in reference holes at each end of the saddle slot and use them as guides.

steps.title: Dry run
steps.detail: With strings off, push the white jig pin into the high-E pin hole and route the golf tee through the jig into the G hole. Hold a transducer on the jig with a small putty ball and rehearse reaching in through the soundhole; check with a mirror that it lands flat, parallel and in place.

steps.title: Glue each transducer
steps.detail: Coat the whole underside with gel CA (generously - too little glue is K&K's number one cause of poor or uneven sound), press into place, hold 30 seconds and leave the jig 5-10 minutes. Good coverage shows glue squeezed out around the entire edge.

steps.title: Route the cables
steps.detail: Slide the cable tube to about 1-2 in from the transducers, fit the jack, and twist it a turn or two before tightening so the cables loop clear of the top and back - no clips needed.

steps.title: Test
steps.detail: String up and play. Weird or hollow sound usually means a transducer is not fully bonded or is misplaced; K&K recommends reinstalling it.

models.note: A weak high E can come from the brace damping the plate near the high strings: keep the E-B transducer right under the string and close to that brace, use a heavier high E, or add a fourth transducer beyond the brace.
Small plates may force a slight transducer overlap (max 1/16 in).
Works without magnets, unlike soundhole pickups.

warnings: CA glue bonds skin instantly and gives off irritating fumes - gloves and ventilation.

sources.title: K&K Sound: Pure Mini installation booklet (PDF)

title: Install a Roland/BOSS GK hexaphonic (synth) pickup
time: 1–2 h (no-drill mount); longer for a permanent install
summary: Mount a GK-3/GK-5 divided pickup between the bridge and bridge pickup so each string feeds a guitar synth or modeler. Placement and string clearance are what make it track well.
tools: Screwdrivers; feeler gauges or a 1 mm reference
Capo (to fret at the last fret while measuring)
Drill and small bits only if screw-mounting
Cleaning wipes for the tape area
parts: GK pickup kit (divided pickup, controller/main unit, mounting parts: tape, spacers, springs, holder)

specs.label: Max distance from bridge (Roland GK-3 kit manual)
specs.value: 20 mm

specs.label: String-to-pickup gap (GK-3 kit manual)
specs.value: 1.0 mm for each string, measured with the string pressed at the highest fret

specs.label: String spacing range (GK-3 kit manual)
specs.value: 9.6–11.8 mm between strings

specs.label: Not compatible
specs.value: 12-string guitars, unusual string setups, nylon or non-metal strings

steps.title: Set the guitar up first
steps.detail: Do your normal setup (relief, action, intonation) before fitting the pickup — the GK gap depends on string height. Remove any battery from the guitar.

steps.title: Find the position
steps.detail: The divided pickup goes between the bridge and the bridge pickup, as close to the bridge as it fits — no more than 20 mm from it. Each string must pass over its own section of the pickup, with the cable end under the low E (6th) string. If there's no room, moving the bridge pickup can help — ask a tech first.

steps.title: Test-fit with tape
steps.detail: Fit the pickup and the controller with the supplied double-sided tape first to find the best spots. Roland notes the tape is for temporary positioning; shocks and long use can make it shift, and removing tape can pull off a poor finish.

steps.title: Set the height
steps.detail: Fret each string at the highest fret and adjust the pickup (spacers or spring-loaded screws) so there's a 1.0 mm gap between the string and the pickup. Tilt it so the gap is the same across all six strings.

steps.title: Mount permanently
steps.detail: Use the supplied spacers and tape, the holder, or screws with springs. Drilling a guitar is permanent — if you're unsure, have a Roland dealer or tech do it.

steps.title: Connect and calibrate
steps.detail: Use only the dedicated GK cable. Wrap the cable around the strap near the end pin to take strain off the jack. Run the string sensitivity calibration on your synth/modeler and fine-tune the height by string if one string tracks badly.

models.note: Usually enough room behind the bridge pickup; tape or spacer mount works well.
Space between the bridge and the bridge pickup is tight on many; check fit before buying.
Mount to the body, not the bridge; check the trem's movement can't hit the pickup.

warnings: Don't bend or twist the divided pickup, or strain its cable.
Tape adhesive may lift weak or old finishes when removed.
pro: Permanent screw mounting, moving a pickup to make room, or installing a GK connector board inside the guitar.

title: Make a custom pickguard from a blank
summary: Cut a new pickguard from sheet material or wood using a template, a flush-trim (bearing) bit and a bevel cutter — for a custom pickup layout, a new material, or a guard that isn't sold off the shelf.
tools: Template material at least 1/2 in thick (MDF, plywood or laminated old guards)
Router table (preferred) or trim router; flush-trim bearing bit; pickguard bevel cutter
Files, scraper, small sanding block, spindle sander (optional)
Super glue or epoxy (to harden template edges)
Safety glasses, dust mask, hearing protection
parts: Pickguard blank (plastic sheet, celluloid, or thin wood)

specs.label: Template thickness (StewMac)
specs.value: At least 1/2 in, so the bearing has enough to ride on

specs.label: Rough-cut oversize
specs.value: At least 1/16 in outside the line

specs.label: Common blank thickness (Allparts)
specs.value: 3-ply 0.090 in; 4-ply 0.100 in

steps.title: Make the template
steps.detail: Trace the old guard or draw the new shape on 1/2 in MDF/plywood (or, as Dan Erlewine does, glue three old plastic guards together so the stack is thick enough for a bearing). Cut and file the outline and cutouts perfectly smooth — the finished edge can only be as good as the template edge. Soak porous template edges with super glue or epoxy, then file and scrape smooth. Check it on the guitar, including the pickups and controls.

steps.title: Rough out the blank
steps.detail: Leave the protective film on the blank until the end. Trace the template, and cut at least 1/16 in outside the line with a bandsaw or coping saw. Drill out the inside of pickup and control cutouts with a Forstner bit to leave little for the router. Brittle celluloid/tortoise material should be warmed slightly before cutting — but only a little, as it shrinks with heat.

steps.title: Attach blank to template
steps.detail: Stick the blank on the template with double-stick tape, keeping the tape back from the edges so the bit doesn't gum up. Drill the screw holes through the template positions now so everything stays aligned.

steps.title: Trim the outline
steps.detail: On a router table with a flush-trim bit, start along a straight edge to get the feel. Feed the work against the bit's rotation, keep the bearing on the template, and at the end of each pass draw the piece away from the cutter. Never push a horn point straight into the cutter — work around to it slowly and firmly. With a handheld router, raise the template on scrap blocks so the bearing doesn't hit the bench, and support thin areas like horns so the base stays level.
steps.warn: Keep fingers well away from the bit, wear eye protection, and practice on scrap first.

steps.title: Cut the inside openings
steps.detail: With the outline done, rout the pickup and control openings with the bearing following the template. Small openings like a switch slot can be drilled at each end and joined with a small saw, then filed.

steps.title: Bevel the edge
steps.detail: Run a pickguard bevel cutter (it rides the same template) to expose the inner plies, or scrape a small bevel by hand with a razor blade held at a slight angle. Finish by hand-sanding or scraping smooth.

steps.title: Countersink and finish
steps.detail: Countersink the screw holes so screw heads sit flush. Add shielding foil to the back (connect it to ground), remove the protective film, and polish scratches out of clear or tortoise-look materials with plastic polish. Wood guards get a light oil or lacquer finish.

models.note: Easiest to copy from the existing guard; make the template from the original so screw holes line up.

Thin self-adhesive material can be cut with scissors from the back, sanded to the line, and laid on with a soapy-water mist so it can be positioned and squeegeed flat. Keep water away from the soundhole and label.

warnings: Router bits can grab thin plastic and fling it — clamp or tape securely.
Plastic dust and celluloid shavings are flammable; vacuum up as you go.

title: Replace or upgrade tuners
summary: Swap tuning machines without cracking the finish or drilling crooked holes: identify vintage press-fit (11/32 in) vs modern threaded-bushing (10 mm) holes, use conversion bushings or a reamer, and align and pilot-drill new screw holes.
tools: Tuner bushing press or homemade puller
Drill with depth-stop bits or tape flag
Tuner pin drill jig (for pin-located tuners)
parts: Hardwood plugs and glue for old holes (optional)

specs.label: Vintage (Kluson-type) peghole
specs.value: 1/4 in hole reamed to 11/32 in (8.8 mm) at the face for a press-fit bushing

specs.label: Sealed modern tuner peghole
specs.value: 3/8 in to 10 mm, drilled straight through (brand-dependent)

specs.label: Gotoh Magnum Lock / Hipshot Grip-Lock
specs.value: 10 mm (13/32 in) peghole

specs.label: Fender modern peghole
specs.value: 10.5 mm (StewMac conversion bushing listing)

specs.label: StewMac 3/8 in conversion bushing
specs.value: For 3/8 in or 10 mm holes, 1/4 in posts; not for 10.5 mm holes; counterbore with a 0.393 in reamer

specs.label: StewMac 10.5 mm conversion bushing
specs.value: Lets 1/4 in-post vintage tuners fit Fender's modern 10.5 mm holes

specs.label: Gear ratios (examples)
specs.value: Kluson Supreme 18:1; Gotoh Magnum Lock-Trad 16:1; Fender locking 18:1; Hipshot Grip-Lock 18:1

steps.title: Identify what you have
steps.detail: Vintage-style tuners use bushings pressed into the face and usually a screw beside each tuner on the back. Sealed modern tuners use a threaded hex bushing and washer on the face and one screw (or locating pins) at the back. Measure the hole with calipers.

steps.title: Choose compatible tuners
steps.detail: Same hole size and screw position is a drop-in. Going vintage to modern means reaming holes up to 10 mm or so. Going modern back to vintage needs conversion bushings so the vintage posts don't wobble. Even the same brand moves the screw tab position between models (StewMac found three Grover models with three tab positions), so expect new screw holes. Some tuners use pins instead of screws.

steps.title: Remove old bushings safely
steps.detail: Press-fit bushings should come out with a bushing press or puller pushing from behind, with a caul on the face, in quarter-turn steps; rushing chips the lacquer. StewMac advises leaving original bushings in place on vintage guitars if you can.

steps.title: Enlarge holes with a reamer, not a drill
steps.detail: A tapered peghole reamer keeps holes round and square. Mark the reamer at the right depth with a marker and stop when the mark meets the surface (StewMac's road-ready method). Clear any finish that rolls over the hole edges with a tiny grinding stone so the bushing seats.

steps.title: Align the tuners
steps.detail: Fit the tuners loosely and line them up with a straightedge (six-in-line) or so the buttons sit at matching angles (3+3). Mark the new screw holes with a sharp scribe.

steps.title: Drill pilot holes
steps.detail: Use a small pilot bit, then one sized for the screw's core, with a depth stop or tape flag so you can't go through the headstock. For pin-located tuners, a tuner pin drill jig keeps the holes perfectly placed; crooked pins mean crooked tuners.

steps.title: Install
steps.detail: Thread bushings by hand, then snug with a nut driver - don't crush the finish. Reuse original screws where they fit to avoid cross-threading. Tighten screws with a properly fitting #00 Phillips.

steps.title: Deal with the old holes
steps.detail: Leave them, fill them with the old screws, or plug them: drill slightly oversize, glue in a side-grain plug of matching wood with hide glue or Titebond, leave it just below the surface and drop-fill. New tuners like the Gotoh Magnum Lock often cover old holes anyway.

models.model: Fender vintage-style (American Vintage, Vintera, Classic Vibe)
models.note: Press-fit bushings in 11/32 in holes; Kluson-style replacements drop in.

models.model: Modern Fender (American Professional, Ultra, Player and some Squier)
models.note: Larger threaded-bushing holes; Fender's modern hole is 10.5 mm. Fender locking tuners for American Deluxe/Elite use dual guide pins and need 10 mm holes.
Vintage Kluson-style or Grover Rotomatic depending on model; Grover Rotomatics need larger holes than Klusons.
Usually modern sealed tuners with threaded bushings; check for pin-located models.

warnings: Modifying a vintage guitar reduces its value - choose exact-spec replacements.
Never oil tuners on the guitar; oil wicks into the wood and can strip screw holes (StewMac).
pro: Enlarging holes in a lacquered vintage headstock, or plugging and redrilling, is best done by a tech - chips around the hole are hard to repair invisibly.

title: Set up for heavy strings, drop tunings or 'baritone' strings
summary: Make a guitar play properly tuned down (Drop C, B standard, etc.) with heavier strings: nut slots, relief, intonation and trem spring balance all change. Also covers bass/guitar detuner levers. A true baritone needs a longer-scale neck, not just strings.
symptoms: New heavy strings sit on top of the nut or bind and ping when tuning
Floating trem tips forward or backward after changing strings
Intonation goes sharp after going to heavier gauges
tools: Nut files matching the new string gauges
Truss rod wrench; ruler for relief/action
Screwdriver for saddles and trem claw
parts: Heavier string set made for the tuning
New nut if old slots end up too wide later

specs.label: Nut slot width (StewMac)
specs.value: Slightly wider than the string; up to 0.004 in oversize is fine

specs.label: Nut slot depth (StewMac)
specs.value: Wound strings sit about half their diameter above the nut

specs.label: Example (StewMac)
specs.value: A .012–.060 set on a 24-3/4 in scale tuned to C standard restores normal tension

steps.title: Pick strings for the tuning
steps.detail: Lower tuning with the same strings makes them floppy. Go heavier so tension returns to near-normal; string makers publish tension charts and 'drop tuning' sets. Shorter scales need heavier gauges for the same tension.

steps.title: Widen the nut slots
steps.detail: Heavier strings jam in old slots (pinging, sticking, going sharp). Open each slot with a nut file matching the new gauge, keeping the slot angled down toward the headstock and not cutting deeper. Polish the slot and lubricate with graphite. See the Frets & Nut guides for slot work.
steps.warn: Only widen — cutting the slot deeper causes open-string buzz, and you can't undo it.

steps.title: Re-check relief
steps.detail: String tension changes, so the neck relief changes. Re-measure and adjust the truss rod per the setup guides.

steps.title: Rebalance the trem
steps.detail: On a floating trem, more (or less) string tension tips the bridge. Retune, then adjust the claw screws in the back cavity (or add a spring) until the bridge sits at your chosen angle, retuning as you go. Blocking or decking the trem is an option for heavy drop tunings.

steps.title: Intonate
steps.detail: Heavier strings generally need saddles moved back from the nut. Intonate each string at the 12th fret; if a saddle runs out of travel, reverse its spring or fit a longer screw/bridge with more travel.

steps.title: Pickups
steps.detail: Heavier strings put out more signal and pull harder magnetically — reset pickup heights.

steps.title: Want instant drop-D instead? Fit a detuner
steps.detail: A Hipshot Xtender (bass) or guitar Xtender replaces the low-string tuner with one that has a lever to drop that string to a preset note. Choose the model that matches your existing tuner's footprint (check Hipshot's fit list) so no drilling is needed, then set the lower stop to your target note.

models.note: Handles lower tunings well with modest gauge increases.
Needs heavier gauges for the same tension when tuned down.
Locking-nut clamping pads and fine tuners: check heavy strings still fit the saddle blocks; rebalance springs.
Detuners (Xtenders) are popular for instant drop D.

warnings: Detune before removing trem springs; spring tension can fling parts.
Large gauge jumps can need a new nut altogether.
pro: Re-cutting a nut for big gauge changes, or converting to a true baritone with a longer-scale replacement neck.

title: Swap active and passive pickups (what changes)
time: 1–3 h (plus routing if a battery box is needed)
summary: Going from passive pickups to active (EMG-type) or back means more than swapping pickups: pot values, the output jack and a battery all change. This is an overview of the hardware differences; the wiring itself is in the Wiring guides.
tools: Router or Forstner bit (only if adding a battery box)
parts: Pots: 25k for actives; 250k (single coils) or 500k (humbuckers) for passives
Stereo (TRS) jack for actives; mono jack for passives

specs.label: Pot values (StewMac)
specs.value: Active electronics 25k; single coils 250k; humbuckers/P-90s 500k; Jazzmaster-type 1M

specs.label: Active power
specs.value: 9V battery switched by a stereo jack (plugging in a mono cable turns it on)

steps.title: Passive to active
steps.detail: Fit the active pickups, replace the pots with the low-value (25k) pots supplied or specified by the maker, and fit a stereo jack — its ring contact switches the battery's negative so the battery only drains when a cable is plugged in. You need room for a 9V battery: in the control cavity (with a foam pad so it can't rattle) or in a dedicated battery box routed in the back.

steps.title: Active to passive
steps.detail: Fit passive pickups, change the pots to 250k/500k as appropriate (low-value active pots make passives sound dull), and you can go back to a mono jack. The battery cavity stays — a cover plate hides it.

steps.title: Mixing active and passive
steps.detail: Possible but needs care: the two have very different output levels and impedances. Follow the pickup maker's diagrams for mixed setups.

steps.title: Wire it
steps.detail: Follow the Wiring guides and the pickup maker's diagram (many actives use solderless connectors).

models.note: Check there's room for a battery before buying actives; a battery box may need routing.
Onboard preamps (e.g. 2- or 3-band EQ) are a separate system from active pickups — follow the preamp's instructions.

warnings: Unplug the cable when not playing an active guitar — the jack is the power switch.
Never leave a dead 9V battery in the cavity; leaking batteries corrode wiring.

title: Add piezo bridge saddles to an electric (Graph Tech Ghost)
summary: Replace your bridge saddles with piezo pickup saddles and add a preamp so the electric can also give an acoustic-type sound (and, with an extra module, MIDI). The saddles are drop-in; getting the wires into the cavity is the tricky part.
tools: Small drill and bits (if a wire channel is needed)
Router (only if the battery box or preamp needs a cavity)
parts: Graph Tech Ghost saddles for your bridge type (Strat, Tele, Tune-o-matic, Floyd Rose-style)
Stereo jack (for separate magnetic/piezo outputs), 9V battery box

steps.title: Buy the right saddles
steps.detail: Ghost saddles are made for specific bridges and string spacings; there are also complete Ghost-loaded bridges. Match your exact bridge model.

steps.title: Plan the wire path
steps.detail: Each saddle has a fine wire that has to reach the control cavity. On some guitars there's an existing route (trem cavity, bridge ground hole); others need a small hole or channel. Graph Tech notes some instruments need modification to pass the piezo wires and offers support for specific guitars.
steps.warn: Fine piezo wires break if pinched under the bridge plate or pulled tight — leave slack.

steps.title: Fit the saddles
steps.detail: Remove strings, swap saddles one at a time so you keep their order and rough height, and feed each wire through to the cavity.

steps.title: Install the preamp and battery
steps.detail: Mount the Acousti-Phonic board in the control cavity, with a battery box where it can be reached. Wire the magnetic pickups, the piezo output and the jack according to the Ghost manual (a stereo jack lets you send the two sounds to separate amps).

steps.title: Set up and balance
steps.detail: Restring, reset action and intonation, then balance string-to-string piezo output — uneven output usually means a saddle isn't seated or a wire is pinched.

models.note: Saddle sets swap straight in; wires usually follow the trem cavity or bridge ground path.
Wires come down through the bridge post area; check the post holes have room.
Ghost makes Floyd saddles; leave a loop of wire so the trem can move freely.

warnings: Unplug the cable when not playing to save the battery.
Piezo saddles can sound harsh until heights and the preamp EQ are balanced.
pro: If the guitar needs drilling or a new cavity for the preamp/battery, or for MIDI (Hexpander) installs.

title: Convert a right-handed guitar to left-handed
time: Half a day (electric); a day or more (acoustic)
summary: Restring a right-handed guitar upside-down for a left-handed player. It always needs a new nut and attention to saddle compensation; electrics also need the pickguard, string trees and controls considered. Some guitars convert well, some barely at all.
tools: Nut files and a nut blank (bone or synthetic)
Small hammer and block (to remove the old nut)
Screwdrivers; saddle height and intonation tools; tuner
Drill and small bits (string trees, strap button)
For acoustics: saddle-slot routing jig, hide glue, rosewood or matching filler
parts: Left-handed pickguard (if available) or a custom guard

specs.label: Nut slot width (StewMac)
specs.value: Just over the string gauge; up to 0.004 in oversize is acceptable

specs.label: Frank Ford acoustic example
specs.value: Original compensation was off by nearly 1/8 in after reversing — saddle slot filled and re-cut

specs.label: Side-dot fix (Frank Ford)
specs.value: 1/16 in holes with 1/16 in white plastic rod on the new top edge

steps.title: Decide if this guitar suits conversion
steps.detail: Symmetrical guitars convert best (Strat-style and other double-cut bodies, classical guitars). On single-cutaway guitars (Les Paul, Tele) the cutaway ends up on the bass side, so upper-fret access is lost. On steel-string acoustics the bracing and the angled saddle are built for right-handed stringing, so a converted acoustic is a compromise.

steps.title: Make a new nut
steps.detail: Reversing the old nut doesn't work: the slot widths and spacing are graded for each string. Remove the old nut, make or fit a new blank and cut slots with files matching the new string positions (bass strings go where the trebles were). Many classical guitars have slots wide enough to reverse-string without changes. See the Frets & Nut guides for nut slotting.

steps.title: Fix the saddle compensation
steps.detail: Electric: adjustable saddles usually have enough travel, but the saddle pattern reverses — on three-saddle Teles and Tune-o-matics you may need to turn saddles around or use compensated saddles. Acoustic: the saddle slot is angled for right-handed stringing; Frank Ford filled the old slot with a glued-in strip (hot hide glue), leveled it and cut a new slot at the reversed angle with a router jig, then fitted a new saddle.

steps.title: Pickguard and controls (electric)
steps.detail: Swap to a left-handed pickguard where one exists (Fender sells left-hand 11-hole Strat guards) or have a custom guard made. On a flipped Strat the controls and jack end up above the strings, and the bridge pickup's slant reverses — both change feel and tone; a lefty guard lets you remount pickups the right way.

steps.title: String trees and strap button
steps.detail: With the headstock flipped, the string order on the posts changes, so string trees may need to move to the new high-string positions for proper down-pressure behind the nut. Move the upper strap button if the balance is wrong, and plug the old hole.

steps.title: Side dots
steps.detail: The fret markers on the edge are now on the floor side. Add dots on the new top edge: Frank Ford drilled 1/16 in holes and glued in 1/16 in white plastic rod, trimmed flush and polished.

steps.title: Set up
steps.detail: Set relief, action and intonation from scratch, and check the truss rod access is still usable.

models.note: Popular conversions. The headstock ends up 'reverse'; check string pull past the nut to the tuners and move string trees as needed.
Not practical — the cutaway ends up on the bass side. Buy a left-handed guitar instead.
Frank Ford calls these almost trivial to convert — symmetrical bracing and a straight saddle.
Needs a new nut and a re-cut saddle slot; pickguard ends up on the wrong side.

warnings: Never just flip the old nut — strings will bind or rattle.
Unplugged pickguard holes look untidy; plan to plug and touch up.
pro: Acoustic saddle slot re-cutting and anything on a vintage instrument.

title: Install an undersaddle piezo pickup (Fishman Matrix, LR Baggs Element type)
summary: An undersaddle pickup is a thin strip under the saddle, wired to a preamp built into the endpin jack (and often a small soundhole control). Success depends on a flat slot, a flat-bottomed saddle that moves freely, a clean hole and tidy wiring.
tools: Drill and small bit matching or slightly larger than the pickup lead/strip
Endpin jack reamer (15/32 or 1/2 in) - see [ac-endpin-jack]
Soundhole clamp (to locate the drill exit)
Soldering iron (if the kit needs it), heat shrink
Two bath towels to protect the top
parts: Undersaddle pickup kit (strip, jack preamp, battery holder/bag, clips)
Bone saddle blank (if a new, taller saddle is wanted)

specs.label: Fishman Matrix element
specs.value: 2.650 in (67.3 mm) long, 2.500 in sensing area; cannot be cut. Slots over 3 in need a 2-piece saddle

specs.label: Fishman slot sizes
specs.value: Narrow for 3/32 in slots (Martin), wide for 1/8 in slots (Gibson). A narrow pickup works in a wide slot, not the reverse

specs.label: Endpin jack hole
specs.value: 15/32 in or 1/2 in depending on the jack (measure it)

specs.label: Saddle height loss
specs.value: Remove the pickup's thickness from the saddle bottom to keep the same action

steps.title: Check the guitar suits it
steps.detail: The saddle slot must be deep enough for the strip plus saddle (StewMac advises against installing in a bridge that has been shaved thin), the saddle slot must not run through the bridge ends (through-cut saddles need a new slot), and the slot bottom must be flat. A very wide heavily compensated saddle may work less well.

steps.title: Prepare the slot
steps.detail: Remove the saddle. Look along the slot bottom: it must be flat end to end with no ridges or debris. StewMac found tiny ridges caused dead strings; a pro will rout the slot flat.

steps.title: Drill the lead hole
steps.detail: Drill at the bass end of the saddle slot (some kits also want a shallow hole at the treble end to tuck the strip end). Use a bit equal to or slightly larger than the strip/lead. StewMac's tip: start the drill steep, then lower to a shallow angle once it bites, and have a soundhole clamp or mirror inside so you see where it will exit and miss the braces and bridge plate edge.
steps.warn: Wear eye protection; drill slowly so the bit does not wander or tear out the plate.

steps.title: Fit the jack
steps.detail: Ream the endpin hole and fit the jack preamp - see [ac-endpin-jack].

steps.title: Feed the strip
steps.detail: Push the strip lead down through the saddle-slot hole into the body and connect it to the jack preamp (plug-in or solder per the kit). Lay the strip flat in the slot, sensing face up as marked.

steps.title: Compensate the saddle height
steps.detail: Mark the strip thickness on the saddle bottom (Frank Ford uses dividers set off the pickup) and sand it off flat on a plate. Check the saddle bottom against a straightedge and strong light - no light should show. The saddle should drop in and lift out easily - not tight - so string pressure reaches the strip evenly.

steps.title: Mount the battery and controls
steps.detail: Place the battery bag/clip where it is easy to reach (often on the neck block or near the soundhole), sanding and sealing the spot first so adhesive holds (Dan Erlewine). Clip the wires with self-adhesive clips so nothing touches the top or back.

steps.title: String up and test
steps.detail: Tune up, plug in and pick each string at equal force. If strings are uneven, see [ac-piezo-string-balance].

models.note: 3/32 in saddle slot - use a 'narrow' strip.
1/8 in saddle slot - 'wide' strip.
Frank Ford routes a short new slot just long enough for the element and leaves the original saddle ends glued in to keep the bridge strong.
Works on nylon (unlike magnetic soundhole pickups).
Fishman makes split elements (1-3/4 in and 7/8 in).

warnings: Hot solder drips burn through lacquer - cover the top with two layers of towel when soldering at the jack (Frank Ford).
Solder fumes: ventilate.
pro: If the bridge is thin, the saddle is glued/through-cut, or the slot needs routing flat, have it installed by a tech.

title: Install or replace a Strat tremolo
time: 1–3 h (replacement); longer for a new body
summary: Swap a Strat-style trem for a better unit, or fit one to an undrilled body, with pivot holes in exactly the right place and the right parts for 6-screw vs 2-point.
parts: Replacement tremolo (match string spacing 2-3/16 in vintage or 2-1/16 in modern, mounting type and block size)

specs.label: Pivot location (StewMac)
specs.value: Pivot screw centres 25.25 in from the nut (for 25.5 in scale)

specs.label: Common Strat saddle spreads (Graph Tech sizes)

steps.title: Match the replacement
steps.detail: Check mounting type (6-screw or 2-point and stud spacing), string spacing, block height and cavity depth before buying. A 2-point bridge will not drop into a 6-screw body without redrilling, and vice versa.

steps.title: Remove the old unit safely
steps.detail: Slacken all strings, remove them, then unhook springs at the claw with a hook. Remove the pivot screws and lift the bridge out. Note the ground wire on the claw.

steps.title: Fitting to an undrilled body
steps.detail: Mark the centre line with tape and a centring rule. Measure 25.25 in from the nut to locate the pivot-screw centres. Centre a Strat trem template on the line with its front edge aligned with the trem cavity rout, hold it with double-stick tape, and drill all six holes with a drill press (or a thick drill guide if hand-held) so they are plumb. StewMac stresses you cannot eyeball it: grain can push the bit off line and a single misaligned hole spoils the bridge's pivot.

steps.title: Test-fit before going further
steps.detail: Drop the bridge in and check the screw holes line up with the plate holes and the block moves freely in the cavity without rubbing.

steps.title: Install and set up
steps.detail: Fit springs and claw, string up, then set it up per [bt-strat-vintage-trem] or [bt-strat-2point-trem].

warnings: Fitting studs for a 2-point means pressing anchors into the body; a misaligned or oversized hole is very hard to correct.
pro: Converting 6-screw to 2-point (or back), plugging old holes, or routing a cavity for a bigger block should be done by a luthier.

title: Rout a single-coil body for a humbucker (HSS conversion)
summary: Enlarge a single-coil pickup cavity so a full-size humbucker fits — the usual route to an HSS Strat — using a template, a palm router and a bearing-guided bit. Check first: many bodies are already routed for it, and single-coil-sized humbuckers need no routing at all.
tools: Palm or trim router (e.g. Bosch Colt) with plunge base if available
Humbucker routing template — body-rout version (StewMac templates are 3/8 in thick acrylic)
Top-bearing (pattern) router bits: 1/2 in for the main cut, 3/8 in for tight corners
Forstner bit and drill press or drill (optional, to remove waste)
Double-stick tape or rolled painter's tape; centerline ruler; pencil
Shims cut from template material (for shallow first passes)
Safety glasses, hearing protection, dust mask
parts: HSS pickguard (or a ring, on top-mounted guitars)
500k pots if the humbucker will be the main pickup (wiring guides)

specs.label: Standard pickup cavity depth (Warmoth)
specs.value: 3/4 in (19.05 mm) for humbucker and Strat single-coil routs

specs.label: Vintage Strat replacement bodies (Warmoth)
specs.value: 5/8 in (15.9 mm) pickup routs

specs.label: Humbucker screw/ear wells
specs.value: Deeper than the main rout; Premier Guitar went about 3/16 in deeper for the mounting-screw areas

specs.label: Router bit shank in collet (StewMac)
specs.value: At least 1/2 in, always

specs.label: Bridge humbucker starting height (Premier Guitar)
specs.value: About 3/32 in from the treble strings (fretted at the last fret), balance bass side by ear

steps.title: Check whether you need to rout at all
steps.detail: Take off the pickguard. Many Strats already have a large 'swimming pool' or HSS-ready rout that takes a full humbucker. If yours has only single-coil cavities, you can avoid routing by using a single-coil-sized humbucker (e.g. Seymour Duncan JB Jr.-type) in the existing hole. Otherwise, plan the rout and buy an HSS pickguard whose cutout matches your humbucker.

steps.title: Strip and protect
steps.detail: Remove strings, pickguard and electronics (photograph the wiring first). Remove the neck if it makes handling easier. Cover the finish around the work area with tape; score the finish along the rout edge with a sharp knife so the bit can't chip it.

steps.title: Position the template
steps.detail: Draw the body centerline. Line up the template's etched centerline with it and place the pickup where the guard's cutout will be (bridge humbuckers are usually angled slightly less than a Strat bridge single coil — follow your pickguard). Check the humbucker drops through the template opening without rubbing. Fix the template with double-stick or rolled painter's tape (strong adhesives can lift finish).

steps.title: Remove waste (optional)
steps.detail: Drill out most of the extra wood inside the outline with a Forstner bit, staying a little inside the line and short of final depth. Less wood for the router to remove means less chance of the bit grabbing.

steps.title: Rout in shallow passes
steps.detail: Set the bit so the bearing rides the template edge (shim the template up for the first shallow passes if needed). Hold the router flat, switch on with the bit clear of the wood, let it reach full speed, then lower into the existing cavity and move it so the cutting edge bites into the wood (not a climb cut). Take several shallow passes rather than one deep one. Once the cavity walls are deep enough for the bearing to ride on them, you can remove the template and keep going down using the walls as the guide.
steps.warn: Switch the router on and off only with the bit clear of the wood, and don't move it while it's speeding up or slowing down. Never let the bit touch the template's tape or screws. Practice on scrap first. Wear eye and ear protection.

steps.title: Go to depth, then cut the screw wells
steps.detail: Rout the main cavity to the same depth as the existing pickup routs (usually 3/4 in; 5/8 in on many vintage-style bodies). Then lower the bit about 3/16 in and cut only the areas under the humbucker's mounting ears/screws so the screws and springs have room. Use the 3/8 in bit only to clean up corners.

steps.title: Clean up and shield
steps.detail: Vacuum, ease any sharp edges, and seal the bare wood with a little lacquer if you like. If the guitar is shielded, extend the shielding paint or foil into the new area and make sure it connects to ground.

steps.title: Test-fit and wire
steps.detail: Mount the humbucker in the new pickguard and check it sits without forcing. Wire it in (see the wiring guides — humbuckers usually want 500k pots), set pickup heights and check the balance between pickups.

models.note: Body routs vary by model and year — many already take a humbucker under the guard. Always pull the pickguard and look before buying parts.
Often only single-coil routs, 5/8 in deep — expect to rout and possibly to deepen for a tall humbucker.
The bridge pickup sits in the bridge plate; a bridge humbucker usually means a humbucker-ready bridge plate as well as routing.
Premier Guitar's routing demo: a P-90 cavity enlarged for a humbucker in a ring, with the pickguard trimmed around the larger ring.

warnings: Routers are dangerous: two hands, eye and ear protection, dust mask, guitar clamped or held firmly.
A bit set too shallow cuts the template; set depth so the bearing always rides on it.
Routing reduces resale value on collectible guitars.
pro: If you've never used a router, or the guitar has value, have a luthier do the rout — it's quick on a bench with the right templates.

title: Convert a hardtail to string-through body
summary: Drill six string holes through the body and counterbore ferrules in the back so strings load from behind instead of through the bridge plate. Accuracy matters: holes must come out exactly in line, so this is drill-press and jig work — usually a pro job.
tools: Drill press with a long brad-point bit and a body support/backer
Transfer punch or bridge used as a template
Forstner bit sized to the ferrules
Arbor press or wooden block and mallet (to seat ferrules)
parts: String-through bridge (Tele-style or hardtail with through holes)
Six string ferrules (or a single string-through back plate)

steps.title: Check it's possible
steps.detail: You need a solid hardtail body area behind the bridge and a bridge with through holes. A Strat with a tremolo rout can't simply be converted — the cavity would need plugging and a new bridge fitted, which is a much bigger job.

steps.title: Mark the holes
steps.detail: Install and position the bridge exactly (scale length set), then mark each string hole through the bridge with a transfer punch. Draw a centerline and check the marks are symmetrical.

steps.title: Drill straight through
steps.detail: Use a drill press with the body flat and well supported, and a sharp brad-point bit. Wood grain can push a bit off line, and even one hole that drifts (StewMac notes this on Strat bridge holes) spoils the row on the back. Many luthiers drill from the front part-way and finish from the back using an alignment pin or jig.
steps.warn: Hand-drilling through a body almost always produces a crooked row of ferrules.

steps.title: Counterbore for ferrules
steps.detail: Measure your ferrules with calipers and use a Forstner bit of the matching diameter to counterbore each hole on the back, centered on the through hole, to the depth that seats the ferrule flush. A drilled strip of hardwood clamped on the back helps keep the row straight.

steps.title: Seat the ferrules
steps.detail: Press them in with an arbor press or tap them in with a hardwood block. They should be a snug press fit.

steps.title: String up and set up
steps.detail: String through the back, check strings sit cleanly in the saddles, then set action and intonation.

models.note: Top-loader bridges can be swapped to a string-through Tele bridge on a body that has the holes; adding the holes is the hard part.
Hardtail bridges with through holes exist; ferrules can be individual or a single back plate.

warnings: Misaligned ferrules can't be hidden — practice on a scrap block of the same thickness first.
Wear eye protection on the drill press.
pro: Recommended for most players: a luthier with a drilling jig will get a straight ferrule row first time.

sources.title: StewMac — How to install a Strat tremolo and get it right (drill press, grain drift)

title: Floyd Rose retrofit and locking nut install
summary: Fitting a double-locking Floyd Rose to a guitar that didn't have one means new routing, precisely placed pivot studs and a locking nut clamped behind the first fret. This outlines the job and the choices (full rout, recessed rout, surface-mount) — it's pro work on most guitars.
tools: Router, Floyd Rose routing templates (standard and recessed versions exist)
Drill press; Forstner bits; drill bits for stud bushings
Manufacturer routing spec sheet for your exact Floyd model
Files to fit the nut shelf; calipers; straightedge
parts: Floyd Rose tremolo (Original, 1000, Special, or FRX surface-mount)
Locking nut of the correct width and radius, with shims

specs.label: Routing specs
specs.value: Use the manufacturer's sheet for your model (StewMac hosts Floyd Rose parts diagrams and routing specs, inches and metric)

specs.label: FRX
specs.value: Surface-mount Floyd with its own bridge, stud and nut spec sheets

specs.label: Saddle radius options (Floyd Rose USA Original saddles)

steps.title: Choose the approach
steps.detail: Full retrofit (rout the body for the Floyd's base plate, sustain block and spring cavity; optionally a recess so the bridge can pull up). Surface-mount (FRX) for guitars where you don't want a big rout. A locking nut alone (no locking trem) is rarely worth it: it stops you tuning at the headstock, and without fine tuners at the bridge tuning becomes awkward.

steps.title: Locate the bridge from the nut
steps.detail: The pivot studs must sit so the saddles land at the scale length plus compensation. Measure from the nut along the centerline and use the routing spec for your model. (For comparison, a vintage Strat trem's pivot screws sit 25.25 in from the nut.)

steps.title: Rout the cavities
steps.detail: Use the matching template and bearing-guided bits in shallow passes (see md-route-humbucker-hss for router practice). The block cavity goes through to the back; the spring cavity is routed from the back.

steps.title: Install the studs
steps.detail: Drill the stud bushing holes on a drill press, perfectly square to the top, and press the bushings in. Studs set the bridge height and knife-edge pivot — misalignment ruins tuning stability.

steps.title: Fit the locking nut
steps.detail: Locking nuts mount either through the neck with a bolt or with screws from behind the nut, and often need a shelf cut at the end of the fretboard. Match the nut's radius to the fretboard, use shims to set string height at the first fret, and fit a string retainer bar between nut and tuners so strings pass flat over the nut.

steps.title: Check the neck angle
steps.detail: A Floyd sits higher than some vintage bridges. If the saddles can't be lowered enough for playable action, a recessed rout or a neck shim is needed.

steps.title: Set up
steps.detail: Balance springs for float, set action and intonation, then lock the nut. See the Bridges & Trems guides for Floyd setup and restringing.

models.note: Needs a much larger rout and new stud holes; plugging the old six-screw holes is usual. Many players buy a Floyd-routed replacement body instead.
A surface-mount FRX avoids a full tremolo rout; compare its stud spec sheet with your guitar before buying.
Most are factory-routed for double-locking trems — swap only between compatible models (check stud spacing and block).

warnings: Detune fully before removing springs — they store a lot of energy.
Routing a vintage-style body for a Floyd is irreversible and reduces value.
pro: Strongly recommended for anyone without router and drill-press experience. A Floyd-routed replacement body or neck is often cheaper overall.

title: Fretless conversion (pull frets, fill slots, coat the board)
summary: Turn a fretted neck (usually a bass) into a fretless: pull the frets without chipping the board, fill the slots with thin strips that become fret lines, level the board, then harden it with a super glue (or epoxy) coating so roundwounds don't chew it up.
tools: Fret pullers (flush-ground nippers); soldering iron to heat frets
Blocks and clamp to bow the neck back
Small rotary tool with a fine bit (to clean/size slots) or a fret saw
Radius block to match the board; precision straightedge
Thin and medium super glue; accelerator; nitrile gloves; respirator
parts: Slot fill strips: plastic binding, veneer or thin wood strips sized to the slot
Optional: new nut (strings sit lower without frets)

specs.label: Erlewine fill (fretless bass)
specs.value: 3/8 in tall black plastic binding, 0.040 in thick, split lengthwise and scraped to about 0.037 in

specs.label: Slot sizing
specs.value: Original slots took a 0.024 in feeler; widened with a 0.031 in rotary bit to about 0.034–0.035 in

specs.label: Glue cure before leveling
specs.value: About 15 min for water-thin super glue

specs.label: Leveling
specs.value: Radius block matching the board (14 in in Erlewine's example), 80 → 120 → 220 → 320

specs.label: Board coating (super glue)
specs.value: 3–4 coats thin/medium CA with accelerator; sand 320 → 800 on a rubber block, wet to 2000, Micro-Mesh 3200–12000, buff

steps.title: Remove the frets cleanly
steps.detail: Take the neck off. Support it on blocks and pull the headstock down gently into a back-bow — this opens the slots slightly so frets come out easily. Heat each fret with a soldering iron (helps if they're glued), then work the fret puller under one end and roll it along, pulling in the direction the fret was installed. Keep the puller jaws on the board to stop chips.
steps.warn: Fret ends are sharp; heat can scorch rosewood — don't let the iron linger.

steps.title: Clean and size the slots
steps.detail: Clean old glue and grime from the slots. Check the width with feeler gauges. Either size your strips to the slot, or widen the slots evenly (Erlewine used a 0.031 in rotary bit) so standard binding or veneer fits snugly.

steps.title: Fit the fill strips
steps.detail: Cut strips taller than the slot depth and just slightly thicker than the slot (scrape to fit — snug, not forced). Tap each in with the rough edge up; plastic binding follows the board's curve. Wick water-thin super glue along both sides of each strip and let it set about 15 minutes. These strips become your fret lines, so a contrasting color (black, white, maple) helps intonation.

steps.title: Level the board
steps.detail: With the truss rod just snug, trim the excess and sand with a radius block matching the board: 80 grit until the strips are nearly flush (stop just short so you don't gouge the board), then 120, 220 and 320. Check with a straightedge that the board is straight and the radius is even end to end.

steps.title: Coat the fingerboard
steps.detail: Clean with naphtha. Wipe on thin, then medium super glue in thin coats, curing each with accelerator (Erlewine applied it with a scrap of sandpaper). After 3–4 coats, level with 320 then 400, 600 and 800 on a rubber block, wet-sand to 2000, then Micro-Mesh up to 12000 and hand-buff with compound. Epoxy coatings are an alternative used by many builders but need longer cures and careful leveling.
steps.warn: Super glue fumes are strong — wear gloves and a respirator and work outdoors or with good ventilation.

steps.title: Reassemble and set up
steps.detail: Restring to pitch and confirm the neck can be adjusted straight. Without frets the strings sit lower at the nut: the nut slots may need lowering (or a new nut), and relief/action are usually set lower than fretted. Flatwound strings are kinder to the board than roundwounds.

models.note: The most common conversion. Rosewood and maple boards both work; maple must be finished/coated.
Frets are often notched over the binding — removal takes more care, and slot ends must be filled neatly.
Possible, but most players find fretless guitar very demanding; consider a replacement neck instead of converting a good one.

warnings: Not reversible without a full refret.
Chipped slot edges show on a fretless board — pull frets carefully.
pro: Pro-level job. Consider buying a fretless replacement neck, or have a luthier convert it if the neck matters to you.

title: Install a sustainer (Sustainiac / Fernandes) — overview
time: Half a day to a day (pro bench time)
summary: A sustainer replaces the neck pickup with a driver coil that keeps strings vibrating indefinitely. This outlines what the job involves so you can plan it — the makers recommend a trained luthier for installation.
tools: Router and templates (for driver, board and battery cavities, where needed)
parts: Sustainer kit (driver, circuit board, switch board, harness)

specs.label: Driver position
specs.value: Neck pickup position; Sustainiac Stealth Pro driver is humbucker-sized and fits a standard neck ring

specs.label: Power
specs.value: 9V battery (Manson × Sustainiac kit)

specs.label: Sustainiac AUX-RG switch board
specs.value: Mounts flat, for cavities under 1.35 in (35 mm) deep

specs.label: Manson AUX board (Manson × Sustainiac kit)
specs.value: 46 × 35 mm, needs 35 mm cavity depth; two toggles 25.4 mm apart (on/off and Harmonic/Mix/Fundamental)

specs.label: Bridge pickup (Manson × Sustainiac kit)
specs.value: Kit is meant for passive bridge humbuckers

steps.title: Check compatibility
steps.detail: The sustainer works together with the bridge pickup. The Manson × Sustainiac kit is specified for passive bridge humbuckers and not for single-coil Teles (the slanted bridge pickup is too far from the neck position). Sustainiac says the Stealth Pro fits many control cavities without extra routing — check its installation drawings against your guitar.

steps.title: Plan the space
steps.detail: You need room for the main board, a switch board (on/off and mode), a battery box and a stereo jack. Measure your control cavity depth and footprint against the board drawings; shallow cavities need the flat-mounting switch board.

steps.title: Fit the driver
steps.detail: The driver replaces the neck pickup. When the sustainer is off, it works as a (single-coil) neck pickup.

steps.title: Wire, shield and ground carefully
steps.detail: Driver and pickup wiring must be routed and shielded to the maker's drawing — stray coupling between the driver and the bridge pickup causes squeals and oscillation. Fernandes systems in particular are described as needing careful shielding and grounding.

steps.title: Test
steps.detail: Check all three modes (fundamental, harmonic, mixed) on every string, battery draw/switching via the jack, and that the neck position still works as a pickup.

models.note: Retrofit kit; driver in the neck position. Sustainiac's own retail sales were suspended in 2025 — kits are sold through dealers such as Gearstreet, and Manson sells a kit with its own switch board.
Usually found factory-fitted; retrofitting is described as a significant modification.
Jackson, Schecter and Fender (EOB Strat) have offered sustainers from the factory — often easier than a retrofit.

warnings: Unplug the cable when not playing so the battery isn't drained (the stereo jack switches it).
Poor shielding causes feedback squeal in the electronics, not just from the amp.
pro: The kit makers recommend installation by a trained, experienced luthier. Treat this guide as planning information.

title: Clean and polish the finish (nitro vs poly)
summary: Safely remove sweat, grime and fingerprints from a guitar's finish. Explains which products are safe on nitrocellulose lacquer and which suit modern poly finishes, how to treat satin finishes, and why vinyl or rubber stands, straps and capo pads can damage nitro.
symptoms: Dull, smeary or sticky body after gigs
Soft, sticky or blistered patches on the finish where a stand, strap or case touched it
Dark marks on the back of the neck that line up with where a rubber-padded capo sat

causes.cause: Vinyl or rubber in contact with a nitrocellulose finish
causes.check: Look for softened, tacky or imprinted areas exactly where stand padding, a vinyl strap, case lining or a capo pad touches the guitar.
causes.fix: Stop the contact at once (wrap stand rubber in a cotton cloth, store the guitar in its case). Damaged finish has to be dissolved back and re-lacquered, which is a professional job.

causes.cause: Sweat, skin oil and dirt build-up
causes.check: Cloudy film or grime that wipes off with a slightly damp cloth.
causes.fix: Clean with a guitar-specific cleaner as in the steps below.

causes.cause: Wrong product used (silicone polish, furniture polish, household sprays)
causes.check: Greasy smear that comes back, or hazy patches after using a household product.
causes.fix: Clean with naphtha on a cloth (ventilate) and switch to a silicone-free guitar polish.

tools: Lint-free microfiber or soft cotton cloths
Nitrile gloves (for very dirty guitars or solvents)
parts: Naphtha (lighter fluid type) for heavy grease — optional
Pure carnauba wax — optional, gloss finishes only
Plain cotton cloth to cover stand padding

specs.label: Never use (Fender)
specs.value: Glass cleaner, anything with ammonia, abrasive or silicone products

specs.label: Also avoid (Premier Guitar)
specs.value: Furniture polish, all-purpose sprays, lacquer thinner, bleach, heavy waxes, petroleum/solvent cleaners on nitro

specs.label: Safest wax if you wax
specs.value: Pure carnauba

specs.label: Satin finishes
specs.value: Clean only — never buff or polish

steps.title: Find out what finish you have
steps.detail: Check the maker's spec sheet for your model. Nitrocellulose lacquer is used on most Gibsons, on Fender American Vintage and Custom Shop models, and on Martin's standard line. Most other Fenders, Taylors (except very early ones) and most imported guitars use a catalyzed poly finish, which is far tougher. Also note whether the finish is gloss or satin (matte), because satin is treated differently.

steps.title: Wipe down after every session
steps.detail: Wipe the strings, neck and bridge with a dry lint-free cloth each time you finish playing. Sweat is acidic, and most finish and fret problems start with sweat left to sit.

steps.title: Routine cleaning
steps.detail: Lightly dampen a cloth with a guitar cleaner (spray the cloth, not the guitar). Wipe the body in small sections, use a Q-tip around the bridge, pickups and controls, then go over the area once more with a clean, barely damp cloth. Never soak the guitar; water near pickup cavities, screw holes or bare end grain can swell the wood.

steps.title: Heavy grime
steps.detail: For a really dirty guitar, wipe with warm water and a little dish soap on a cloth, mopping up dirty water as you go. Naphtha on a cloth or brush loosens grease and grime and is safe on most finishes and hardware. On an old nitro finish test it in a hidden spot first.
steps.warn: Naphtha is flammable and toxic: open a window, wear gloves and a mask, and keep it away from any flame or spark.

steps.title: Polish (gloss finishes only)
steps.detail: Rub a silicone-free guitar polish on with soft flannel and buff off. If you want wax, pure carnauba is the safest choice. A buffing compound or swirl remover actually cuts finish away, so use it only to fix swirls on newer gloss guitars (see md-buff-swirls-scratches), and leave the worn patina of a vintage nitro guitar alone — removing it lowers the value.

steps.title: Satin finishes: clean, don't polish
steps.detail: Use the routine cleaning step only. Buffing or polishing a satin finish creates shiny, blotchy patches that cannot be blended back without refinishing.

steps.title: Hardware
steps.detail: Polish metal parts with a soft dry cloth; no spray is needed. Keep metal polish off the finish.

steps.title: Protect nitro from vinyl and rubber
steps.detail: Plasticizers in vinyl (and to a lesser extent rubber) soften nitrocellulose and leave sticky blisters. Avoid vinyl straps, gig bags and case linings, rubber stand padding, rubber capo pads and surgical-tubing stand covers in long-term contact. Gibson's advice is to drape a soft cotton cloth over the stand's rubber and to use stands only short-term (for example at a gig) — the case is the safest place. Gibson also warns that clip-on tuners can mark nitro. Bug spray and some colognes attack nitro too. Heat makes all of this worse, so never leave a nitro guitar in a hot closed case with vinyl inside.

models.note: Gibson USA guitars are nitrocellulose: cover stand rubber with cloth and store in the case. Gibson does not cover stand damage under warranty. Most Epiphones are poly.
American Vintage and Custom Shop models are nitro. Most other Fender and Squier models are poly — still use guitar-specific cleaners, never household sprays.
Martin's standard line has been nitro since about 1930 (the D-1 family used a cross-linked polymer). Taylor uses a catalyzed finish, apart from very early guitars, which were lacquered.
Most imported steel-string guitars, mandolins and banjos use a catalyzed polymer that is largely immune to vinyl reactions.

warnings: Naphtha and other solvents are flammable: ventilate and keep away from flames.
Every polish with abrasive in it removes some finish. Don't use it as a weekly cleaner.
Never buff a satin finish.
pro: If the finish has gone soft, sticky or blistered from a stand, strap or case, a finish tech has to dissolve the damaged layer, re-color and re-lacquer it. Don't try to sand it off yourself.
