title: Remove swirls and fine scratches (buffing out)
summary: Bring back a gloss finish dulled by swirl marks, belt-buckle haze and light scratches using polishing compounds, and wet-sand scratches you can feel before buffing. For gloss finishes only.
symptoms: Fine circular swirl marks visible under a light
Hazy, dull patches where an arm or belt rubs
Light scratches that catch a fingernail only slightly
tools: Medium and fine polishing compounds (e.g. ColorTone medium/fine)
Separate foam pads or soft cotton cloths for each compound grade
Optional: foam pad on a variable-speed polisher or drill
Micro-finishing papers 1200–2000 grit (for scratches you can feel)
Small sanding block (cork, felt or rubber backed)
Bowl of water with a drop of dish soap, or naphtha, as lubricant
Eye protection and a dust mask/respirator when machine polishing

specs.label: Start compound to match last sanding grit (StewMac)
specs.value: 800 grit → coarse; 1200–1500 → medium; finish with fine/swirl remover

specs.label: Polyester / polyurethane finishes
specs.value: Sand no coarser than 1500–2000 grit before buffing; 1200 is too coarse for a clean rub-out

specs.label: Fresh nitro: wait before wet sanding
specs.value: At least a week (StewMac); 10–14 days per StewMac's nitro schedule

steps.title: Decide what you're dealing with
steps.detail: Drag a fingernail across the mark. If it doesn't catch, it's surface haze or swirls and compounds alone will fix it. If it catches, the scratch must be leveled by wet sanding first (step 6) or filled (see md-drop-fill-chips). Don't buff satin finishes, and think twice before buffing a vintage nitro guitar — wear and patina add value.

steps.title: Clean and mask
steps.detail: Clean the area first (see md-clean-polish-finish) — grit left on the surface creates new swirls. Mask off logos, pickups, binding you want to keep matte, and any open holes or cavities.

steps.title: Compound by hand
steps.detail: Put a small amount of medium compound on the pad or cloth (not on the guitar). Rub with firm, overlapping circles over a small area, then let it cool and wipe the residue off with a clean soft rag. Use a fresh pad for each grade.

steps.title: Fine compound / swirl remover
steps.detail: Repeat with fine compound or swirl remover on a fresh pad until the swirls are gone. Swirl remover also works by hand for a high shine.

steps.title: Machine polishing (optional)
steps.detail: With a foam pad at 1500–2500 rpm: spread the swirl remover over the area with the pad before switching on, polish at medium pressure, ease off as it dries, and wipe off the residue with a damp cloth before moving on. Don't work in direct sun or on a hot surface. Keep the spinning pad moving and stay off sharp edges and corners, where the finish is thinnest.
steps.warn: Wear eye protection and a mask with a rotary polisher. A pad that dwells in one place can heat and cut through the finish.

steps.title: Wet-sand scratches you can feel
steps.detail: Soak micro-finishing paper overnight. Wrap a 2–4 in square around a small block. Using water with a drop of soap (or naphtha) as lubricant, sand only the scratched area with the finest grit that will remove it (1500–2000 on poly; 1200–1500 on nitro). Dip the paper often and wipe the slurry off about once a minute. Dry the area and look: keep going until the scratch is gone and the patch is evenly dull. Then compound, starting with the grade that matches your last grit.
steps.warn: Water can swell bare wood at f-holes, pickup cavities and exposed end grain, and lift lacquer there. Keep it away from openings or use naphtha.

steps.title: Final polish
steps.detail: Finish with a guitar polish on soft flannel.

models.note: Very hard finish. Use fine grits (1500–2000) and expect compounding to take longer.
Softer and buffs easily — but it's also easy to cut through. Leave genuine vintage patina alone.
Don't buff or polish at all; it leaves shiny blotches.

warnings: Every buffing removes some finish. Do it rarely.
Edges, corners and the tops of carved surfaces have the thinnest finish — burn-through shows as a light patch of color or bare wood.
Wear eye protection with any rotary tool.
pro: If you sand or buff through to the color coat or wood, stop: that needs spot re-spraying and blending by a finish tech.

title: Steam out dents in wood
summary: Swell crushed wood fibers back up with heat and moisture. Works best on raw or oil-finished wood; it can work through a finish but risks clouding or blistering lacquer.
symptoms: A smooth-bottomed dent where the wood is pushed in but not torn
Dings on raw or oiled necks and bodies
tools: Soldering iron (hot) — tin the tip afterwards to keep it clean
Damp cotton rag (old T-shirt) or wet paper towel
Heat gun or hair dryer (optional, for drying)
For finished surfaces: cork block, 1000–2500 grit wet-or-dry, kerosene as lubricant

specs.label: Works only on
specs.value: Compressed fibers — not cut, torn or chipped wood

specs.label: Frank Ford example
specs.value: A 0.011 in deep dent in lacquered spruce steamed for about 10 min

specs.label: Wait before sanding level
specs.value: About a day (the wood shrinks back slightly as it dries)

steps.title: Check the damage
steps.detail: Look closely: if the fibers are crushed or cut through, or wood is missing, steam won't raise it and you'll need filler (md-drop-fill-chips). A smooth dent with intact fibers is a good candidate.

steps.title: Wet the dent
steps.detail: On raw or oil-finished wood, put a drop of water in the dent and let it soak in a minute. On a finished surface the steam has to get through the finish — it goes in faster if the finish is already cracked.

steps.title: Steam it
steps.detail: Wring the rag out so it's damp, not dripping, and lay it over the dent. Press the hot iron tip onto the rag right over the dent for a few seconds — you'll hear it hiss. Lift and check. Repeat, letting the area cool between applications, until the dent rises. Stubborn dents may take many applications.
steps.warn: The iron and steam burn. On lacquer, too much heat makes the finish turn white, blister or melt — go slowly and let it cool between hits.

steps.title: Dry and wait
steps.detail: Let it dry (a heat gun on low speeds this up), then wait about a day before sanding. The steamed area swells slightly proud and settles back as the moisture leaves.

steps.title: Level
steps.detail: Raw wood: sand the raised grain smooth with 320 and re-oil. Finished wood: level with a cork block and 1000 grit (Ford uses kerosene as lubricant), then buff. If a shallow dip remains, drop-fill it.

models.note: Ideal — steam goes straight into the wood and there's no finish to damage.
Frank Ford found catalyzed finish tolerated steaming well, though it took a long time to work through.
More heat-sensitive; old lacquer may blush, blister or melt. Test cautiously.

warnings: Don't sand or polish right away — the dent can reappear as the wood dries.
Keep the hot iron off bare finish; it marks instantly.
pro: Deep dents in a valuable lacquered guitar, or anything on a vintage finish.

sources.title: StewMac — Fixing a guitar dent by steaming it out
Frets.com (Frank Ford) — 'Steaming out' dents
Premier Guitar — How to refinish a guitar

title: Aerosol (rattle-can) nitro refinish, day by day
time: 5–6 spraying days + 2 weeks cure + 1 day sanding and buffing
summary: Spray a prepared body or neck with aerosol nitrocellulose lacquer — sealer, color, clear — and get a smooth, buffable finish without a spray gun. Assumes the wood is already stripped, sanded and grain-filled (md-refinish-overview).
tools: Aerosol sealer, color lacquer and clear gloss lacquer from one system (Premier Guitar's body example used 1 can of color and 3 of clear)
Sink or bucket of hot tap water to warm cans
Body holder or scrap-wood handle bolted into the neck pocket; a hook to hang it to dry
320, 400, 600 and 800 grit paper; 1200 micro-finishing paper for wet sanding
Medium and fine polishing compounds, swirl remover, soft cloths

specs.label: Room conditions (ColorTone)
specs.value: About 70°F (21°C) and 50% humidity or lower

specs.label: Warm cans (StewMac)
specs.value: 15–20 min in very hot tap water; keep can and guitar at similar temperatures

specs.label: First coats
specs.value: Light tack coat, then a wet coat (StewMac: about 45 min later; Premier Guitar: several minutes later)

specs.label: Coats per day
specs.value: 2–3 per day, 1–2 h apart (StewMac); Premier Guitar's schedule uses 60–90 min

specs.label: Clear coats
specs.value: 4–10 thin coats; 6–12 total coats including sealer and color (beginners 10–12)

specs.label: Cure before sanding
specs.value: 10–14 days (ColorTone); two weeks warm and dry (Premier Guitar)

specs.label: Leveling and polish
specs.value: Dry 800 to a flat dull sheen, wet 1200, then medium and fine compound

steps.title: Set up a safe spray area
steps.detail: Spray outdoors in still air or in a ventilated booth, warm and dry, with no flames, heaters with open elements or sparks nearby. Wear a respirator, gloves and eye protection.
steps.warn: Nitro lacquer and its propellant are highly flammable and harmful to breathe.

steps.title: Warm and prime the cans
steps.detail: Stand cans in very hot tap water for 15–20 minutes and shake for at least a minute after the ball starts to rattle. Warm lacquer atomizes finer and spits less. Swap to a freshly warmed can when the one in use feels cold. Clear the nozzle by spraying upside down for 2–3 seconds.

steps.title: Spraying technique
steps.detail: Hold the guitar close to level on a holder rather than spraying it while it hangs — lacquer runs downhill on vertical surfaces. Start and stop each pass off the guitar, keep the can roughly level and the distance constant (about 8–10 in), spray at a slight angle so the mist settles rather than splatters, and overlap each pass by about half. Do the edges and sides first, then the flat faces. Turn the nozzle to change the fan direction for flat areas. Aerosols put out more than you'd expect: start farther back and move in only if the coat looks dry. Hang the guitar only to dry.

steps.title: Day 1 — sealer
steps.detail: Spray a light tack coat, then a wetter coat. Build 2–3 coats total with 1–2 hours between them. Let dry overnight (24 hours before color if the sealer maker says so).

steps.title: Day 2 — color
steps.detail: Scuff flat areas lightly with 320 to give the color something to grip, tack off the dust, and spray 2–3 color coats 60–90 minutes apart until coverage is even. Dry overnight.

steps.title: Days 3–5 — clear
steps.detail: Each day: scuff with 320 until most shiny spots are dull (go gently on edges so you don't sand through the color), tack off, and spray about 4 clear coats 60–90 minutes apart. Dry overnight. Aim for 10–12 total coats if you're a beginner — extra build gives you room when leveling.

steps.title: Fix runs
steps.detail: Don't touch a run while it's wet. Let it harden 24 hours, level it with 400 on a block, then carry on spraying.

steps.title: Cure
steps.detail: After the last coat, scuff lightly with 600 to help solvent escape, then leave the parts somewhere warm and dry for at least two weeks (10–14 days minimum). The finish keeps shrinking as it cures; sanding too early means the grain shows through again later.

steps.title: Level
steps.detail: Dry-sand with 800 on a block until the surface is flat and evenly dull, removing orange peel without over-sanding. Then wet-sand with 1200 micro-finishing paper that has soaked overnight, rinsing it in soapy water as you go. Be very light on edges and corners.

steps.title: Buff and reassemble
steps.detail: Polish with medium compound, then fine, using a separate soft cloth for each, and finish with swirl remover (md-buff-swirls-scratches). Reassemble once the finish is hard.

steps.title: Look after the nozzles
steps.detail: After each session, turn the can upside down and spray until only clear gas comes out, then wipe the tip with thinner. A clogged tip (spattering or blotchy spray) can be popped off and soaked in lacquer thinner for a couple of minutes.

models.note: Mask the fretboard and frets if it's rosewood/ebony; on maple boards spray clear over the whole face and clean the frets afterwards. Mask the neck heel where it sits in the pocket.
Mask or later scrape the binding clean of color before clear coats.
Apply any waterslide decal before the clear coats (md-headstock-decals).

warnings: Never spray near a flame, pilot light or spark source.
Cold cans spit droplets; humid air can cloud lacquer.
Don't hurry the cure — two weeks is a minimum, not a target.
pro: Sunbursts, metallic or candy colors and multi-color jobs are much easier with a spray gun and experience — consider a finish shop.

title: Drop-fill finish chips and dings (super glue or lacquer)
time: 1–2 h of work; cure overnight (super glue) to 3 weeks (lacquer)
summary: Fill a chip or ding in the finish so it's level and nearly invisible. Super glue (CA) is quick and suits poly finishes; nitrocellulose lacquer melts into a nitro finish but needs a long cure before you can level it.
symptoms: Small crater where finish has chipped off, often down to color coat or wood
Dent edges where the finish has broken
tools: Medium-viscosity super glue (e.g. StewMac #20) or clear nitro lacquer (thickened from an aerosol)
Drop-fill toothpicks or a fine artist's brush
Acetone (to soften the dent for lacquer fills)
Naphtha or a fast solvent on a Q-tip (to preview color)
Liquid stain to match missing color
Micro-finishing papers 1000–2000 and Micro-Mesh pads up to 12000 (or 1200 wet-or-dry with kerosene)
Medium polishing compound and guitar polish

specs.label: Super glue cure before leveling (StewMac)
specs.value: Several hours minimum; overnight is better

specs.label: Lacquer fill: thicken a puddle (Erlewine)
specs.value: Nickel-sized drop left about 1 h

specs.label: Lacquer fill: next drop
specs.value: After 4–5 h; repeat with smaller drops over about 2 days

specs.label: Lacquer fill cure before leveling (Frank Ford)
specs.value: At least 3 weeks after the last drop

specs.label: Nitro lacquer solids
specs.value: About 25% — roughly 75% of what you apply evaporates, so overfill

specs.label: Tape on razor (depth stop)
specs.value: About 0.002 in plastic tape on each end

specs.label: Leave after scraping (Ford)
specs.value: About 0.001–0.002 in proud, then sand

steps.title: Pick the filler
steps.detail: Use thin layers of nitro lacquer on a nitro guitar: it bonds into the old finish. Use medium (or thick gap-filling) super glue on poly, polyester or UV-cured finishes, or when you need a fast fix. For very deep dents, Frank Ford fills most of the depth with a non-shrinking catalyzed filler first and tops off with lacquer.

steps.title: Clean and preview the color
steps.detail: Pick out loose flakes, wipe with naphtha and let dry. Dab a little fast solvent on the chip with a Q-tip — while wet it shows roughly how the chip will look under clear finish. If bare wood or primer shows up lighter, you need to add color.

steps.title: Add color if needed
steps.detail: Thin a drop of liquid stain with alcohol or acetone and touch it into the chip only, building up slowly until the wet color matches. Let it dry.

steps.title: Fill with super glue
steps.detail: Put a puddle of medium super glue on a scrap of plastic. Pick up a drop on the tip of a toothpick and touch it into the chip so it flows in. Build it slightly higher than the surrounding finish, letting each drop harden before the next. Leave it to cure — overnight if you can. Glue that isn't fully hard will smear and tear when you level it.
steps.warn: Super glue fumes sting eyes and noses: ventilate and wear safety glasses.

steps.title: …or fill with lacquer
steps.detail: Spray a nickel-sized puddle of lacquer onto a plastic lid and leave it about an hour to thicken. Brush a drop of acetone onto the dent to soften it, then with the same brush place a drop of thickened lacquer in the dent, feathering it onto the edges. It will sink as it dries. Add another, smaller drop after 4–5 hours and keep going for about two days until the fill stays above the surface. Then let it cure — Frank Ford waits at least three weeks — because lacquer keeps shrinking as solvent leaves.
steps.warn: Lacquer and acetone are flammable; ventilate and keep away from flames.

steps.title: Level with a taped razor
steps.detail: Draw the edge of a fresh single-edge blade along a steel vise jaw or other hard steel to raise a small burr. Wrap thin tape around both ends of the blade so only the width of the fill is bare — the tape rides on the finish and stops the blade cutting into it. Pull the blade across the fill with light pressure until it stops cutting.

steps.title: Strip-sand flush
steps.detail: Cut narrow strips of paper and pull them across the fill under a fingertip, changing direction: 320 or 400, then 600, then 800 — under a minute per grit, touching the surrounding finish as little as possible. Then use a small flat block with 1000–2000 grit to make it perfectly level.

steps.title: Polish
steps.detail: Wet-sand with soaked Micro-Mesh pads (3600 up to 12000) or 1200 paper lubricated with kerosene, then buff with medium polishing compound on a soft paper towel and finish with guitar polish.

models.note: Lacquer drop fills melt into the old finish and become nearly invisible. Allow weeks of cure before final leveling.

models.model: Fender, Ibanez, PRS, most imports (poly/polyester/UV finishes)
models.note: Thick or medium super glue is the usual filler; it can take up to about five minutes to set for thick gel unless you use accelerator.
Color matching is the hard part. Practice on a scrap or hidden area.

warnings: Don't sand or scrape soft fill — wait for full cure.
Keep the razor taped so it can't cut into the surrounding finish.
Super glue, acetone and lacquer all need ventilation.
pro: Large chips, chips on a sunburst edge, metallic or translucent colors, or a valuable vintage guitar — a finish tech can blend these properly.

title: Fix stripped screw holes (neck, strap button, pickguard)
summary: Permanently repair a screw that spins without tightening — a strap button, pickguard screw or bolt-on neck screw — by drilling the hole out, gluing in a hardwood dowel and drilling a fresh pilot hole. Toothpicks and matchsticks are only a stop-gap.
symptoms: Screw turns but never tightens
Strap button wobbles or pulls out
Neck shifts in the pocket or loses its setup
tools: Drill (drill press for necks) and bits: 3/16 in, 7/64 in, 5/64 in; for necks #14 (0.182 in), #13 (0.185 in), #51 and #30 (0.128 in)
Calipers or a drill gauge to measure screws
Masking tape as a drill depth stop
Low-tack tape to protect the finish
parts: 3/16 in hardwood dowel (maple, poplar, basswood, or matching wood such as mahogany)
Wood glue (Titebond) or medium super glue
Beeswax or paraffin for the screw threads
New screw if the old one is worn

specs.label: Strap button (StewMac)
specs.value: Drill out 3/16 in, glue in 3/16 in dowel, pilot 7/64 in (for its ~0.153 in screw)

specs.label: Pickguard screw (Premier Guitar)
specs.value: Drill 3/16 in about 1/32 in deeper than the screw; pilot 5/64 in, typically about 3/8 in deep

specs.label: Bolt-on neck screw (Erlewine)
specs.value: Stripped hole measured 0.173 in; drilled with #14 (0.182 in); 3/16 in dowel sized through a #13 (0.185 in) hole; pilot #51 then #30 (0.128 in)

specs.label: Glue time before redrilling
specs.value: Super glue about 20 min (Erlewine); wood glue about 1 h minimum (StewMac), overnight (Premier Guitar)

steps.title: Remove and measure
steps.detail: Take the screw out and clean the sawdust from the hole. Measure the screw's outer thread diameter (tells you the hole you'll drill out) and the solid core between the threads (tells you the pilot size). Only plug holes that are actually loose.

steps.title: Drill out the old hole
steps.detail: Put a tape flag on the bit at the depth of the hole and drill straight in — no wobbling or angling — with a bit slightly smaller than your dowel (3/16 in hole for a 3/16 in dowel, or a few thousandths under for a tight fit as Erlewine does on necks). Support a neck face-down on a radius block or padded surface so it can't rock.
steps.warn: On a neck, never drill deeper than the original hole — you can come out through the fretboard.

steps.title: Prepare the dowel
steps.detail: Cut the dowel to the hole depth (or a little longer to trim later). Chamfer the end and file a couple of shallow grooves along it so excess glue can escape. Erlewine sizes neck dowels by driving them through a hole drilled in steel plate so they're perfectly round.

steps.title: Glue it in
steps.detail: Tape around the hole to catch squeeze-out. Coat the inside of the hole and the dowel with wood glue (Premier Guitar thins Titebond II 50/50 with water for pickguard holes) or use medium super glue, then tap the dowel home. Let it cure — overnight for wood glue.

steps.title: Trim flush
steps.detail: Cut the dowel flush with a flush-cut saw or pare it with a sharp chisel. Don't use side-cutters, which crush the dowel. On a hidden area like a strap button or neck pocket, a dab of lacquer seals the end grain.

steps.title: Mark the new hole
steps.detail: For pickguards and neck plates, put the part in place and mark through its hole (tap a Phillips screwdriver into the dowel to make a center mark). For strap buttons, mark the center with an awl so the bit can't wander.

steps.title: Drill the pilot
steps.detail: Drill the pilot hole straight, to the screw's depth, at the size of the screw's core (e.g. 7/64 in for a strap button, 5/64 in for a pickguard screw). On necks, Erlewine starts with a tiny #51 bit to keep it centered, then opens up to #30 — slightly larger than factory because the dowel is softer than the neck wood.

steps.title: Reinstall
steps.detail: Rub beeswax or paraffin on the threads and drive the screw until snug. Stop there — over-tightening strips the new wood. A strap button should grip firmly and not spin.

models.note: Use a drill press with the neck supported on a radius block. Hard maple dowel is ideal.
Match the plug wood to the body if possible (mahogany plug in mahogany).

models.model: Acoustic end pin / heel strap button
models.note: Frank Ford fills with a small dowel and wood glue, then hides the hole with a cosmetic plug and touched-up finish — consider a pro if the finish must be invisible.

warnings: A loose strap button can drop your guitar — fix it properly, don't rely on toothpicks.
Drill straight; an angled hole won't hold.
Vintage guitars: let a qualified luthier decide on repairs.
pro: Vintage instruments, holes near an edge or in cracked wood, or neck holes that are close to coming through the fretboard.

title: Headstock logos and waterslide decals
time: 1 h + 12 h dry + clear coats + 1–3 days cure
summary: Apply a waterslide decal to a headstock (a new build, refinish or replacement logo) and seal it under clear lacquer so it looks factory-made.
tools: 1000–1500 grit wet-or-dry paper (to scuff an existing gloss)
Clear lacquer (aerosol) compatible with the existing finish
800–3000 grit paper for optional leveling; polishing compound

specs.label: Soak (Nitorlack)
specs.value: 20–30 s in lukewarm water, until it slides freely

specs.label: Dry before lacquering
specs.value: At least 12 h

specs.label: First coat
specs.value: Very light mist/dust coat, wait 15–20 min

specs.label: Build
specs.value: 4–6 thin coats with flash-off time between

specs.label: Cure before handling
specs.value: 24–72 h (longer before leveling)

specs.label: Decal film thickness (StewMac examples)
specs.value: Lacquer waterslide film about 0.0015 in; Mylar overhead film about 0.004 in

steps.title: Prepare the surface
steps.detail: On a refinish, apply the decal over the color or first clear coats, before the main clear coats. On an existing gloss headstock, scuff lightly with 1000–1500 grit just until the shine goes, wipe with a damp cloth and let dry. Mask the rest of the neck if you're only coating the face.

steps.title: Trim and soak
steps.detail: Trim the decal close to the design. Drop it in lukewarm water for 20–30 seconds until the film slides on the backing — don't force it.

steps.title: Position
steps.detail: Put a drop of water on the headstock so the decal can float into place. Slide it off the backing onto the headstock and nudge it straight with a wet fingertip or swab.

steps.title: Remove the water
steps.detail: Blot gently with paper towel from the center outward to push out water and bubbles. Press, don't rub.

steps.title: Let it dry
steps.detail: Leave at least 12 hours. Lacquering over trapped moisture causes bubbles and wrinkles that can't be fixed.

steps.title: Seal with a mist coat
steps.detail: Spray a very light dust coat just to anchor the decal — a wet coat can make it swim or wrinkle. Wait 15–20 minutes. Lacquer solvent can soften some decal inks, so keep early coats dry.

steps.title: Build clear coats
steps.detail: Spray 4–6 thin coats with flash-off time between. Heavy coats run, orange-peel and can lift the decal edges. Keep building until the decal edge disappears into the clear.

steps.title: Cure, level and buff (optional)
steps.detail: Let it cure (24–72 hours to handle; longer before sanding). For a factory look, wet-sand very lightly from 800 up to 3000 and buff. The decal sits in a very thin layer — sand only enough to remove the edge ridge and orange peel.
steps.warn: Sanding through the clear destroys the decal. Go gently near it.

models.note: Scuff the existing finish well and test your lacquer on a hidden area first — fresh nitro doesn't always bond well to old poly.
New nitro lacquer bonds into the old finish. Gibson's logos are inlaid, not decals — a decal is a replacement look only.

warnings: Don't put another company's trademarked logo on a guitar you sell or present as genuine — that's counterfeiting.
Lacquer is flammable; spray with ventilation and a respirator.
pro: Matching a vintage logo or refinishing over an inlaid logo.

sources.title: Nitorlack — How to install a decal on a guitar headstock and lacquer it correctly
StewMac — Custom peghead decals
StewMac — Waterslide decal to repair a guitar finish

title: Relic (aged) finish basics
summary: Make a guitar look and feel played-in: fake finish checking, dull the gloss, wear the neck and fretboard edges, and age plastics and logos. Every step is permanent, so plan from photos of real worn guitars.
tools: Utility knife blade or knife point; magnifier
Fine and very fine steel wool (#0000)
Lacquer-compatible pigment or stain for darkening cracks; amber tint for plastics and logos
Round steel bar (a slide or large screwdriver shank) for rolling fretboard edges
Masking tape; newspaper for the bench

specs.label: Faking checks on a body (StewMac example)
specs.value: Under 2 h by hand with a knife point

specs.label: Wipe pigment out of the checks
specs.value: Immediately with naphtha; buff after about 10 min

specs.label: Breaking fretboard edges (Premier Guitar)
specs.value: Round bar at about 45°, roughly 10–15 min per edge

specs.label: Airbrush de-gloss (StewMac)
specs.value: 2–3 light passes at 15–20 psi

steps.title: Plan the wear
steps.detail: Study photos (with magnification) of genuinely worn guitars of the same model: where the forearm rubs the top, belt wear on the back, pick wear below the strings, thumb wear on the neck, and the pattern real checking makes. Mark the areas lightly with tape. Mask parts you want to keep original, like the headstock face.

steps.title: Fake the checking
steps.detail: Scratch fine check lines into the finish with a knife point or the corner of a stiff utility blade, following the patterns you studied. Vary the shapes — repeated identical marks look fake. Go slowly; this is the step that makes or breaks the look.

steps.title: Color the cracks
steps.detail: Thin a lacquer-type pigment with naphtha, wipe it over the checks so it settles into them, then immediately wipe the surface clean with a naphtha-dampened rag. After about ten minutes, buff the area so the lines don't look sharp and new.
steps.warn: Don't let pigment dry on the surface — it stains.

steps.title: Dull the shine
steps.detail: Rub worn areas and the back of the neck with very fine steel wool to break the gloss. (StewMac's advanced trick: mix a little of the milky settled stearate from the bottom of an unshaken can of vinyl sealer into lacquer thinner and airbrush 2–3 light passes at 15–20 psi.)

steps.title: Age the fretboard and edges
steps.detail: Clamp the neck, then run a round steel bar along each fretboard edge at about 45°, roughly 10–15 minutes per edge, checking often. This crushes the edge fibers the way years of hand pressure do, rather than sanding a bevel. A rosewood board can then be darkened with a rosewood dye (mask the binding/edges, Vaseline on the dots) and finished with a hard fretboard wax rather than oil.

steps.title: Age the plastics and logo
steps.detail: Knock the shine off the nut, truss rod cover, pickup covers and logo with steel wool, then build up thin layers of amber tint with a Q-tip, and rub in a little dust and grime. Don't reshape the headstock or swap the logo.

steps.title: Bare-wood tone (advanced)
steps.detail: On worn-through bare spruce or maple, luthiers use oxalic acid to lighten and dilute potassium permanganate to darken (oxalic acid also pulls permanganate color back out). Apply in thin coats and judge color only when dry.
steps.warn: Oxalic acid is mildly toxic; keep it off skin. Potassium permanganate is highly reactive and can ignite violently with glycerol or simple alcohols — keep it away from other chemicals.

models.note: Classic wear spots: forearm contour, belly cut, pick area under the strings, lower bout edges. Maple necks wear through the clear where the hand slides.
Arm wear on the top edge, belt wear on the back, checking across the top. Aged binding is amber/yellow.

warnings: Relicing can't be undone and usually reduces resale value unless done very well.
Dyes stain permanently: cover the bench and keep rags handy.
Steel wool fibers stick to pickup magnets — cover or remove pickups first.
pro: For a convincing Custom Shop–style relic, or on any guitar with collector value, use a specialist.

sources.title: StewMac — Relic finish: faking age cracks on a 1956 Strat
Premier Guitar — How to relic your guitar neck, Pt. 1
StewMac — Mamie Minch on guitar oxidation: instant aging

title: Body cracks and broken horns (solid bodies)
summary: Reglue a cracked or snapped-off horn, a cracked body edge or a split around a cavity on a solid-body guitar, then touch up the finish. Clean breaks with all the pieces present glue back strongly; missing wood or old repairs are pro work.
symptoms: A horn that has cracked through or snapped off after a fall
A crack that opens when you flex the body near a cavity or jack
Finish lifting along a line in the wood
tools: Glue syringe with blunt needles and a small glue brush
Clamps (cam clamps, bar clamps) and rubber clamping bands
Cauls shaped to the body, with wax paper so they don't stick
Small hardwood wedges to open a crack slightly
Q-tips, warm water and a cloth for squeeze-out
Bone burnisher; touch-up marker or tinted lacquer; fine brush or knife tip
Thin super glue and accelerator (for small chips)
parts: Aliphatic wood glue (StewMac used Titebond III for its strength and longer open time) or hide glue

specs.label: Clamp time (StewMac broken SG neck)
specs.value: At least a day — about 24 h

specs.label: Glue choice
specs.value: Wood glue (Titebond) or hide glue for structural joints; thin super glue is brittle — use it only for small chips

steps.title: Strip the area and save every piece
steps.detail: Remove strings, pickguard, electronics near the break and anything heavy (StewMac even removed the tuners on a broken SG). Save every splinter and finish chip, and don't knock loose pieces out — disturbing them makes the fit worse. Leave any old glue that helps the parts locate.

steps.title: Dry-clamp first
steps.detail: Rehearse the clamp-up with no glue: cauls in place, clamps set, seams lining up flush on every face. If parts won't close without forcing, stop and find out why (debris, a missing chip, old glue). Make cauls that spread pressure and won't mark the finish; line them with wax paper.

steps.title: Get glue deep into the break
steps.detail: For a crack that's still attached, open it slightly with small wedges and inject glue with a syringe until it seeps out the other side; gently flex the joint to wick it in. For a horn that came off, brush glue thinly on both faces along the grain (check brushes don't shed bristles).

steps.title: Clamp and clean
steps.detail: Clamp using the rehearsed setup, checking the edges and faces line up as pressure comes on. Clean squeeze-out with damp Q-tips — little water, and don't soak the finish. Leave clamped at least 24 hours.

steps.title: Clean up and replace chips
steps.detail: Remove dried glue with a barely damp cloth. Push any raised wood edges down with a polished bone burnisher rather than sanding (sanding removes wood and color; burnishing suits thin finishes, not thick poly). Reattach saved finish chips with a touch of thin super glue and accelerator.

steps.title: Touch up the finish
steps.detail: Work a matching color (touch-up marker dispensed onto glass, tinted lacquer) into the crack line with a fine tool, wipe off any that lands on the surface, and test in a hidden spot first. Then drop-fill and level any remaining gap (md-drop-fill-chips).

steps.title: Restring and watch
steps.detail: Restring and keep an eye on the joint for a week or two. A properly glued joint is usually stronger than the wood around it.

models.note: Thin mahogany horns and long horns snap in falls. Set-neck joints may be involved — if the neck tenon is cracked, it's a pro repair.
Cracks often start at the jack cavity or from screws driven into end grain near edges.

warnings: Don't use super glue for structural joints — it's brittle and very hard to reglue over later.
Old vintage solder joints are fragile when removing electronics.
pro: Missing wood, broken set-neck joints, breaks that have been glued badly before, or a crack across a carved top. Also see a pro for headstock breaks.

sources.title: StewMac — Real Repairs: fixing a broken SG neck
StewMac — Gluing a broken peghead
StewMac — Using three different glues: where and why
Premier Guitar — Using super glue in guitar repair

title: Finish cracks and checking
time: 1–2 h of work; up to a month of drying for lacquer fills
summary: Understand and, where worthwhile, repair cracks in the finish: weather checking in nitro, seam cracks at neck joints and binding, and lifted edges. Often the right answer is to leave age checking alone.
symptoms: Fine hairline cracks in the lacquer, often running across the grain
A crack or chip line in the finish at the neck heel or along binding
White or silvery lines where finish has lifted from the wood

causes.cause: Temperature shock / aging of nitrocellulose lacquer
causes.check: Many fine parallel or crazed lines across a nitro finish, often after the guitar was cold. Cold temperatures can trigger checking.
causes.fix: Usually leave it — it's normal aging and doesn't hurt the wood. Repair only a single noticeable check on a fairly new guitar (Method B). Prevent it by letting a cold guitar warm up in its closed case before opening.

causes.cause: Wood movement at joints (neck heel, binding, end grain)
causes.check: A crack or chip that follows the seam between two parts, sometimes with white lifted finish beside it.
causes.fix: Stabilize and fill with ultra-thin super glue (Method A).

causes.cause: Impact
causes.check: Star-shaped or circular crack around a dent.
causes.fix: Treat as a ding: see [md-steam-dents] and [md-drop-fill-chips].

causes.cause: Crack in the wood itself, not just the finish
causes.check: The crack line opens or moves when you flex the area gently, or shows in raw wood on the inside/back.
causes.fix: Structural repair — see [md-body-crack-broken-horn] or a luthier.

tools: Ultra-thin and medium super glue (e.g. GluBoost Fill n' Finish) with accelerator
Small pipette or fine applicator tips
600, 1000, 1200 grit paper (wet-or-dry for the fine grits); 2500 grit for lacquer fills
For nitro checks: slow lacquer solvent (Frank Ford used Cellosolve), clear nitro lacquer, fine brush, glass microscope slide

specs.label: Seam crack fill (StewMac)
specs.value: 1–2 drops ultra-thin CA, accelerator, level with 600, wet-sand 1000 then 1200, buff

specs.label: Nitro check fill drying (Frank Ford)
specs.value: About one month before leveling

specs.label: Final sanding of check fill (Ford)
specs.value: 2500 grit wet-or-dry on a block, then buff

steps.title: Decide whether to repair at all
steps.detail: Weather checking on a nitro guitar is normal aging, and Frank Ford usually advises against repairing it. Repairs make sense for an isolated check on a new guitar, or a seam crack where finish may flake off. Never widen or 'clean out' a crack with a knife — it only makes the damage bigger.

steps.title: Method A — seam cracks with thin super glue: mask
steps.detail: Lay fine-line tape right up to both sides of the crack to control the glue and catch drips.

steps.title: Wick the glue in
steps.detail: With a small pipette, put one or two drops of ultra-thin super glue on the crack and let it wick underneath. Where the lacquer stays white (air under it), prick a tiny pinhole with a thumbtack so glue can get underneath — the white disappears when it's wetted. Mist with accelerator.
steps.warn: Wear safety glasses; ventilate.

steps.title: Build up low spots and skim
steps.detail: If there are still low spots, add a thicker grade of glue. Before removing the tape, skim the excess lightly with a razor blade, then pull the tape.

steps.title: Level and polish
steps.detail: Level with 600 grit on a hard block, wet-sand lightly with 1000 then 1200, and buff with a heavier-cut polish followed by swirl remover.

steps.title: Method B — single nitro check (Frank Ford)
steps.detail: Drop a tiny bead of slow lacquer solvent into the check so it softens and fuses the lacquer around it. A few hours later, brush a fine line of clear nitro lacquer along it. Next day brush on a second line so the fill stands above the surface. Let it dry about a month.

steps.title: Level the lacquer fill
steps.detail: Scrape the fill down to the original surface with a glass slide or taped razor (tape its edges so it can't scratch the surrounding finish), block-sand with 2500 grit wet-or-dry, and buff to match the surrounding gloss.

models.note: Prone to weather checking; protect from sudden temperature changes. Checking is cosmetic.
Rarely check, but can crack around impact points or at the neck joint; use the super glue method.

warnings: Solvents and lacquer are flammable; ventilate.
Don't cut into or widen cracks.
A crack that goes into the wood is structural — don't just fill the finish.
pro: Widespread checking (a pro can 'amalgamate' the whole surface or refinish), cracks over sunburst or metallic color, or any crack that is in the wood itself.

sources.title: Frets.com (Frank Ford) — Repairing a lacquer check
StewMac — Guitar finish repair (Tips du Jour mailbag)

title: Full refinish: strip, prep, grain-fill and choose a finish
time: 1–2 days of prep + spraying days + 2–3 weeks cure
summary: The plan for refinishing a solid body or bolt-on neck: choosing nitro, 2-part urethane or a wipe-on finish, stripping the old finish, repairing and sanding, grain-filling open-pore woods like ash and mahogany, and sealing. Spraying itself is covered in md-aerosol-nitro-refinish.
tools: Heat gun (lowest setting) and putty/seam-separation knives, scrapers
Flat sanding pad/blocks; 120, 180/220, 320, 400 grit (silicone-free paper such as 3M Gold)
Grain filler, plastic spreader or old card
Naphtha and clean rags; tack cloth
Respirator with organic-vapor cartridges; eye protection
Body holder or handles made from scrap wood; a way to hang parts to dry
parts: Sealer (vinyl or sanding sealer for nitro; waterbase sealer when going from stripped poly to nitro)
Grain filler (powdered water-mix or epoxy) for porous woods
Color and clear finish of one compatible system

specs.label: Prep sanding (Premier Guitar/StewMac)
specs.value: 120 → damp-wipe to raise grain → 220 → raise grain → 320, always with the grain

specs.label: Porous woods that need grain filling
specs.value: Ash, mahogany, rosewood, koa, walnut, wenge

specs.label: Non-porous woods (no filler needed)
specs.value: Maple, alder, basswood, spruce

specs.label: ColorTone powdered grain filler mix
specs.value: 1 part water : 2 parts powder

specs.label: Grain filler timing (ColorTone)
specs.value: Squeegee after 5–10 min at 45° to grain; 1 h between fills; 24 h before nitro (2–4 h before waterbase)

specs.label: Epoxy pore fill (StewMac, SilverTip)
specs.value: 10 g resin : 4 g hardener by weight; sand next day with 240–320

specs.label: Nitro schedule (StewMac)
specs.value: Sealer 3–4 coats, color 1–3, clear 4–10; 2–3 coats per day, 1–2 h apart; 6–12 coats total (beginners 10–12)

specs.label: Nitro cure before wet sanding
specs.value: 10–14 days (StewMac); two weeks warm and dry (Premier Guitar)

specs.label: 2-part urethane (StewMac)
specs.value: Mix 1:1, thin about 20%; 3–4 coats 45–60 min apart, no more than four coats per session; level after 4–6 days with P800–P1500, then P2000–P3000

specs.label: Runs and sags
specs.value: Let harden 24 h, level with 400 grit on a block

steps.title: Choose the finish
steps.detail: Nitrocellulose lacquer: thin, traditional, easy to touch up because new lacquer melts into old, sprayable from aerosol cans — but it cures slowly, checks with age and reacts with vinyl. Two-part (2K) urethane: very hard and fast-curing, but it needs a spray gun and serious respiratory protection; best left to experienced finishers. Wipe-on poly or oil finishes: no spray gear, thin satin feel, easy to repair, less protection — a good first project (StewMac sells a wipe-on poly kit with its own schedule). Whatever you choose, use one maker's sealer, color and clear together.

steps.title: Strip the guitar down
steps.detail: Photograph the wiring, then remove strings, neck, all hardware and electronics, and bag the screws by part. If you'll keep the pickups, protect them from dust.

steps.title: Strip the old finish
steps.detail: Heat gun on its lowest setting, kept moving: when the finish softens, slide a sharp knife or scraper under it and lift it off in sheets. Do the cavities too. Chemical strippers turn modern poly into a slurry and rarely give a clean strip; sanding works but is slow. Expect a base coat or sealer under the color — remove it with a final heat-and-scrape pass. Be aware that solid-color factory finishes often hide multi-piece bodies.
steps.warn: Heat scorches wood easily, and fumes from hot finish are harmful — ventilate and wear a respirator. Light scorch marks can sometimes be bleached or hidden under a burst.

steps.title: Repair
steps.detail: Steam out dents (md-steam-dents), fill chips, and plug any holes you won't reuse with glued hardwood dowels (md-stripped-screw-holes).

steps.title: Sand
steps.detail: On a flat pad, sand with the grain only: 120 grit to remove all old finish and sealer, wipe with a damp cloth to raise the grain, let dry, 220, raise the grain again, then 320. Wipe with naphtha to remove oils and wear clean gloves from now on.

steps.title: Grain-fill ash, mahogany and other open-pore woods
steps.detail: Mix powdered filler with water (1 part water to 2 parts powder) to a ketchup-to-sour-cream consistency. Brush it on generously with the grain, then across it. After 5–10 minutes squeegee off the excess with a card held at 45° to the grain, wipe the haze off with a dry cloth once it's dry, and sand lightly with 320. Repeat after an hour if pores are still open. Wait 24 hours before spraying nitro. Filler can be tinted with stain — black filler in ash gives the classic contrasting-grain look.

steps.title: Seal
steps.detail: Spray 2–4 thin coats of sealer 1–2 hours apart, sanding very lightly with 320 on a block between coats without going through to wood. Let the last sealer coat dry 24 hours before color. If you've stripped a factory poly finish and are going to nitro, seal the bare wood first (StewMac used a couple of light coats of waterbase sealer, cured overnight and leveled with 400) because leftover poly sealer can stop nitro adhering.

steps.title: Spray color and clear
steps.detail: Follow md-aerosol-nitro-refinish for spraying by day. Test-fit and pre-drill hardware before the clear goes on so you don't drill into fresh finish.

steps.title: Cure, level and buff
steps.detail: Let nitro cure 10–14 days (longer is better) somewhere warm and dry, then wet-sand and buff (md-buff-swirls-scratches). 2K urethane can be leveled after 4–6 days.

steps.title: Reassemble
steps.detail: Clear finish out of screw holes and the neck pocket, reinstall, and do a full setup.

models.note: Modern bodies are usually poly over alder or ash; vintage-series and Custom Shop are nitro. Ash bodies need grain filling for a smooth gloss.
Mahogany needs grain filling. Bound guitars need the binding masked or scraped clean of color. Set necks mean you'll be finishing the whole guitar at once.
Refinishing a vintage guitar greatly reduces collector value — have a pro advise first.

warnings: Lacquer, thinners and sealers are flammable and harmful to breathe: spray outdoors or in a ventilated booth, with a respirator, and no flames or sparks nearby.
Two-part urethanes contain isocyanate hardeners; read the maker's safety data sheet and use the respiratory protection it calls for.
Don't touch wet lacquer — fingerprints in fresh finish are hard to remove.
pro: 2K urethane or polyester spraying, sunbursts, vintage or valuable guitars, and set-neck/bound guitars are worth taking to a finish shop.

title: Change bass strings
summary: How to restring a bass so the strings seat properly, wind neatly and stay in tune: top-load versus through-body, where to cut, winding direction, and the special rules for taper-wound, flatwound and tapewound strings.
parts: String set of the right scale/wound length for your bass

specs.label: Fender wrap length past the post, standard keys
specs.value: 4th string 3 in (76 mm); 3rd, 2nd, 1st 3-1/2 in (89 mm); 5th (B) 3 in (76 mm)

specs.label: Fender wrap length past the post, vintage keys
Fender manual method
specs.value: Leave enough for at least 3 wraps; mark; kink the string 45 degrees 1 in before the mark; cut at the mark

specs.label: Rule for all strings (La Bella)
specs.value: Only the silk/tapered part may wrap the post; the silk must start after the nut

steps.title: Detune and remove
steps.detail: Detune each string until slack before taking it off or cutting it. On a bolt-on bass you can change one string at a time to keep tension on the neck, or all at once to clean the board. Wipe the fingerboard and frets while the strings are off.

steps.title: Feed the ball end
steps.detail: Top-load bridge: thread the string through the hole at the back of the bridge plate. Through-body: feed it from the back of the body through the ferrule. Pull it through until the ball end sits fully home and check the string is not twisted - La Bella notes a twisted or unseated string causes buzz, poor tuning and breakage.

steps.title: Check what sits on the saddle
steps.detail: For a taper-wound string, the exposed core (without outer wraps) should sit on the saddle. The thick ball-end wrap should be behind the saddle, never on it. See [bs-ball-end-saddle].

steps.title: Measure and cut
steps.detail: Pull the string past its tuner post. Either use Fender's wrap lengths from the specs (measured past the post), or follow the manual: leave enough for at least three wraps, mark that point, put a 45-degree kink in the string 1 in before the mark, and cut at the mark. The kink stops the windings from loosening.
steps.warn: Do not cut flatwound or tapewound strings anywhere except the silk end - cutting through the tape makes a tapewound string unravel, and wrapping the metal of a flatwound around the post breaks it.

steps.title: Insert and bend
steps.detail: Push the cut end straight down into the centre hole of the post and bend it over into the slot (Fender style split posts).

steps.title: Wind downward, no overlaps
steps.detail: Hold the string taut and wind so each wrap sits below the last, finishing near the base of the post. Wraps must not cross over each other. The string should leave the post on the side facing the nut slot so it runs straight in: on a Fender-style 4-in-line headstock that is counter-clockwise as you look at the face of the headstock; on the treble side of a 2+2 headstock it is the opposite direction.

steps.title: Tune and stretch
steps.detail: Bring to pitch, then grab each string in the middle, tug it gently up and down to take out slack, and retune. Repeat two or three times. La Bella advises not to tug flatwounds before installing; a few hours of playing breaks them in.

steps.title: Check intonation and setup
steps.detail: Fender recommends checking intonation after every string change, and a new gauge or brand may change relief too. See [bs-fender-bass-setup].

models.note: Vintage keys need longer wraps (see specs) because the post is thinner.

models.model: Through-body Fender basses (e.g. American Deluxe bent-plate bridge)
models.note: Need strings long enough for the run through the body. Most flatwounds cannot be strung through the body - La Bella says they break unless you use a through-body model.
Different system - see [bs-headless-string-change].

warnings: Cut string ends are sharp; bend them in or trim close and wear eye protection when cutting.
Never cut a string at full tension - detune first.
pro: Not usually needed; take it to a tech if new strings will not fit through the bridge or nut slots without forcing.

title: Choose bass strings: scale, gauge, flats vs rounds
summary: How to pick a bass string set that actually fits your bass (wound length, not just scale) and which construction - roundwound, flatwound, halfwound, tapewound, taperwound, coated - suits your sound and fingerboard.

specs.label: Scale lengths
specs.value: Short 30 in or less, medium 32 in, standard 34 in, long 35 in

specs.label: La Bella wound lengths
specs.value: Short 32-1/4 in, medium 34-1/4 in, long 36-3/4 or 37 in, extra long 38 in

specs.label: Gauge when tuning down (Music Man)
specs.value: About one gauge step heavier for every half step down

specs.label: Strandberg Boden Bass
specs.value: D'Addario NYXL super long; tuner and lock bore 4 mm (.157 in) including any double-wound ball-end wrap

steps.title: Measure wound length
steps.detail: Measure from the ball-end seat (bridge or back of body) to just past the nut. Choose a set whose silk/taper starts after the nut - only the silk or taper may wrap the post.

steps.title: Roundwound
steps.detail: Bright, punchy, most common. Grooves the board on a fretless and wears frets faster.

steps.title: Flatwound
steps.detail: Smooth, thumpy, long-lasting, kind to fretless boards. Can sound dull at first; La Bella says a few hours of playing usually evens the tone and raising the pickup a little helps. Most flatwounds cannot go through-body.

steps.title: Halfwound / groundwound
steps.detail: Rounds ground partly flat: a hybrid between the two in feel and tone.

steps.title: Tapewound
steps.detail: Metal core with a nylon/plastic outer wrap: very soft, upright-like thump. Cut only at the silk.

steps.title: Taperwound
steps.detail: The string thins near the ball end so only the core sits on the saddle. Often chosen for B strings and high-mass bridges.

steps.title: Coated
steps.detail: A thin synthetic coating slows corrosion so the strings stay bright longer.

steps.title: Gauge and tuning
steps.detail: Lighter sets are easier to play but floppier; heavier sets are firmer and need more relief and possibly wider nut slots. If you tune down, go up roughly a gauge step per half step to keep the feel.

models.note: Not compatible with double-ball strings; the 5-string B is tapered and needs a speaking length of about 37.5-38 in, so buy super-long-scale sets.
Double-ball strings, or single-ball with Steinberger's headpiece adaptor.

title: Set up a Fender P or J bass
summary: A full Fender-style bass setup in the order Fender recommends: relief, string height, pickup height, then intonation, using Fender's published factory numbers. Do this after every string-gauge change, a big weather change, or whenever the bass feels stiff or buzzes.
tools: 6 in steel rule with 1/64 in or 0.5 mm marks
Truss rod tool that fits your bass (hex key at the headstock on modern models, large Phillips screwdriver at the heel on vintage-style models)
Small Phillips screwdriver or hex keys for the saddles
Fingerboard radius gauge (if you do not know your radius)
parts: Fresh set of strings in your usual gauge

specs.value: .014 in (0.35 mm) at the 8th fret

specs.label: Relief, 9.5-12 in radius
specs.value: .012 in (0.3 mm) at the 8th fret

specs.label: Relief, 15-17 in radius
specs.value: .010 in (0.25 mm) at the 8th fret

specs.label: Relief, older Fender bass manual (2013)
specs.value: .012-.014 in at the 7th fret

specs.label: String height at 17th fret, 7.25 in radius
specs.value: Bass side 7/64 in (2.8 mm), treble side 6/64 in (2.4 mm)

specs.label: String height at 17th fret, 9.5-12 in and 15-17 in radius

specs.label: Pickup height, standard P/J and Special Design humbuckers (setup article and manual)

specs.label: Micro-Tilt
specs.value: 1/4 turn of the 1/8 in hex screw changes action about 1/32 in (0.8 mm)

specs.label: Neck shim alternative
specs.value: .010 in thick x 1/4 in wide x 1-3/4 in long shim raises action about 1/32 in (0.8 mm)

steps.title: Fit strings and tune
steps.detail: Fit the strings you will actually use (see [bs-string-change]), tune to pitch and stretch them by pulling each one gently away from the fingerboard in the middle, then retune. Every measurement below assumes the bass is at pitch, in playing position or lying on its back with the neck supported.

steps.title: Find your fingerboard radius
steps.detail: Fender's numbers depend on radius. Vintage-style necks are usually 7.25 in, most modern ones 9.5-12 in, some 15-17 in. If unsure, lay radius gauges across the frets around the 12th fret and use the one that sits flush.

steps.title: Measure relief
steps.detail: Put a capo at the 1st fret. Hold the 4th (E) string down at the last fret (on a 5- or 6-string use the B string, as Fender's manual does). Slide feeler gauges between the bottom of the string and the top of the 8th fret. The gauge that just slips through without lifting the string is your relief. Compare with the spec for your radius.

steps.title: Adjust the truss rod
steps.detail: Slacken the strings a little first (Fender's instruction). Too much relief (neck too concave, action high): turn the rod nut clockwise. Too little or a back-bow (strings hitting low frets): turn counter-clockwise. Turn in small steps - a quarter turn is already a lot - then retune and measure again. On heel-adjust vintage models you may need to loosen the strings and either loosen the neck screws or lift the pickguard to reach the nut.
steps.warn: If the nut will not turn with normal hand pressure, stop. Forcing it can strip the nut or snap the rod. See the pro note.

steps.title: Bi-Flex rods (two-way)
steps.detail: Many American and American Deluxe basses have a Bi-Flex rod. Tightening bends the neck back as usual; loosening first reaches a neutral point with no force, and loosening past that pushes the neck forward. So if the nut goes slack and then gets stiff again while loosening, you have passed neutral - that is normal on a Bi-Flex.

steps.title: Set string height at the 17th fret
steps.detail: With no capo, measure from the bottom of each outer string to the top of the 17th fret with the steel rule. Raise or lower each saddle with its two height screws until you hit the spec for your radius. Keep both screws on a saddle at the same height so the saddle sits level and does not rock. Set the two middle strings so they follow the fingerboard curve between the outer ones.

steps.title: Check the nut
steps.detail: If the first few frets feel stiff or notes there play sharp, the nut slots may be high; if open strings buzz, they may be low. Nut work is a separate job - this setup does not cut the nut.

steps.title: Set pickup height
steps.detail: Hold the 1st and 4th strings down at the last fret. Measure from the bottom of the string to the top of the pole piece on each side of each pickup and set the screws to the table for your pickup type. Fender's rule of thumb: pickups end up closest to the strings at the 1st-string side of the bridge pickup and farthest at the 4th-string side of the neck pickup. Heavier strings and 5-strings need a little more clearance. Then fine-tune by ear: too close sounds harsh or makes notes warble as the magnet pulls the string.

steps.title: Rough-set intonation
steps.detail: Measure from the inside edge of the nut to the centre of the 12th fret and double it: that is your scale (34 in on a standard Fender). Set the 1st-string saddle's witness point at that distance from the nut. Set each following saddle back from the previous one by roughly that string's gauge (for a .060 in string about 1.5 mm further back). For a taper-wound string use its full gauge, not the thin tapered part.

steps.title: Fine-tune intonation
steps.detail: Turn the volume and tone fully up (selector in the middle on switched models). Tune each string with its 12th-fret harmonic, then fret the 12th fret normally. Fretted note sharp: turn the saddle's length screw clockwise to move the saddle back toward the end of the body. Fretted note flat: counter-clockwise to move it toward the neck. Retune after every change; recheck all strings at the end.

steps.title: Micro-Tilt or shim only if the saddles run out
steps.detail: If you cannot get low enough action with the saddles bottomed out (or high enough with them topped out), change the neck angle. Micro-Tilt models: loosen both neck screws next to the access hole at least four full turns, turn the 1/8 in hex screw about 1/4 turn (about 1/32 in of action change), then retighten the neck screws. Without Micro-Tilt, remove the neck and fit a shim of the size given above. Fender notes the factory neck angle rarely needs changing.

steps.title: Play-test and recheck
steps.detail: Play the whole neck with your normal attack, including hard digging-in. Retune, recheck relief the next day (necks keep moving for a few hours after a rod change) and touch up if needed.

models.model: Fender vintage-style P Bass / Jazz Bass (heel adjust)
models.note: Rod nut at the neck heel, turned with a large Phillips or flat screwdriver. Fender's manual says you may need to take the strings off and loosen the neck screws or remove the pickguard to reach it.

models.model: Fender American Standard / Professional / Deluxe (headstock adjust)
models.note: Hex key at the headstock. Many have the two-way Bi-Flex rod described above.
Use the B string to check relief (Fender manual) and allow a little extra pickup clearance.
Use the same procedure and the Fender numbers for your radius. If replacing Affinity tuners, Hipshot says its HB7 fits the post hole but the old screw holes must be filled and redrilled.

warnings: Strings under tension store a lot of energy; detune before removing a string or cutting it, and wear eye protection when snipping string ends.
Do not force a stiff truss rod nut.
Make relief changes in small steps and let the neck settle before judging.
pro: Take it to a tech if the truss rod is at the end of its travel or will not turn, if you still get buzz after relief and height are in spec (likely uneven frets), or if the neck needs a shim and you are not comfortable removing it.

title: Set up a Gibson Thunderbird or EB bass
summary: Gibson basses use a Gibson-style truss rod at the headstock, three-point or adjustable bridges and, on EB models, a 30.5 in short scale. Gibson does not publish bass setup numbers on the pages we could reach, so this guide uses the general bass procedure with Fender's published numbers as a starting point.
tools: 5/16 in truss rod wrench (Gibson-style rod nut)
Small screwdriver for the truss rod cover
Screwdriver or hex key for bridge height and intonation

specs.label: Scale length, Thunderbird
specs.value: 34 in (Gibson's first 34 in scale model)

specs.label: Scale length, EB-0 / EB-3 era short scale
Starting relief (Fender bass figure, 9.5-12 in radius)
specs.value: .012 in at the 8th fret

specs.label: Starting action (Fender bass figure)
specs.value: 6/64 in bass side, 5/64 in treble side at the 17th fret

steps.title: Fit the right strings
steps.detail: A Thunderbird is 34 in scale and takes long-scale sets. An EB-0 or other 30.5 in Gibson needs short-scale strings so the wound part ends after the nut (see [bs-choose-bass-strings]).

steps.title: Measure relief
steps.detail: Tune to pitch, capo the 1st fret, hold the E string at the last fret and measure the gap at the 8th fret with feeler gauges. Around .012 in is a sensible starting point; adjust to taste.

steps.title: Adjust the rod
steps.detail: Remove the bell-shaped cover on the headstock. Use a 5/16 in socket or box wrench on the rod nut: clockwise to reduce relief, counter-clockwise to add. StewMac's Dan Erlewine suggests marking the nut with ink to count turns and notes that a whole turn would be a lot. If the nut is stiff, back it off, put a dab of petroleum jelly on the threads and the washer face, and snug it again.
steps.warn: Gibson rod nuts sit in a deep, narrow cavity - use a wrench that fits squarely so you do not crack the finish around the opening.

steps.title: Reduce strain on a stiff neck
steps.detail: If a neck needs a lot of correction, take the load off the rod: with a helper holding the body, gently pull back on the neck (or clamp a padded caul at frets 7-9 over a support) while you snug the nut, rather than making the rod do all the work.

steps.title: Set string height
steps.detail: On a three-point bridge, the two height posts raise or lower the whole bridge; individual saddles may also have height screws on later bridges. Aim for around 6/64 in on the bass side and 5/64 in on the treble side at the 17th fret, then adjust by feel.

steps.title: Set pickup height and intonation
steps.detail: Hold the outer strings at the last fret and set each humbucker so the bass side sits a little lower than the treble side; balance by ear between pickups. Intonate each saddle with the 12th-fret harmonic versus fretted note: sharp, move the saddle back; flat, forward.

steps.title: Deal with neck dive
steps.detail: Both the reverse-body Thunderbird and SG-shaped EB basses have a long neck relative to the body and can drop toward the floor on a strap. See [bs-neck-dive].

models.note: Original Thunderbirds were neck-through with body wings glued on; the 1966 non-reverse redesign used a set neck. Bicentennial (1976) and later reissues use a three-point bridge. For a drop-D key, Hipshot says the GB7 Xtender fits Thunderbirds with Gotoh-style tuners, and the 3/8 in Ultralite Xtender fits mini-clover / Y-key versions.
Some cheaper Epiphone versions use a bolt-on neck instead of neck-through; same setup procedure.
30.5 in scale; early bar bridges were not adjustable, mid-1960s bridges have adjustable saddles, later models moved to the three-point bridge.

warnings: Do not force the rod nut.
Short-scale Gibsons need short-scale strings.
pro: If the rod is at the end of its travel, the neck has a twist, or a neck-through bass has a neck problem (it cannot simply be swapped), see a tech.

title: Set up a modern bass (Ibanez SR, Warwick, Schecter, Squier)
summary: Most modern basses - thin-necked Ibanez SRs, Warwicks with an adjustable nut, Schecters and Squiers - set up the same way: relief, height, pickups, intonation. This guide gives the order and two sets of published modern targets to aim for.
tools: Steel rule or string action gauge (mm or 1/64 in)
Truss rod key for your bass (usually a hex key at the headstock)
Hex keys or screwdriver for the saddles; Hipshot bridges use a .050 in hex for height

specs.label: Relief, Fender 9.5-12 in radius
specs.value: .012 in (0.3 mm) at the 8th fret

specs.label: Relief, Strandberg bass spec
specs.value: .015-.020 in (0.40-0.50 mm) at the 9th fret, capo at 1, D string held at the last fret

specs.label: Action at 17th fret (Fender, 9.5-12 in radius)
specs.value: Bass side 6/64 in (2.4 mm), treble side 5/64 in (2.0 mm)

specs.label: Pickup height (Strandberg bass)
specs.value: Neck 2.8 mm bass side / 2.4 mm treble side; bridge 2.4 mm / 2.0 mm (string held at last fret)

specs.label: Hipshot A-style bridge placement (34 in scale)
specs.value: Mount screw holes 34-3/4 in from the nut (3/4 in behind the scale line)

steps.title: Fresh strings, tuned
steps.detail: Fit the strings you will use and tune to pitch. Relief depends on string tension, so never set up with old or different-gauge strings.

steps.title: Relief first
steps.detail: Capo the 1st fret, hold a middle-to-low string at the last fret, and measure at the 8th or 9th fret with feeler gauges. Pick one of the targets above. Tighten (clockwise) to reduce relief, loosen to add, a quarter turn at a time, retuning between turns.

steps.title: Action second
steps.detail: Measure each string at the same fret (17th for Fender-style figures, 19th for Strandberg's per-string figures). Raise or lower each saddle. Strandberg's rule if you cannot hit exact values: a thinner string should never sit lower than the thicker string next to it.

steps.title: Pickup height third
steps.detail: Hold the outer strings at the last fret and measure string-to-pole-piece on both sides of each pickup. Set to the figures above and then balance by ear.

steps.title: Intonation last
steps.detail: Harmonic at the 12th versus fretted 12th; sharp, lengthen the string (saddle back); flat, shorten (saddle forward). Retune after each change.

steps.title: Check spacing on Hipshot bridges
steps.detail: Hipshot A-style and KickAss bridges allow sideways saddle moves: loosen the saddle's locking screw (1/16 in hex on A-style, .050 in on KickAss), slide the string, retighten firmly but do not overtighten (it can push the A-style barrel out of place).

models.note: Thin, flat necks respond quickly to the rod, so use small turns. Ibanez publishes bridge-specific manuals (SR, SRMS multiscale, SRF fretless and others) on its manuals page. Hipshot notes SR bridges sit in a routed pocket, so a retrofit like the SR605 needs a shim or rerouting plus new screw holes; matching Hipshot bridges are the 5-string A Style in .656 in spacing or the 5-string KickAss.

Many Warwicks have the height-adjustable Just-a-Nut, so first-fret height can be raised or lowered instead of filing slots; use the tool and instructions supplied with the bass. For a drop-D key Hipshot recommends the GB7 Xtender but notes it usually cannot drop a full step because the lever hits the next tuner.
Same procedure. Hipshot lists the 3/8 in Ultralite or Licensed Ultralite as replacement tuners for the Stiletto and the 3/8 in Ultralite or GB7 as Xtenders.
Use the Fender numbers and procedure in [bs-fender-bass-setup].

warnings: Do not force a truss rod.
Retune after every adjustment - each one changes the others.
pro: Rod at the end of travel, neck twist, high frets, or a bridge retrofit that needs rerouting are tech jobs.

title: Set up a Music Man StingRay (truss rod wheel)
summary: Music Man basses use a spoked truss-rod wheel at the body end of the neck that you can turn with any rod that fits, with the strings at full pitch. This guide covers relief, string height, pickup height and intonation using Music Man's own FAQ numbers.
tools: Small hex key, small screwdriver or similar rod that fits the holes in the truss rod wheel
Steel rule (1/64 in or 1/32 in marks)
Hex key or screwdriver for the saddles
parts: Strings: Music Man ships 4-strings with .045-.065-.080-.100 (Ernie Ball Super Slinky 2834) and 5-strings with .045-.065-.080-.100-.130 (Regular Slinky 5, 2836)
9 V alkaline battery (Music Man recommends Duracell because battery sizes vary)

specs.label: Relief test (Music Man)
specs.value: Lowest string held at the 2nd and 12th frets; gap in the middle no more than a business card

specs.label: String height, 5-string low B
specs.value: 7/64 in (other strings as 4-string)

specs.label: Pickup height, single pickup
specs.value: 6/32 in from the top of the pickup cover to the bottom of the G string; bass side parallel to the pickguard

specs.label: Pickup height, two pickups
specs.value: Bridge 6/32 in, neck 8/32 in

specs.label: Pickup height, three pickups
specs.value: Bridge 6/32 in, middle 7/32 in, neck 8/32 in

specs.label: Battery life
specs.value: About 6 months average with an alkaline 9 V

steps.title: Tune up - do not slacken the strings
steps.detail: Music Man says to adjust the rod with the strings at playing tension. Tune to pitch first.

steps.title: Check relief
steps.detail: Hold the lowest string down at the 2nd fret and the 12th fret at the same time (a capo on the 2nd fret frees a hand). Tap the string around the 7th fret. It should just move - no more than a business card's thickness. A forum moderator suggests 0.25-0.35 mm as a sensible range if you use feeler gauges; Music Man itself only gives the business-card test.

steps.title: Turn the wheel
steps.detail: Push a hex key or small rod into one of the holes in the wheel at the end of the fingerboard and lever it a quarter turn. To straighten the neck (less relief, lower action), turn the wheel clockwise as seen from the bridge looking up the neck - on a bass lying face-up in front of you, that is pushing the top of the wheel toward the G-string side. To add relief, turn it the other way (top of the wheel toward the E-string side). Play after each quarter turn.
steps.warn: Music Man's FAQ wording on direction is easy to misread. Always confirm by re-measuring after the first quarter turn. If the wheel will not move with moderate pressure, stop - only forcing a stuck rod breaks it.

steps.title: Read the buzz pattern
steps.detail: Music Man's guide: buzz from open to about the 5th fret means the neck needs more relief; buzz from the 5th to the 12th fret means it needs to be straighter; buzz all over the neck means the string height is too low.

steps.title: Set string height
steps.detail: Raise or lower each saddle with its height screws until you reach the ranges above (measure from the top of the fret to the bottom of the string; the 12th fret is the usual reference). Lower within the range for a light touch, higher for a heavy attack.

steps.title: Set pickup height
steps.detail: Measure from the top of the pickup cover to the bottom of the G string and set 6/32 in on a single-pickup StingRay. Then set the bass side so the pickup sits parallel to the pickguard. On HH or HS models set the bridge pickup at 6/32 in and the neck at 8/32 in.

steps.title: Intonate
steps.detail: Compare each string's 12th-fret harmonic with the fretted 12th note. Sharp: turn the saddle screw clockwise to lengthen the string. Flat: counter-clockwise. Make sure each string leaves the saddle in a straight line, not arched sideways. Retune and recheck after each change.

steps.title: Battery check
steps.detail: If the bass distorts or sounds weak, change the 9 V battery. Unplug the cable when you finish playing - the jack switches the preamp on, so a cable left in drains the battery.

models.note: Spoked wheel at the neck end; use the 4-string numbers above.
Low B at 7/64 in; factory strings add a .130 B. See [bs-five-six-string-setup] for B-string tips.
Bongo 6 high C at 2/32 in. For a drop-tuner on the Bongo, Hipshot lists the BT13 Xtender; for most other Music Man basses the BT1 short key.

warnings: Do not leave the cable plugged in overnight - it keeps the preamp powered.
Never force the wheel.
pro: If the wheel is seized, turns with no effect, or the neck stays bowed at the end of the rod's travel, have a tech look at it.

title: Set up a short- or medium-scale bass
summary: Short-scale (30 in or less) and medium-scale (32 in) basses use lower string tension, so they need the right-length strings, a bit more care with relief and action, and attention to where the string's wrapped ends land.
parts: Short- or medium-scale string set matched to your bass's wound length

specs.label: Short scale
specs.value: 30 in (76 cm) or less

specs.label: Medium scale
specs.value: 32 in (81 cm)

specs.label: La Bella wound lengths (ball end to start of silk)
specs.value: Short 32-1/4 in, medium 34-1/4 in, long 36-3/4 or 37 in, extra long 38 in

steps.title: Measure scale and wound length
steps.detail: Scale = twice the distance from the nut to the 12th fret. Then measure from where the ball end sits (in the bridge or through the body) to just past the nut: that is the wound length you need. La Bella stresses that scale alone does not decide the set - the silk/taper must start after the nut.

steps.title: Fit and tune
steps.detail: Fit the strings. Check that the thick ball-end wrap is not sitting on the saddle (short bridges and string-through designs can cause this) - see [bs-ball-end-saddle].

steps.title: Relief
steps.detail: Measure with a capo at 1 and the E held at the last fret, at the 8th fret. Lower tension means the neck moves less from string pull, so small rod turns go a long way. Use the Fender figure for your radius as a starting point (.012 in for 9.5-12 in).

steps.title: Action
steps.detail: Slacker strings swing wider, so short-scale basses often need slightly more height than a 34 in bass to avoid rattle. Start at Fender's 6/64 in bass side and 5/64 in treble side at the 17th and raise a little if needed.

steps.title: Pickups and intonation
steps.detail: Set pickups a little further away if the strings warble (low tension strings are pulled more easily by magnets). Intonate at the 12th; heavy flatwounds on a short scale may need the saddle well back.

models.note: 30.5 in; short-scale sets; prone to neck dive - see [bs-neck-dive].
Use short-scale sets. Hipshot lists specific bridge and tuner upgrades for the Mustang PJ and for the Squier VM Jaguar short scale on its FAQ.

warnings: Long-scale strings on a short-scale bass can put the thick wound section over the nut and around the post, which can break the string.
pro: If saddles run out of travel or the bridge is in the wrong place for the strings you want, see a tech.

title: Set up a 5- or 6-string bass
summary: Five- and six-string basses set up like a 4-string, but the low B needs more room to vibrate, the wide neck is more prone to twist, and the B string's wound length and taper must suit the bass. Covers relief, B-string height, pickups, string spacing and the high C.
tools: Saddle hex keys/screwdriver (.050 in hex on Hipshot KickAss and Vintage bridges)
parts: 5-string set of the right wound length (Music Man's factory B is .130)
6-string set adds a high C (tuning B-E-A-D-G-C)

specs.label: Tuning
specs.value: 5-string B-E-A-D-G; 6-string B-E-A-D-G-C

specs.label: Relief (Fender manual method)
specs.value: .012-.014 in at the 7th fret, measured with the B string held at the last fret and a capo at the 1st

specs.label: Low B height (Music Man 5-string)
specs.value: 7/64 in; other strings as 4-string (bass side 3/32-7/64 in, treble 5/64-7/64 in)

specs.label: Low B height (Strandberg, 19th fret)
specs.value: 1.75 mm, with E at 1.60 mm

specs.label: String wrap past the post, 5th string (Fender)
specs.value: 3 in (76 mm) on standard keys, 3-1/2 in (89 mm) on vintage keys

specs.label: Hipshot KickAss bridge
specs.value: Largest recommended string about .170 in; rear hole is .187 in

steps.title: Check the B string fits
steps.detail: Before setting up, make sure the B is the right wound length: the silk or tapered end must start after the nut, and only the thin part should wrap the tuner post (La Bella). On a through-body bass the string must be long enough for the extra run through the body.

steps.title: Relief with the B string
steps.detail: Capo the 1st fret and hold the B at the last fret. Measure at the 7th or 8th fret. Then check the treble side the same way with the G (or C). Big differences between the two sides suggest twist - see the pro note.

steps.title: Adjust the rod in small steps
steps.detail: Wide necks carry more total tension, so changes can take longer to settle. Quarter turns, retune, wait, re-measure.

steps.title: Set the B higher than the E
steps.detail: The B swings in a wider arc. Set it a little higher than the E - Music Man uses 7/64 in, Strandberg 1.75 mm at the 19th against 1.60 mm for E. Then set E-A-D-G (and C) so heights step down smoothly across the radius.

steps.title: High C on a 6-string
steps.detail: The thin high C can go lowest of all (Music Man's Bongo 6 spec is 2/32 in). Follow Strandberg's rule across all strings: a thinner string should never sit lower than the thicker string next to it.

steps.title: Pickup height with extra clearance
steps.detail: Fender advises a bit more pickup clearance on 5-strings and heavy gauges. Hold the B and the G at the last fret, set the bass side of each pickup a little lower than the treble side, and listen for a balanced B: if the B sounds woolly or warbles, lower the bass side of the pickup.

steps.title: Spacing and intonation
steps.detail: On adjustable-spacing bridges, centre the strings over the pole pieces and fingerboard edges first, then intonate. The B saddle usually sits furthest back; if it runs out of travel see [bs-low-string-intonation].

models.note: Fender checks relief with the B string; 5th-string wrap 3 in on standard keys.
Factory .045-.130 on 5-strings; B at 7/64 in; Bongo 6 high C at 2/32 in.
Thin, wide necks: small rod turns. Hipshot's matching 5-string bridges for the SR605 are the A Style in .656 in spacing and the KickAss.
Multiscale 33-35 in; B at 35 in carries about 34.1 lb with a .130 NYXL, similar to the E. See [bs-multiscale-setup].

warnings: Wide necks can twist; do not try to fix twist with the truss rod.
pro: If relief on the B side and the treble side differ a lot (neck twist), or the B still buzzes with correct relief and height (likely high frets), take it to a tech.
