title: Set up a fretless bass
summary: On a fretless the string stops on the fingerboard itself, so the setup aims for a near-straight neck, low action, careful intonation by ear and tuner, and protecting the fingerboard from string wear.
tools: Tuner (a steady one, not a hyper-sensitive strobe)
Straightedge long enough to span the fingerboard
parts: Flatwound or tapewound strings (gentler on the fingerboard)
Lemon oil or fingerboard conditioner for unfinished boards

steps.title: Pick strings
steps.detail: Roundwounds give the classic singing fretless sound but grind grooves into an uncoated board. Flatwounds or tapewound strings wear the board far less. Flatwound and tapewound strings must not be cut or wrapped in the wrong place - see [bs-string-change].

steps.title: Straighten the neck
steps.detail: Tune to pitch. Lay a straightedge along the fingerboard (or hold a string at the first position and the last position and look at the gap in the middle). Fretless players normally want the neck very close to straight - just enough relief that the strings do not rattle against the upper board when played open. Adjust the rod in quarter turns, retuning each time.

steps.title: Set action low but clean
steps.detail: Lower the saddles until notes played hard start to choke or rattle, then come back up a little. A slight 'buzz' as the string touches the board is part of the fretless 'mwah' sound - you are listening for notes that die early, not for that growl.

steps.title: Nut height
steps.detail: With no first fret, the open strings should sit just clear of the board at the nut so notes near the nut are easy to stop in tune. If the low positions feel stiff or play sharp, the nut slots may be high - a nut job.

steps.title: Intonate by ear and tuner
steps.detail: Play the 12th-position harmonic, then stop the string exactly on the 12th marker or line (on a lined board stop directly on the line; on an unlined board use the side dots). Adjust saddles so the stopped note matches the harmonic. Because your finger position also changes the pitch, repeat a few times and average. Also compare octaves by ear across the neck.

steps.title: Look after the fingerboard
steps.detail: Wipe strings and board after playing. On an unfinished rosewood or ebony board condition it occasionally. Watch for grooves under the most-played spots (often the low strings in the first five positions).

steps.title: Worn or grooved boards
steps.detail: Shallow grooves can be filled and levelled; badly grooved boards need to be re-levelled and re-radiused. Some players have the board coated with a hard finish (epoxy or polyester) to protect it from roundwounds. StewMac shows a related super-glue fill-and-level technique for worn necks, done in thin coats and levelled with files and fine abrasives - practise on scrap first.
steps.warn: Coating or re-levelling a fretless fingerboard is precise work; uneven results cause dead notes.

models.model: Factory fretless models (Fender Jazz fretless, Ibanez SRF and others)
models.note: Ibanez publishes a separate manual for its SRF fretless bridge on its manuals page.
Shipped with D'Addario XL Chromes (flatwounds).

warnings: Do not wrap the metal part of a flatwound around a post - it breaks.
Cutting a tapewound string through the tape (not the silk) makes it unravel.
Solvents and coatings need good ventilation and gloves.
pro: Fingerboard re-levelling, groove filling across the whole board and epoxy/poly coating are bench jobs for a luthier.

title: Adjust Rickenbacker 4003 dual truss rods
time: 30 min per session, spread over 1-3 days
summary: Rickenbacker basses have two truss rods side by side, one under the bass strings and one under the treble strings, and older ones use a fragile rod design that must never be cranked against a bowed neck. This guide shows how to tell which rods you have and how to adjust each side safely.
tools: Thin-wall 1/4 in socket or nut driver on a screwdriver-style handle (not a T-handle)
Feeler gauges or a business card
Towel and a sturdy table (older rods)

specs.label: Target
specs.value: Neck essentially straight (Rickenbacker's John Hall: necks should be straight); a business-card gap at frets 7-9 is a common player target

specs.label: Maximum per day
specs.value: 1/4 turn per rod (Rickenbacker guidance)

specs.label: Rod design change
specs.value: Around September 1984

steps.title: Identify the rod type
steps.detail: Remove the truss rod cover on the headstock. Rods made before about September 1984 are each a steel bar folded in two; the nut pushes an aluminium spacer block, and you can often see two channels in the wood behind the spacer and the end of the shorter bar. Later rods use a thin steel washer-like spacer and no channel is visible. Old rods can only hold a neck in position; later ones can be adjusted under string tension like a modern rod.
steps.warn: On pre-1984 rods, tightening against a bowed neck can pull the fingerboard off the neck. If in doubt, treat it as an old rod or take it to a tech.

steps.title: Measure each side separately
steps.detail: Tune to pitch. Capo the 1st fret, hold the E string down near the last fret and look at the gap around frets 7-9. Repeat on the G string. Each side has its own rod, so each side can need a different setting - it is normal for the treble rod to be barely snug and the bass rod tighter.

steps.title: Fit the right tool
steps.detail: Use a thin-wall 1/4 in socket or nut driver with a screwdriver-style handle. Rickenbacker's advice is to avoid a T-handle: a screwdriver handle slips in your hand before the rod breaks, a T-handle gives enough leverage to snap it.

steps.title: Later rods (post-1984): adjust each side
steps.detail: With the strings at pitch, turn the nut on the side that needs it: clockwise (tightening) reduces relief on that side, counter-clockwise adds relief. Turn no more than a quarter turn, retune and re-measure both sides - the rods sit close together, so changing one affects the other a little. Stop for the day after a quarter turn per rod, play the bass, and continue the next day if needed.

steps.title: Older rods (pre-1984): position the neck, then snug
steps.detail: Lay the bass on a towel on a sturdy table with the headstock off the edge and have a helper hold the body. Gently pull the headstock down so the neck goes slightly straighter (you will see the strings move toward the frets). Keep that pressure on and snug each rod nut only until it is firm - the rod then holds the neck where you put it. Release, retune, check. Repeat in small amounts.
steps.warn: Do not try to pull a bowed old neck straight by tightening the nuts alone.

steps.title: Wait and recheck
steps.detail: Leave the bass tuned for about 24 hours before judging. Expect two or three sessions to get both sides even.

steps.title: Re-set action and pickups
steps.detail: Once the neck is straight, you may want to lower the bridge and the pickups slightly to keep the same feel and sound. Then check intonation.

steps.title: If a rod rattles
steps.detail: Rickenbacker says a rattle is usually a loose rod nut or the rod knocking in its channel. Snug the nut first. If it continues, the fix is to wrap each rod in masking tape - that means taking the strings off and removing the rods, which is a bench job.

models.note: Uses the older style rods; treat with the older-rod method.
Newer-style rods, adjusted per side under tension. Rickenbacker FAQ notes later 4003s have larger rounded holes at the neck end for the rod nuts.
Very early 4003s may have older rods; check before adjusting.

warnings: Never more than a quarter turn per rod per day.
No T-handle wrenches.
Never tighten old-style rods against a bowed neck.
pro: Any pre-1984 Rickenbacker with a bowed neck, a rod that will not turn, a lifting fingerboard, or a rod rattle that needs the rods out should go to a tech experienced with Rickenbackers.
